PREFACE 

During the author's experience at the Bar, the need for a Practice Book that would answer quickly, accurately and in practical fashion, the what, when, and how questions, became increasingly apparent a book that would serve as a handbook and guide, yet be sufficiently comprehensive to meet the routine needs of the busy office regardless of the existing books on Practice it may own. Such is the purpose of this Book. 

An attempt is made to describe briefly and simply, in chronological order, the steps of a litigation beginning with the preparation of the summons, through to the final entry of judgment, proceedings supplementary to judgment, and the steps of an appeal.

Although the author would have preferred to cite more law governing the different situations, and discuss further points, the need for brevity was deemed most important and reference is therefore frequently made to more extensive works on Practice, to meet the further needs of the lawyer.

In short, the book represents an attempt to provide a guide to Practice and to answer the Practice questions most frequently arising in every day experience. It is hoped that it will serve as a remembrancer to the experienced members of the Bar, as well as a guide to those less experienced. That this will be accomplished is the sincere wish of the author.

NEW YORK, May 1, 1938 S. MORRIS

§ 1. In General. 

Experience has shown that the manner in which a law office is conducted is a fair indication of the manner in which that particular office conducts its litigation. If, for example, the office has a definite plan which enables it to keep full and complete records of every transaction, so that every point of information with respect to a particular matter can be obtained quickly, and every paper used in the case can be found easily and without the resultant confusion and clash of tempers, a client may feel confident that his case will be handled in a thorough, efficient and successful fashion. And to put a client's mind at ease in this respect brings its rewards in more business and better fees. Take the instance of a client

82 

who calls upon his lawyer to discuss the status of a pending case. During the discussion, the meaning of a clause in the contract is questioned. The attorney immediately calls in his file clerk and asks that the contract be brought in so that he may study it. Word comes back that it cannot be found. The effect upon the client is immediate and obvious. Again, the client may have been informed that a motion has been made to dismiss the complaint. 

The client, who is the defendant, is pleased and anxiously awaits the day of the hearing, when, if successful, the suit against him may be terminated. He asks when the hearing will be heard. An examination of the records shows that no entries have been made with reference to that particular case. A further examination discloses the fact that although the necessary papers were filed in the action, the attorney was not informed of the return day and as a result did not appear in court and no hearing was had. Or if the client happens to be the plaintiff in the action and his attorney fails to appear in court when an application is made to dismiss the complaint, he may find that his case has been thrown out of court without the opportunity of a hearing. Such occurrences are inexcusable and unfair to the client.

It is, therefore, manifestly more expedient to employ an efficient system so that when a client is present, one may with confidence send for the file in that particular case and find each paper properly filed and indexed, and each step in the action properly performed and recorded. 

§ 2. The Managing Attorney-His Duties. 

The work of the managing attorney is, perhaps, the most important contributing factor toward a smoothrunning office. This is true because of the need of some one responsible person who may be charged with and held accountable for the proper performance of the great amount of detail which is ever present in the

2 3 

OFFICE ROUTINE. 

average sized law office. In an office where there is more than one attorney, there is the tendency of one attorney to shift detail work on to another with the result that in the general confusion, the work remains undone. 

Serious results follow. For example, a failure to prepare, serve and file a notice of appeal. Such neglect can never be remedied because no court has the power to extend the time to appeal. In the many cases where judgments have been reversed on appeal, it is obvious that if the timely service of the notice of appeal had been overlooked, such negligence would have proved an irreparable loss to an otherwise successful litigant.

Again, where an attorney fails to serve an answer within the time limited therefor, and no extension of time to do so has been secured, the adverse attorney may obtain a judgment by default with the result that at the expense of time and trouble, efforts must be made to vacate the default and in some instances, it may be necessary to secure a bond to do so. Where, however, there is one individual whose duty it is to oversee detail work, who must either personally perform such work or see that it is properly done, the possibility of such serious results is negligible, because he realizes that it is inexcusable and he will have to answer for it, regardless of whose fault it may actually be, and however innocent he may be of any wrongdoing. The managing attorney is soon made to realize that where there is the slightest defect in an otherwise smooth-running office, the cause thereof will be placed at his door. And, only one who has actually been a managing attorney knows how amazing and positively ingenious are the methods employed to fasten blame upon him.

Realizing the value of such an individual, the majority of law offices containing more than one lawyer employs a managing attorney. A single practitioner, if his practice is large enough to warrant it, requires the services

8 2 

of a managing attorney. The specific duties of the managing attorney are difficult to specify because they vary with the individual. He is, as a rule, an attorney, and thus, if his ability warrants it, he may be called upon to perform the duties of an attorney, to wit: interview clients, gather evidence, prepare cases for trial and actually try cases. But while he is doing this, he is not permitted to lose sight of ordinary routine work. It may well be that there are a number of attorneys in the office, to each of whom a specific case has been assigned and for which that attorney is ultimately held responsible; nevertheless, the managing attorney must be well-informed with respect to every case and be acquainted with every step which has been taken therein. If he does not personally prepare the necessary papers, argue motions, try cases and argue appeals, he must call the attention of the person who is handling the particular case, to the necessity of doing these things and make certain that the work is done in the time allowed. In other words, what he does not do himself, he must see is done by someone else.

A few of his duties may be more specifically enumerated as follows:

Upon his arrival at the office in the morning, he examines the diary (§ 4) to see what cases or motions will be called that day in court. Following this, he examines the Law Journal or other local paper which contains the various court calendars and checks them to see if such motions and cases appear thereon. See

Chapter XVII. If they do, he arranges to have them answered. He may do this personally; he may delegate the work to a clerk or office boy; or it may be taken care of by one of the various agencies which answers calendars and reports the disposition thereof. Where the service of an agency is required, the matter should be attended to the evening before.

5 

OFFICE ROUTINE. 

10 He makes a daily check of the Law Journal for decisions affecting office litigation. Where a decision has been rendered, he prepares the judgment or order as the case may be and takes the necessary subsequent steps. 

After a case has been noticed for trial, he examines the Law Journal for calendar calls and announcements with respect thereto. In this way, he determines the probable date that a case will be reached for trial and notifies the person in charge thereof so that the case may be properly prepared for trial in advance of the date of trial.

Every paper which is served upon the office and concerns litigation, is immediately delivered to the managing attorney. He marks upon the original paper the following notation known as an admission of service:

Copy Received February 6, 1936. 

Roland Manners,

Attorney for Defendant 

(or Plaintiff).

He notes upon the copy the day it was received and properly records it in the litigation register (§ 3). If it is a motion paper, the return day thereof is entered in the diary. If it is a complaint, or an answer containing counterclaims, the time to serve the answer or the reply as the case may be is noted in the diary. And, unless he is to take the subsequent steps as required by the service of that paper, he may deliver it to the attorney who is in charge of the matter. 

Every paper which concerns litigation, and which is prepared by the office for service upon a party, attorney or witness, must first be delivered to the managing attorney so that he may make the proper entry in the litigation register and diary as already described, after which he arranges with a clerk or office boy for its

8 3 

service and the return to him of the original thereof with admission of service. If the original is required to be filed, he must see that this is done. 

He prepares the record on appeal, takes the steps necessary for placing the appeal on the calendar for a hearing, follows the matter until it is ready to be argued and continues along with whatever subsequent steps are required. 

§ 3. Litigation Register. 

The litigation register or docket corresponds to the ledger employed by business firms. One page or more is devoted exclusively to each case. It contains the title and index number of the action or proceeding. Then follows a chronological account of every step taken in the action together with a proper notation as to the time when and the nature of every paper received and served thus:

CHARLES ROBERTS, Plaintiff,

Index No. 3822-1936 

-against- 

(Name and address of adverse attorney, thus:)

Defendant's Attorney. 

1936 

George Arnold 

119 Broadway 

New York. 

Jan. 3. Served summons and complaint in action to recover 

Five Thousand Dollars on promissory note. 

9. Signed stipulation extending defendant's time to answer to February 20th. 

Feb. 20. Received answer containing counterclaims. 

Mar. 12. Served reply. 

14. Served order to show cause returnable February 19th for examination before trial.

$ 7 

OFFICE ROUTINE. 

§ 4. The Diary. 

All future engagements of an attorney with respect to pending litigation are recorded in the diary. Where a summons and complaint have been received and properly noted in the register, the next step is to make a note in the diary of the last day to serve the answer. Where practice motions are necessary, the last day to make them should be noted. One should also make note of trial dates and of the return days of motions. 

§ 5. List of Pending Cases. 

As soon as a case is noticed for trial, it is given a number by the clerk of the court. This is known as a calendar number. It shows the position of the case on the general calendar of the court and is some indication as to when it will be reached for trial. If, for example, the number is 5280 and 5000 cases have already been tried, and we know that the Supreme Court of New York County disposes of an average of twenty cases a day, we know that the case may be reached within approximately fourteen court days. Therefore, as soon as a case receives a number, it is placed on what is known as a list of pending litigation. This list sets forth the names of the cases which have been noticed for trial, their calendar numbers and the names of the courts in which they will be tried. These numbers are changed about once a year in some of the courts so that it is necessary to watch for the announcement of such changes and obtain new numbers before the opening of court in the Fall.

§ 6. Day Sheets. 

Every attorney should prepare a day sheet which gives a complete account of the day's occurrence, with respect to a pending matter, such as the time spent in the research of law, the fact that a client called and conferred with respect to the case or phoned, and a recital of the papers prepared or received. Day sheets are kept in loose-leaf book form made for the particular purpose, and obtainable at stationery stores. The initials of the attorney at the foot of the sheet indicates that he has read it and that it is correct. It may read as follows:

DAY SHEET Date February 20, 1936. 

Name R.N. 

Briggs v. Ford 

Research law, one hour. 

Meeker v. Brooks 

Phone conf. client.

Sullivan v. Peabody 

Drew summons and complaint.

Wills v. 

Watson for trial.

Conf. client this office three hours-preparing case 

§ 7. History Cards. 

R. N.

A history card is just what the name implies. It contains a list of every occurrence in a case and is made up of items taken from day sheets. The day sheet may

88 

contain the day's happenings in a number of cases, whereas a history card is devoted to one particular matter. The purpose of such a card is to enable the attorney to compute the amount of fee to be charged. 

And where a client objects to the amount, and it is desired to convince him as to the reasonableness thereof, he may be furnished with an itemized statement of services prepared by transcribing the items from the history card. The cards are filed alphabetically under the name of the case, the client's name appearing first, and read as follows: 

Anderson v. Loeb 

1936 

Jan. 7

R. N. 

Research of law, one hour.

L. F. 

Conf. client, one hour. 11 

Studied complaint. Drew answer. 

§ 8. Tickler Sheets. 

Tickler sheets although not necessary are nevertheless helpful as reminders. If one writes a letter and wishes to follow the matter, he makes a copy of the letter on the tickler sheet and checks the date and month thereon so that on that particular day and month the tickler sheet is placed on his desk for further action, reading thus:

§ 9. Inter-Office Memoranda. 

It is very good practice to give written rather than oral instructions in order to avoid misunderstandings. 

This also applies to any items of information. Printed forms for the purpose may be purchased and read as follows: 

From: R. N. 

OFFICE MEMORANDUM 

February 21, 1936.

To: L. F. 

Re: Anderson v. Leob 

Clerk of Trial Term, Part I, phoned. Informed case would be called for Trial to-morrow morning, February 23, 1936, at ten. 

§ 10. Printed Forms. 

One should obtain from any law stationer a catalogue of printed forms and check those forms which will be more frequently used by the particular office. Some of those in common use are the following: 

1. Summons With Notice 2. Summons Without Notice (Various Courts) 3. Judgment After Trial (Municipal Court) 

4. Judgment on Default (Municipal Court) 

5. Bill of Costs

$ 10 

6. Subpoena 7. Subpoena Duces Tecum 8. Contempt Order 9. Short Form Orders 

10. Order for the Appointment of a Receiver.

11. General Release 12. Satisfaction Piece 13. Stipulations to Extend Time to Serve Pleadings 14. Note of Issue 

In addition, real estate forms should be obtained from title companies and surrogate's forms from the various surrogate's courts. These forms are filed in steel cabinets provided for the purpose. The forms as checked may be given numbers in the catalogue in the order in which they appear, and the drawers may be given numbers corresponding thereto. In this way, one saves time unnecessarily spent in ex mining form books for the correct form and the additional time spent in dictating it. 

§ 11. Filing System. 

Each case is provided with a folder, in the upper lefthand corner of which is pasted a small square of white paper containing the number of the file and the title of the case, the client's name being placed first, and the attorney's name thus:

CHARLES ROBERTS 

—against— Plaintiff 

File No. 26  

ROLAND MANNERS, 

140 E. 42nd St.

§ 13 

OFFICE ROUTINE. 

Where the client is the defendant, his name will appear first, and the word "advs." will be substituted for the word "against." The folder may contain one or more inner white folders in accordance with the requirements of the particular case. The inner folders may be labelled as follows: 

1. Correspondence Folder (contains copies of all letters) 

2. Pleadings or Court Papers 3. Examination Before Trial 4. Bill of Particulars 5. Memoranda (Law Memoranda, briefs, etc.) 6. Copies of Court Papers 7. Client's Papers 8. Appeal Papers 

A card index is used which gives the title and number of each case. Two cards are provided for each case in order to facilitate the finding of a folder by cross-reference. 

§ 12. Closed Files. 

As soon as a case has been tried or otherwise terminated, the file should be stamped "closed" and taken out of its regular position in the filing cabinet and placed in another cabinet provided for the purpose. Where space is limited and closed files too numerous, the practice of the larger offices is to store them in a warehouse. 

§ 13. Safe Files. 

Very often valuable papers are left by a client which should be kept in a safe or vault rather than in the regular filing cabinet. Regular safe folders are used for this purpose. These are carefully labelled and numbered and a card index is used.

§ 14. Affidavit-Defined-Form. 

An affidavit is a voluntary sworn declaration before a competent authority by a witness known as the affiant. 

It consists of the following: 

Title 

Venue 

Body of Affidavit 

Jurat 

Signature of Affiant and is in the following form: 14

$ 15 

SUPREME COURT-Albany County. 

JOHN DOE, being duly sworn, deposes and says: 

(Statement of Facts) 

day of 19.... 

(Name of officer and official title) 

(Signature of Affiant) 

Title. An affidavit is entitled in the action or special proceeding in which relief is sought, where one has been commenced; that is, it bears the entire heading consisting of the name of the court and the names of the parties. 

Baxter v. Seaman, 1 How. Prac. 51; Bowman v. Sheldon, 7 N. Y. Super. Ct. (5 Standf.) 657, 10 N. Y. Leg. Obs. 339.

Venue. The venue follows the title or heading and reads thus: 

STATE OF County of 

... ... 

(Add City of 

SS.: 

if verified by commissioner of deeds.)

The purpose of this is to show that the affidavit was taken within the jurisdiction of the officiating officer. 

Leavitt v. Thornton, 123 A. D. 683, 108 N. Y. S. 162, citing

8 14 

Rogers v. Pell, 154 N. Y. 529, and Thompson v. Burhans, 61 N. Y. 52; Cook v. Staats, 18 Barb. 407. An affidavit wanting a venue or a statement in the jurat as to where it was taken, contains no evidence that it was sworn to within the jurisdiction of the officer administering the oath, and is prima facie a nullity. But if in fact it was sworn to within the jurisdiction of the officer, the omission of the venue does not invalidate the oath. Smith v. 

Collier, 3 N. Y. St. Rep. 172. The omission of the venue from an affidavit is not fatal if the instrument or any part thereof expressly or by implication shows where it was taken. In re McCarthy, 119 Misc. 257, 196 N. Y. S. 

265, aff'd 203 A. D. 833, 196 N. Y. S. 937. The omission of the letters "ss" from the venue is immaterial. Babcock v. Kuntzsch, 85 Hun 33, 32 N. Y. S. 587.

Body of Affidavit. Following the venue, is the name of the affiant or deponent reading, "John Doe, being duly sworn, deposes and says:" Here follows a statement of the facts in support of whatever claim is made or relief prayed for. See affidavits in this volume. It should not contain conclusions. Town of Duanesburgh v. Jenkins, 40 Barb. 575. It should, where possible, be made by the person having first-hand knowledge of the facts. But where this is not possible, the affidavit is made on information and belief, giving the source of information and the grounds of belief. This is done, so that the courts or official officers who are asked to act on such affidavits may decide whether the affiant is justified in his belief or not and thus draw their own conclusions. Penn Oil & 

Supply Co. v. Cohn, 131 A. D. 929; 116 N. Y. S. 124.

It may be that the attorney himself will be obliged to make the affidavit because of facts which are unknown to a party but peculiarly within the knowledge of the attorney. In re Ries, 170 A. D. 951, 155 N. Y. S. 1156.

Some courts require the affidavit to read in the first person. City Court of the City of New York Rule IX.

$ 17 

Jurat and Signature of Officer. The jurat follows the body of the affidavit and appears to the left thereof reading thus: 

 day of ....." 19.... 

(Signature and official title of officer)

It imports that the statements were sworn to be true. 

Crosier v. Cornell Steamboat Co., 27 Hun 215, 15 N. Y. 

Wkly. Dig. 34, aff'd 92 N. Y. 627. In Snyder v. Olmsted, 2 How. Prac. 181, the venue of an affidavit was Albany

County. It was, however, sworn before, and the jurat subscribed to by a "Judge of Rensselaer County Courts", etc. The court held that the affidavit could not be read on the motion, on the ground that the officer before whom it purported to have been sworn had no jurisdiction to take it. In re McCarthy, 119 Misc. 257, 196 N. Y. S. 265, aff'd (1922) 203 A. D. 833, 196 N. Y. S. 937, the affidavit bore no venue but it was held that in view of Executive Law, § 105, subd. 2, authorizing a notary public to take affidavits anywhere within the state, and in view of the presumption that a notary public had performed his duty, where the jurat was signed by the notary public and bore the words "K. County", it was evidence that the affidavit was taken in such county and the omission of the venue was not fatal.

The jurat is signed by the officer who administers the oath and his official title is indicated thereon. Where a notary public or commissioner of deeds takes an affidavit, the usual practice is to sign his name and affix his stamp containing the name and official title. In 

Brooklyn City Railroads v. City of New York, 139 Misc. 

691, 248 N. Y. S. 196, a notice of claim bore a stamped signature of the claimant and of the notary public and the court refused to receive it unless it bore the autographed signature of the notary public and of the 2

$ 15 

claimant. It was held that there was no proof that the claim was not verified and the fact that the signature was stamped did not establish that the claim was verified, and further held that generally, a signature may be printed, lithographed or typewritten as well is written, citing David v. Williamsburgh City Fire Ins. Co., 83 N. Y. 

265, Gen. Const. Law, § 46. 

Signature of affiant. Although the signature of the affiant is not necessary, nevertheless, it serves to identify the affidavit. If the affidavit commences with the deponent's name, it need not be subscribed by him. Soule v. 

Chase, 24 N. Y. Super. Ct. (1 Rob.) 222, 1 Abb. Prac. (N. S.) 48, judgment reversed 39 N. Y. 342 (7 Transc. 

App. 161). 

§ 15. Acknowledgment-Defined. 

An acknowledgment is a certificate of an officer duly empowered to take an acknowledgment or proof of the conveyance of real property, that on a specified date "before me personally came.........., to me known and known to me to be the individual described in and who executed the foregoing instrument and acknowledged to me that he executed the same." The object and purpose of acknowledgment and record is to make the title secure and prevent frauds in conveyancing, as well as to furnish proof of the due execution of conveyances. 

If not duly acknowledged, an instrument is not properly on record, and if not properly on record, it is not constructive notice. Armstrong v. Combs, 15 A. D. 246, 44 

N. Y. S. 171. 

See form of acknowledgment, § 482, and also in Wait's

N. Y. Practice Vol. 1 (3rd Ed.) page 292. 

Real Property Law, § 303, provides that an acknowledgment shall not be taken by any officer unless he knows or has satisfactory evidence that the person making it is the person described in and who executed the instrument. Gross v. Rowley, 147 A. D. 529, 132 N. Y. S.

$ 19 

541. A notary public's certificate of acknowledgment to a deed is prima facie evidence only of its due and proper execution which may be rebutted by a party affected thereby. Albany County Savings Bank v. 

McCarty, 149 N. Y. 71. 

§ 16. Officers Before Whom Affidavits May be Taken. 

C. P. A. 357 provides as follows: 

"An oath or affidavit, required or authorized by law, except an oath to a juror or a witness upon a trial, an oath of office, and an oath or acknowledgment required by law to be taken before a particular officer, may be taken before a judge, an official examiner of title, official referee, clerk, deputy clerk, or special deputy clerk of a court, a notary public, mayor, justice of the peace, a city magistrate of any of the cities of this state, or police justice thereof, surrogate, special county judge, special surrogate, county clerk, deputy county clerk, special deputy county clerk, or commissioner of deeds, within the district in which the officer is authorized to act, except that a justice of the peace may take such oath or affidavit anywhere in the county containing the town or city in which he is authorized to act; and when certified by the officer to have been taken before him may be used in any court or before any officer or other person. 

Of the aforementioned officers, the public generally, is perhaps more familiar with the notary public and commissioner of deeds and therefor their powers and duties and manner of appointment will be briefly considered. 

§ 17. Notary Public-Qualifications. 

An applicant for appointment as notary public must be, among other things, of full age, a citizen of the United States and a resident of the county for which he is appointed. Public Officers Law, § 3.

$ 20 

§ 18. Manner of Appointment. 

One applies for appointment as notary public by writing to the Secretary of State for an application blank. 

If the applicant is an attorney and counsellor at law, he is required to do nothing more than fill in the blank form and return it to the Secretary of State. With respect to other persons, the recommendation of a judge or justice must accompany the application unless the notary public applies for reappointment before the expiration of his term or six months thereafter. Execu tive Law, § 101. 

§ 19. Notice of Appointment. 

Thereafter, the applicant is notified of his appointment by the county clerk of the county wherein he made application and within fifteen days after the receipt of said notice or within fifteen days after the commencement of the term for which he is appointed, he files his oath as notary public therein. Executive Law, § 103. 

§ 20. Qualifying in County of Appointment and Else where.

Where a notary public, for example, is appointed in New York County, he personally appears at the office of the county clerk and signs his name in a book kept for that purpose, and pays a fee of ten dollars. Executive 

Law, §§ 102, 103. If he resides in a city having a population of more than 50,000 and less than 600,000, the fee is five dollars; and where he resides elsewhere, the fee is two and one-half dollars. Executive Law, § 103.

It may be that, in addition to exercising his duties in the county of his appointment, he may also wish to qualify and exercise the functions of his office in other counties. Under such circumstances, he may ask for and receive from the county clerk as many certificates as the number of counties in which he wishes to qualify. He will then proceed to file the certificates in the several

22 21 

counties, and upon payment of one dollar filing fee, he will be qualified to perform the duties in those counties. 

In addition, he will secure further certificates for filing with the register of deeds where such register has an office in the county where he desires to qualify. When the certificate is filed in the register's office and the twenty-five cent filing fee is paid, instruments acknowledged by him may be recorded therein. Executive Law, $ 103. 

A notary public from any other county may file his certificate with the county clerk of New York County upon payment of a fee of $7.50. Executive Law, § 103. 

§ 21. Term of Office. 

The term of office is for two years where the appointment takes effect on the thirty-first day of March and expires on the thirtieth day of March. But where the appointment takes place on a day other than the thirtyfirst day of March, the term expires on the thirtieth day of March first occurring after the thirty-first day of 

March next following the date of appointment. Execu tive Law, § 101. 

§ 22. Manner of Administering Oath. 

The form of oath most commonly used is "You do solemnly swear that the contents of this affidavit subscribed by you is correct and true?" Bookman v. City of N. Y., 200 N. Y. 53. However, the form is immaterial.

It must be in the presence of an officer authorized to administer it, and it must be an unequivocal and present act by which the affiant consciously takes on himself the obligation of an oath. Bookman v. City of New York, 200 N. Y. 53, citing People ex rel. Kenyon v. Sutherland, 81 N. Y. 1; O'Reilly v. People, 86 N. Y. 154. Very often, however, there are persons who will produce a signed affidavit, saying that the signature is that of a friend, and request the notary to sign his name and affix his stamp

$ 23 

and seal. Or someone may telephone that he cannot appear in person but that he is sending the affidavit to the notary public for his signature. This, of course, is an imposition upon the notary public, to say the least, because an affidavit or acknowledgment taken without the presence of the affiant is illegal and constitutes serious professional misconduct on the part of the notary public. 

Matter of Napolis, 169 A. D. 469, 155 N. Y. S. 416. 

§ 23. Powers and Duties of a Notary Public. 

With respect to the powers and duties of a notary public, section 105 of the Executive Law provides that a notary public has authority: 

1. (Negotiable instruments and commercial usages)

Anywhere within the state to demand acceptance and payment of foreign and inland bills of exchange, and of promissory notes, and may protest for the nonacceptance or nonpayment thereof, to exercise such powers and duties as by the laws of nations and according to commercial usage, or by the laws of any other government, state or country, may be performed by notaries. 

2. (Oaths and acknowledgments) In the county in and for which he shall have been appointed and elsewhere, as provided in section one hundred and two of this chapter, to administer oaths and affirmations, to take affidavits and certify the acknowledgment or proof of deeds and other written instruments to be read in evidence or recorded in this state, in all cases in which commissioners of deeds may now take and certify the same, and under the same rules, regulations and requirements prescribed to said last-mentioned officers, not inconsistent with any of the provisions of this chapter; except that a county clerk's certificate authenticating the official character and the signature of such notary shall not be necessary to entitle any deed or other instrument so proved or acknowledged, to be read in evidence or recorded in a county in which the autograph signature and certificate

24 23 

of appointment and qualification of such notary shall have been filed, pursuant to section one hundred and two of this chapter, provided, however, that such exemption shall not be deemed to include any instrument so proved or acknowledged, to be recorded in the office of the register of deeds, in any county in which there is a register of deeds as well as a county clerk, unless such notary public shall also have filed in the office of the register of deeds of such county, his autograph signature and a certificate, as provided by section one hundred and three of this chapter. A notary public also has authority anywhere within the state to administer oaths and affirmations, to take affidavits and certify the acknowledgment or proof of deeds and other written instruments to be read in evidence or recorded in this state, in all cases in which commissioners of deeds may now take and certify the same within the state, and under the same rules, regulations and requirements prescribed to said lastmentioned officers, not inconsistent with any of the provisions of this chapter, provided that said deeds or other written instruments so proved or acknowledged are to be read in evidence or recorded only in the county for which the notary public shall have been appointed, or in which the autograph signature and certificate of appointment and qualification of such notary shall have been filed pursuant to section one hundred and two of this chapter. 

The acts authorized by this subdivision may be performed by such notary without official seal. For any misconduct in the performance of any such powers, a notary public shall be liable to the parties injured for all damages sustained by him. See also Executive Law, § 105a. 

§ 24. Notarial Stamp and Seal. 

When a notary public qualifies in the office of the county clerk or in that of the register of deeds, he is given certain numbers. In the counties of New York and Bronx, he is required to affix to each instrument acknowledged

$ 24 

or proved, in addition to his signature, his official number or numbers. For convenience, a stamp is used and appears thus:

MARY SMITH NOTARY PUBLIC, NEW YORK COUNTY N. Y. Co. Clk's No. 448, Reg. No. 6-M-587 Kings Co. Clk's No. 182, Reg. No. 6372 Queens Co. Clk's No. 773, Reg. No. 3143 Bronx Co. Clk's No. 42, Reg. No. 152-M-30 Commission Expires March 30, 1936 

However, the failure to affix the official numbers does not affect the validity of the instrument or acknowledgment or proof. Executive Law, § 105. 

In addition, a notary may obtain a seal which he may affix to the instrument. It has the words "Notary Public" in the center and is surrounded by the name of the notary public and that of the county of appointment. 

There is, apparently, no direct statutory requirement for a notarial seal, nevertheless it is used because certain statutes refer to the official seal. See C.P.A., §§ 366, 368;

R.P.L., § 312; N.I.L., § 261; Executive Law, § 105. 

A notary public cannot take an acknowledgment in a county in which he is not qualified except for use in a county where he is qualified and his subsequent qualification will not validate a previously unauthorized act done by him. Op. Atty. Gen. 1918. 

The filing of a certificate by a notary public of Westchester County in the office of the register of deeds of one of the counties of the City of New York, does not qualify the notary to act in such county. Such procedure merely allows instruments taken in the county where the notary public is qualified, to be recorded with such register of deeds without the necessity of a county clerk's certificate. Op. Atty. Gen. 1932, 45 St. Dept. 154.

26 25 

§ 25. County Clerk's Certificate. 

Section 103 of the Executive Law provides that the county clerk of a county in whose office any notary public has so filed his autograph signature and such certificate, shall, when so requested, subjoin to any certificate of proof or acknowledgment signed by such notary, a certificate under his hand and seal, stating that such notary public has filed a certificate of his appointment and qualifications with his autograph signature in his office, and was at the time of taking such proof or acknowledgment duly authorized to take the same; that he is well acquainted with the handwriting of such notary public and believes that the signature to such proof or acknowledgment is genuine, and thereupon the instrument so proved or acknowledged and certified shall be entitled to be read in evidence or to be recorded in any of the counties of this state in respect to which a certificate of a county clerk may be necessary for either purpose.

Instruments verified or acknowledged out of the state require the county clerk's certificate of the foreign state, and likewise an affidavit verified or acknowledgment taken in this state for use out of the state requires the county clerk's certificate to be subjoined thereto. 

§ 26. Commissioner of Deeds. 

Except the city of New York, commissioners of deeds in the cities of the State of New York are appointed by the common councils. Executive Law, § 106. In New 

York City, application blanks may be secured from the city clerk. Commissioners of deeds hold office for two years from the date of appointment. 

In the cities of New York, except New York City, after the appointment is made by the common council by resolution, the city clerk files a certificate thereof with the county clerk of the county wherein the city is situate. The county clerk notifies such persons and they must qualify

8 27 

within ten days by taking the oath and paying the fee.

Executive Law, § 106. In New York City, the applicant is notified by and is required to take the oath in the city clerk's office within thirty days from such appointment.

Greater New York Charter, § 58. 

§ 27. Powers and Duties of Commissioners of Deeds. 

Executive Law, § 106, provides as follows: 

"Every such commissioner shall have authority, within the city, county, municipality or other political subdivision for which he is appointed, and in the manner such acts are performed by authorized officers within the state: 

1. To take the acknowledgment or proof of the execution of a written instrument, except a bill of exchange, promissory note or will, to be read in evidence or recorded in this state. 

2. To administer oaths."

The powers of a commissioner of deeds appointed under this section are expressly limited to performing the official acts of a commissioner of deeds within the city or district for which he is appointed. Op. Atty. Gen. (1914) 62. 

An instrument proved or acknowledged within the City of New York before a commissioner of deeds of that city is entitled to be read in evidence or to be recorded in the county in which the officer resides without authentication by the certificate of the clerk of that county, provided the officer has filed in such county clerk's office the oath of office required by law. In the other counties, however, although embraced in whole or in part within the city, there must be such authentication. People v. Haggerty, 22 Misc. 296, 50 N. Y. S. 32.

§ 28. Action Defined. 

PAGE 

27 28 28 28 29 30 30 31 Where one seeks to enforce or protect a right, to redress or prevent a wrong, he does so by an "ordinary prosecution in a court of justice". C.P.A., § 4. This is known as bringing an action. There are two kinds of actions-civil and criminal. This book will deal with civil actions only, which include any action except those brought in the name of the State against one charged with a crime. In order to obtain the intervention of the court, however, the burden is upon the one who brings the action to prepare the necessary papers and follow certain prescribed rules of procedure in order that the court may have notice of what relief a party seeks and to determine whether or not he is entitled to it. In bringing a civil action, therefore, certain steps are required to be taken both to commence it and to conclude it. Such steps, which will be more fully discussed in the various chapters of this book, are briefly described under the separate headings which follow. 27

$ 31 

§ 29. Summons and Complaint. 

To commence an action, a summons which is a mandate of the court is issued. It is prepared by the plaintiff's attorney, who merely fills in a blank form obtainable at all law stationers. The summons is then served upon the defendant. With it or at a prescribed subsequent date, the complaint is served. The complaint is also known as a pleading, and recites the nature of the claim which is being asserted by the plaintiff against the defendant. 

§ 30. Joinder of Issue. 

After the plaintiff has served his complaint, the defendant serves his pleading, which is known as an answer. 

In it, he states how he intends to oppose the claim thus set up in the complaint. He may, for example, deny the validity of the claim. He may admit the claim, but set up a defense which, if successfully proved, may ultimately defeat the plaintiff's claim. And, finally, he may admit the validity of the claim, but assert an independent claim which he has against the plaintiff and which is known as a counterclaim. If a counterclaim is alleged, the plaintiff is given an opportunity to serve a reply setting forth how he in turn intends to resist the claim thus set up in the defendant's answer. The service of the last pleading is known as joinder of issue.

Thereafter, there may or may not follow applications to the court to correct or dismiss the various pleadings; to obtain more definite particulars; or to examine the adverse party in person concerning the claim. 

§ 31. Trial. 

After each side has had the opportunity to serve its respective pleading, a reading of which will acquaint the court as to the nature of the controversy which it will be called upon to decide, the plaintiff's attorney serves upon the defendant's attorney a note of issue, which states the

$ 29 

OUTLINE OF STEPS TAKEN IN ACTIONS. 

nature of the action, the names of the attorneys, the date of the joinder of issue and the term for which it has been set down for trial. See § 252. A copy of the note of issue is filed with the Calendar Clerk, who gives it a number and places it upon his general calendar of trials. The case is reached in its regular order unless it is entitled to a preference by statute or the special rules of the court. 

When the case is called in court for trial, it is assigned to a particular judge. The plaintiff then proceeds with the aid of witnesses, or such other proof as he may have, to substantiate his claim, while the defendant in turn seeks to defend his position by offering his witnesses and such proof as he may have. The proceedings are recorded by the court stenographer in the presence of the judge who decides the controversy. If either party has demanded a jury, then the jury, the members of which have been chosen to the satisfaction of both sides, remain in the jury-box throughout the entire proceedings, after which they are given a brief summary of the evidence together with instructions of the law applicable thereto, by the judge. They then retire to the jury room to deliberate. After they have decided the controversy, they return to the jury-box and announce their verdict. 

§ 32. Entry of Judgment. 

At the conclusion of the trial, the winning party draws the judgment which briefly describes the time when, the place where, and before whom the trial was had; the decision of the judge or the verdict of the jury; a direction that the winning party recover from the losing party an amount therein specified; and a direction to the clerk to enter the judgment. This the clerk does by carefully examining the paper as to form, and the correctness of the amount. He then places his signature at the foot thereof, recording the exact time by his watch of his doing so.

8 34 

§ 33. Collection of Judgment. 

A copy of the judgment is served upon the attorney for the losing party, who is known as the judgment debtor. If the judgment is paid, there is nothing further to do. If it is not paid, the following steps are taken: 

1. The judgment debtor is served with a subpoena to appear at a designated time and place to be examined as to what assets he may have and which may be taken to satisfy the judgment. If it is found that he has nothing, the matter is dropped there to be renewed again when the debtor is known to have come into possession of money or property. If, however, it is found that the debtor is able to pay the judgment, the next step is followed. 

2. If the debtor has a bank account steps are taken to cause the bank to deliver to the judgment creditor a sum sufficient to satisfy the judgment. If the debtor is employed and receives a salary, his employer is served with notice to deduct a certain amount of the salary if and when paid and deliver it to the marshall or sheriff who in turn delivers it to the judgment creditor's attorney to be applied on account of the judgment. If he receives no salary and has no bank account, it may be that he has property of some sort such as jewelry, etc., in which case, the application is made for the appointment of a receiver. It may be that some third person owes money to the judgment debtor whereupon the said third person may be served with a subpoena directing him to appear and be examined as to the indebtedness and cause him to pay it directly to the judgment creditor. 

§ 34. Appeal. 

It may be that the losing party feels he did not have a fair trial in which case he may proceed to apeal from the judgment. He does so by preparing an account of all the proceedings of the trial, known as the record, together with a brief containing the legal authorities on

$ 31 

OUTLINE OF STEPS TAKEN IN ACTIONS. 

which he relies to support his contention, and brings the appeal on for hearing in the appellate court. In as much as the winning party is entitled to collect the judgment immediately, the losing party, pending the hearing and determination of the appeal, gives to the winning party a bond which secures the payment of the judgment. The upper court, upon review may sustain the determination of the lower court, in which case the amount will have to be paid. It may reverse the decision or in addition send the case back for a new trial. There may also be an appeal from an order which is a direction of a court or judge in an action or special proceeding. 

C.P.A., § 127. 

§ 35. Special Proceeding Defined. 

Every other prosecution to protect a right or to redress or prevent a wrong is known as a special proceeding, instances of which are habeas corpus and arbitration proceedings. C.P.A., § 5. Unlike an action, there are only two stages. It is commenced by an application to the court for an order and concluded by the entry of a final order which is really the court's decision upon the application.

§ 36. Interviewing Client. 

PAGE 

32 34 35 37 38 39 40 40 41 41 42 46 46 46 Before any thought is given to the preparation of the summons, the service of which will officially commence the action, effort should be made to obtain from the prospective client a complete and detailed set of facts upon which the alleged claim is based. During the interview it should be ascertained whether the client is an infant. If he is, it will be necessary for him to appear by a guardian ad litem, and application for the appointment of one must be made before the action is commenced. See Chapter XXIX. If the client is a non-resident and his claim is such that it is assignable, an assignment should be executed, otherwise the client will be required to furnish a bond as security for the payment of any costs which may be assessed against him after the termination of the suit. See Chapter XXXIV. 

If a claim is made against the city, inquiry should be made if six months have elapsed. If it has, the client, of course, is barred from asserting the claim. Considera- 32

& 33 

tion should be given to the statute of limitations in so far as it governs the particular claim involved. C.P.A., § 

10-61. One should also ascertain whether the client consulted an attorney on any previous occasion with respect to the claim in question in order that any lien for services which the previous attorney might have, may be taken care of and a consent to substitution of attorneys executed. See Chapter XXXIV. In addition, one should secure from the client every paper which may have any bearing on the claim including all correspondence, contracts or leases, promissory notes, etc.

The next step is to investigate all facts which require investigation and finally search the law for authorities in support of the propositions raised by the claim. A memorandum of the law is prepared and filed for future use.

The importance of following the procedure as outlined cannot be overestimated, when one realizes the results which may follow from a failure to do so. The client may, for example, state that the X Company owns and operates the surface car from which he fell and was injured. The attorney, without investigating the matter, brings suit against the X Company to recover for the damages sustained. The case is prepared for trial, the necessary disbursements in connection with having the case placed on the calendar for trial are paid, and after a period of two and one-half or three years of waiting, the case is finally reached for trial. The client and witnesses come to court and in the midst of the trial the attorney hears the judge order the case dismissed for the reason that the Y Company owned and operated the car line and not the X Company. The attorney is then obliged to commence suit against the Y Company, but in addition to paying further disbursements and delaying the matter for a further period of two and onehalf or three years, his client will be liable to the X Company for certain statutory costs. Again, a client 3

$ 37 

may wish to sue a former employee, a salesman, for an overdraft; that is, the difference between the amount of commissions actually earned and the amount paid as advance against commissions. The attorney in his eagerness to commence the action is interested only in the question as to whether the employee expressly agreed to repay the overdraft. The client answers in the affirmative and suit is commenced immediately. Just before the case is reached for trial, the attorney sends for his client and for the first time, proceeds to examine the correspondence between his client and the former salesman. There, he finds a statement to the effect that the employee agrees to pay the overdraft only out of the commissions earned and that if no commissions are earned, the employee is not to reimburse the client any money received in excess of commissions earned. The attorney realizes that he cannot go to trial and is therefore obliged to discontinue the action after time and money has been expended. 

§ 37. Summons-Form and Requisites. 

With the preliminary work completed, the next step is to prepare a summons. This is done by the attorney and not by the court. In the New York Municipal Court, however, a party who does not wish to retain an attorney, may ask the clerk of the court to issue a summons. Blank forms may be obtained at all law stationers. They may be obtained for each of the courts separately or blank court summons may be secured, in which case the name of the court may be inserted.

The summons contains certain requisites. C.P.R. 45. 

It must state the court in which the action is brought, the names of the parties, and in the Supreme Court, the county which the plaintiff designates as the place of trial. The body of the summons directs the defendant to serve an answer to the complaint within a prescribed period of time or if the complaint is not served with the

$ 35 

summons, then, the defendant is required to serve a notice of appearance within the same period of time, otherwise a default judgment will be taken against him. 

It is subscribed with the name and address of the plaintiff's attorney. The form reads as follows: 

SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK. 

County of Albany. 

CHARLES ROBERTS, Plaintiff, -against- 

GEORGE CASE, Plaintiff designates Albany County, as the place of trial.

SUMMONS: 

Defendant. 

TO THE ABOVE NAMED DEFENDANT: 

YOU ARE HEREBY SUMMONED, to answer the complaint in this action, and to serve a copy of your answer, or, if the complaint is not served with this summons, to serve a notice of appearance on the Plaintiff's attorney within twenty days after the service of this summons, exclusive of the day of service. In case of your failure to appear, or answer, judgment will be taken against you by default, for the relief demanded in the complaint. 

Dated February 6th, 1936.

RONALD MANNERS, 

Office & P. O. Address, 

140 East 42nd Street,

Borough of Manhattan,  

The New York City Court summons provides a shorter period within which to serve an answer or notice of appearance; to wit, six days. See § 50 for form of summons used in the New York City Municipal Court. 

§ 38. The Court-Helpful Hints. 

The first consideration is the court in which the action is to be commenced. This must be clearly indicated.

$ 38 

At the outset one may feel somewhat confused and bewildered by reason of the great number of courts which are to be found in the City of New York and perhaps be at a loss to know in which one of these he may commence his action. His problem will be a simple one if he will consider the following:

Amount of Claim. If the amount sued for is not in excess of one thousand dollars, exclusive of interest, suit may be brought in the Municipal Court. If action is brought to recover a greater amount but not in excess of three thousand dollars and interest, suit is brought in the City Court. Suits to recover amounts in excess of three thousand dollars are brought in the Supreme 

Court. And where the sum demanded is three thousand dollars, exclusive of interest and costs, and the controversy is between citizens of different states, the action may be brought in the Federal Court. 

The jurisdiction of the supreme courts is the same throughout the state. This is also true with the county courts. The lower courts however vary and one should, therefore, consult the local court acts. For example, where the sum claimed does not exceed two thousand dollars exclusive of interest and costs, the action may be brought in the City Court of the City of Albany; on the other hand, the amount claimed in the New York City Court may be three thousand dollars and interest. 

If the sum claimed is not in excess of three thousand dollars exclusive of costs, it may be brought in the Municipal Court of the City of Syracuse; whereas in the Municipal Court of the City of New York, the amount claimed cannot exceed one thousand dollars exclusive of interest and costs. 

Speedy Trial. Litigants often bring suit in the

Supreme Court to recover large amounts, when as a matter of fact the claim is not worth more than one thousand dollars and the parties are willing to settle

$ 37 

for much less. Under such circumstances and in view of the fact that speedy trials are desirable, suit should be brought in the lower courts where the trial calendars are not so congested and therefore cases can be reached at a much earlier date.

Territorial Limits of Court. The residence of the parties must be taken into consideration to determine the court in which suit may be brought. If a resident of the Borough of Manhattan, for example, were to bring suit to recover the sum of one thousand dollars, he would bring the action in the Municipal Court, provided the defendant resided within the city limits, for the reason that the process of the Municipal Court cannot be served beyond the city limits. But if the defendant resided in some other part of the state, it would be necessary to bring the action in the Supreme Court because the process of that court reaches throughout the state. It could also be brought in a local court situated in that part of the state where the defendant resides and which has jurisdiction of the defendant. 

Nature of Jurisdiction. Before commencing an action, it is advisable to study the statute or other court act with respect to the nature of the actions of which the particular court has jurisdiction. For example, matrimonial actions; that is, actions for divorce, annulment and separation are always brought in the Supreme Court; whereas actions known as landlord tenant actions are brought in the Municipal Court. 

§ 39. Supreme Court. 

Unlike any other court, this court has unlimited jurisdiction. It has general jurisdiction in law and equity. 

C.P.A., § 64; Const. Art. 6, § 1. It has both original and appellate jurisdiction in civil as well as criminal cases. Although there is no restriction upon the amount for which suit may be brought, actions to recover an

8 40 

amount less than three thousand dollars are not encouraged. In fact, the statute provides that in contract actions where less than fifty dollars are recovered, costs are awarded against the plaintiff, whereas in tort actions, if the recovery is less than fifty dollars, the costs cannot exceed the damages. C.P.A., § 1471-1475.

The reason for this is that inferior courts are provided to take care of smaller causes and thus relieve an already congested calendar of the higher court. 

Except real property actions and actions to recover a penalty or a chattel restrained, an action, as a general rule, is brought in this court in the county wherein one of the parties resides at the commencement thereof. C.P. 

A., § 182. If neither party then resides in the state, it may be tried in any county which the plaintiff designates for that purpose in the title of the summons. 

§ 40. County Court. 

A county court may be found in each county of the state. With the exception of the county courts of Kings, Bronx, Queens and Richmond which have jurisdiction of criminal cases only, the county court of all other counties has limited jurisdiction in both civil and criminal cases. It has jurisdiction of all actions wherein the complaint demands judgment for a sum of money only not exceeding three thousand dollars, but its jurisdiction is limited to the residents of the county and to domestic corporations or joint-stock companies whose principal place of business or any part of its plant is located within the county, and in no case does it have jurisdiction of a foreign corporation, doing business here although its principal place of business and its plant may be located within the county. Wachtel v. 

Diamond Slate Engineering Corp., 215 A. D. 15; 213 

N. Y. S. 77. A counterclaim in any amount, however, may be interposed, but where it is in excess of three

41 39 

thousand dollars, either party may have the cause removed to the Supreme Court. It also has jurisdiction in actions for the partition of real property, dower, foreclosure, the specific performance of a contract relating to real property, to enforce or foreclose a mechanic's lien on real property, of any value, where the real property is situated within the county; and in actions to foreclose a lien on a chattel within the county and not exceeding the sum of three thousand dollars. C.P.A., 

§ 67. 

Service of its process may be made in any part of the state. 

§ 41. City Court of the City of New York. 

This court is vested with jurisdiction of all civil actions and proceedings which, prior to January 1, 1927, was vested in the county courts of Kings, Bronx, Queens and Richmond. Those courts retained jurisdiction in criminal prosecutions and proceedings only. It has original jurisdiction concurrent with the Supreme Court in actions for the recovery of money only, or, to recover chattels in which the complaint demands judgment for a sum not exceeding three thousand dollars and interest, in actions of replevin, foreclosure of mechanic's liens and liens on personal property, the taking and entry of judgment upon confession, where the sum sought to be recovered does not exceed three thousand dollars and interest, in marine cases, irrespective of amount, in actions on a bond given in an action or special proceeding in the City Court. The jurisdiction of this court over counterclaims is unlimited. Its process and mandates may be executed in any part of the City of New 

York. City Court Act, §§ 16, 18, 27. 

The jurisdiction of the court may be said to correspond to that of the Municipal Court of the City of 

Syracuse. Syracuse Municipal Court Code, § 6.

$ 43 

§ 42. Municipal Court of the City of New York. 

The several boroughs composing the City of New York are divided into districts, each of which has a municipal court. N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 5. The number of districts vary in each borough. For example, the Borough of 

Manhattan has ten such districts; while the Borough of the Bronx has two districts, and that of Brooklyn has eight districts. In addition, there is a Central Jury 

Part in each of the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn to which jury cases from the various district courts of the particular borough are transferred when a jury has been demanded. In the Borough of Manhattan, some of the non-jury cases are also transferred from the district court to Central Jury Part. 

This court has jurisdiction in the following actions when the amount claimed in the summons does not exceed one thousand dollars, exclusive of interest and costs: an action upon a contract, express or implied, other than a contract to marry; an action to establish a mechanic's lien on real property; an action to foreclose a lien on a chattel; an action to recover damages for fraud or deceit, or for personal injury or an injury to property; an action for an accounting; an action to recover a chattel, the aggregate value of which does not exceed one thousand dollars with or without damages; and summary proceedings between landlord and tenant for the recovery of real property regardless of the amount. N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 6. 

§ 43. Justice Court. 

The jurisdiction of this court is limited to the recovery of sums not in excess of two hundred dollars in actions for breach of a contract, express or implied, other than a promise to marry; to recover damages for personal injury, or injury to property; to recover for a fine and to recover a chattel. It also has jurisdiction of dis-

45 41 

possess proceedings.

Its jurisdiction over counter claims is unlimited. Justice Court Act, § 3. 

This court may be found in towns and some cities. 

Actions and special proceedings are heard and tried by a justice of the peace, and where provision is not otherwise made, he is vested with all the necessary powers possessed by the Supreme Court. The jurisdiction of this court is not limited to civil actions but has some criminal jurisdiction. As to the method of commencement of actions and who may appear as attorneys, see Sections 32, 33, 44 of the Justice Court Act. 

§ 44. Federal Court. 

Where the controversy is between citizens of different states and the amount involved is in excess of three thousand dollars, exclusive of interest and costs, the action should be brought in a federal court which may be found in each of the four federal districts, into which the State of New York is divided. The Northern District is in Albany and Malone, the Western District is in 

Syracuse and Buffalo, the Eastern District in Brooklyn and the Southern District in the Borough of Manhattan. 

In addition to the type of controversy already mentioned, this court also has jurisdiction of actions for infringement of copyright, admiralty and bankruptcy matters. 

In addition to its civil jurisdiction, it also has criminal jurisdiction involving the violation of Federal laws. 

§ 45. Other Courts. 

The process of the Surrogate's Court is a citation to show cause, an order to show cause, or such other process and mandate as the surrogate is or shall be authorized to issue. Proceedings are commenced by the filing of a petition. Surr. Ct. Act, §§ 48, 52. This court, among other things, has jurisdiction of all matters relating to decedents. The surrogate hears all cases which arise in connection with such matters. The court

8 46 

takes proof of wills, admits them to probate, grants letters testamentary and letters of administration. It concerns itself with the payment of debts and legacies. 

It determines the validity, construction or effect of any disposition of property contained in wills proved by the court. Surr. Ct. Act, § 40. 

The subject of criminal courts and procedure in connection therewith is not within the scope of this book. 

Such information may be obtained by a reference to the Code of Criminal Procedure, a book similar to the 

Civil Practice Act. 

Appellate Courts are discussed under the Chapter on 

Appeals. 

§ 46. Parties-Joinder and Manner of Naming. 

The next consideration is to determine who the parties to the action shall be; that is, who shall sue and who shall be sued. The former is known as the plaintiff, and the latter as the defendant. There may be one or more plaintiffs as well as one or more defendants. In either case, the names of the parties must appear in the caption. As to the question of joinder of plaintiffs, generally, the statute provides that all persons may be joined in one action as plaintiffs, in whom any right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same transaction or series of transactions is alleged to exist, whether jointly, severally, or in the alternative, where, if such persons brought separate actions, any common question of law or fact would arise. C.P.A., § 209. Where, however, two or more persons are entitled to sue by reason of their joint interest, they must all appear as plaintiffs. In the event that one of them refuses to join the others in bringing suit, he must be named as one of the defendants, the reason being stated in the complaint. C.P.A., § 194. But where the persons claiming a joint interest are too numerous, or it is impracticable to bring them all before the court, one may sue

46 

43 

Atkins v. Towerbridge, Where persons entitled interest in the subject on behalf of all. C.P.A., § 195; 

162 A. D. 161; 147 N. Y. S. 275. to sue, have only a common matter of the suit, one may sue on behalf of all others, regardless of whether they are numerous. Brock v. 

Poor, 167 A. D. 784; 153 N. Y. S. 332.

With respect to the joinder of defendants, generally, the statute provides that all persons may be joined as defendants against whom the right to any relief is alleged to exist, whether jointly, severally or in the alternative; this does not mean that each defendant shall be interested as to all the relief prayed for, or as to every cause of action included in any proceeding against him. C.P.A., §§ 211, 212. The section merely contemplates a case where a fundamental, common set of facts either entitles a plaintiff to relief against all the defendants even though such relief may be predicated upon different relationships or in the alternative against one of two or more defendants. A plaintiff may if he wishes, sue all who are liable or less than all. In a tort action for instance, where more than one person is liable, he may elect to sue one or all. Where the plaintiff is in doubt as to the person from whom he is entitled to redress, he may join two or more defendants, so that the question as to which, if any, of the defendants is liable, and to what extent, may be determined in the action. See Wait's N. Y. Practice Vol. 8 [3rd Ed.] 

324-396. 

It must be remembered that the question of who shall sue and who shall be sued is not one to be determined by guesswork nor by the client's demand. As already stated, a careful search of the authorities must be made in order to determine whether the client has the right to sue and whether the persons whom he wishes to sue are in fact liable in the matter. After the question is settled

8 46 

in the lawyer's mind, some difficulty may arise as to the manner of indicating or naming the parties. 

If either party is an individual, the name will be indicated simply as 

RAYMOND SMITH 

Where, however, the plaintiff is ignorant of the name or part of the name of the defendant, he may designate that defendant by a fictitious name or by as much of his name as is known, adding a description identifying the person intended. C.P.A., § 215. Or, if the defendant is unknown, he may designate that person as unknown, adding a description tending to identify him thus: 

John Smith, first name being fictitious, defendant's real first name being unknown to the plaintiff. or 

John Smith, name being fictitious, defendant's true name being unknown to the plaintiff, person intended residing at 131 East 38th St. Borough of

Manhattan, City of New York. 

When the name becomes known, application is made to the court for an order that the proceedings already taken be deemed amended by the insertion of the true name in the place of the fictitious name and that all subsequent proceedings be taken under the true name. 

Where the individual is an infant, the suit cannot be brought in its name alone, but must be brought through someone appointed by the court for the specific purpose of the action. Such person is known as a guardian ad litem and is indicated thus: C.P.A., § 202. 

John Burke, an infant, by Richard Burke, his guardian ad litem.

If the plaintiff sues as assignee of the claim, he is the owner of the claim and his name alone appears. C.P.A.,

It may be that an individual is doing business under an assumed name and may be indicated thus:

If the party is an unincorporated association of more than seven persons, suit is brought against the president or treasurer in his official capacity thus: (Gen. Assoc.

§ 47. Body of Summons. 

This part of the summons is specifically prescribed as to form by the statute. C.P.R. 45. See form, § 37. 

§ 48. Subscription. 

This part of the summons consists of the typewritten name of the attorney, his office and post office address. 

§ 49. Supplemental Summons. 

If, after the commencement of the action, it becomes necessary to bring in additional parties defendant, a

$ 47 

new summons is drawn. This is known as a supplemental summons. It is in the same form as the original summons except that in the body thereof it must require the new defendant to answer the original or the amended complaint and the supplemental complaint or either of them as the case requires. C.P.R. 48. Application, however, is first made for leave to bring in the additional parties. Where the defendant himself moves for the order, no supplemental summons need be served upon him. The manner of service of the supplemental summons is the same as that of the original summons. After the new defendants are given an opportunity to serve their answer, the action proceeds in the usual manner. C.P.A., 

§§ 219, 220.

§ 50. Serving Summons Without Complaint-Generally and in Particular Instances. 

A summons may be served with a complaint or it may be served alone and the complaint served at a later stage. 

Where a defendant is about to depart from the State for a lengthy visit abroad, it may become necessary to effect immediate service in order that the court may acquire jurisdiction of the defendant and the action proceed without delay. Under such circumstances, there would probably be no time within which to prepare a complaint. Again, some debtors refuse to pay a claim until action is commenced. In such case, a summons will 48

$ 49 

often suffice. In certain instances where the complaint does not accompany the summons, a notice is served in lieu thereof for reasons depending upon the nature of the action. In other instances, a particular endorsement must appear on the face of the summons. 

Amount Fixed or Ascertainable. Where an action is brought to recover a sum of money which is either fixed by the terms of the contract or capable of ascertainment by computation and the complaint is not served, the summons may contain a notice on the face of the summons stating the sum of money for which judgment will be taken in case of default. C.P.R. 46.

C.P.R. 46. This facili tates the entry of judgment; for, if the defendant ignores the summons and does not serve a notice of appearance as required by the summons within the time limited therefor, the plaintiff may file with the clerk of the court the original copy of the summons with notice, proof of the service thereof, (§ 53) and an affidavit that the defendant has not appeared. The clerk will enter judgment accordingly. C.P.A., §§ 485, 486. 

Actions Affecting Property-No Personal Claim Notice 

There is another form of notice which is used to accompany a summons, and found most frequently in foreclosure actions. In actions affecting specific real or personal property and in which no personal claim is made against the defendant, a notice is served with the summons. It states the object of the action, contains a description of the property affected and states that no personal claim is made against the defendant. The purpose of this is to prevent unnecessary delay and if the defendant despite the notice, unreasonably defends the action, costs may be awarded against him. The notice reads as follows: (C.P.A., § 1478.)

Matrimonial Actions. In matrimonial actions where the summons alone is served, the statute requires that the summons have plainly endorsed on the face thereof, the words "Action for a Divorce", "Action for a Separa tion", or "Action to Annul the Marriage", depending on the nature of the action. C.P.A., § 1167; C.P.R. 47, 53. In 

Actions to Recover a Penalty or Forfeiture. 

actions to recover a penalty or forfeiture in the Municipal Court and the Justice Court, where the complaint does not accompany the summons, the latter must bear the endorsement "According to the provisions of," naming the statute or ordinance to which it relates. 

N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 24; Justice Ct. Act, § 49. Albany City Ct. Act, § 35. Syracuse Municipal Ct. Code, § 25. 

Execution Against the Person. In an action where execution against the person may issue upon a judgment of the Municipal Court, if no verified complaint accompanies the summons, the latter must bear the endorsement "Plaintiff claims defendant is liable to arrest and imprisonment in this case". N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 25.

Municipal Court Actions Generally. Unlike the usual summons, if no written complaint is annexed, the common practice in the Municipal Court is to recite the nature of the claim on the back of the summons. This is known as an oral complaint. See § 110. This court also has a prescribed form of summons. N. Y. Mun. Ct. 

Code, §§ 19, 20. In addition to the usual form, the added features are as follows: 

1. Address of the plaintiff. 

2. Classification numbers. A recent rule of this court classifies all types of actions, giving to each such type a number. This number appears upon the face of the summons and is the means of identifying the kind of

§ 51. Service of Summons-Generally. 

The original summons is placed in the office file pending service. A copy is delivered to the person who is to serve it upon the defendant. This person must be upwards of the age of eighteen years and not a

$ 52 

party to the action. It may be served by someone in the attorney's office, or it may be sent to a regular process server. The fee for serving a summons is one dollar and fifty cents unless it is a difficult service. If the defendant resides at a great distance, the summons may be sent directly to the sheriff of the county wherein the defendant resides. He will serve it within his county or if necessary outside of his county.

The summons may be served in one of the three following ways: C.P.A., § 220-235; See also Wait's

N. Y. Practice Vol. 1 [3rd Ed]. 560-606. 

Personal service

Substituted service 

Service by publication § 52. Personal Service. 

The defendant may be served personally by delivering to him a copy of the summons. If the defendant refuses to accept it, the process server may permit the summons to fall to the floor or he may place it on a table or other convenient place nearby and leave. He must not take it back because the defendant has been served. The process server, however, must be certain that the person served is actually the defendant. He should obtain a description of the defendant in advance of the service, and when effecting service, he may inquire whether the person served is the defendant named in the summons thus: "Are you Mr. Burke?" If the answer is in the affirmative, the summons is delivered to him. 

The service must be made peacefully and quietly. No attempt may be made to entice a non-resident into the state on some pretext in order to serve him. Garabettian v. Garabettian, 206 A. D. 502; 201 N. Y. S. 548. In other words, one cannot resort to tricky service.

§ 53. Proof of Service-Form. 

After the summons has been served, the next step is to prepare and annex to the summons proof of the service. The statute provides in detail the manner in which such proof shall be made. C.P.R. 53. Generally speaking, proof may be made in either of the following ways: 

Affidavit. The person who serves the summons signs an affidavit which states that he is upwards of eighteen years of age, the time when, the place where he served the summons, and that he knew the person so served to be the person mentioned and described in the summons as the defendant. Printed copies of the following affidavit are available at law stationers: (C.P.R. 53).

Deponent knew the said person so served as aforesaid to be the same person mentioned and described in said summons as the defendant therein.
