Where service is made by a sheriff within the territorial limits of his county, he need furnish a certificate only. C.P.R. 53, Subd. 1. Where,

$ 54 

however, he effects service outside his county, he must furnish an affidavit.

In matrimonial actions, the sheriff must furnish, in addition to the certificate, an affidavit that he knew the person served to be the same person named as defendant in the summons and also state the source of his knowledge. C.P.R., 53, Subd. 3. And where the summons is served without the complaint, the certificate must recite the fact that the summons contained the required notice. 

§ 54. Filing Summons-Index Number. 

Unless the adverse party demands the filing thereof, where a defendant is served personally, it is not necessary to file the summons in actions pending in the 

Supreme Court or the New York City Court. 

A summons is filed by delivering to the clerk of the court wherein the action is pending, the original summons to which is annexed the affidavit or certificate of service. The clerk places it in an individual folder wherein from time to time are placed further papers in the case as subsequent steps are taken. The folder bears a file number which together with the year of filing, as for example 31246-1936, constitutes the index number. The number is obtained when the first paper in the action is filed. It is noted in the litigation register for future use; for the clerk will refuse to accept any paper which does not have endorsed thereon, the index number. This facilitates an orderly and time-saving means of preserving the record in the case. N. Y. 

County Supreme Court Trial Term Rule VIII. 

In the Municipal Court, the summons with oral or written complaint together with the affidavit of service must be filed within three days after the service thereof. 

N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 22, Subd. 3. If this is not done, and no stipulation is obtained which extends the time for filing, the clerk will refuse to accept the summons at

$ 59 

a subsequent time with the result that the action may be dismissed. N. Y. Mun. Ct. Rule VIII. The plaintiff may, however, obtain permission of the court to file the summons nunc pro tunc; that is, as of the date it should have been filed. N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 22, Subd. 4. 

§ 55. To Compel Filing. 

One may compel a party in whose behalf they are served, to file the summons and each pleading in the action with the clerk of the court by serving a notice on such party requiring such filing within five days after demand. And, on failure to comply with the demand, the court may order that the summons or pleading be deemed abandoned. C.P.A., §§ 100, 101. 

§ 56. Substituted Service. 

Frequently, a defendant may learn in advance that a summons is to be served upon him and will attempt to evade the service thereof. As a result, the process server will experience difficulty in effecting service. 

When he calls at the defendant's residence, he will be informed that the defendant is "out", and it is not known when he will return. The process server may also experience difficulty in effecting service upon a domestic corporation when none of its officers who may be served, can be found. Under such circumstances, if the process server will not be able with due diligence to serve the defendant personally, application may be made to the court for an order directing that service be made by substituted service. C.P.A., § 230. This is done in the 

An order is prepared reciting the fact that the court is satisfied from a reading of the papers annexed thereto that the defendant is evading service and that personal service cannot be made upon him, although

$ 56 

diligent efforts to do so have been made and directing that service of the summons be made (1) by leaving a copy thereof, and of the order, if the defendant is a domestic corporation or joint-stock or other unincorporated association at its principal place of business, or if a natural person, at the residence of the defendant, with a person of proper age, if upon reasonable application admittance can be obtained and such person found who will receive it; or (2) if admittance cannot be so obtained nor such person found, by affixing the same to the outer or other door of the defendant's said place of business or office, or of his residence, and by depositing in a post-office another copy thereof, properly inclosed in a post-paid wrapper addressed to the defendant at its said principal office or place of business, or to him at his place of residence. C.P.A., § 231. 

Where no residence of a natural person can be found, service may be made in such manner as the court directs. 

It may even direct service by publication as hereinafter discussed. 

An affidavit of the process server is annexed to the order. The affidavit, among other things, states the time when, the place where and the conversation, if any, which took place on the occasion of each attempt on the part of the process server to serve the defendant; and that he will be unable to serve the defendant personally although he has made diligent efforts to do so. An affidavit should also be annexed to the order reciting the fact that a registered letter was sent to the defendant acquainting him with the fact that efforts have been made to serve him and that the writer desired to be advised of a time and place convenient to the defendant where he could be served, and that no reply was received.

57 61

§ 58. Affidavit-Form. 

An affidavit in support of an order for substituted service, reads as follows:

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York.

§ 59. Submitting Order for Signature. 

The original order, affidavit, summons with or without the complaint, a copy of the letter and the registered receipt, are submitted to the Clerk of Special Term Part II for the judge's signature, or such other part wherein ex parte business is transacted. 

§ 60. Service of Order. 

When the order is signed, two conformed copies of the complete set of papers are delivered to the process server and he makes the service as directed in the order. 

§ 61. Proof of Service. 

The process server prepares an affidavit reciting the time when, the place where and the manner of service. 

C.P.R. 53. This he forwards to the attorney. The latter annexes it to the original set of papers. 

§ 62. Filing Order. 

The order and the papers on which it was granted must be filed, service made and proof of service filed within twenty days after the order is granted; otherwise the order becomes inoperative. Service is complete ten days after proof thereof is filed. C.P.A., § 231; N. Y.

City Ct. Act, § 51. In the Municipal Court, the order with proof of service, must be served and filed within five days after it has been signed. N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, 

§ 23. 

§ 63. Service by Publication. 

Except in Municipal Court actions, the statute makes provision for another method of service; to wit, service by publication, under certain prescribed conditions. C.P.A., § 232; N. Y. City Ct. Act, § 51; N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 21. They arise in a case where, among other things, the defendant to be served is a foreign corporation; or

$ 65 

is a joint-stock association or other unincorporated association neither of whose president and treasurer is a resident of the state; or being a domestic corporation, where after diligent effort, service cannot be made within the state upon those of its officers who may be served; or where the plaintiff is unable to ascertain whether the defendant is or is not a resident of the state; where the defendant being a resident of the state departed therefrom with intent to defraud his creditors or to avoid the service of a summons or keeps himself concealed therein with like intent; or where title to real property is affected, or where property of the defendant within the state has been levied upon pursuant to a warrant of attachment. 

It will be observed that although non-residents as well as residents may be served by publication, the provision does not offend against the rule that the courts of the state cannot reach outside its prescribed territorial limits. The court's jurisdiction in such a case extends only to the property, real or personal which is within the state. Beyond that it cannot go. One cannot, for example, serve a non-resident defendant by publication in an action upon a debt and recover judgment for a sum of money, where that defendant has no property within the state. Where, however, it can be shown that the defendant has property within the state, the plaintiff would also have to show that a warrant of attachment has been levied against such property before an order of publication could be obtained. 

The procedure is briefly as follows: 

An order is drawn which among other things directs that the service of the summons be made by publication thereof in two newspapers in the English language therein designated; that such notice appear for a specified time, not less than once in each of six successive weeks. It also contains a direction that on or before the

$ 64 

day of the first publication, the plaintiff send to the defendant by mail one or more sets of copies of the summons, complaint and order, and of the notice required, or a statement that the court or judge being satisfied by the affidavit annexed to the order that it cannot be ascertained with due diligence where the person would receive such mail, dispenses with the mailing thereof. C.P.R. 50.

In addition to the order, a verified complaint is prepared to be annexed thereto and any other papers which may be necessary under the special circumstances of the case. The complaint shows the existence of a cause of action. The affidavit shows extraneous facts as in a case brought to recover a sum of money and it it necessary to show that a levy has been made on the property of the defendant within the state, or where it is necessary to show what diligent efforts have been made to serve the defendant within the state without success. 

When these papers have been prepared, they are submitted for the judge's signature in the same manner as the order for substituted service. 

§ 64. Procedure After Order is Signed-Form of Notice. 

After the order has been signed, and as provided therein, one or more sets of copies of the summons, complaint, order and notice are mailed to the defendant unless such mailing has been dispensed with. C.P.R. 50.

A copy of the summons is sent directly to the designated newspapers or to any of the various advertising agencies. 

The latter in turn sends it to the newspapers, obtains and forwards to the attorney proofs of the summons as it is to appear in the newspapers. In addition to the summons, the following notice is sent along to be subjoined to and published with the summons. C.P.R. 52. 

TO GEORGE CASE: The foregoing summons is served upon you by publication pursuant to an order of the Honorable Hiram S.

$ 67 

Black a Justice of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, dated the 10th day of September, 1936, and filed with the complaint in the office of the Clerk of the  at the Supreme Court Building, in the Borough of Manhattan, City, County and State of New York. 

Dated: September 11, 1936. 

RONALD MANNERS, 

140 East 42nd Street,.

If the action be brought to recover a judgment affecting the title to or the possession, use or enjoyment of real property, the notice shall also briefly state the object of the action and give a brief description of the property.. 

§ 65. Time of First Publication-When Service Com plete. 

The first publication must be made within three months after the order is granted. Service by publication for the purpose of reckoning time to answer, is complete on the forty-second day after the first publication. C.P.R. 51. 

§ 66. Proof of Service. 

Where service is made by publication, an affidavit showing, among other things, that the summons and subjoined notice did appear in the designated papers and the length of time they appeared, is prepared by the printer, publisher, foreman or principal clerk. The advertising agency takes care of forwarding the affidavit to the attorney. 

§ 67. Filing Order. 

If service is made by publication, or without the statein lieu thereof, the summons, complaint and order and the papers on which the order was made must be filed with

$ 69 

the clerk on or before the day of the first publication or the day of personal service. C.P.R. 52. 

§ 68. Service Without the State in Lieu of Publication. 

See C.P.A., § 233; C.P.R. 53. 

§ 69. Personal Service Out of the State Without Order. 

See C.P.A., § 235; C.P.R. 53.

§ 70. Asking Relief of Court-Contested Motions. 

93 During the pendency of the action and before the actual trial thereof, application may be made to the court for various kinds of relief. Such relief may consist, among other things, of asking the court to vacate the service of the summons; to dismiss the complaint; to strike out defenses; to strike out an entire answer and thus secure judgment without the necessity of a trial and the attendant delay and expense; to be furnished with a bill of particulars of the adversary's claim in order to properly prepare for trial; to obtain an examination before trial and an opportunity to examine the adversary's books in order to establish one's own case; to obtain an order of 69

8 70 

arrest; and to attach property. One makes application for such relief by motion which is defined as an application to a court or judge for an order. C.P.A., §§ 113, 115. 

Ordinarily, motion papers consist of a notice of motion, one or more supporting affidavits and exhibits. In certain instances, only a notice of motion is required. See $ 124. A notice of motion may be described as follows: 

1. It is entitled in the action. 

2. It is directed to the adversary's attorney or to the adverse party in person, if the latter is not represented by counsel. 

3. It makes specific reference to all papers which will be used at the hearing, in support of the motion. 

4. It states the time when and the place where the motion will be brought on for hearing. 

5. It states that application will be made for an order directing that certain specific relief be granted. 

6. It contains at the end thereof, the phrase, to wit, "and for such other, further and different relief as to the court may seem just and proper in the premises". 

7. It is subscribed by the attorney for the moving party.

Annexed to the notice and made part thereof is an affidavit which may be described as follows: 

1. It is entitled in the action. 

2. Directly beneath the title, appears the venue, to wit: 

State of New York,  SS.: 

3. The name of the deponent appears as follows: 

John Doe, being duly sworn, deposes and says:

$ 71 

4. Brief description of the deponent. 

5. Status of the case. 

6. Facts showing why the moving party is entitled to the relief prayed for. 

7. Any other matter which is required by statute or the rules of the court. 

8. Prayer for relief. 

9. Signature of the deponent. 

10. The jurat and signature of the officer who administers the oath.

It should be remembered that every fact necessary to entitle the moving party to relief must be established in the affidavit. The motion papers are served upon the adversary's attorney the required time before the hearing. See § 77. This is known as a contested motion because the adversary is given an opportunity to be heard on the return day of the motion and to file an opposing affidavit setting forth the reasons why the relief should not be granted. 

Where, for example, a defendant wishes to dismiss the complaint and thus terminate the action because the summons alone was served on the defendant and the plaintiff failed to serve the complaint within the time limited therefor, the defendant's attorney prepares a notice of motion and affidavit as hereinafter described. 

§ 71. Notice of Motion-Form. 

A notice of motion to dismiss the complaint in a case where an action was commenced by the service of a summons, but no complaint was served within the time limited therefor, may read as follows:

$ 71 

CHARLES ROBERTS, Plaintiff, -against-

Manhattan, City of New York, on the 22nd day of October, 1936, at 10:00 o'clock in the forenoon of that day, or as soon thereafter as counsel can be heard, for judgment dismissing the complaint herein for the failure of the plaintiff to serve his complaint, and for such other, further and different relief as to this Court may seem just and proper in the premises, together with the costs of this motion.

ROLAND MANNERS, ESQ., 

140 East 42nd Street,

Yours, etc.,

Borough of Manhattan, New York City.

$ 74 

§ 73. Ex Parte Applications. 

Although it is the usual practice to give notice whenever a motion is made, nevertheless, there are instances where such applications may be made ex parte; that is, without giving the adversary an opportunity to be heard in opposition. Examples of ex parte applications are as follows: 

1. Applications for provisional remedies. 

2. Orders to show cause. 

3. Motions to extend time. (Note exceptions.) 4. Orders supplementary to execution. 

Where, however, an ex parte order has been granted without notice to the adversary, the latter is not without a remedy. If, for example, the ex parte order is an attachment or order of arrest, and the adverse party feels ag grieved thereby, he may proceed by notice of motion or order to show cause to vacate the ex parte order. Upon the hearing, the court determines whether the order has been properly granted. 

§ 74. Order to Show Cause-Form. 

If it is desired to shorten the time required to be given by notice of motion and thus bring the hearing on sooner, or when pending the motion, and before its hearing and determination, it is desired to stay the proceedings so that the rights of the parties will not be prejudiced, one proceeds by order to show cause which is similar to, and takes the place of the notice of motion. It is distinguished from the notice of motion in the following respects: 

1. It states the manner and time of service. 

2. Instead of being subscribed by the attorney for the moving party, it must be signed by a judge. 

3. The affidavit must state why a shorter notice than that usually required is necessary (C.P.R. 60); and whether any previous application has been made for the same or similar relief. C.P.R. 61.

$ 75 

Procedure by order to show cause also gives one, in some instances, the additional advantage of securing relief regardless of the outcome of the motion as in the instance where a motion is made to make a pleading more definite and certain. Unlike other motions addressed to the pleading, this motion does not extend the time of the defendant to answer. The defendant, therefore, in order that he may not be in default pending the decision, provides for an extension of time by inserting a direction in the order to show cause as follows: "It is ordered that the defendant's time to answer be and the same hereby is extended to five days after the service of an order entered upon the determination of the within motion."

Instead of proceeding by notice of motion to dismiss the complaint as already considered, the defendant could proceed by order to show cause if he desired to bring the hearing on sooner than the five day period required by notice of motion. Where, for example, the plaintiff is in default for failure to serve a complaint but nevertheless disregards the default and moves for an order requiring the defendant to appear for an examination before trial in order that the plaintiff may obtain the necessary information to frame a complaint, the defendant could move by order to show cause to dismiss the complaint and thus secure his relief before the return day of the plaintiff's motion.

Under such circumstances, the defendant's attorney would proceed to draw an order to show cause in the following form:

874 

CHARLES ROBERTS, GEORGE CASE, Plaintiff, -against- 

Defendant. 

Upon the annexed affidavit of George Arnold, duly verified the 

16th day of October, 1936, it is hereby

ORDERED, that the plaintiff show cause at Special Term, Part III of this Court to be held at the Courthouse, Pearl and 

Centre Streets, in the Borough of Manhattan, City of New York, on the 19th day of October, 1936 at 10:00 o'clock in the forenoon of that day, or as soon thereafter as counsel can be heard, why an order should not be made to dismiss the complaint herein, for the failure of the plaintiff to serve his complaint, and for such other, further and different relief as to this Court may seem just and proper in the premises; and it is further 

ORDERED, that all proceedings on the part of the plaintiff be stayed pending the hearing and determination of this motion except to vacate this order.

Sufficient reason appearing therefore, service of this order and the annexed affidavit upon the attorney for the plaintiff made on or before the 18th day of October, 1936, shall be deemed sufficient.

Dated: New York, October 16, 1936. 

SAMUEL ROSENMAN, Justice of the Supreme Court. 

The above order to show cause takes the place of the notice of motion. And annexed thereto is an affidavit in the form already considered but adding a paragraph explaining why the plaintiff proceeds by order to show cause and also a paragraph reading thus: "That no previous application has been made to any other court or judge for the same or similar relief prayed for herein."

$ 77 

In some instances, proceedings must be initiated by order to show cause instead of a notice of motion if the statutes or rules of the court so provide. Where this is the case, the same period of notice is given as required when proceeding by notice of motion unless otherwise provided. 

§ 75. Submitting Order for Signature. 

As soon as a notice of motion is prepared, it may be immediately served with the accompanying affidavit, but an order to show cause requires the signature of a judge before service. The judge's signature is obtained by submitting the order to show cause and the affidavits annexed thereto to the clerk of the part of the court wherein ex parte business is transacted. This may be in Special 

Term, or Special Term, Part I or Part II. Assuming that it is a Supreme Court action in New York County, or Kings County, the order to show cause and affidavit are presented to the Clerk of Special Term, Part II. N. Y. 

Supreme Ct. Spec. Term Rule IV; Kings County Su preme Ct. Rule XIV. In Bronx County, the papers are submitted to the Clerk of Special Term, Part I. Bronx

County, Supreme Court, Special Term, Rule VII. After he has examined the papers, and is satisfied that they comply with statutory requirements and otherwise correct as to form, he sends them to the judge for signature. 

The same procedure is followed in the City Court in the 

Borough of Manhattan. In the New York Municipal 

Court, however, it is common practice to present the papers to the judge personally or to his secretary, either at Trial Term or in the judge's chambers. In the congested areas such as the counties of New York, Kings and the Bronx, the order may be submitted on any day of the week except Sundays, and on Saturdays if a judge can be found in chambers. But in the sixth judicial district, for example, applications may be made at Supreme Court chambers at Oneonta, Binghamton, Cortland or

$ 77 

Norwich on Saturdays of each week except during the months of July and August when the resident justice is not otherwise engaged. Supreme Ct. Rules, 6th Jud. Dist. 

When the order has been signed, a conformed copy thereof is made and served upon the adversary's attorney. 

§ 76. Kinds of Relief to Specify. 

The motion or order to show cause may specify one or more kinds of relief or in the alternative or otherwise. 

C.P.A., § 117. 

§ 77. Service of Motion Papers and Opposing Affida vits-Form of Affidavit of Service. 

The original notice of motion or order to show cause, together with a conformed copy thereof, and supporting affidavits are sent to the office of the adversary's attorney. There, the managing attorney or other person charged with the duty of receiving papers, retains the copy and endorses upon the back cover of the original papers an admission of service. See § 2. If an admission of service cannot be obtained, the copy is left at the office, and the person who served the same signs an affidavit of service to be annexed to the original motion papers which reads thus: 

CITY COURT OF THE CITY OF NEW YORK: 

County of New York. 

CHARLES ROBERTS, Plaintiff, -against- 

Affidavit of Service on

Person in Charge. 

FREDERICK SMITH being duly sworn, deposes and says that he is upwards of the age of eighteen years; that on the 11th day

$ 79* 

of October, 1936, between the hours of four and five in the afternoon, he served the annexed notice of motion and affidavit on Ronald Manners, the attorney for the plaintiff in the above entitled action; at his office, 140 E. 42nd St. in the City of New

York by delivering the same to and leaving the same with a person in charge of said office, said attorney being absent therefrom at the time of said service.

FREDERICK SMITH. 

11th day of October, 1936.

MARION BROWN, Notary Public-New York County. 

In the usual case, where the attorneys for the parties. reside in the same city, the attorney for the moving party serves a copy of the motion papers upon the attorney for the adversary five days before the day set for the hearing. C.P.R. 60. In the City Court, motion papers may be served four days before the return day, and in the Municipal Court three days' notice is sufficient. N. Y. 

City Court Act, § 29, Subd. 4; N. Y. Mun. Ct. Rule X. If the attorneys do not have their offices in the same city, eight days' notice is required. The moving party may give his adversary ten days' notice of motion and insert in the notice of motion the requirement that the affidavit of the adversary to be used in opposition to the motion be served on the moving party five days before the return day. If the adversary fails to serve the answering affidavit in advance of the hearing, as directed, he will not be permitted to read it in opposition to the motion, unless the court, for good cause shown, shall otherwise direct. 

Where, however, the answering affidavit is thus served, the moving party may serve a reply affidavit thereto at least two days before the hearing. C.P.R. 64. Again, the moving party may, if he wishes, give eight days' notice of motion, in which case the adversary must serve at least one day prior to the day on which the motion is to be heard, upon the attorney for the moving party, a copy- 10

$ 79 

of the affidavit which he expects to read in opposition to the motion. C.P.A., § 117. By giving longer notice, the moving party has the advantage of learning what the adversary's line of attack will be and he can thus be better prepared to meet it.

An order to show cause and the affidavit in support thereof may be served two or more days in advance of the return day, depending on the direction contained in the order. 

§ 78. Cross Motion. 

Where the moving party gives eight days' notice of motion, and the adversary, upon receipt of the motion papers, decides that he, too, will require certain relief and will want the court to hear his application on the return day of the original application, he may serve upon the attorney for the moving party a notice, with or without affidavits or other papers in support thereof, specifying any kind or kinds of relief in the alternative or otherwise to which he claims to be entitled in the action; whether the relief so asked for, be responsive or not to the relief asked for by the moving party. C.P.A., § 117. 

§ 79. To Bring Motion on For Hearing-Form of Note of Issue. 

The practice of bringing a motion or order to show cause on for hearing varies in the different courts. It is therefore advisable to consult the clerk of the court or the local court rules. Motions may be noticed for any day in the term, except Saturdays and holidays, unless otherwise provided.

The first thing to remember is to place the index number on the back cover of the motion papers before filing. 

Assuming that the motion is made in an action pending in the Supreme Court of New York County, the notice of motion or order to show cause and affidavit with proof of service thereof are filed in advance of the return day with

$ 81 

the clerk of the part wherein it is returnable, except that an order to show cause which is returnable in less than two days may be filed at any time; that is, either before or after the calendar call on the return day. If the motion is to be heard in Special Term, Part I, such as a motion for an examination before trial or a bill of particulars, the papers are filed with the Clerk of Special Term, Part I. 

N. Y. Cty. Supreme Ct., Spec. Term, Rule II. If, on the other hand, the motion is one that is to be heard in Special Term, Part III, such as a motion to strike out defenses or for judgment on the pleadings, the papers are filed with the clerk of Part III. N. Y. Cty. Supreme Ct.,

Spec. Term, Rule III. In certain other courts, all motions are heard in one Special Term Part. The clerk then proceeds to place it upon his calendar of motions to be called on the day specified in the motion papers. 

In the Supreme Court of Kings County, instead of filing the original motion papers, the rules require that a note of issue be filed with the clerk of the part in which the motion is returnable, two days before the return day, except in the case of an order to show cause, which may be filed at any time before the hearing. Kings Cty. Sup. 

Ct., Spec. Term, Rule 12.

The note of issue is in the following form: 

CHARLES ROBERTS, Plaintiff, -against- 

Motion to dismiss complaint

Returnable October 22, 1936, 

Ronald Manners, Attorney for the plaintiff. Office and Post

Office Address: 140 E. 42nd St.,

$ 80 

George Arnold, Attorney for the defendant. Office and Post

Office Address: 119 Broadway,  

Note of issue filed by the defendant.

On the hearing of the motion the original motion papers are filed with the clerk who calls the calendar or other clerk present therein to receive them.

In the City Court, New York County, both the note of issue and the motion papers are filed with the clerk one day in advance of the return day.

In the Municipal Court of the Borough of Manhattan, the motion papers are filed with the clerk of the court before nine-thirty on the return day. 

§ 80. Hearing. 

Assuming that the motion is returnable in Special 

Term, Part I, of the Supreme Court, New York County, the calendar of motions to be heard in that part will appear in the New York Law Journal on the return day thus: 

SUPREME COURT-SPECIAL TERM, PART I. 

(ROOM 300, Third Floor.) Before Mr. Justice ROSENMAN-Court opens at 10A.M. 

RULE II. 

Motion Calendar.

Motions may be noticed for any day in the term. The clerk of Special 

Term, Part I, shall make up a calendar for each day. cause or notice of motion, with proof of service thereof, must be filed with the clerk before the date on which the motion is noticed to be heard, except where an order to show cause is granted returnable in less than two days upon proof of service thereof, the clerk at any time may place the motion on the calendar. This calendar will be called at opening of the court, and no motion will be heard unless it is on the calendar. On the hearing of a motion only one counsel on each side will be heard for not more than fifteen minutes unless the court shall otherwise order.

During the July, August and September terms, or at any other time when Part III of the Special Term is not in session, any motion directed by Rule 111 to be heard in that part may be noticed for and made at Part I 

of the Special Term. The justice presiding at Special Term, Part I, may adjourn the motion to the next term of Special Term, Part III, if he does

$ 83 

not deem it important that such motion should be heard during the time when Part III is not in session. 

NOTE.-Filed papers that are to be used on motion must be sent to clerk's office of this part before the call of the calendar. 

The calendar of Special Term, Part I, will hereafter be called by the clerk at 10 A.M. for the purpose of noting defaults, adjournments and motions ready for argument and allow submission of motions where the papers are complete.

The motions not thus disposed of will be heard in their regular order by the justice presiding.

Upon the submission or argument of all motions requiring a consideration of the pleadings a copy of the pleadings properly marked to indicate denials and admissions must be submitted by the moving party.

At ten o'clock in the morning of the return day, the attorney or his clerk attends upon the call of the calendar. The clerk calls the motions in Room 300, in the order in which they appear on the calendar. Answer is made in accordance with the manner of disposition. 

If the attorneys wish to argue the motion, each side answers thus: "Plaintiff ready to argue; Defendant ready to argue". If they do not wish to argue but merely desire that the judge read the papers at his convenience, they answer "Submitted". The courts, as a rule, refuse to hear argument on such motions as those for bills of particulars and examinations before trial. These motions are therefore marked "Submitted". 

It is advisable to consult the clerk of the court to learn whether the court will hear argument on the particular motion. If the parties have settled their differences and wish to withdraw the motion, they answer "Withdrawn". If they desire an adjournment, they may request the court to put the motion over to a specified later date. If neither side appears on the call of the calendar, the clerk marks the motion "Off". If the moving party alone appears, the motion is granted on default. 

At the close of the calendar call, the clerk makes a list of the motions which are to be argued. The attorneys remain in court and await their turn. Upon the argument, the attorney for the moving party argues in favor of the granting of the motion by stating orally every fact contained in the moving affidavit. The adversary's attorney then argues in opposition to the motion. He too, states orally every fact contained in the opposing affidavit which he files with the clerk at the time of the

$ 85 

argument, at the same time giving a copy to the adversary's attorney. The attorneys must refer to those papers only which are before the court and of which. both parties have copies. If, when the adversary's. attorney completes his argument, the moving party desires to answer matter contained in the opposing affidavit, he asks leave to serve and file a reply affidavit.. 

In the Supreme Court, New York County, the usual! practice is to serve the reply affidavit on the adversary's. attorney and file it together with admission or affidavit of service with the clerk with whom the original papers were filed, before four o'clock on the same day on which the motion was argued unless a longer period of time has been granted. 

§ 81. The Decision. 

After a motion has been argued or submitted to the court, the next step is to watch the Law Journal each day until the decision appears. The decisions of the 

New York Municipal Court, however, are not published in the Law Journal and it is therefore necessary to make a daily examination of the court docket. This is a book in which the clerk records every step in the action in so far as it has taken place in the court. 

To find a decision published in the Law Journal, it is necessary to look for it under the name of the judge who heard the argument and the part in which the judge was sitting. The decision on a motion heard in Part I before Mr. Justice Rosenman would appear thus: Decisions.

The short form order is made by the court. It is annexed to the motion papers and remains on file in the court.

Printed forms for the different courts are available at law stationers. A conformed copy is made and served with notice of entry on the adverse attorney. See § 87. 

§ 83. Long Form Order-Form. 

This form of order is, as a rule, prepared by the attorney for the party in whose favor the decision has been rendered, but may be prepared by the adverse attorney. Briefly, it contains the following: 

1. A caption beginning with the words, "At a Special

Term Part "giving the name of the part in which the motion was heard; the name and address of the court, and leaving a blank space for the judge to fill in the date when he signs the order. 

2. Name of the judge who heard the argument. 

3. The title of the action. 

4. Statement of the time when and the place where the motion was heard together with a brief description of the relief prayed for. 

5. Recital of the papers read in support of and in opposition to the motion. 

6. Names of the attorneys representing the parties together with the names of the individuals who argued the motion. 

7. The ordering clauses which set forth the decision of the court 

8. The word "Enter" which is a direction to the clerk to enter the order. 

9. The initials or name of the judge, followed by

& 89. 

either words or initials to indicate the name of the court wherein he sits as justice, thus: Justice of the Supreme Court (J.S.C.); Judge of the City

Court (J.C.C.); or Judge of the Municipal Court (J.M.C.). C.P.R. 70. 

The order is drawn in the following form:

§ 85. Submitting Order for Signature. 

In the Supreme Court of New York County, the original proposed long form order with proof of service thereof is filed with the clerk of the part wherein it was heard, before noon on the return day. See other local court practice. The clerk in turn sends it to the same judge who heard the motion originally. In order to learn when the judge has signed the order, it is necessary to examine the list of signed orders as they daily appear in the Law Journal under the appropriate court, part and judge. 

§ 86. Counter Order. 

If the adversary objects to the form of the proposed order, he may submit his own proposed counter order before noon on the return day of the notice of settlement, in the form he desires, together with a separate memorandum in which he briefly states why his order should be signed rather than that of the moving party. As a rule, the court signs the proposed order of the moving party if its terms are in accordance with the decision. 

§ 87. Service of Order With Notice of Entry-Form. 

If the court has entered a short form order as already described, the next step is to go to the clerk's office, and make two copies of the order which will be found in the court file of the particular case and serve a copy thereof with notice of entry upon the adverse attorney. 

A printed blank form of the notice generally appears on the back cover, otherwise a notice may be prepared to read as follows:

The same procedure is followed in the case of a long form order after it has been signed. An admission or affidavit of service is obtained on the office copy. Because the time to appeal starts to run from the day of service of the order, with notice of entry, one should serve the order immediately in order to limit the time therefor. 

§ 88. Reargument. 

After an order has been served with notice of entry, the aggrieved party may appeal. Before doing so, he may wish to ask the court to reconsider its decision.

$ 93 

One proceeds in the usual way by notice of motion or order to show cause and affidavit for a re-hearing or reargument of the original motion. On the return day, if a judge other than the one who heard the original motion, is sitting in that particular part, the attorney for the moving party may ask that the motion be referred to the same judge who decided the original motion, because the judge who heard the original motion is obliged to pass upon an application for reargument. 

As soon as the request is granted, the attorneys attend at the chambers of the judge to whom the motion has been referred and arrange with the secretary for a time when the judge will hear reargument. While some judges will hear argument, others will refuse to do so but will insist upon a mere reading of the papers. Still others refuse to entertain such motions at all. See

N. Y. City Court Rule XIV. 

§ 89. Resettlement. 

If the aggrieved party desires to do so, he may proceed immediately to take an appeal from the order. But before doing so, he should examine the order carefully for any defects. For example, the order may fail to recite all the papers on which the order was based; that is, those papers which were before the court on the hearing of the motion such as the affidavit of the moving party. This defect must be cured in order that the affidavit may be used upon the appeal, for only those papers which are recited in the order may be made part of the record. C.P.R. 234, Matter of Brady, 155 Misc. 

242; 280 N.Y.S. 887; O'Brien v. Weisbecker, 196 A. D. 

971; 188 N.Y.S. 940. Again, the order may not comply with or otherwise state the exact terms of the decision. 

The remedy is to resettle the order. This must be done within the time permitted to appeal; to wit, thirty days, otherwise it would in effect be extending the time within which to appeal. No court can do this.

$ 89 

The procedure is to serve upon the adverse attorney a copy of the proposed resettled order together with notice of resettlement. The notice is in the same form as the notice of settlement except that the prefix "re" is added to the word "settlement" wherever it appears in the notice. The original proposed resettled order with notice of resettlement and proof of service thereof is submitted to the clerk of the part wherein the motion was heard. The latter submits it to the same judge who signed the original order. The steps following the signing thereof correspond to those following the signing of the long form order. The adversary may file a memorandum opposing the resettlement unless, of course, the original order was defective. 

One may also proceed by notice of motion to resettle the order, annexing thereto a supporting affidavit and the proposed resettled order.

A resettled order takes the place of the original order theretofore entered and an appeal is taken from the said resettled order.

§ 90. General Appearance-Form. 

It has been previously stated that an action is commenced by the service of a summons and in this way the court acquires jurisdiction of the defendant. Very often, however, the defendant does not wish to be annoyed or embarrassed in either his home or his office by the presence of a process server. He may therefore waive service by asking his attorney to accept service in his behalf. This his attorney does by communicating with the plaintiff's attorney, and requesting the latter to serve upon him a copy of the summons and receive in return, a copy of a notice of appearance. The service of the notice of appearance means that the defendant has appeared generally in the action thus conferring jurisdiction upon the court, and is equivalent to personal service on the defendant. C.P.A., § 237.

A notice of appearance reads as follows: 

95

$$ 90 

- 

SIR: 

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that the defendant William Rice hereby -appears in this action, and that I have been retained as attorney for said defendant and demand that you serve a copy of all papers in this action upon me at my office, No. 112 Broadway, Borough of Manhattan,  

Dated: New York, November 15, 1936. 

MARTIN ADAMS, Attorney for Defendant. 

Office & Post Office Address, 

112 Broadway,

New York City. 

"To: 

MILTON BARTLETT, 

New York City. 

A notice of appearance is required to be served when no complaint is served with the summons. See § 91. It may also be served when the purpose is to waive objection to the service of the summons. This happens when, after a summons and complaint have been served personally on the defendant, the latter's attorney requests further time beyond the statutory period to serve an answer. The plaintiff's attorney consents to the extension upon receipt of a notice of appearance so as to be assured that during the stipulated further time, the defendant's attorney will not object to the court's juris-

$ 97 

APPEARANCE. 

diction by moving to set aside the service of the summons on the ground of an alleged irregular service and thus unnecessarily delay the joinder of issue. Reed v. 

Chilson, 142 N. Y. 152; See also Wait's N. Y. Practice,

Vol. 1, [3rd Ed.], 611-616. 

§ 91. Time Within Which to Serve Notice of Appear ance. 

Where the summons alone has been served upon the defendant, the latter's attorney must serve a copy of the notice of appearance upon the plaintiff's attorney within the period of time required to serve an answer; to wit, twenty days from the date of the service of the summons, in a Supreme Court action; and six days in a New York City Court action. 

§ 92. Notice of Appearance and Waiver in Foreclosure. 

In foreclosure actions, where the defendant has no defense to the action and therefore does not intend to interpose an answer, but nevertheless desires notice of each subsequent step in the action, he may serve upon the plaintiff's attorney the equivalent of a general appearance; to wit, a notice of appearance and waiver. 

See & 428 for form. 

§ 93. Special Appearance-Form. 

The plaintiff's attorney should not serve a general appearance if there has been any irregularity in service and it is desired to object to the court's jurisdiction on that ground. Where, for example, a defendant has not been personally served but finds a copy of a summons in his mail-box and upon investigation, learns that the plaintiff has not obtained an order permitting service by publication or substituted service, he may appear specifically and move to set the service aside; whereas if he serves a general appearance or an answer, he will be deemed to have waived the defect in service. Further-

8 93 

more, upon finding the summons in the mail-box or under his door, the defendant cannot sit by and ignore the service in the mistaken belief that because he has not been properly served, the plaintiff will be unable to proceed in the matter, for if he does, he will find that a judgment by default has been entered against him and he will be obliged to move to set it aside. 

The same applies to a foreign corporation which cannot be sued if it is not doing business in this state. 

If the plaintiff purports to have effected service upon the foreign corporation in this state, the defendant corporation may move to set it aside. 

The following is a form of special appearance: 

SIR: 

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that the defendant William Rice appears specially in this action and that I have been retained specially as attorney for the said defendant for the sole purpose of vacating and setting aside the service of the summons and to dismiss the complaint herein on the ground that the defendant has not been properly served with the said summons and complaint herein. 

Dated: New York, November 15, 1936. 

MARTIN ADAMS, 

Attorney for Defendant,

Appearing Specially. 

Office & Post Office Address, 

112 Broadway,

§ 94. Procedure After Appearing Specially. 

A copy of the notice of special appearance is served upon the plaintiff's attorney. The original is not required to be filed. Thereafter, within the time required to serve an answer, a motion is made to set the service aside; and to dismiss the complaint, if a complaint has been served. But in order to prevent a default, in the event the service is sustained, it is advisable to proceed by order to show cause and provide therein for an extension of time to plead. 

§ 95. Order to Show Cause-Form. 

An order to show cause to set aside the service of the summons and to dismiss the complaint on the ground of defective service may read as follows:

Upon the annexed affidavits of William Rice and Robert Siddons duly verified the 15th day of November, 1936, and upon all the pleadings and proceedings heretofore had herein, it is hereby 

ORDERED, that the plaintiff show cause at Special Term, Part I 

of this Court to be held at the County Courthouse, Pearl and 

Center Streets, in the Borough of Manhattan, City of New York on the 18th day of November, 1936, at 10 o'clock in the forenoon

$ 96 

of that day or as soon thereafter as counsel can be heard, why an order should not be made herein vacating and setting aside the service of the summons and dismissing the complaint herein on the ground that the defendant was not personally served with the said summons and complaint herein; and that the defendant have such other further and different relief as to the court may seem just and proper in the premises, and it is further ORDERED that pending the hearing and determination of this motion that all proceedings on the part of the plaintiff be stayed except to review this order, and it is further ORDERED that if the service be sustained that the time of the defendant to serve his answer be and the same hereby is extended to ten days after the service of an order with notice of entry upon the defendant's attorney.

Sufficient reason appearing therefor, service of a copy of this order and the annexed affidavits upon the attorney for the plaintiff if made on or before the 15th day of November, 1936, shall be deemed sufficient.

Dated: New York, November 15, 1936. 

H. B. J. S. C. 

§ 96. Affidavit-Form. 

A supporting affidavit in the following form may be drawn: 

SS.: 

WILLIAM RICE, being duly sworn, deposes and says that he is the defendant in the above entitled action.

$ 101 

APPEARANCE. 

Deponent makes application by order to show cause for an order to vacate and set aside the service of the summons and to dismiss the complaint herein on the ground that the deponent was not duly personally served therewith. 

That on or about the 5th day of November, 1936, deponent was obliged to leave the City and go to Chicago on a business matter. 

That about ten days later upon his return to his home in the Hotel Madison, he called at the desk for his mail. The clerk gave him, among other things, a large sealed envelope. Upon opening it, deponent found a summons and complaint. That, as appears from the annexed affidavit of Robert Siddons, he questioned the clerk and was informed that a young man who refused to reveal his identity had called a number of times and asked for the deponent. That on his third visit upon being informed that the deponent was absent from the city, he gave the clerk the aforesaid sealed envelope with instructions that he deliver it to the deponent on the latter's return to the city. 

That no application for the same or similar relief has been made to any other court or judge.

Wherefore deponent respectfully requests that an order be entered herein to vacate and set aside the service of the summons and to dismiss the complaint. 

15th day of November, 1936.

MARY BROWN, Notary Public-New York County. 

WILLIAM RICE.

§ 97. Traverse-Practice in New York Municipal Court. 

In the Municipal Court, a special appearance is known as a traverse. The form already considered may be used. It must, however, be accompanied by an affidavit of the party stating in particular the ground of his objection. N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 88, Subd. 1. 

§ 98. Filing of Traverse and Effect Thereof. 

Unlike the procedure in the higher courts, after a copy of the traverse and the accompanying affidavit has been served upon the adverse attorney, the original with proof of service thereof is required to be filed with the clerk of the court on or before the last day for answering. This operates as a stay of proceedings and the defendant is not obliged to serve an answer until the question of the service is decided. 

§ 99. Notice of Hearing-Form. 

If upon receipt of the traverse, the plaintiff's attorney is convinced that the defendant has actually been served, he may have the court decide the issue of service by serving a notice of hearing upon the adverse attorney and filing the original with proof of service thereof upon the clerk. The latter places the matter upon the court calendar for a hearing for the day mentioned in the notice. The hearing is noticed for not less than three nor more than five days. If either party appears in person, the clerk sets the matter down for hearing. N. Y.

Mun. Ct. Code, § 88, Subd. 1. 

The notice served by the attorney, reads as follows:

§ 100. Hearing. 

The procedure upon the hearing is in the nature of The process server is questioned about the a trial.

8 100 

manner of service and is asked to point out the defendant who may be in a crowded room of spectators. 

Section 88 of the New York Municipal Court Code as recently amended provides that upon the hearing, if the court shall sustain the objection, it shall dismiss the action or counterclaim as the case may be with costs in the discretion of the court in an amount not to exceed the sum of twenty-five dollars. If the court shall overrule an objection based upon an alleged defective service of the summons, it shall impose costs in its discretion in an amount of not more than twenty-five dollars and shall grant leave to the party interposing such objection to plead further only upon the payment of such costs as imposed. If the court shall overrule any other objections so interposed, it shall grant leave to plead further upon such terms and conditions as in its discretion are just in the premises.

§ 101. When to Serve and File Complaint. 

PAGE 

105 106 107 107 108 110 110 110 112 115 116 116 117 118 118 119 

The first pleading is the complaint. C.P.A., § 254. It is prepared by the plaintiff's attorney and may be served upon the defendant with the summons or if it does not accompany the summons, it must be served upon the defendant's attorney twenty days after receipt of a notice of appearance. If the defendant's attorney fails to serve a notice of appearance, the plaintiff's attorney is not obliged to serve a complaint but may proceed at once to enter judgment by default. In New 

York City Court actions, where the complaint does not accompany the summons, the complaint is served six days after the receipt of the notice of appearance. In 

Municipal Court actions, unless the oral complaint is endorsed upon the summons, a written complaint usually accompanies the summons. 105

§ 102 

The complaint is not required to be filed in actions pending in the Supreme Court or the New York City

Court unless demand therefor is made. C.P.A., § 100. 

§ 102. Drawing the Complaint. 

Before the complaint is drawn, the plaintiff's attorney should determine upon what theory the action shall be based. For example, where the action involves a contract, the question may arise as to whether to regard it as a valid and subsisting agreement and sue to recover damages for its breach or whether to regard it as invalid and sue to rescind and set it aside. The reason for this is obvious; in as much as the theories are inconsistent. One cannot ask a court to declare a contract invalid and at the same time hold that it is valid in order to recover damages for its breach. Again, it may be necessary to determine whether to sue on contract or in tort. Having decided upon the theory, the next step is to draw it in proper form, setting forth the facts upon which it is based in a plain and concise manner, bearing in mind that a complaint must contain certain allegations, the omission of any one of which may be ground for dismissal of the one or more causes of action contained in the complaint.

It is true, of course, that after the type of action is determined upon, one need only consult the regular form books, nevertheless in addition, it is advisable to examine the provisions of the Civil Practice Act applicable thereto, and the annotated cases found therein for an interpretation and better understanding of the reasons for the provisions. The Rules of Civil Practice and the rules of the various courts found in the same volume and following the text of the Act should also be consulted. 

For example, where the action involves the sale and delivery of goods or performing of work, labor and services, one could simply sue and set forth the ultimate

$ 107 

facts but the Statute provides that if the plaintiff annexes to the verified complaint, a schedule in which are set forth and numbered the items of the claim and the reasonable value or agreed price of each, the defendant in turn will be compelled by his verified answer to indicate specifically the items, if any, which he disputes in respect to delivery, or performance, reasonable value or agreed price. C.P.A., § 255a. See form § 109. The purpose of this section is to narrow and define the field of controverted facts primarily for the convenience of the plaintiff and incidentally to save the time of the court; for should the defendant merely interpose a general denial, no issue would be raised. Innis, Pearce & Co. v. 

Poppenberg, 213 A. D. 789; 210 N. Y. S. 761.

Again, a resident of New York County may be planning to commence suit in the Supreme Court of Westchester County against a resident of the latter county to recover damages for breach of contract. But upon examining the rules of the Supreme Court, it will be found that because the plaintiff is a resident of New York County at the time the action arose, he will be entitled to a preference if he brings the action in New 

York County rather than in Westchester County. N. Y.

County Supreme Court Trial Term Rule V. 

§ 103. Contents of Complaint. 

The complaint must contain the title of the action, a statement of each cause of action, and a demand for judgment. C.P.A., § 255. 

§ 104. Title of Complaint. 

The title or caption is the same as that of the summons. 

Since each part of the title was taken up under the Chapter on Preparation of Summons, it may be briefly stated that the title specifies the name of the court in which it is brought; if it is brought in the Supreme

105 

Court, the name of the county which the plaintiff designates as the place of trial; and the names of all parties to the action, plaintiff and defendant. 

§ 105. Pleading Each Cause of Action Separately. 

Where the parties are not individuals, there will follow certain preliminary allegations which will serve to describe or introduce the parties. For example, where either party is a corporation, the complaint shall so state, also whether it is a domestic or foreign corporation, if the latter, the state, country or government by or under whose laws it was created thus: (C.P.R. 93). 

That at all the times hereinafter mentioned, the defendant was a corporation duly organized and existing under and by virtue of the laws of the 

State of New York. 

or That at all the times hereinafter mentioned, the defendant was and still is a foreign corporation organized and existing under and by virtue of the laws of the Dominion of Canada, having its principal office in Montreal, Canada.

Also, where one sues in a representative capacity as administrator, executor or receiver, there follows an allegation about the appointment, and due qualifications.

In other words, there is an allegation of facts showing the right to sue or be sued as such. 

Following this, is a plain and concise statement of the facts constituting the claim. C.P.A., § 241. It may be that the complaint will set out more than one cause of action. If so, each separate cause of action shall be separately stated and numbered and shall be divided into paragraphs numbered consecutively, each as nearly as may be, containing a separate allegation. An allegation contained in a separately numbered paragrah of

$ 109 

one cause of action may be incorporated in another cause of action in the same pleading by reference and need not be repeated. C.P.R. 90. One cannot, of course, combine different causes but must set forth each cause separately, and under each cause state the ultimate facts constituting that cause. One must not set forth the evidence by which the facts are proved but neither may one plead a conclusion. One cannot, for example, state that certain acts were fraudulent without stating the facts from which the conclusion of fraud can be inferred. 

Swift v. Chester Carbon Co. Inc., 223 A. D. 808; 228

N. Y. S. 475. In this way the defendant is given an opportunity to properly prepare for trial because he is apprised of the facts and knows how to meet them. The 

Statute, however, provides an exception to this rule. In pleading the performance of a condition precedent in a contract, it is not necessary to state the facts constituting performance, but the party may state in general terms that he or the person whom he represents, duly performed all the conditions of such contract on his part to be performed. C.P.R. 92.

Exception is also made in certain other instances so as to render it unnecessary to set forth complete facts. 

Where suit is brought on an account, it is not necessary to set forth the items of the account therein alleged. 

C.P.A., § 246; See also Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 3, [4th Ed.] 556. In suing on an instrument for the payment of money, the party may set forth a copy of the instrument and state that there is due to him thereon from the adverse party a specified sum which he claims. 

See § 108; C.P.R. 94; Kahnweiller v. Salomon, 107 Misc. 

602; 177 N. Y. S. 739; Cohu v. Husson, 113 N. Y. 662.

Other exceptions are found in the case of pleading a judgment or determination, also a private statute. C.P.R. 

95; 98.

If the complaint is to be verified, the manner of

108 

pleading these facts will depend on whether the person swearing, knows the facts of his own knowledge or whether he obtained the information through other sources. In the former instance, he may plead without qualification. In the latter, he may plead on information and belief, as for example where the person who has first-hand information is absent from the county wherein the attorney has his office at the time the complaint is drawn, but has communicated all the necessary facts and sent papers containing the required information to his attorney. In such a case the attorney may allege the facts on information and belief and so swear. 

§ 106. Demand for Judgment. 

The complaint must contain a demand for the judgment to which the plaintiff supposes himself entitled by reason of the facts alleged therein. C.P.A., § 255, Subd. 3. 

§ 107. Subscription. 

The complaint is subscribed with the name of the attorney for the party or of the party if appearing in person. C.P.R. 91.

§ 111. Verification-In General. 

If the complaint is to be verified or sworn to, one annexes thereto an affidavit to the effect that the person so swearing has read the pleading, that it is true to the knowledge of the deponent, except as to the matters therein stated to be alleged on information and belief, and as to those matters believes it to be true. The affidavit is signed by the party in whose behalf the pleading is served or by another person authorized by statute. And where a person, other than the party, signs the affidavit, he must set forth the grounds of his belief as to all matters not stated upon his knowledge and the reason why it is not made by the party. C.P.R. 

99; 100. 

Unless required by statute, a complaint need not be verified. If it is verified, all subsequent pleadings must be verified except the general answer of an infant by his guardian ad litem and except as otherwise specifically prescribed by statute. C.P.A., § 248–252. If a verifica tion is defective, the pleading may be treated as an unverified pleading provided the attorney who receives it gives the adverse attorney notice of his election to so treat it. C.P.A., § 253. 

§ 112. Verification By Individual-Form. 

Rule 99 of the Rules of Civil Practice provides that the verification of a pleading must be made by the affidavit of the party, or, if there are two or more parties united in interest and pleading together, by at least one of them who is acquainted with the facts, except as otherwise provided therein.

An affidavit by an individual is in the following form: 

HAMILTON BOWERS, being duly sworn, deposes and says: 

That he is the plaintiff in the within entitled action; that he

& 117 

has read the foregoing complaint and knows the contents thereof and that the same is true to his own knowledge, except as to the matters therein stated to be alleged on information and belief, and as to those matters he believes it to be true. 

16th day of January, 1936.

MARY BROWN, Notary Public-New York County. 

HAMILTON BOWERS. 

§ 113. Verification By Corporation—Form. 

Rule 99 of the Rules of Civil Practice provides that if the party be a domestic corporation, the verification must be made by an officer thereof. The rule further provides that if the party be a foreign corporation, or be not within the county where the attorney has his office; or if there are two or more parties united in interest and pleading together where none of them acquainted with the facts is within that county; or if the action or defense be founded upon a written instrument for the payment of money only which is within the possession of the agent or the attorney; or if the material allegations of the pleading be within the personal knowledge of the agent or the attorney, the verification may be made by such agent or attorney. 

A verification by a corporation is in the following form: 

  

EDWARD ARNOLD, being duly sworn, deposes and says: That he is the President (or any other officer) of Arnold Galleries, Inc., the plaintiff in the above entitled action; that he has read the foregoing complaint and knows the contents thereof; that the same is true to his own knowledge, except as to the matters therein stated to be alleged upon information and belief, and as to those matters he believes it to be true. 

That the reason why this verification is made by deponent and

8 115 

not by plaintiff is that plaintiff is a domestic corporation and deponent is an officer thereof, to wit, its President. 

EDWARD ARNOLD. 

11th day of November, 1933.

MARY BROWN, Notary Public-New York County. 

§ 114. Amended Complaint. 

The plaintiff may, without applying to the court, prepare an amended complaint and serve a copy thereof on the defendant's attorney twenty days after the original complaint has been served; or within the same period of time after the answer has been served, or twenty days after the service of a notice of motion addressed to the complaint. Although the right to thus amend once, as of course is an absolute one, the court may, nevertheless, upon the application of the adversary, strike it out for cause. If the plaintiff desires to amend the complaint again, he may do so only by leave of the court. He may proceed by notice of motion and annex to the motion papers a copy of the proposed amended complaint. The court may grant the application if it is convinced that the plaintiff desires the amendment in good faith and not to delay the trial of the action. The amended complaint takes the place of the original complaint and the defendant serves his answer thereto disregarding the original one entirely. C.P.A., § 244. 

The form is the same as the original except that in the opening statement, the word "amended" precedes the word "complaint". See Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 3, 

§ 115. Supplemental Complaint. 

If subsequent to the service of the complaint, material facts occur which it is necessary to plead, the plaintiff

119 

must obtain leave of the court to serve a supplemental complaint. C.P.A., § 245. This is also true where the plaintiff desires to allege any new or additional causes of action, even though such additional causes came into existence after the commencement of the action. C.P.A., § 245a. This he may do by notice of motion annexing thereto an affidavit and a copy of the proposed supplemental complaint. The application may be for leave to make a supplemental complaint, either in addition to or in place of the original complaint. C.P.A., § 245; See also Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 3, [4th Ed.] 549–553. 

§ 116. Further Considerations. 

If the complaint has been carefully prepared and is not open to attack by the adversary, the plaintiff will, after the defendant serves an answer, proceed to examine the defendant concerning the allegations of the complaint as a first step in preparation for trial. See Chapter

XIII.

§ 117. In General. 

As soon as the defendant's attorney receives a complaint, note should be made in the litigation register of the date it was served upon the defendant, or if not served simultaneously with the summons, then the date it was served upon the attorney. A diary entry is then made of the last day to serve an answer or make a motion with respect to the complaint. 

§ 118. Examining the Complaint. 

The defendant's attorney proceeds to examine the complaint as follows: 

120

& 121 

HOW TO EXAMINT A COMPLAINT. 

1. Is the venue proper, if not, serve demand for change to proper county; or for convenience of witnesses, etc. 

2. Is plaintiff a non-resident, if not known, serve demand for address. 

3. If plaintiff is a non-resident, make application for a non-resident bond. 

4. If the action is between citizens of different states. and the amount in dispute exceeds the sum of three, thousand dollars exclusive of interest and costs, make application for removal to the federal court. 

5. Does the complaint state a cause of action, if not, move for a dismissal thereof upon that ground or upon the thirteen additional grounds provided by statute. 

6. If the complaint is defective in other respects, move to correct or strike out certain parts thereof. 

7. If particulars of the claim are desired, serve a. demand or move for a bill of particulars. 

§ 119. Venue. 

If an action is brought in a county other than the proper one, it will be tried in that county unless steps are taken by the defendant to transfer it. The county may be improper because neither party resides nor has a place of business therein; but even though the county is proper, a change may be sought for the convenience of witnesses or because an impartial trial cannot be had in the county designated. See Chapter XXVII for further discussion and procedure. 

§ 120. Demand for Address-Form. 

If the defendant desires to obtain the plaintiff's address either to determine whether he is a non-resident; to question the venue; or for any other reason, he may serve a written demand therefore upon the plaintiff's

$ 120 

attorney. The plaintiff also may obtain the defendant's address; for Rule 9a of the Rules of Civil Practice provides that any party to an action or proceeding, by notice in writing, may demand of any other party a verified statement setting forth his post office address and his residence, in sufficient detail to permit ready location. If the party whose post office address and residence are demanded is a corporation, such demand may include, in addition, the names, post office addresses and residences of any officers thereof specified in the same. In the case of an assigned cause of action, any party may demand of any other party a verified statement of the post office address and residence of the original owner of the claim and any assignee thereof. 

The address must be furnished within ten days after the service of the demand, otherwise a motion may be made staying all proceedings until the information is provided. 

The demand may be in the following form:

SIR: 

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that you are hereby required to serve and file a verified statement of the plaintiff's residence address, stating street, number, city or village, county and state, and if the same is in an apartment house, the number of the apartment, including whatever information is necessary to locate the place of residence of the said plaintiff, within ten days after the service of this demand upon you, otherwise a motion will be

$123 

made for an order staying all proceedings until the information demanded is furnished.

Dated: New York, February 20, 1936. 

Yours, etc.,

To: 

Attorney for Plaintiff, 

MARTIN ADAMS, § 121. Non-Resident Bond. 

Attorney for Defendant.

Office & Post Office Address, 

112 Broadway,

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. 

Where the plaintiff, among other things, is a nonresident or a foreign corporation, the defendant may apply to the court for an order, ex parte, requiring the plaintiff either to pay into court the sum of two hundred fifty dollars or file a bond in the same amount. 

The reason for this is that the court wishes thereby to insure to its resident defendant payment of costs to which he will be entitled if he is successful in the action; otherwise he might have to seek payment from the plaintiff in the foreign state of the latter's residence. See Chapter XXVIII for further discussion and procedure. 

§ 122. Removal to Federal Court. 

If the action is between citizens of different states and the amount in controversy is in excess of three thousand dollars, exclusive of interest and costs, the defendant may, if he wishes, remove the action to the Federal

Court. There, the practice is similar to that of the

§ 123 

state court unless otherwise prescribed.

See Chapter 

XXX for procedure. 

§ 123. Determining Whether Complaint States a Cause of Action. 

When an attorney prepares a complaint, he experiences little difficulty because he follows a form but when he receives a complaint drawn by another attorney, he must rely on his own ingenuity to determine whether it is drawn in proper form, and to find all the defects which may be present therein. Perhaps the application most frequently made with respect to a complaint is that for dismissal thereof on the ground that it does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. 

Every complaint is made up of certain allegations. 

These in turn are based upon and supported by recitals of such facts and circumstances from which the inference of the allegation can be drawn. For example, where the plaintiff seeks to set aside an agreement on the ground that it was executed under duress and coercion, it is not sufficient to allege that at the "persuasion, nagging and coercion of the defendant, the plaintiff joined in the execution of the contract"; for that would be a mere conclusion unsupported by facts constituting a legal basis for the charge. To properly allege duress, the courts hold that the plaintiff must plead the words or substance which constitute duress and coercion. Cross ways Apartments Corporation v. Amante, 213 A. D. 430; 

210 N. Y. S. 346. In this connection, it is interesting to note that the court in Sylvan Mortgage Company v. 

Stadler, 113 Misc 659; 185 N. Y. S. 293, states that it is impossible to lay down a general rule to determine what facts are necessary to plead or prove in order to show that one possessed with fear was deprived of the free exercise of his will, but, as already stated, there must

$125 

be allegations of such facts and circumstances as will warrant the inference.

In certain instances, the Rules of Civil Practice go to the extent of prescribing the particularity with which a cause must be pleaded. In an action for separation, for example, wherein the complaint, among other things, is based on cruelty, the plaintiff may not recite that the defendant treated the plaintiff in a cruel and inhuman manner, in that the defendant was abusive and neglected the plaintiff; for that would be a mere conclusion unsupported by facts and not in accordance with Rule 280 of the Rules of Civil Practice. 

Where a complaint omits any of the essential allegations or pleads such allegations generally or as conclusions without facts to support them, the complaint is insufficient. This means that the defendant need not serve an answer or take the usual steps in preparation for trial, but may move immediately to dismiss the complaint. Where this is done, and the motion is granted the action is at an end and judgment may be entered, terminating the action. But if the court is of the opinion that the defect can be cured by amending the complaint, the plaintiff will be given an oportunity to do so. 

To determine whether the complaint states a cause of action, one should read it carefully and ascertain, first of all, what the nature of the action is; that is, whether it is a matrimonial action; one for breach of contract; for fraud; specific performance, etc., then one may con sult Wait's New York Practice Volume 3 (4th Ed.), pages 66-487, wherein are discussed the essentials of the various causes of action. One may also consult Abbott's Forms of Pleading which contain copious footnotes in connection with the particular form of complaint. Reference should furthermore be made to the 

Civil Practice Act and the Rules of Civil Practice which may provide in some instances with respect to certain

$ 124 

allegations which are required to be pleaded or in what manner they are required to be set forth. 

If, after an examination as above outlined, the complaint is found to state a cause of action, there still remains thirteen further grounds for dismissal. See § 129. And where no defect is present which would be ground for dismissal, consideration should be given to the advisability of moving to strike out certain parts of the complaint or as the circumstances may require, to compel the plaintiff to correct the complaint. See § 130-134. If, however, the complaint is proper in every respect, there is nothing further to be done, but to serve the answer.

But where one finds that the complaint is subject to attack on the ground of insufficiency, the next step is to proceed to dismiss the complaint. 

§ 124. Notice of Motion to Dismiss Complaint Form. 

Assuming that the complaint lacks one or more of the essential allegations and is therefore insufficient on the face thereof, a motion may be made pursuant to Rule 106 of the Rules of Civil Practice to dismiss the complaint. 

A notice of motion only, is required. man, 118 Misc. 276; 194 N. Y. S. 191.

Velsor v. Free- 

No affidavit is necessary because the court must consider and pass upon the complaint alone. 

The notice of motion if returnable in New York

County, reads as follows:

$ 127 

SIR: 

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that upon the complaint herein the undersigned will move this Court, at Special Term Part III, thereof to be held at the County Courthouse, in the Borough of Manhattan, City of New York, on the 20th day of February, 1937, at ten o'clock in the forenoon of that day or as soon thereafter as counsel can be heard for judgment dismissing the complaint herein on the ground that it appears on the face thereof that it does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, and for such other, further and different relief as to the court. may seem just and proper in the premises. 

Dated: New York, February 15, 1936.

MARTIN ADAMS, Attorney for Defendant.
