§ 125. Serving Notice of Motion. 

A copy of the notice of motion is served upon the plaintiff's attorney within twenty days after the complaint is served. The attorneys may stipulate to extend

§ 127 

the time to answer, but this is not necessary, because the service of the notice of motion automatically extends the defendant's time to serve an answer until ten days after the service of an order determining the motion unless the court is of the opinion that the objections are frivolous. C.P.A., § 283. 

§ 126. Filing Notice of Motion. 

The original notice of motion with admission of service thereof is filed simultaneously with a copy of the complaint with the clerk of the part wherein it is made returnable, and he makes up his calendar of motions and includes it for the day mentioned therein. 

§ 127. The Brief or Memorandum of Law. 

The next step is to prepare a brief or memorandum of law in support of the motion which contains the following: 

1. Title of action. 

2. Statement of the nature of the motion. 

3. A summary of what the complaint contains. 

4. Points urged as grounds for dismissal, together with authorities to support the contentions. 

The function of the brief is two-fold. Firstly, it serves to point out to the court the defects in the complaint, and cites authorities in support thereof. Secondly, it gives the adverse attorney an opportunity to read the defendant's brief in advance of the hearing and draw his brief in opposition to meet the defendant's claim by showing why the complaint is proper and cite cases to support his contention. Then, upon the hearing, the judge need only examine the complaint, hear oral argument of counsel if they so wish, and refer to the briefs as a guide to the law and render his decision.

The brief is typewritten on regular brief paper. copy of the brief is served upon the plaintiff's attorney

128 129 

two days before the return day. The original brief, together with proof of service thereof, is presented to the judge upon the hearing. The plaintiff's attorney is not required to serve a copy of the opposing brief upon the defendant's attorney in advance of the hearing, although he may do so if he wishes. He, too, presents his brief to the judge upon the hearing and at the same time the defendant's attorney may request a copy and ask permission of the court to serve and file a reply brief in order to answer the arguments set up in the opposing brief. N. Y. Cty. Supreme Court, Spec. Term, Rule III. 

See pertinent rule of other courts. 

§ 128. Decision. 

The judge may decide the motion upon the hearing, but as a rule he reserves decision, and it subsequently appears in the Law Journal. He may decide it in one of three ways, as follows: 

1. Deny the motion. 

2. Grant the motion without qualification if he is convinced that the defect is such that it cannot be cured by the service of an amended complaint. 

3. Grant the motion but permit the plaintiff to serve an amended complaint within a specified period, usually ten days after service of a copy of the order with notice of entry upon the plaintff's attorney.

If the motion is denied, the defendant may serve his answer within ten days after the service of the order determining the motion. If the motion is granted without leave to serve an amended complaint, the defendant may treat the case at an end and proceed to draw a judgment and tax costs. If the plaintiff is permitted to serve an amended complaint, the defendant's attorney examines it for defects and proceeds in the same manner as he did with the original complaint. If the amended complaint is proper, he serves an answer to it, disregarding the original complaint entirely.

$ 129 

§ 129. Further Grounds for Dismissal. 

In addition to the foregoing, thirteen additional grounds for dismissal are available. Consideration has been given to one of the five grounds for which a dismissal may be granted where the defect appears on the face of the complaint. The procedure with respect to the remaining four is the same as already outlined. 

The five grounds are enumerated under Rule 106 of the 

Rules of Civil Practice as follows: 

1. That the court has not jurisdiction of the person of the defendant. (If a foreign corporation is not doing business in the state, or a non-resident person has no property within the jurisdiction of the court, neither party would be subject to the court's authority.) 

2. That the court has not jurisdiction of the subject of the action. (A suit brought in the New York Municipal 

Court to recover a sum in excess of one thousand dollars in other than dispossess proceedings, would not be within its jurisdiction, and therefore subject to dismissal.) 

3. That the plaintiff has not legal capacity to sue. (Where the complaint alleges that the plaintiff is an infant and it does not appear that a guardian ad litem has been appointed, the plaintiff would not be able to maintain the suit.) 

4. That there is another action pending between the same parties for the same cause. 

5. That the complaint does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. (Previously discussed.) 

Objection on some of the aforementioned grounds may be waived unless taken by motion. C.P.A., § 278, subd. 1.

Objection to the court's lack of jurisdiction, however, cannot be waived.

Rule 107 of the Rules of Civil Practice provides nine further grounds for dismissal where the defect is not apparent on the face of the complaint. The procedure

$ 131 

is the same as already outlined, except that an affidavit accompanies the notice of motion to explain the defect and may, therefore, be used upon the hearing. The rule includes the first four grounds enumerated under Rule 106, and in addition those of res adjudicata, statute of limitations, statute of frauds, general release, and other disability of defendant, such as infancy. 

§ 130. Motion to Strike Out-In General. 

Where ground does not exist for the dismissal of a complaint, nevertheless it may be such that it is either inadvisable or impossible to serve an answer thereto unless and until it is either corrected or matter stricken out. The statute provides that if any matter contained in a pleading be sham, frivolous, irrelevant, redundant, repetitious, unnecessary, impertinent or scandalous, or may tend to prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of the action, such matter may be stricken out. C.P.R. 

103. For example, in a libel action, it was held that the repetition in the final defense of the facts which appeared in each of the preceding defenses was redundant and prejudicial and should be stricken out. Burnham v. Hornday, 130 Misc. 207; 223 N. Y. S. 750.

A motion to strike out matter is made within twenty days after the service of the complaint unless the time to do so has been extended. C.P.R. 105. One proceeds by notice of motion accompanied by affidavit. 

§ 131. Notice of Motion-Form. 

Care should be taken to make reference in the notice of motion to the specific parts which are objectionable, otherwise the court may deny the application. Schwartz v. Marjolet, Inc., 214 A. D. 530; 212 N. Y. S. 464. The notice of motion reads as follows:

$131

-against-

§ 132. Affidavit-Form. 

An affidavit in support of the motion to strike, may read as follows: 

HAMILTON BOWERS, V. 

GREENLAND FURS CO., INC., Plaintiff,

Defendant. 

  

MARTIN ADAMS, being duly sworn, deposes and says: That he is the attorney for the defendant in the above entitled action. 

That your deponent is familiar with all the facts and circumstances hereinafter mentioned.

That this action was commenced by the service of the summons and complaint upon an officer of the defendant corporation on September 9th, 1936, and is brought to recover a judgment against the defendant "for the possession of the said merchandise, or if possession cannot be given to plaintiff to the sum of twenty-five hundred ($2500) dollars representing the reasonable value thereof together with the sum of twenty-five thousand ($25,000) dollars damages for the unlawful withholding of the said merchandise, 

It is submitted that this action, as indicated by the prayer for relief, is one to recover a chattel and for damages for the unlawful withholding thereof.

This motion is made to strike out certain paragraphs of the complaint upon the ground that the matter contained therein is immaterial and unnecessary and would tend to embarrass and delay a fair trial of this action, and otherwise prejudice the defendant. 

Paragraph "Third" of the complaint alleges, in substance, that the plaintiff was a manufacturing furrier and that certain

8 133 

customers of his delivered their garments to him for repair and storage. 

Paragraph "Fourth" of the complaint alleges, in substance, that the plaintiff rendered such services to such customers and acquired a lien on the garments delivered to him for that purpose. 

Paragraph "Tenth" of the complaint alleges, in substance, that thereafter one of plaintiff's customers demanded the return of her coat, and upon the failure of the plaintiff to produce and return the same to the said customer, plaintiff was charged with larceny of said coat and held in bail. 

Paragraph "Eleventh" of the complaint alleges, in substance, that by reason of the said charge of grand larceny made against the plaintiff, he has been compelled to expend large sums of money, to the damage of his business and reputation, in the sum of $25,000.

It must be evident that the foregoing allegations are not material or necessary in so far as an action to recover chattels or their value is concerned. It is likewise evident that the inclusion of these allegations in the complaint would tend to prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair trial of this action.

Defendant therefore respectfully requests that an order be made herein striking out said matter from the complaint, and directing the plaintiff to serve an amended complaint omitting said matter, pursuant to Rule 103 of the Rules of Civil Practice. 

MARTIN ADAMS. 

 25th day of September, 1936.

MARY BROWN, Notary Public-New York County. 

§ 133. Procedure After Preparation of Motion Papers. 

A copy of the notice of motion and affidavit is served upon the adverse attorney. The originals with proof of service thereof are filed with the Clerk of Special Term, Part I. A brief may or may not be prepared by either side for use by the court upon the hearing of the motion. 

If it is prepared, and it is advisable to do so, a copy of

$ 135 

the brief in support of the motion is not required to be served in advance of the hearing. The decision of the court may be to the effect that the pleading will be deemed amended, or it may require the plaintiff to serve an amended pleading omitting the objectionable matter. 

§ 134. Motion to Correct. 

Separately State and Number. It may sometimes happen that one who drafts a complaint may wholly ignore Rule 90 of the Rules of Civil Practice and thus omit to separately state each separate cause of action and also omit to divide each such separate cause into paragraphs consecutively numbered. He may be likely to go so far as to combine the causes of action and set out all the allegations in one paragraph. This would render it impossible for the defendant's attorney to prepare an answer thereto in proper form, denying each allegation of each separate cause of action as he is required to do. 

The defendant's attorney would, therefore, make application to compel the plaintiff to comply with Rule 90 of the Rules of Civil Practice. 

Where, for example, one sues for commissions and also sets out a cause of action based upon conspiracy and fraud on the part of the defendant to deprive the plaintiff of his commissions, the cause of action based upon conspiracy and fraud is entirely separate from the cause of action for commissions and should be separately stated. Popper v. Korn, 218 A. D. 513; 218 N. Y. S. 631.

The procedure is the same as outlined under a motion to strike.

Where Indefinite, Uncertain and Obscure. Provision is made whereby an amended pleading will be required to be served where matter contained therein be so indefinite, uncertain or obscure that the precise meaning or application thereof is not apparent, or if there be a misjoinder of parties plaintiff, or a defect of parties plaintiff or defendant. C.P.R. 102. The first of these defects

$ 135 

may require explanation. A complaint may be indefinite where, for example, there is more than one defendant and a cause of action is alleged against the defendant but it is not clear which defendant is intended; or where, as in a representative action by stockholders, there is an allegation that the defendants have profited "by the aforesaid and other similar stock transactions". In the latter instance, the court held it was indefinite and ordered the words "other similar stock transactions" to be stricken out. Deininger v. Ward, 218 A. D. 235, 218 N. Y. S. 337.

The procedure is the same as outlined under motions to strike out. The notice of motion and affidavit must be served within twenty days after the service of the complaint.

It should be noted that, unlike motions for the dismissal of a complaint, a motion to correct the complaint does not automatically extend the time to answer. 255 Fifth Avenue Corporation v. Freeman, 120 Misc. 472, 199 N. Y. S. 

519. Under such circumstances, one may stipulate to extend the time to answer, or proceed by order to show cause and provide therein for the extension. 

§ 135. Bill of Particulars. 

If the complaint is in all respects proper, the defendant's attorney may find that he desires particulars with respect to the claim set forth in the pleading. In such event, the next step is to ask for a bill of particulars.

The bill does not make the complaint good nor does it cure any of the defects. It serves merely to explain and make definite the allegations set forth in the pleading and thus limits the proof to be offered at the trial. Har mon v. Peats Co., 243 N. Y. 473. See Chapter XII for procedure.

§ 136. Defined. 

The answer is what the name itself implies. It is the defendant's retort to the plaintiff's claim as set forth in the complaint, thus serving to create an issue which is subsequently decided by a court with or without a jury. 

It is the only pleading served on behalf of the defendant. 

C.P.A., § 260. 

137

§ 138 

§ 137. What to Contain. 

The answer bears the same title as the complaint. The statute provides that the answer of the defendant must contain the following: (C.P.A., § 261) 

1. A general or specific denial of each material allegation of the complaint controverted by the defendant, or of any knowledge thereof sufficient to form a belief. 

2. A statement of any new matter constituting a defense or counterclaim.

In addition, the answer contains a demand for judgment dismissing the complaint. And where the defendant deems himself entitled to an affirmative judgment by reason of a counterclaim interposed by him, he must demand the judgment in his answer. C.P.A., § 262. This pleading also contains the subscription of the defendant's attorney. 

§ 138. Preparation of Answer-How to Plead. 

Before any attempt is made to draw the answer, the defendant and his attorney carefully examine each of the allegations of the complaint. Starting with the first allegation, if the client finds that it is not true, he will ask his attorney to deny it in the answer. The attorney, for his own convenience, notes in the margin of the first allegation the word "deny". With respect to the allegations, the defendant may 

1. Deny without qualification. 

2. Deny upon information and belief where his knowledge is not first-hand. 

3. Deny that he has knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief. For example, if the plaintiff alleges that it is a domestic corporation, the defendant may deny he has any knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief that it is a corporation because he will not, as a rule, know that the defendant has been duly incorporated, and he can therefore neither deny nor admit its existence.

$ 139 

THE ANSWER. 

4. Admit part and deny the balance.

The attorney makes the pertinent notation in accordance with the above and continues with his client to examine each allegation until they have disposed of all the allegations. See Marked Pleadings, § 151. 

§ 139. Defenses. 

After the allegations of the complaint have been disposed of, the defendant's attorney may consider the question of raising the following possible defenses:

Payment. The plaintiff may claim that the defendant owes him money. The defendant's answer is that he has paid the claim and so alleges. 

Statute of Limitations. Although a plaintiff may be entitled to sue for a debt owed him, nevertheless if he did not sue within a prescribed period of time, which in the particular instance is six years, he is barred from asserting his claim.

Statute of Frauds. If the plaintiff bases his claim upon an oral contract which should have been in writing, the defendant may set up the statute of frauds as a bar to the maintenance of the action. 

Accord and Satisfaction. Where there is a dispute as to the amount actually due and owing and the defendant settles for a sum which the plaintiff accepts, the plaintiff is bound thereby and cannot subsequently sue for the full amount.

General Release. Where a claim is settled, it is common practice to ask for and receive a general release, which is to the effect that in consideration of the payment of a certain sum, the plaintiff releases the defendant from any and all claims which he had from the beginning of the world to the date of the release. And, should the plaintiff at a subsequent date bring suit on the claim, the execution of the release may be set up as a bar. 

The foregoing defenses are complete defenses and so labelled in the answer. But where matter tends only to

8 142 

mitigate or reduce damages, it constitutes a partial defense and must be expressly stated to be a partial defense to the entire complaint or to one or more separate causes of action therein set forth. C.P.A., § 262. See Wait's 

N. Y. Practice, Vol. 3 [4th Ed.], 497, for a discussion of other defenses. 

§ 140. Counterclaim. 

The next consideration is the setting up of a possible counterclaim. The defendant may, for example, be able to show that he in turn has a claim against the plaintiff which he is entitled to set up as an independent action. 

C.P.A., § 262. In such a situation he is not required to bring a separate action, unless the court later determines that the interests of justice require it, but may set it up as a counterclaim to the end that the claims of both parties may be determined in one suit. And under the recently amended statute which was enacted to liberalize procedure and expedite litigation, a counterclaim may be any cause of action in favor of the defendants or some of them against the plaintiff or some of them, a person whom a plaintiff represents or a plaintiff and another person or persons alleged to be liable. C.P.A., § 266. 

§ 141. Set-off. 

Finally, it may be that although the defendant is in fact indebted to the plaintiff, the latter in turn owes the former money which may be alleged as a set-off. 

§ 142. General Denial-Form. 

When the attorney has carefully planned the defendant's answer, the next step is to draw it in proper form. 

The one provided herein is used in all courts and is known as a general denial; that is, it denies that which is alleged in the complaint and contains no defenses or counterclaims thus:

141 

THE ANSWER. 

The defendant above named, by his attorney, Martin Adams, answering the plaintiff's complaint herein: 

1. Denies each and every allegation contained in paragraphs marked or numbered "Second", "Third", "Fourth", "Fifth" and "Sixth" in said complaint contained.

Wherefore defendant demands judgment dismissing the plaintiff's complaint herein, together with the costs and disbursements of this action.

MARTIN ADAMS, 

Attorney for Defendant.

Office & Post Office Address, 

112 Broadway,

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York.

§ 145. Verification. 

Where the complaint is verified, the answer must be verified except in the following instances: 

1. General answer of an infant by his guardian ad litem. C.P.A., § 248. 

2. Except where otherwise specially prescribed by law, where the defendant would be privileged from testifying as a witness concerning an allegation or denial contained in the pleading. C.P.A., § 248. 

3. Where the answer contains a counterclaim which charges adultery, it must be verified in respect of such counterclaim where the complaint is verified. C.P.A., 

§ 1148. 

4. Where defendant is charged with criminal libel.

The answer must be verified in an action against a corporation to recover damages for the non-payment of a promissory note, or other evidence of debt for the absolute payment of money. C.P.A., § 252.

Where the complaint, however, is not verified, and the answer sets up a counterclaim in addition to a defense, the verification may be made to refer exclusively to the counterclaim, and the provisions of statute or rules relating to the construction of the allegations, their effect, the person by whom the verification is made and the form of verification apply to the counterclaim as if it were a separate pleading. C.P.A., § 249. 

A defense which does not involve the merits of the action must be verified. C.P.A., § 251.

$ 147 

THE ANSWER. 

§ 146. Service of Answer. 

In Supreme Court actions, within twenty days after the service of the complaint, unless the time to answer has been extended by consent or order of the court, a copy of the answer is served upon the plaintiff's attorney. 

C.P.A., § 263. The original with proof of service is retained pending the trial. In City Court actions, the answer must be served within six days after the service of the complaint, N. Y. City Ct. Act, § 50; while in the 

Municipal Court, the period is five days. N. Y. Mun. Ct. 

Code, § 78, subd. 2. 

§ 147. Extending Time to Answer or Move-Form of Stipulation. 

If the defendant's attorney finds that he cannot prepare and serve an answer within the required period of time, he may ask the plaintiff's attorney for more time.

If the latter consents, a stipulation is prepared by the defendant's attorney and signed by the plaintiff's attorney. An extension of time to answer does not include the right to make a motion with respect to the complaint, so that if it is desired to move at a later time, provision therefor should be made in the same stipulation. 

Further extensions may be granted from time to time in the same manner.

If the plaintiff's attorney refuses to consent to an extension, the defendant may apply to the court ex parte therefor, because the defendant is entitled to the first extension, as of course, unless the action is based upon a promissory note, or other written evidence of debt for the unconditional payment of money. C.P.R. 86; C.P.A., $ 98. 

Applications for further extensions require two days' notice to the adverse attorney. C.P.R. 87. The usual notice of motion or order to show cause accompanied by an affidavit of merits is necessary. C.P.R. 88. Such affidavit must allege facts showing that the defendant has a

$ 148 

good and meritorious defense and intends in good faith to defend the action.

The following is a form of stipulation extending the defendant's time to answer:

It is hereby stipulated, consented and agreed that the time. for the defendant to serve his answer or otherwise move with respect to the complaint herein be and the same hereby is extended to and including the 15th day of February, 1937. 

Dated: New York, February 2, 1937. 

MILTON BARTLETT, 

§ 148. Service of Answer Containing Counterclaim to Bring in Additional Party. 

Where a defendant sets up any counterclaim which raises questions between himself and the plaintiff along with any other person, he may serve the answer containing the counterclaim upon the third person, and if the latter is not already a party, the service of the answer is just as effective in making such person a party as if he had been served with a summons. C.P.A., § 271. His name is added to those already appearing in the caption. 

Within twenty days after the service of the answer, the co-defendant may serve his reply thereto. The evident purpose of this section was to cover a case where a defendant, who is sued upon a several liability, has, in turn, a counterclaim against the plaintiff and another person who are jointly indebted to him on such counterclaim.

$ 

THE ANSWER. 

149 

Youngman v. New York Indemnity Co., 120 Misc. 687, 

199 N. Y. S. 420.

Where the rights of two or more defendants as between themselves are involved, a defendant who requires a determination of such rights must demand it in his answer and at least twenty days before the trial serve a copy upon the attorney for each of the defendants to be affected thereby, or upon such defendants personally who have not duly appeared therein by attorney. $264. 

§ 149. Filing Answer. 

C.P.A.,

The answer is not required to be filed in actions pending in the Supreme Court and the New York City Court unless a demand to do so has been served. C.P.A., § 100. 

In the Municipal Court, however, the answer must be filed within three days after the service of the summons (N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 22, subd. 3); unless additional time has been obtained, in which case the summons is filed at such subsequent date together with the original stipulation extending the time to answer, if any. 

§ 150. Amended and Supplemental Answer. 

The same rules apply to the service of amended and supplemental answers as to the service of amended and supplemental complaints. C.P.A., §§ 244, 245; see §§ 114, 115. The practice in the Municipal Court, how ever, differs somewhat in that the defendant who desires to amend his answer may declare his intention so to do by the service of a notice to that effect, thus: (N. Y. Mun. 

Ct. Code, § 93, subd. 2).

§ 151. How to Examine an Answer-Marked Pleadings. 

As soon as the plaintiff's attorney receives an answer to the complaint, he should examine it to see if it contains a counterclaim. If it does, a diary entry should be made twenty days hence, exclusive of the day of service as the last day to serve a reply thereto in Supreme Court actions, C.P.A., § 273; six days in City Court actions, N. Y.

City Ct. Act, § 50. The failure to serve a reply has the same effect as the failure to serve an answer to the complaint, the defendant being in the position to enter judgment upon the counterclaim by default. In New York

151 

THE ANSWER. 

Municipal Court actions, however, it is not necessary to serve a reply. N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 87. This is also true in Albany City Court actions. Albany City Ct. Act, 

§ 160. See other local court acts. A diary entry ten days hence should also be made for the purpose of moving to strike out defenses or to dismiss the counterclaim. 

C.P.R. 109, 110.

The next step is to examine the answer together with the complaint. In the margin of the complaint, beside each allegation, a notation is made of the manner in which the particular allegation is disposed of in the answer thus: 

Denies knowledge or information sufficient to form belief. 

Second: That at all the times hereinafter mentioned the defendant was a corporation duly organized and existing under and by virtue of the laws of the State of New York. 

This is done on a copy of the complaint, which becomes known as a "marked pleading". When pleadings are submitted to the court upon the trial they must be marked in this manner. This is very helpful, especially where the complaint is lengthy in that it enables the court, as well as the attorney, to know what the issues are by reading the complaint alone. The answer may be marked in similar manner where a reply is served. 

After this is completed the next consideration is to determine which of the following motions should be made: 

§ 152. Motions After Joinder of Issue. 

To strike out all or part of the answer: 

1. Strike defenses. 

2. Dismiss counterclaim. 

3. Strike out sham answer pursuant to Rule 104. 

4. Motion for judgment on pleadings to strike answer. 

5. Motion for summary judgment to strike answer.

$ 154 

To correct answer: 

1. Separately state and number defenses. 

2. Make matter more definite and certain. 

3. Strike out sham and frivolous matter.

Additional motions: 

1. Motion for bill of particulars of defenses or coun terclaim. 

2. Motion for examination before trial. 

3. Motion for judgment on pleadings to dismiss complaint. 

§ 153. Striking Out Defenses-In General. 

Where the answer contains defenses, the question to be determined is whether they are sufficient in law. For example, in a libel action based upon an item which appeared in a newspaper, the defendant may interpose a defense of privilege on the ground that the news item is a fair and true report of a judicial, legislative or other public and official proceeding. C.P.A., § 337. But if the plaintiff can show that the report was based on an inquiry before the Attorney General, which was not judicial, legislative or public, but on the contrary was both secret and non-judicial, the plea of privilege is unavailing, and the plaintiff is entitled to have the defense dismissed as insufficient in law. C.P.R. 109, subd. 6; 

Levey v. N. Y. Evening Journal, 237 A. D. 255, 260 N.

Y. S. 654. 

For a discussion of sufficient and insufficient defenses, see footnotes in connection with the particular defense in Abbott's Forms of Pleading, Volume 3 (3rd Ed.), pages 2402-2823. 

§ 154. Procedure to Strike Defenses-Form of Notice of Motion. 

The procedure on a motion to strike out a defense is similar to that previously discussed under a motion

The notice of motion only is prepared. and served within ten days after the service of the answer. A copy thereof is served upon the defendant's attorney. The original with proof of service is filed with the Clerk of Special Term, Part III. Two days before the return day, a copy of the brief in support of the motion is served upon the defendant's attorney and the original with proof of service thereof is submitted upon the hearing. N. § 155. Dismissing Counterclaims. 

If the answer contains a counterclaim, it is helpful to remember that it may be treated in practically the same manner as if it were a complaint. It may be dismissed for defects appearing on its face on four grounds, which are analogous to the last four grounds of Rule 106, considered under the dismissal of the complaint, and on the further ground that the counterclaim is not one which may be properly interposed in the action. 

C.P.R. 109. The procedure is the same as outlined under a motion to dismiss the complaint pursuant to Rule 106. No affidavits are admissible. The motion must be made within ten days after the service of the answer. 

A counterclaim may also be dismissed for defects not appearing on its face on five grounds analogous to five of the nine grounds considered under Rule 107 for the dismissal of the complaint. C.P.R. 110. The procedure is the same as outlined under Rule 107. Affidavits are admissible.

$155 

THE ANSWER. 

§ 156. Striking Out Sham Answer. 

If the entire answer is sought to be stricken out on the ground that it is sham or frivolous, the statute provides for such relief pursuant to Rule 104 of the Rules of Civil Practice. The motion, however, must be brought within twenty days after the service of the answer.

No affidavits may be submitted upon the hearing. Levan v. American Safety Table Co., 222 A. D. 110, 225 N. Y. S. 

583. This rule is seldom used perhaps because it limits the time within which to make the application; whereas a motion for summary judgment pursuant to Rule 113, may be made at any time before trial and the same relief is available thereunder. 

§ 157. Judgment on Pleadings. 

If the parties have not moved within the time limited therefor, to dismiss the complaint or a counterclaim contained in the answer, or to strike out the answer or a defense contained therein pursuant to the pertinent rule, application may be made at any time before trial pursuant to Rule 112 for similar relief.

The procedure on such a motion is discussed under 

Chapter XV. 

§ 158. Summary Judgment. 

Although this motion is discussed under Chapter XIV, it is well to note that both bench and bar widely acclaim the usefulness of this rule. It was formerly limited to cases wherein the damages were liquidated, but has been liberalized to include cases wherein damages are unliquidated with the result that more litigants can avail themselves of a rule, the purpose of which is to prevent the delay of judgment by a denial, good on its face, but without actual support in fact.

§ 160 

§ 159. Motions to Correct Answer. 

The plaintiff's attorney may proceed to have the answer corrected in the same manner as outlined with respect to the complaint; that is, move under Rule 90 to separately state and number each defense and counterclaim; move under Rule 102 to make more definite and certain the particular parts of the answer which require it; and finally to move under Rule 103, to strike out such parts as may be sham, frivolous, irrelevant or redundant or may tend to prejudice or delay the fair trial of the action. A motion under Rule 90 should, of course, be made before the reply is served. Motions under Rule 102 or 103 are made within twenty days after the service of the answer. C.P.R. 105. 

§ 160. Additional Motions. 

If the answer is found to be in proper form, the plaintiff's attorney may commence preparation for trial by securing a bill of particulars of the defenses and counterclaims contained in the answer. The subject is more fully discussed in Chapter XII. 

The plaintiff's attorney may also proceed with a motion to examine the defendant before trial with respect to the allegations of the complaint. This motion is more frequently made after joinder of issue, but there are instances where it may be made before action commenced and also after the service of the summons but before the complaint is prepared. The motion is discussed more fully under Chapter XIII.

§ 161. When to Serve. 

If the answer contains a counterclaim and it is so labelled, a further pleading on the part of the plaintiff is required. This is known as a reply and must be served within twenty days after the service of the answer, otherwise the defendant is in a position to take judgment thereon by default. C.P.A., § 273. The reply is served within six days in New York City Court actions. 

N. Y. City Ct. Act, § 50. The reason for this is that each material allegation of new matter in the answer, not controverted by the reply where a reply is required, must be taken as true. C.P.A., § 243. One need not, however, serve a reply in a New York Municipal Court action unless compelled to do so by the court. N. Y. Municipal 

Ct. Code, § 87. This is also true in Albany City Court actions. Albany City Ct. Act, § 160. See other local court acts. 

162. What to Contain. 

The statute provides that the reply must contain a general or specific denial of each material allegation of 157

8 164 

the counterclaim controverted by the plaintiff, or of any knowledge or information thereof sufficient to form a belief; and it may set forth new matter not inconsistent with the complaint constituting a defense to the counterclaim. It may contain two or more distinct avoidances of the same defense or counterclaim. C.P.A., § 272. 

§ 163. Preparation of Reply. 

Following the same procedure as outlined under Preparation of Answer, the plaintiff's attorney consults with his client and together they examine the counterclaim contained in the answer noting in the margin of each allegation how it is to be disposed of. See § 151. 

§ 164. The Reply-Form. 

The reply is similar to the answer in form, thus:

The plaintiff above named, by his attorney, Milton Bartlett, for his reply to the counterclaim contained in the defendant's answer herein 1. Denies each and every allegation contained in paragraphs marked or numbered "3", "4”, “5”, “6", "7", and "8" in the said answer contained.

Wherefore plaintiff demands judgment dismissing the counterclaim herein, together with costs.

Office & Post Office Address, 

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York.

THE REPLY. 

§ 165. Verification. 

If the answer is verified, the reply must be verified, except as otherwise specially prescribed by statute. 

The verification may be omitted in a case where it is not otherwise specially prescribed by law, where the party pleading would be privileged from testifying as a witness concerning an allegation or denial contained in a pleading. C.P.A., § 248. 

§ 166. Filing Reply. 

As in the case of other pleadings, it is not necessary to file the reply unless compelled to do so by the service of a demand therefor by the adverse attorney. C.P.A., 

§ 100. 

§ 167. Compelling Reply-In General. 

As already stated, unless an answer contains a counterclaim and so labelled, it is not necessary to serve a reply. 

But where an answer contains new matter constituting a defense by way of avoidance, the defendant may compel the plaintiff to serve a reply, in order to narrow the issues and prevent surprise at the trial. In other words, the defendant will be better prepared for trial if he knows in advance what the plaintiff's answer to his charge will be. In a case, for example, where the defense sets up a general release, the courts will compel a reply because they hold that the defendant should be given an opportunity before trial to know what the plaintiff intends to urge as the ground for the invalidity of the release; furthermore, that justice will be promoted by having the issue as to the validity and sufficiency of the release clearly defined. Writting v. N. Y. and Long Island Traction Co., 91 Misc. 231, 153 N. Y. S. 1081. 

One proceeds by notice of motion or order to show cause and supporting affidavits.

8 168

§ 170. Procedure After Preparation of Motion Papers. 

A copy of the motion papers is served on the adverse attorney. The original with proof of service thereof is filed with the Clerk of Special Term, Part I. Although it is not necessary to do so, the defendant's attorney may prepare a memorandum of law citing, if possible, authorities to show that the matter pleaded is new matter which warrants the court in compelling the plaintiff to serve a reply thereto. The memorandum is filed with the court upon the hearing of the motion. 

The statute authorizes the court in its discretion to compel a reply where new matter is set up as a defense by way of avoidance and this discretion, as a general rule, is freely exercised if the court can see that the matter if true is of such character that it may avoid surprise and shorten the trial. Dittenfass v. Horsley, 171 A. D. 507 at page 508; 157 N. Y. S. 632. If the motion is granted, the next step is to serve upon the adverse attorney a copy of the order entered thereon with notice of entry and await the service of the reply. See Chapter 

VI on Motions and Orders. 

§ 171. Procedure Upon Receipt of a Reply. 

Upon receipt of the reply, one makes a diary entry ten days hence, exclusive of the day of service as the last day to make a motion to strike out the reply or a separate defense therein contained on the ground that it is insufficient in law on the face thereof. C.P.R. 111. 

If any other kind of motion is to be made, the particular diary entry should be noted. 

§ 172. Examining the Reply. 

One proceeds to examine the reply in the same manner as already outlined under the examination of the answer. 

The answer is so marked as to indicate in the margin how each allegation of new matter set up in the defense or counterclaim is disposed of by the reply.

$ 172 

The next step is to determine if the reply or defenses therein set forth are insufficient in law. If they are, the procedure is the same as that outlined under a motion to strike out the defense contained in the answer. § 154156; C.P.R. 111. The reply may also be stricken pursuant to Rule 104, if it is sham or frivolous. Consideration should be given to the motions pursuant to Rules 

90, 102 and 103 as outlined under motions to correct the answer.

§ 173. Who May Ask for a Bill. 

Because, as has been stated, only ultimate facts are required to be stated in a pleading, it often becomes necessary to secure details with respect to these facts, which although they have no place in a pleading, nevertheless are required for a better understanding of the adverse party's claim. And to these details, each party, within certain limits, is entitled. The plaintiff may demand of the defendant particulars concerning defenses and counterclaims interposed in the answer. The 165

$ 175 

defendant, in turn, may demand from the plaintiff particulars concerning the allegations of the complaint as well as the defenses in the reply. C.P.R. 115, 116. 

§ 174. When to Ask for a Bill. 

One may apply for a bill at any time before trial but it is advisable to apply for it sometime after issue is joined for the reason that if one delays until just before the trial, the court may refuse to grant the request on the ground of laches. 

§ 175. Function of Bill. 

The courts have held that a bill is intended to define the issues, limit the proof, to make certain that which is uncertain, and to apprise the defendant of what he is required to meet. Bjork v. Post & McCord, 125 A. D. 

813; 110 N. Y. S. 206. In a case, for example, wherein it was alleged the conversion by defendants of a certificate of stock, the property of the plaintiff, and the refusal of the defendants to return the same upon demand, the court held that the defendants were entitled to be informed in advance of the trial as to what were the particular acts on their part, or upon the part of any other person or persons which plaintiff claimed constituted a conversion, and if committed by any person other than the defendants, when and where committed, and what were the relations which plaintiff claimed existed between such person or persons and the defendants. 

Schirmer v. Kline, 180 A. D. 812, 168 N. Y. S. 67. This does not mean that a party is at liberty to pry into the adverse party's case. Under no circumstances will a party be compelled to divulge its evidence in advance of the trial. For example, a party is not entitled to the address of any of the witnesses of the adverse party. 

Steinleger v. Frankel, 117 Misc. 693, 192 N. Y. S. 74.

Very often, the adverse party will oppose the granting of a bill claiming that the party requesting the bill

$167 

already has full knowledge of the particulars which he seeks. The court's attitude, however, is that despite what the party knows, he is, nevertheless entitled to know what the adverse party claims the facts to be. 

Furthermore, the courts say that a party cannot successfully urge that the adverse party has sufficient knowledge to guess at a particular occurrence but the latter is entitled to know, and not be relegated to conjecture concerning what is actually claimed by the plaintiff in that regard. Adams v. Dodge, 114 Misc. 565, 187 N. Y. S. 688. 

§ 176. Procedure Generally. 

To obtain a bill, two methods are available. A party may serve a demand therefore or proceed by notice of motion. To save time, however, a party may apply by notice of motion in the first instance so that the court may upon the hearing thereof immediately determine the propriety of the items to which objection is made. 

Where, however, a party proceeds by service of a demand, the adverse party is permitted five days after the service thereof to move to modify it in respect to the items that are claimed to be improper, and an additional five days is required by the service of the notice of motion. C.P.R. 115. 

§ 177. Procedure by Demand-Form. 

To prepare a demand for a bill of particulars, the attorney examines each allegation of the complaint or of a defense, or counterclaim, as the case may be, and determines what particulars he will want. Where, for example, suit is brought to recover damages for breach of a contract and the complaint alleges that there was an agreement by the defendant to employ the plaintiff, the defendant's attorney will want to know whether the agreement of employment was oral or in writing; if in writing, he will ask that an exact copy be annexed to

§ 177 

the bill; if oral, he will ask that the substance thereof be stated, but he may not ask for the conversation which took place on the occasion of entering into the oral agreement; for that would be evidence. He is also entitled to know the time when and the place where the contract was entered into. And where either of the parties is a corporation or partnership, he may ask the name of the person who acted on behalf of such corporation or partnership. If an allegation sets forth the fact that certain professional services were rendered, he is entitled to ask for and receive an itemized statement of such services. If he desires certain information but questions his right to it, he should, of course, first search the authorities to find if he is entitled thereto. 

A copy of the demand is served upon the adverse attorney and the original is retained with proof of service.

Each item of the demand is separately listed and numbered in the following manner:

ARNOLD BROWN, Plaintiff, -against- 

WILLIAM BERGER, Defendant. 

SIR: 

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that pursuant to Rule 115 of the Rules of 

Civil Practice, you are hereby required to serve upon the attorney for the defendant a verified bill of particulars as follows: 

1. State the time when and the place where the alleged agreement referred to in paragraph marked "Second" of the complaint was entered into. 

2. State whether the alleged agreement was oral or in writing; if oral, state the terms thereof; if in writing, annex a copy thereof.

$ 169 

3. Set forth an itemized statement of the services alleged to have been rendered by the plaintiff for the defendant as referred to in paragraph marked "Third" of the complaint. 

4. State the names of all persons who were present at the time the alleged agreement was entered into. noted here for purpose of motion to vacate.) 

Dated: New York, February 5, 1937. 

(Improper item 

Yours, etc.,

To: 

MARTIN ADAMS, 

Attorney for Defendant.

Office & Post Office Address, 

112 Broadway,

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. 

§ 178. Procedure Upon Receipt of Demand. 

Upon receipt of a copy of the demand, the adverse attorney proceeds to examine each item thereof, to determine if it is proper. If he finds that some of the items are not proper, he may communicate with the attorney and advise the latter that he will furnish a bill with respect to certain of the items but disputes the right to particulars with respect to the remaining items. 

If the attorney who served the demand still believes that the disputed items are proper, he may cite authorities to support his contention. In this way, it is possible for the attorneys to agree among themselves upon the items. But where they cannot so agree, the attorney upon whom the demand was served, may move to vacate or modify it and thus cast upon the court the burden of determining which of the items are proper.

§ 180 

§ 179. Time to Move to Vacate or Modify Demand and Procedure in General. 

Rule 115 of the Rules of Civil Practice as recently amended, provides that where a party upon whom the demand is served is unwilling to furnish the particulars demanded, in whole or in part, he may move to vacate or modify such notice by serving his motion papers within five days after the receipt thereof. If no motion is made, a bill of particulars is required to be served within ten days after the demand therefor is served. 

The motion papers are served and filed and the motion comes on for hearing in the usual manner. Upon the determination of the motion, a copy of the order entered thereon is served with notice of entry and a bill of particulars is furnished in compliance therewith. 

§ 180. Notice of Motion to Modify Demand—Form. 

A notice of motion to modify the demand by striking out an improper item, may read as follows:

§ 184. Serving and Filing Motion Papers. 

A copy of the motion papers is served on the adverse attorney. The original papers with proof of service are filed with the Clerk of Special Term, Part I. 

§ 185. Hearing. 

When the motion is called on the return day, a copy of the pleadings is delivered to the clerk and the motion is marked "submitted". Because a great deal of time would be required to hear argument on both sides for each item, the courts refuse to hear oral argument. The judge merely reads the papers. Under the circumstances, it is advisable to submit a brief citing authorities showing why the moving party is entitled to the items. The adverse party may submit either an opposing affidavit together with a brief citing authorities to prove that the moving party is not entitled to the particular items to which objection is made, or the brief alone. If there is a possibility of an appeal, it is more advisable to serve an affidavit in addition to the brief, to the end that the affidavit may be made part of the record. 

§ 186. Decision and Service of Order Entered Thereon. 

In due time, the decision appears in the Law Journal, and the order entered thereon will direct which items are allowed and which are not. A copy of the order with notice of entry is served on the adverse attorney and another copy with proof of service is retained for future use. Upon the expiration of the time mentioned in the order, the bill must be served unless the parties consent by stipulation to extend the time. 

§ 187. Time to Serve Bill. 

The bill of particulars must be served within ten days after the demand therefore unless the court or judge shall otherwise direct. C.P.R. 115.

100. C.P.R. 117. If the party is without knowledge with respect to any of the particulars required, the order entered on the motion provides, as a rule, that he may state such lack of knowledge under oath in lieu thereof. 12

§ 190. Procedure Upon Failure to Serve Bill. 

In the event that a party fails to serve a bill of particulars, or a copy of the items of an account, pursuant to the demand or order modifying the demand, or other order for a bill of particulars, the adverse attorney may move for an order to preclude such party from giving evidence at the trial of the items of which particulars have not been furnished. C.P.R. 115, subd. c.

§ 193. Procedure Upon Receipt of Defective Bill. 

If a bill of particulars served pursuant to the demand or order is regarded as defective or insufficient, by the party upon whom it is served, the latter may make an application upon notice for an order of preclusion as already described or for an order directing the service of a further bill. C.P.R. 115, subd. d.

In the absence of special circumstances, the motion papers are served ten days after the receipt of the defective bill.

$ 181 

§ 194. Decision Upon Application to Preclude. 

Rule 115, subd. e of the Rules of Civil Practice has been twice amended recently and is now to the effect that the preclusion order may provide that the same be effective unless a proper bill is served within a specified time thereafter. 

§ 195. Municipal Court Practice. 

In Municipal Court actions, one proceeds, as a rule, by the service of a demand rather than by a notice of motion. The defendant may serve and file the demand with the answer and it is convenient to do so especially when the printed forms which combine the answer and the demand are used. See § 144.

Section 78, subd. 7 of the New York City Municipal 

Court Code as recently amended, however, provides that the procedure for obtaining a copy of the items of an account, or a bill of particulars, shall be that prescribed in the civil practice act and rules adopted pursuant thereto except that the periods of time prescribed by any rule of civil practice relating thereto, may be changed by rule of the court. The original bill of particulars, or items of an account, shall be filed with the clerk within the same time that service of a copy thereof must be made on the adverse party or his attorney.

§ 196. Who May Ask for Examination Before Trial and 

Nature Thereof.

Where the party has the burden of proof, he may in aid of such proof and before the trial, obtain from the adverse party whatever information is material and necessary. In other words, where the plaintiff sets up the various allegations which comprise the complaint, he must prove all those allegations in order to succeed. upon the trial. And with respect to those allegations, he may examine the defendant. This of course, does not apply to the allegations which have been admitted by the defendant in the answer. For example, where the complaint states a cause of action for goods sold and delivered and alleges that between January 1, 1934 and 

January 1, 1936, the defendant purchased certain merchandise and the answer is a general denial, the burden is upon the plaintiff to prove that the defendant did purchase the merchandise as alleged. He may, among other things, examine thus: 

Q. Do you know the plaintiff? 

A. Yes. 

Q. Did you, on or about and between January 1, 1934, and January 1, 1936, have any business dealings with the plaintiff ? 

A. Yes. 

Q. And what was the nature of those dealings?

A. I bought some laces from him. 

Q. I show you a series of invoices and ask you whether they represent the merchandise purchased by you.

If the defendant identifies all of the invoices, the trial will be a comparatively simple matter, for the plaintiff will merely have to produce the invoices. But if the defendant admits the purchase of merchandise described in only part of the invoices, then with respect to the

§ 196 

balance, the plaintiff, when preparing for trial, will realize that he will have to bring along witnesses or such other proof as he may have, to show that the goods were ordered; that they were shipped and delivered to the defendant and accepted and retained by him. The plaintiff is thus better prepared for the trial; for he has by the examination, secured the defendant's admission as to part of the cause of action and as to the balance, he knows how much proof he will be required to furnish. The plaintiff may also examine as to the defenses set up by him in the reply. Although one may examine as to those matters of which he has the affirmative, nevertheless, the test is rather as to whether the matter is material and necessary in the prosecution or defense of the action. New York City Car Advertising 

Co. v. Regensburg & Sons, Inc., 205 A.D. 705, 200 N. Y. S. 

152; Combes v. Maas, 209 A.D. 330, 204 N. Y. S. 440. In other words, the testimony sought to be adduced must be material and necessary for the use of the party seeking to elicit it and to establish some fact which he must affirmatively prove. Oakes v. Star Co., 119 A.D. 358, 104 N. Y. S. 244.

The defendant, in turn, and in like manner may examine the plaintiff concerning the defenses and counterclaims set up in the answer and which he has the burden of establishing. But he must remember that he may not set up matter as a defense which may otherwise be proved under a general denial; for an examination will not be permitted. For example, where a plaintiff sues upon a contract and alleges due performance, the defendant cannot, by setting up non-performance as a defense, examine the plaintiff in order to establish non-performance because it is not a defense and furthermore proof of non-performance is admissable under a general denial. 

Kessler v. North River Co., 169 A.D. 814, 155 N. Y. S. 

799. Such being the case, matter concerning non-per-

$ 185 

1 formance is neither material nor necessary to the defendant's case but on the contrary, it is matter which tends to disprove the plaintiff's case. The courts, under such circumstances, hold that a party, plaintiff or defendant, may examine his adversary before trial only for the purpose of proving facts necessary to the examining party's affirmative case or defense, but not for the purpose of disproving facts which the adversary must affirmatively prove in order to succeed. 

§ 197. When Examination May be Had. 

After Issue Joined. Applications for an examination before trial are perhaps more frequently made to obtain facts material and necessary in the prosecution or defense of the action as already described than for any other reason. Such applications are made after issuejoined because the court cannot determine whether the testimony sought is material and necessary until after the answer has been served. Kardonsky v. Tozzi, 217 

A.D. 753, 216 N. Y. S. 418. Before taking up the question of procedure to obtain the examination, it may be interesting to note on what other occasions an examination may be sought. 

After Commencement of Action to Frame Complaint.. 

Where the plaintiff finds that he does not have sufficient information to enable him to draw a complaint, he is permitted by statute to obtain such information. But unlike the previous situation, he cannot serve a demand therefor. He must apply for an order on notice and present proof by affidavit that he has a meritorious cause of action, for until that is shown, it cannot be determined that the testimony is material for the plaintiff to frame. 

his complaint. Ashton v. Baker Manufacturing Corpora tion, 206 A. D. 343; 201 N. Y. S. 259; C.P.A., § 295; C.P.R. 

122. The prospective defendant may, of course, show by his affidavit in opposition to the motion, that the plaintiff is not entitled to the relief sought. This he may proceed

8 197 

to do by reading the affidavit in support of the motion carefully to see what facts the plaintiff already has. He will then determine what the essentials of such a complaint should be. See § 123. Very often he will find that the plaintiff actually has sufficient facts to set forth the essential allegations but requires information to definitely state the amount of damages. Under such circumstances, the defendant may point out that the motion should be denied, because the plaintiff may state his general damages at an amount sufficient to cover the estimated loss; and furthermore, that the purpose of an examination to frame a complaint is not to seek additional facts of which he is ignorant but rather evidence in support of facts which are claimed to enable him to maintain his suit. Newman v. Potter, 201 A. D. 335; 194 

N. Y. S. 207; Matter of La Grave, 132 A. D. 108; 116 

N. Y. S. 465.

Before Commencement of Action to Perpetuate Testi mony. Testimony which is material to an expected party in the prosecution or defense of an action about to be brought in a court of record may be taken at his instance, by deposition, if the taking or preservation thereof is necessary for the protection of his rights. The testimony may be taken only in pursuance of an order. On application for such an order, which may be made ex parte, the applicant must set forth in the affidavit the nature of the controversy which is expected to be the subject of the action and the circumstances which render it necessary for the protection of the applicant's rights that the testimony of the witness be perpetuated. Matter of Richey, 217 N. Y. S. 819; aff'd 218 A. D. 732; 218 N. Y. S. 879;

C.P. A., § 295; C.P.R. 123. 

During Trial or After Judgment. The applicant is required to obtain an order for such an examination. He moves upon notice and proof of facts and circumstances which render proper the taking of testimony by deposi-

$ 187 

EXAMINATION BEFORE TRIAL, 1 tion during the trial of the action, or after judgment, in order to carry the judgment into effect. C.P.A., § 293. 

Testimony of Person in Prison. Again an order is re quired where a party or other person whose testimony is sought, is confined in a prison or jail within the state, under a sentence for a felony. The granting of the order is discretionary. The order must include a direction requiring the production of the prisoner at the prison or jail. C.P.A., § 297. 

§ 198. Persons to be Examined. 

The statute provides that any party to an action may cause to be taken by deposition before trial his own testimony, or that of any other party; or that of the original owner of the claim; or that of any other person where such person is about to depart from the state, or is without the state, or resides at a greater distance from the place of trial than one hundred miles, or is so sick or infirm as to afford reasonable grounds of belief that he will not be able to attend the trial, or other special circumstances, where such testimony is material and necessary in the prosecution or defense of the action. C.P.A., $288. 

§ 199. Procedure Generally. 

Unless the statute specifically provides that the testimony may be taken only in pursuance of an order, one may secure an examination in either of the following two ways: 

1. Service of notice to take testimony accompanied by a subpoena 

2. Notice of motion or order to show cause

§ 202. Service of Subpoena and Notice. 

A copy of the subpoena and a copy of the notice are served personally upon the person to be examined, five days before the day set for the examination. C.P.R., 121; C.P.A., § 300. Where the person to be examined is a resident of the state, he may not be required to attend in any county other than that in which he resides, or where he has an office for the regular transaction of business. If he is not a resident, he cannot be required to attend in any other county than that wherein he is served with a subpoena; except that where the examination is

204 191 

held pursuant to an order, he may be compelled to attend in any county specified in the order. 

At the time of service, the witness must be paid what is known as a subpoena fee, consisting of fifty cents a day for one day's attendance, and where he resides more than three miles from the place of attendance, eight cents for each mile going to the place of attendance. C.P.A., 

§§ 404, 1539. 

§ 203.

Motion to Vacate or Modify the Notice-In 

General. 

After the person has been served, a copy of both the subpoena and the notice may, as a matter of courtesy, be served upon his attorney, although it is not necessary to do so. In the interim between the day of service and the day set for the examination, the attorney for the party to be examined may move to vacate, modify or limit the notice. C.P.R. 124. In other words, the burden is upon the person to be examined to show that the testimony sought is not material or necessary. Hillick v. Edwards, 143 Misc. 277; 256 N. Y. S. 313; Citizens Trust Company v. Prescott & Son, Inc., No. 1, 221 A. D. 420; 223 N. Y. S. 

184. Any question as to the right to take testimony, or as to the time or place, or as to the matters as to which the testimony is to be taken, or as to the persons before whom it is to be taken, may be raised by a motion to vacate or modify the notice. C.P.A., § 291. 

It is well to note that where the parties stipulate to adjourn the examination, the right to question the regularity of the notice is waived unless such right is reserved therein. W. L. Sutphin Realty Co. v. Breinig, 206 A. D.. 

713; 200 N. Y. S. 839. 

§ 204. Notice of Motion to Vacate or Modify—Form.

An affidavit in support of a motion to modify the notice, may read as follows:

That the deponent consents to item numbered "1" but objects to items numbered "2", "3", "4" and "5" on the ground that they are improper. Deponent submits that the information regarding the items to which objection is made is peculiarly within the knowledge of the plaintiff and therefore the examination as to those matters is a mere "fishing expedition". 

Deponent further submits that it is obvious on the face thereof that items numbered "2" and "4" are improper for the reason that the defendant would have no opportunity of learning the contents of the bag which the plaintiff alleges it checked with 13

the defendant and therefore would not be able to testify thereto nor as to the value thereof.

§ 206. Service of Motion Papers Operates as Stay. 

Annexed to the motion papers is a copy of the notice. 

If objection is made to the service of the subpoena, it too, is annexed. If the motion is brought on by order to show cause, the order may contain a stay; otherwise 

C.P.A., § 291 provides that the service of the notice of motion, if made for the first term or sitting of court at which the motion can be heard, shall operate to stay the taking of the testimony until the determination of the motion. Where in an action pending in the Supreme

Court of New York County, a notice for examination was served January 21st, returnable January 28th, a notice to vacate served January 26th returnable January 

31st was held timely. Hand v. Haiduck, 122 Misc. 528, 204 N. Y. S. 214. On the other hand, in an action, where the place of trial was Saratoga County, the plaintiff's attorney served the notice for examination on June 21st, returnable June 27th in  The defend ant's attorney served a notice of motion to vacate on 

June 23rd, returnable July 8th in Saratoga Springs.

The court held the service was not timely because it was not the first term at which the motion could be heard; that a special term was appointed to be held in Albany 

County, June 24th and in Schenectady County, July 1st

$ 195 

and thus could have been brought on sooner than by the special term of Saratoga Springs. Richmond v. Joseph thal, 203 A. D. 281, 196 N. Y. S. 571. 

§ 207. Hearing. 

The original motion papers to modify, with proof of service thereof are filed with the Clerk of Special Term Part I. Upon the hearing, the moving party submits a copy of the pleadings, and if he wishes, a memorandum of law citing authorities to prove that the items are improper. The adverse party may submit an opposing affidavit; or better still a memorandum citing authorities to support the contention that the items are material and necessary. If the court finds that the testimony sought is not material and necessary to the one who served the notice, or for any reason that the interests of justice would not be subserved by such an examination, an order may be made, vacating and setting aside the notice or limiting the scope of the examination and directing that the examination proceed at the place stated in the subpoena or other place, on a specified date. C.P.R. 124. Where the service has been questioned, on the ground that the subpoena was served less than five days before the return day, the court may set aside the service of the subpoena and vacate the notice. 

§ 208. Service of Order With Notice of Entry. 

copy of the order entered upon the motion to modify, with notice of entry is served upon the attorney for the party to be examined. The party must attend at the time and place specified or be liable to punishment. If no application is made to modify or vacate the notice, the witness must attend pursuant to the subpoena and at the time and place specified therein. He is, as a rule, accompanied by his attorney.

$ 210 

§ 209. Production of Books Upon Examination. 

In addition to testifying upon the examination, the witness may be required to produce all books and papers in his possession which relate to the matters upon which he is to be examined. This he does where a subpoena duces tecum has been served upon him, or where an order of the court provides therefor. See §§ 210, 215. 

The books, so produced however, may be used only for the purpose of refreshing the witness' recollection. New 

York City Car Advertising Co. v. Regensburg & Sons, 

Inc., 205 A. D. 705, 200 N. Y. S. 152. In other words, the witness is asked to bring along books and records so that when a question is asked, he will not be able to say, "I don't know", or "The information may be found in by books"; for the records will be there so that he may refer to them. The examining party, however, will not be permitted "to roam through such papers at will". Klink v. Hershon, 191 A. D. 504, 181 N. Y. S. 

459. If the circumstances are such as to make it necessary for him to examine the books, he must apply for such relief by order to show cause for discovery and inspection. C. P. A., § 324, C.P.R. 140. He may combine the two prayers for relief, to wit; examination before trial, and discovery and inspection in the one order to show cause. Keon v. N. Y. Traprock Corporation, et al., 228 A. D. 795, 239 N. Y. S. 668; Matter of 

Smathers, 152 Misc. 774, 274 N. Y. S. 109; see also Wait's

N. Y. Practice, Vol. 4 [3rd Ed.] 123-131. 

§ 210. Subpoena Duces Tecum-Form. 

A subpoena duces tecum is one of the means whereby a person may be compelled to produce upon the examination before trial or other hearing or a trial, a book of account. It must be served upon the witness five days before the day that he is required to attend. C.P.A.,

$ 197 

8 411. The production of a book or paper belonging to or under the control of a corporation may be compelled in like manner by the service of the subpoena duces tecum which is directed to the president, or other officer in whose custody is the book or paper. C.P.A., § 413. 

In such case, the subpoena is deemed to be sufficiently obeyed if the book or paper is produced by a subordinate officer or employee of the corporation who possesses the requisite knowledge to identify it and to testify with respect to the purposes for which it is used. If, however, the personal attendance of the officer is required, then in addition, a regular subpoena in the form already described must also be served upon him. C.P.A., § 414. 

Printed forms of a subpoena duces tecum are available which read as follows: 

THE PEOPLE OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK: 

TO BERGER BUS LINES, INC., by William Berger, its President, Greeting: 

WE COMMAND YOU, that all business and excuses being laid aside, that you appear and attend before Raymond Marsh, a

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York, on the 10th day of

February, 1937, at ten o'clock in the forenoon and give evidence as an adverse party, in an examination before trial in a certain action now pending in the Supreme Court of the State of New 

York,  between Arnold Brown, Plaintiff, and Berger Bus Lines, Inc., Defendant, on the part of said plaintiff, and that you bring with you and produce at the time and place aforesaid, letters dated April 15th and 30th, 1933, written by the plaintiff to the defendant, now in your custody, and all other deeds, evidences and writing, which you have in your custody or power, concerning the premises. And for a failure to attend, you will be deemed guilty of a contempt of Court, and liable to pay all loss and damages sustained thereby to the party aggrieved, and forfeit fifty dollars in addition thereto.

8 212 

WITNESS Honorable Samuel Rosenman, one of the justices of the said court at chambers the 3rd day of February, 1937.

MILTON BARTLETT, 

Attorney for Plaintiff, 

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. 

§ 211. Procedure by Motion—In General. 

If, for any reason, the person to be examined cannot be served personally, or if one wishes to proceed at once, without the delay occasioned by the service of a notice which may be followed by a motion to vacate in order to test the materiality or necessity of the items, he may do so by notice of motion, in the first instance, supported by affidavit. C.P.A., § 292. In this way, also, one can provide in the order entered on the motion that the defendant be directed to produce upon the examination books and papers and thus obviate the necessity of serving a subpoena duces tecum therefor. Matter of Sands, 98 A. D. 148, 90 N. Y. S. 749. One may also proceed by order to show cause. 

§ 212. Order to Show Cause-Form. 

An order to show cause for an examination before trial may read as follows:

§ 214. Procedure Following Preparation of Order to Show Cause. 

After the order to show cause has been signed by a judge, a copy thereof and of the affidavit, are served upon the attorney for the party to be examined. The original papers with proof of service thereof are filed with the Clerk of Special Term Part I. On the return day, a copy of the pleadings and a memorandum of law are submitted on behalf of the moving party. The adverse attorney may submit an opposing affidavit and memorandum of law. The service of the memorandum of law, of course, is optional. The court does not hear oral argument, but examines the items and the allegations of the particular pleading to which they refer to determine whether the items are material and necessary in the prosecution or defense of the action, as the case may be. The order entered upon the decision is usually

8 215 

in long form. It is prepared by the moving party and submitted to the judge for signature. A conformed copy of the signed order with notice of entry thereof, is served upon the attorney for the person to be examined.

§ 216. Stipulation Changing Place of Examination- Form. 

As already pointed out, a subpoena and notice may provide that the examination be held at the attorney's

office but where application is made to the court in the first instance, the order will usually direct that the examination proceed at Special Term Part II. The attorneys, however, may stipulate to hold the examination at the office of the examining attorney in the following manner:

217. Conducting the Examination. 

If the examination is held at the courthouse, the attorneys for both sides meet with the person to be examined in Special Term Part II. After the witness is sworn by the clerk, all proceed to the room provided for the holding of examinations and the examining attorney conducts the examination. If the testimony

217 205 

is recorded in longhand, then, at the conclusion thereof, the witness is again brought before the clerk to be sworn that the answers given by him are true and he so signs. 

The examination is thereupon closed or it may be adjourned from time to time. C.P.R. 127. It is common practice, however, to enter into a stipulation for at least one adjournment. The testimony may be taken down in shorthand, transcribed and thereafter signed by the witness. The only advantage of conducting an examination in a court is that in the event the witness refuses to answer a question or the adverse attorney will not permit him to answer on the ground that it is not within the scope of the examination, the attorneys may conveniently consult the judge sitting in Special

Term Part II (or in such part in other courts where judges hear ex parte matters), who will make an immediate ruling so that the examination may proceed. C.P.R. 

129. Where, however, the attorneys are congenial and can settle their arguments amicably without the intervention of the court, then of course, it is more convenient to conduct the examination at the office of the examining attorney before a notary public. Section 301 of the Civil Practice Act provides that the examination may also be taken before any judicial officer, commissioner of deeds, or attorney and counsellor at law. If disputes do arise, as they will, then the objection may be noted, and the examination proceeds to the point where objection has been made to a number of questions. 

The attorneys may then adjourn the examination and in the interim consult the judge of Special Term Part II for a ruling upon the objectionable questions. 

The examination is, as a rule, oral; but the parties may stipulate otherwise. C.P.A., § 302. The examining party alone, asks the questions. There is no crossexamination. Objections to any questions need not be noted, and may be raised upon the trial, unless it is an objection to form only, which must be noted; otherwise

§ 218 

it is deemed to have been waived. C.P.R. 129. When books or papers are referred to, they may be marked for identification, and the examining attorney or his secretary notes upon the exhibit the words, "Plaintiff's Exhibit I for Identification", if it is offered by the plaintiff. If it is introduced on behalf of the defendant, the word, "Defendant's" is substituted for the word "Plaintiff's". 

Before commencing the examination, the attorney should have before him the notice or order containing the list of matters upon which the examination is based. 

This will serve not only as a guide for him, but in the event a dispute arises as to whether a question is within the scope of the examination, reference thereto can be made without unnecessary delay. 

§ 218. The Examination-Form. 

The testimony may be recorded in the following form:

ARNOLD BROWN, 

-against-

Defendant. 

Examination Before Trial of Berger

President, as an adverse party, held on 

February 18, 1937, pursuant to the order of Mr. Justice Leary, dated Febuary 14, 1937, the parties having stipulated that the examination be held at the office of Milton Bartlett, the attorney for the plaintiff.
