§ 219. Testimony May be Changed Before Signing Transcript. 

A witness who has been examined in this manner is not required to subscribe the exact transcript of the testimony. He may revise it to conform to his more deliberate recollections of the facts. Van Sow v. Herbst, 215 A. D. 563, 214 N. Y. S. 272. Where the examination is conducted at the attorney's office, a copy of the testimony as transcribed is sent to the adverse attorney who consults with his client. The latter examines it, makes any changes which he desires and arranges to go to the office of the examining attorney to sign the original before a notary public. 

§ 220. Filing of Deposition. 

The deposition must be filed within ten days after its completion and return, in the office of the clerk of the court in the county in which the action is triable or special proceeding pending unless the filing thereof is waived by stipulation. The usual practice, however, is to enter into a stipulation of this sort at the commencement of the examination. C.P.R. 132; see form of stipulation § 218.

$ 209 

§ 221. Use of Deposition. 

One seeks by an examination to obtain, wherever possible, admissions which will aid his case. But the deposition taken within the state except that of a party taken at the instance of an adverse party, or a deposition taken in pursuance of a stipulation, may not be read in evidence unless the deponent is then dead or out of the state or at a greater distance than one hundred miles from the place where the court is sitting, or that by reason of insanity, sickness or other infirmity or imprisonment he is unable to travel or appear at the court, or for any reason his attendance cannot be compelled by subpoena with the exercise of reasonable diligence. 

C.P.A., § 304. 

§ 222. Effect of Deposition. 

A deposition may be read in evidence by either party.

Nat. Fire Ins. Co. v. Shearman, 223 A. D. 127, 227 N. Y. S. 

522. A deposition which is read in evidence has the same effect and no other, as the oral testimony of the witness would have. C.P.A. § 303, 305. Any objection to the competency of the witness, or to a question or answer may be made as if the witness were being personally examined except that where objection to the form of question has not been noted upon the examination before trial, it shall be deemed to have been waived. 

§ 223. Penalty for Failure to Attend Upon Exam ination.

In order that a witness may be punished for contempt for failure to attend upon an examination before trial or to attend and bring with him a book or paper, it is necessary that he be served personally with a subpoena or order requiring his attendance or the production of the book or paper. The punishment is the damages sustained by the party aggrieved in consequence of the failure, and fifty dollars in addition thereto. And if 14

$ 225 

the witness is a party to the action, the court, as an added punishment, may strike out his pleading. C.P.A., § 405. 

Thus, where a notice to take testimony was served upon the attorney only, and no subpoena or order was served upon the defendant, and the latter failed to appear upon the examination, the court pointed out in Levine v. 

Moskowitz, 206 A. D. 194, 200 N. Y. S. 597, that it could not inflict upon the defendant, the penalty of striking out the pleading because the penalty has inherently the same nature as that of punishment for contempt through disobedience of an order or subpoena, and the same considerations govern its uses. 

§ 224. Commission to Take Testimony. 

Where for some reason, a witness cannot attend upon the trial of an action, or resides outside the state and it is necessary to secure his testimony for the trial, one may move for an order directing that a commission issue to take such testimony in the part of the state where he resides or in a foreign state. C.P.A., §§ 301, 302. This means that someone, designated in the commission, usually a notary public, although not limited to such officer, residing where the witness is, will record all answers given by the witness in response to a set of questions known as interrogatories which are furnished to the commissioner in advance of the examination, by the attorneys. The testimony may be taken wholly or partly on written interrogatories. The privilege of examining a witness orally may be secured only by showing valid reasons therefor, and should be conditioned on the payment, in advance, of the costs and expenses incurred by the opposing party in attending the examination. Boza v. National Surety Co., 192 N. Y. S. 648. 

§ 225. Procedure-Interrogatories and Cross-Interroga tories-Form.

The attorneys may move for a commission to issue or may stipulate therefor. A notice of motion and

$ 211 

affidavit are prepared in the same manner as when seeking an examination before trial. C.P.R. 126. The adverse party usually consents to such a motion. The order is granted as a matter of course. If the order relate to the taking of testimony without the state, it either may direct the issuance of a commission or that the testimony be taken before an authorized officer or person. C.P.A., § 294. The moving party serves the order with notice of entry on the adverse attorney and proceeds to draw a list of questions known as interrogatories which corresponds to questions he would ask the witness if the latter were present at the trial in order to prove his case. The examination may be wholly or partly oral. C.P.A., § 294; C.P.R. 126. Where, however, it is taken upon written interrogatories, proposed interrogatories are served upon the adverse attorney within ten days after the entry of the order, or the filing of the stipulation which provides for written interrogatories. C.P.R. 126. Assuming that the action is based upon a foreign judgment and the defense is lack of jurisdiction in that the attorney had no authority to represent the defendant in the action which resulted in the alleged judgment, the notice of proposed interrogatories would be in the following form:

MUNICIPAL COURT OF THE CITY OF NEW YORK Borough of Manhattan: Ninth District. 

ARTHUR BINNS, Plaintiff, -against- 

HAROLD TILDEN, Defendant. SIR:

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that the following are the plaintiff's proposed interrogatories in the above entitled action.

§ 225 

Q. 1. State the time when and the place where the defendant authorized Clarence Moore to represent him in the action which resulted in the judgment upon which suit is brought in New York.

A. 1. 

Q. 2. State whether the authorization was oral or in writing.

If oral, state the substance thereof. If in writing, annex a copy thereof.

A. 2. (Add all further interrogatories)

Dated: New York, February 1, 1937. 

Yours, etc.,

To: 

MARTIN ADAMS, ESQ., 

Attorney for Defendant. 

112 Broadway,

MILTON BARTLETT, 

Office & Post Office Address, 

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. 

Ten days after the service of the interrogatories, unless a different time is fixed by order or consent, the adverse attorney must serve his cross-interrogatories. 

This is a list of questions which he in turn would use to cross-examine the witness if the latter were present at the trial. If he fails to serve cross-interrogatories within the time limited therefor, he will be deemed to have waived the right to propound cross-interrogatories; but where the examination may be partly oral, he may appear and cross-examine orally as to the matters elicited by the adverse party by oral questions. C.P.R. 

126. They are served in the form used for interrogatories as already described but prefixing the word "interrogatories" by the word "cross".

§ 226. Objections to Interrogatories-Form.

§ 227. Notice of Settlement of Interrogatories-Form. 

If the attorneys can agree upon the interrogatories and cross-interrogatories, they may be settled by consent. The purpose of the settlement of interrogatories is to authenticate them as those which the commissioner is authorized to propound to the witness. Wanamaker v. Megraw, 168 N. Y. 125. If they are not so settled, then within two days after the time to serve crossinterrogatories has expired either party may serve on the adverse party a notice of not less than two nor more than ten days of the settlement of the interrogatories and cross-interrogatories before a justice of the court or a county judge. Either party shall be allowed to insert any question pertinent to the issue. If neither party serve such a notice within the time limited therefor, the interrogatories and cross-interrogatories are deemed settled as served and are allowed without notice. C.P.R. 126. 

The notice of settlement may read as follows:

§ 228. Procedure Following Settlement of Interroga tories.

In the case where a commission is directed to issue, when the interrogatories and cross-interrogatories are settled, they are annexed to the commission to take testimony. This is a printed form which may be obtained at law stationers. It runs in the name of the people of the State of New York, addressed to the commissioner notifying him of his appointment and his authority to act and instructing him how to proceed. It contains a copy of Title 15 of the Rules of Civil Practice and of Article 29 of the Civil Practice Act. C.P.R. 128. 

Rule 130 of the Rules of Civil Practice provides that an officer or person before whom testimony is taken without the state shall comply with the following direc tions:

8 228 

1. If an exhibit be produced and proved, he shall annex to the deposition the exhibit, or a copy thereof if the original be not surrendered, subscribed by the witness proving it, and numbered or otherwise identified, in writing thereon, by the officer or person taking the deposition, who must subscribe his name thereto; 

2. He shall subscribe his name to each single sheet of the deposition; 

3. He shall annex to the deposition the papers authorizing him to proceed with the examination, together with the interrogatories, if any; 

4. He shall annex to each deposition his certificate setting forth: a. That the witness was duly sworn, and that the deposition was duly taken and is a true record of the testimony of the witness and of all questions and answers required to be inserted; b. That the signature of the witness to the deposition and any exhibit or copy attached thereto is genuine ; c. A statement of all appearances by the parties and attorneys. 

5. On the completion of the examination, he shall inclose in a single packet, securely sealed, the deposition or depositions and all papers required to be annexed thereto; 

6. If the notice, stipulation or order contain a direction to return the deposition by mail, or if there is no direction, as to the manner of return, he must immediately deposit the packet in the post office, postage prepaid, and addressed to the clerk with whom it is required to be filed at his office; 

7. If there be a direction to return the same by an' agent of the party, at whose instance the testimony was taken, the packet so addressed must be delivered to the agent;

$ 217 

8. A notice, stipulation or order for the taking of a deposition before two or more persons may be executed by one or more of them.

Each deposition, and the papers required to be annexed thereto, are required to be filed, within ten days after its completion and return in the office of the clerk of the court, in the county in which the action is triable or special proceeding pending unless the filing is waived by stipulation. The deposition and papers annexed, remain open to the inspection of the parties, each of whom is entitled to make copies thereof. C.P.R. 132. 

§ 229. Suppression of Deposition. 

If the deposition taken without the state has been improperly or irregularly taken or returned or there has been any fraud or unfair conduct with respect thereto, the aggrieved party may move for an order for the suppression of the deposition after notice to the adverse party. And if it appear that a resident of the state whose deposition was taken without the state could have been subpoened to attend the trial, his deposition may be suppressed unless he resides more than one hundred miles from the place of trial. C.P.R., 133. A party who has knowledge of the facts, waives his right to suppress the deposition, if he fails to make the motion before the trial. Van Pelt v. Barrett, 205 A. D. 332, 199 N. Y. S. 509. 

§ 230. Use Upon Trial. 

At the trial and just before the introduction of the testimony taken by commission, the judge briefly explains to the jury that because of the absence of the witness, it was necessary to take his deposition and that they are to regard it in the same manner as if the witness were testifying before them in person. The attorney then proceeds to read the interrogatories and answers

$232 

thereto. The adverse attorney may read the crossinterrogatories and the answers thereto. And either attorney may read the entire deposition. William L. 

Schupp & Sons, Inc. v. Barnett, 210 A. D. 546, 206 N. Y.

S. 553. Each side, of course, may object to the questions in the same manner as if the witness were present in court and testifying orally. 

§ 231. Procedure to Obtain Testimony of Witness Residing in a Foreign Country. 

One proceeds to obtain the testimony of a witness residing in a foreign country by the issuance of a commission either in whole or in part on written interrogatories as already described. 

§ 232. Letters Rogatory. 

In the usual case, one may apply for the issuance of a commission to take the testimony of a witness residing in a foreign country. But where, as in some countries which do not enforce the execution of a commission to take the deposition of a witness because they have no authority to compel such witness to testify under a commission issued from a foreign jurisdiction, our courts have inherent authority to issue letters rogatory and such authority is given by express provision of 

C.P.A., § 309. Decauville Automobile Co. v. Metropoli tan Bank, 124 A. D. 478, 108 N. Y. S. 1027; Bowen v. 

Havana Electric Ry. Co., 146 A. D. 672, 131 N. Y. S. 536.

This is a formal request by our court to a court in the foreign state or country to summon the witness named and take his testimony upon written interrogatories annexed to the letters and after the completion thereof, to return the same to our court. See forms in Brad bury's Lawyer's Manual, Fourth Edition, pages 568-575.

§ 233. When to Make Motion. 

227 After the service of the answer and at any time before trial, the plaintiff may move for summary judgment; that is, ask the court to strike out the answer on the ground that it is sham and frivolous and interposed only for the purpose of delay. C.P.R. 113. See Wait's

N. Y. Practice Vol. III. [4th Ed.] page 607. The motion is, as a rule, made immediately after the service of the answer, so that if the plaintiff is successful, he will be in a position to enter judgment immediately and it will not be necessary to incur expense to notice the case for trial nor to wait the long period of time ordinarily required for a case to be reached for trial. 

Before proceeding with a motion of this sort, outside of the First and Second Departments, it may be well to consult the local court acts and rules of the courts other than the supreme court and county court, because although many of them make provision for this remedy; (Albany City Court Act, § 148); nevertheless it is not available, for example, in the Buffalo City Court. A. D.

Deemer Furniture Co. v. G. H. Poppenberg, Inc., 127 

Misc. 117, 216 N. Y. S. 72. 219

$ 235 

§ 234. Nature of Action in Which Motion May be Made. 

Rule 113 was at one time very limited in scope but both bench and bar soon appreciated the usefulness of the rule with the result that it became liberalized by amendment from time to time so as to include various types of cases. One may now move for summary judgment in actions (1) to recover a debt or liquidated demand arising on a contract express or implied in fact or in law, sealed or not sealed; (2) to recover a debt or liquidated demand arising on a judgment for a stated sum; (3) on a statute where the sum sought to be recovered is a sum of money other than a penalty; (4) to recover an unliquidated debt or demand for a sum of money only, arising on a contract express or implied in fact or in law, sealed or not sealed, other than for breach of promise to marry; (5) to recover possession of a specific chattel or chattel with or without claim for the hire thereof or for damages for the taking or detention thereof; (6) to enforce or foreclose a lien or mortgage; (7) for specific performance of a contract in writing for the sale or purchase of property, including such alternative and incidental relief as the case may require; (8) for an accounting arising on a written contract, sealed or not sealed.

The rule also applies to a counterclaim as if it were an independent action. 

§ 235. Nature of Motion Generally-Test is to Deter mine if Triable Issue Exists.

The hearing on the motion may be said to correspond to a trial in only one respect and that is, where the motion is granted, the action is terminated and judgment may be entered immediately to the same effect as if there had been a trial. But it differs from a trial in that no witnesses are called upon to testify and the court therefor does not have to consider their credibility. The

§ 221 

sole duty of the judge is to determine from the facts whether there is a triable issue; that is, whether there is conflicting evidence on a material issue which might be submitted to a jury. Continental Securities Co. v. 

Interborough R. T. Co., 118 Misc. 11, 193 N. Y. S. 892; aff'd 200 A. D. 794, 193 N. Y. S. 903. This he does by hearing the oral argument of counsel, if they so wish, and by reading the papers submitted by both sides. If the defendant by affidavit, or other proof can show that he has a meritorious defense, he will be permitted to defend the action, otherwise he will not. Applebaum v. 

Gross, 117 Misc. 140, 191 N. Y. S. 710. If the judge finds that a triable issue exists, he must deny the motion and permit the parties to settle their differences upon a trial. If he finds that no triable issue exists, he has no alternative but to grant the motion. 

A plaintiff may, for example, before commencing action, write to the defendant demanding payment for certain goods sold and delivered, and receive a reply in which the defendant acknowledges the indebtedness but requests further indulgence by reason of his present inability to pay. The plaintiff may, after further delay and repeated demands finally decide to bring the action to recover the claim. But the defendant who is still unable or unwilling to pay, interposes a general denial in the hope of obtaining further delay for at least the period of time required for the case to be reached for trial. The plaintiff may, nevertheless, move immediately for summary judgment and produce upon the hearing of the motion, the defendant's letter to prove to the court that there is no defense to the action and thus no reason for delaying the entry of judgment. In such case, the motion will be granted.

Another very common example is where suit is brought upon a promissory note. Terner Bros. v. Glickstein & Terner, 263 N. Y. 555. The indorser may, for example,

$ 235 

set up a general denial and a defense to the effect that he received no notice of protest and is therefore released from obligation. But the plaintiff may have in his possession proof that the note was protested and that the defendant received notice thereof. The plaintiff would thereupon proceed to draw a notice of motion in the usual form and annex thereto his affidavit stating the nature of the action, the status of the matter, the facts concerning the making, delivery, presentment and protest of the note. He would also state his belief that there is no defense to the action. He would refer to and annex the affidavit of the notary public to the effect that he duly protested the note and duly notified the defendant thereof. Annexed to the motion papers would be a photostatic copy of the note as well as copies of the evidence of protest and due notice thereof. The original note and other evidence would be submitted upon the trial for the court's inspection. The defendant would then in turn be obliged to prove by affidavit or other proof that he did not in fact receive the notice; otherwise the plaintiff would be entitled to judgment. 

From the foregoing it is clear how a motion for summary judgment might readily be granted, but an interesting situation may arise where the motion would have to be denied. Assuming that suit is brought against a resident of New York to recover upon a judgment alleged to have been recovered in Oklahoma, and that the defendant interposed a general denial setting up the defense of lack of jurisdiction alleging that the attorney was not authorized to appear for him in the Oklahoma action. The plaintiff in moving for summary judgment would proceed upon the theory that the court would have to recognize the judgment of record of the court of a sister state under the full faith and credit clause of the Constitution of the United States. The defendant, however, never appeared in the action as alleged and he

236 223 

is prepared to prove that not only did he leave the foreign state wherein the judgment was recovered a number of years prior to the commencement of the action, but that he had never communicated with the attorney who claims to have represented him. Under the circumstances, the defendant would have a valid defense and would proceed to cite authorities to show that he may set up the defense of lack of jurisdiction and prove that fact by extrinsic evidence even though it contradict the judgment itself which states that the attorney duly appeared on behalf of the defendant. National Exchange Bank v. Wiley, 195 U. S. 257; White v. Glover, 138 A. D. 797, 123 N. Y. S. 482. And thus, the defendant having shown to the court that an issue of fact exists; to wit, lack of jurisdiction of the foreign court to enter judgment, he is entitled to defend the action and the motion will be denied.

§ 237. Affidavit-Form. 

The affidavit in support of a motion for summary judgment may be made by a party or any other person having knowledge of the facts, setting forth such evidentiary facts as shall, if the motion is made on behalf of the plaintiff, establish the cause of action sufficiently to entitle plaintiff to judgment, and if the motion is made on behalf of the defendant, such evidentiary facts, includ-ing copies of all documents, as shall fully disclose defendant's contentions and show that his denials or defenses are sufficient to defeat plaintiff, together with the belief of the moving party either that there is no defense to the action or that the action has no merit, as the case may be. C.P.R. 113, Divan v. Massarene, 199 A. D. 872; 

192 N. Y. S. 577. The affidavit may read as follows:

This action is brought to recover the sum of $2,526.89 and is based upon a judgment recovered by the plaintiff's assignor against the defendant in an action instituted by the plaintiff's assignor against the defendant in the Superior Court of Tulsa in the State of Oklahoma.

That annexed hereto and made part hereof is an exemplified copy of the judgment. Prior to the commencement of this action the said foreign judgment was duly assigned to the plaintiff. The said assignment is annexed hereto and made part hereof.

§ 238. Procedure After Preparation of Motion Papers. 

A copy of the motion papers is served on the adverse attorney and the original with proof of service thereof is filed with the clerk of the part wherein it is returnable unless a note of issue is required to be filed. If the action were pending in the Supreme Court, New York County, it would be returnable in Special Term, Part III and filed with the clerk thereof. If it is returnable in the City 

Court of the City of New York, it is made returnable in 

Special Term Part I and a note of issue is required to be filed.

Wherever a question of law is involved, it is advisable to prepare a brief and submit it upon the hearing. In the case of the suit upon the note previously referred to, the defendant would cite authorities which hold that failure to give the indorser due notice of protest releases him from liability thereon. And as already pointed out in the case of the suit based upon the foreign judgment, the defendant would cite cases which hold that lack of jurisdiction is a valid defense and that extrinsic evidence may be used to contradict the judgment itself. 

In this way, unless it is a clear case which entitles the plaintiff to summary judgment, the defendant can show that his answer creates a triable issue and that the defense therein contained is a valid one supported by authority. 

§ 239. Decision. 

The court may grant the motion or deny it as a whole. 

It may in a proper case, decree partial judgment and direct a trial of the issues as to the balance. The rule provides that in the cases referred to in subdivisions 3, 4, and 5 where either party fails to show facts as may be deemed by the judge to present a triable issue other

240 227 

than the question of damages for which judgment may be granted, an assessment to determine such amount is forthwith ordered for immediate hearing before a referee, by the court alone, or by the court and a jury whichever is appropriate. This means that in an action where a jury trial is a matter of right and the defendant has not waived that right, the appropriate method of assessing the damages is to produce proof to the court and jury in practically the same manner as upon a trial. C.P.A., § 426. Where, however, the right to a trial has been waived, the court alone may assess the damages, but where the matter is involved, the court may refer it to a referee or the parties may consent to a reference. And, upon rendering of the assessment, judgment may be entered thereon. 

The rule further provides that when in any actions in cases set forth in subdivisions 6, 7 and 8, the judge hearing the motion has been convinced that there is no preliminary triable issue of fact, the court shall forthwith render an appropriate judgment or order and thenceforth the action shall proceed in the ordinary course.

If upon such motion made on behalf of a defendant, it shall appear that the plaintiff is entitled to judgment, the judge may award judgment to the plaintiff, even though the plaintiff has not made a cross motion therefor. 

Where the defendant moves for summary judgment with respect to a counterclaim, the court may, in its discretion, provide that the entry of judgment thereon be withheld pending the disposition of the issue in the main case. C.P.R. 113. 

§ 240. Service of Order With Notice of Entry. 

If the plaintiff succeeds on the motion, he serves a copy of the order with notice of entry upon the adverse attorney and proceeds to enter judgment and tax costs. 

If the plaintiff is not successful, he notices the case for trial.

§ 241. Nature of Motion. 

232 After issue joined and at any time before trial, a motion may be made for judgment on the pleadings. C.P.R. 112; 

Klippel v. Weil, 204 A. D. 323, 198 N. Y. S. 13; see also

Wait's N. Y. Practice Vol. 3 [4th Ed.] 602. This motion is nothing more or less than a motion to test the sufficiency of the pleadings; that is, a motion to dismiss the complaint on the ground that it does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action; or a motion to treat the answer as a nullity pursuant to Rule 104 on the ground that it is frivolous; or that the defenses therein contained are insufficient in law. Doppelt v. 

Raeden, 118 Misc. 203, 192 N. Y. S. 835. It will be remembered that these latter motions were required to be made within a limited time. If, for any reason, they were not so made, one may still obtain such relief by moving for judgment on the pleadings. This motion may also be made to test the sufficiency of the reply or the defenses therein contained. However, it is important to note in this connection that where, at some prior time, a motion was made pursuant to the pertinent rule attacking the sufficiency of a pleading or defense and 228

242 229 

JUDGMENT ON THE PLEADINGS. 

denied, that decision is res adjudicata and may not be reviewed by another judge under a motion for judgment on the pleadings. Aldrich v. Newburgh, 70 Misc. 126, 128 N. Y. S. 51. To permit such a thing would set a bad precedent for it would in effect be asking judges of equal rank; that is, judges at different times sitting in the particular part where the motion was heard, to rule upon the decision of the other. This of course, is never permitted. The remedy is by appeal to a higher court. Endurance Holding Corporation v. Kramer 

Surgical Stores, Inc., 227 A. D. 582, 238 N. Y. S. 377.

An interesting situation arose in this manner. complaint alleged three causes of action. The defendant moved to dismiss the complaint pursuant to Rule 106 on the ground that it did not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action. The court, in rendering its decision, held the first cause of action insufficient but denied the motion as a whole on the ground that although the complaint set forth three separate causes of action, the defendant moved against the complaint as a whole and not with respect to each separate cause of action stated. And, under such circumstances, the motion must be denied where any one of the three is sufficient. The defendant then sought a means whereby he could have the first cause of action dismissed, but realized that he had already lost his right to move separately with respect thereto pursuant to Rule 106, because the twenty day period had expired. He found, however, that he could obtain the desired relief by moving for judgment on the pleadings. Strauss v. Strauss, N. Y. Law Journal, February 11, 1936; April 16, 1936. 

§ 242. When to Make Motion. 

Although the motion may be made at any time after joinder of issue, it may be advisable to do so after a bill of particulars is obtained, if there is reason to believe

8 245 

that a bill is necessary. Hubbs & Co. v. Richard, 119 

Misc. 436, 197 N. Y. S. 45, aff'd 212 A. D. 868; Richardson v. Gregory, 219 A. D. 211, 219 N. Y. S. 397, aff'd 245

N. Y. 540. The reason for this is that although the court must determine the motion on the pleadings alone, nevertheless, for the purpose of this motion, a bill of particulars is a pleading and may be considered by the court. Merchants Loan & Investment Corporation v. 

Abramson, 214 A. D. 252, 212 N. Y. S. 193; Kronman &

Co., Inc. v. Public National Banks of N. Y., 218 A. D. 

624, 218 N. Y. S. 616. And where there is a variance between the allegations of the complaint and the statements in the bill of particulars, the latter controls. Al 

American Securities Co., Inc. v. Foundation Co., 211 A. 

D. 684, 208 N. Y. S. 328. 

§ 243. Motion May be Made in Any Action. 

Unlike a motion for summary judgment, a motion for judgment on the pleadings may be made regardless of the nature of the action. 

§ 244. By Whom Made. 

Either party may make the motion and the rule provides that if either party be entitled to judgment on the pleadings, the court will grant the relief without regard to which party makes the motion. 

§ 245. Procedure. 

Where one moves for judgment on the pleadings, attacking the complaint for insufficiency, for example, the procedure is the same as outlined under a motion to dismiss the complaint for insufficiency pursuant to Rule 106; that is, the notice of motion alone is served. 

The motion is determined solely on the pleadings. 

Germini v. N. Y. Central Railroad Co., 209 A. D. 442, 204 

N. Y. S. 603; Lewis v. City of Lockport, 251 A. D. 159, 296 N. Y. S. 385.

§ 249. In General. 

As already pointed out, in actions pending in the Supreme Court and the New York City Court, unless the adverse party serves a demand therefor, no papers are required to be filed until the trial of the action. Thus, the court has no way of knowing that a controversy exists until some step is taken to call the matter to the court's attention and request in effect that a trial be granted as soon as those who have given previous notice have had their cases tried. This is done by preparing a note of issue and serving a copy upon the adverse attorney and filing the original with the court. In the New York City 

Municipal Court, although papers are required to be filed in advance of the trial, nevertheless they will remain in the files unless the attorney for either party serves a copy of a notice of trial upon the adverse attorney and files the original with the clerk, since the court cannot know that a trial is desired for it may well be that the parties will be able to settle the matter without a trial. 233

$ 250 

§ 250. When to Notice Case and Caution Against Unnecessary Delay. 

Unless the answer is sham and frivolous and the attorney can be reasonably certain of success upon a motion for summary judgment, a case should be noticed for trial not later than twenty days after joinder of issue in Supreme Court actions, and six days after joinder of issue in New York City Court actions. This permits time within which to serve an amended pleading. Under Rule 

150 as recently amended, however, one may file a note of issue forty days after service of the summons irrespective of joinder of issue. In New York Municipal Court actions, a notice of trial should be served immediately upon receipt of the answer. The sooner the case is noticed for trial, the sooner it will be tried. And, certainly, in fairness to the client, this step in the case must not be neglected, for a long delay may seriously prejudice the client's rights. For example, the defendant may be in sound financial condition when the action is commenced and continue so to be for some time thereafter. Later, perhaps, the defendant may experience financial reverses with the result that when the judgment is ultimately recovered, he may not be in a position to satisfy it. Again, witnesses may die and render it difficult to prove the case; or the action may fail and abate.

Thus, it is the duty of the attorney to notice the case for trial without unnecessary delay not alone to protect his client's rights but that he may not himself be subject to censure as a result of complaints to the Grievance Committee of the Bar Association. There are instances, of course, where the attorney may not be wholly to blame. 

For example, a client may refuse to furnish the necessary costs to enable the attorney to place the case on the calendar. In this event, if the attorney does not wish to advance the costs himself, he must advise the client by letter that he will be unable to notice the case for trial unless he receives the necessary disbursements. If no

§ 235 

reply is received, and the client persists in his refusal to furnish the costs, the attorney may write him again insisting that he forward the costs or seek other counsel. 

Again, where the client has moved and has left no forwarding address and the attorney is unable with due diligence to determine his whereabouts, he may send a registered letter to the last known address advising the client why the case has not been noticed for trial. Then, if the question arises at some future time, the attorney is protected because his records will show that he was not guilty of laches. 

§ 251. Procedure in Supreme Court-In General. 

In actions pending in the Supreme Court, the attorney for either party may place a case on the calendar for trial by serving and filing a note of issue; and if the case is entitled to a preference, steps are taken to obtain the same by a demand contained in the note of issue or by an application for an order therefor. The plaintiff's attorney, as a rule, prepares and serves these papers. 

§ 252. Note of Issue-Form. 

The note of issue states the title of the action, the names and addresses of the attorneys, the time when the last pleading was served, whether the action is triable by a jury or by the court without a jury, the term at which a trial of the action is desired, the specific nature and object of the action, and if such action be entitled to a preference under sections 138 or 139 of the Civil Practice Act, a demand therefor. C.P.R. 150. It is made returnable the first Monday of the month. Four copies are prepared, two of which are duplicate originals. The third copy is served upon the adverse attorney and the fourth is retained. The original with proof of service is filed with the county clerk at any time after issue is joined, or forty days after the service of the summons irrespective of the joinder of issue and twelve days before the return

$ 252 

day. At the same time, the duplicate original with proof of service and bearing the file number, is filed with the trial term calendar clerk and the calendar fee of twenty dollars and a trial fee of five dollars are paid. N. Y. 

County Supreme Court Rule II, subd. 3; C.P.A., § 1557a, subd. 3,1. The calendar clerk thereupon places the case upon what is known as a general calendar. This contains a list of all cases which are awaiting trial. There are three such calendars, to wit, Equity, Jury and Non-Jury.

Although the case is not reached for trial on the day for which it is noticed, it remains on the calendar until it is disposed of, and it is not necessary to file a new or further note of issue for a succeeding term.

Rule 150 provides that a party who brings in a new party shall within five days thereafter serve such new party or his attorney, if he has one, with a copy of the note of issue, and shall also within the same five-day period file a statement with the clerk advising him of the bringing in of such new party and of any change in the title of the action, together with proof of due service of the note of issue, upon the new party, or his attorney, and of such statement upon the attorneys for all parties who have appeared in the action. The cause in such case retains its position on the calendar unless the court otherwise directs.

Where, however, the case is about to be reached for trial and the new party so brought in can show that he will be prejudiced thereby; that his time to appear or plead or that his time to amend a pleading as of course, or the time to move with respect to the pleadings, has not expired, he may move by the usual notice of motion, based upon affidavit, for an order striking the cause from the ready calendar or for such other relief as the circumstances require.

The note of issue reads as follows:

$ 237 

RAYMOND FOLEY, Plaintiff, -against- 

EDWARD CARSON, Defendant. 

Action for libel. 

Issue joined February 3, 1937 by the service of the defendant's answer. 

Milton Bartlett, Attorney for plaintiff, Office and Post Office

Martin Adams, Attorney for defendant, Office and Post Office 

Address, 112 Broadway, Borough of Manhattan, City of New

Action noticed for trial for March, 1937. Jury demanded.

§ 253. Calendar Number. 

When the case is placed upon the calendar by the clerk, it is given a number. Where, for example, there are 

1199 cases on the calendar awaiting trial, the case is given the number of 1200. It is, as a rule, marked or stamped on the receipt for filing fees. It also appears in the New York Law Journal when the list of new issues is published. When received, the number, together with the name of the case, is placed on the list of pending cases and carefully kept; for it will be the only means of knowing when the case will be reached for trial. § 254. Jury Demand-Form. 

If the party who first serves a note of issue desires a jury, he must serve a copy of a jury demand with the note

8 254 

of issue upon the adverse attorney. N. Y. County Supreme Court, Trial Term, Rule II, subd. 3; N. Y. Const., Art. 1, subd. 2; C.P.A., §§ 425-430; 1023; 1142; 1149.

The original jury demand, with proof of service, is filed with the calendar clerk within three days after the service thereof. The fee for filing a jury demand is twelve dollars. C.P.A., § 1557a, subd. 4. If the party who serves the note of issue does not desire a jury and thus serves no demand therefor, any other party may, within six days after the service of the note of issue, serve a jury demand upon the adverse attorney and file the same with proof of service with the calendar clerk within three days thereafter, whereupon the action is placed upon the calendar for trial by jury. If neither party serves a jury demand, but a note of issue alone is served and filed, the case is placed upon a calendar of cases to be tried without a jury. See local court rules. See pertinent Civil

Practice Act sections with respect to fees charged by the county clerks in the different counties.

Before requesting a jury, it may be well to consider whether one desires an early trial and thus forego a jury. 

In Supreme Court actions in New York County, where a jury is demanded, one must wait for a period of from two and a half to three years for the case to be reached for trial; whereas non-jury cases are reached for trial shortly after the day for which they were originally noticed.

§ 255. Preference-Procedure Therefor-Form. 

In certain instances, the parties will not be obliged to await the trial of an action in its regular order if it comes within the statute or rule entitling it to a preference. 

C.P.A., §§ 138, 139. See also local rules. 

If the case is one enumerated in Section 138 of the Civil Practice Act, it is preferred over the issues of the term only; that is, where, for example, an action is noticed for the February term and one hundred cases which are not within that section have already been noticed for that term, the preferred case will be called for trial before any one of the one hundred cases. Heep v. Cabel, 240

A. D. 859, 267 N. Y. S. 301, citing Yorkshire Ins. Co., Ltd. 

v. Raw Fur & Skin Trading Co. of N. Y., 233 A. D. 905, 

265 N. Y. S. 945. Thus, if a case would ordinarily be reached in three years, a preference of this sort in New York County Supreme Court, for example, may reduce this period by approximately six months. But under subdivision 20 of this section, a case may be set down for an immediate trial for a day certain if the plaintiff can show special circumstances; to wit, that as a result of defend-

$ 255 

ant's conduct the plaintiff has been incapacitated for work, or that his business or profession has been damaged to the extent that he is in dire distress and has become a public charge. 

If application is made for a preference pursuant to the rules of the court, as, for example, Rule V of the Rules of the Supreme Court of New York County, the action will be set down for immediate trial for a day certain. 

In general, where application is made pursuant to Section 138, a demand therefor may be made in the note of issue, specifying the provision of the law under which the demand is made. Where, however, the right depends on facts which do not appear in the pleading or other papers upon which the cause is to be tried, one must secure an order therefor. But in the Counties of New York, Bronx, Kings, Queens, Richmond, Erie, Onondaga and the seventh judicial district, the party must apply to the court for a preference. This is done by serving with the note of issue, a notice of motion in the regular form to the effect that an application will be made to the court at the opening thereof, or to such justice or other term of court or at such other time as shall be prescribed by the general or special rules of practice, for leave to move the same as a preferred cause. It should be noted that unless the notice of application accompanies the note of issue, an absolute right to the preference is lost. Pistell, Deano &

Co. v. Wood, 232 A. D. 411, 250 N. Y. S. 92. The notice of motion alone is sufficient if the reason therefor is apparent on the face of the pleadings as in a libel action. 

If the reason for the preference is not apparent, as, for example, where special circumstances are required to be shown, an affidavit must accompany the notice of motion. 

C.P.A., § 141. 

In New York County, the notice of motion is returnable in Trial Term, Part II, on the first Monday of the term; 

that is, the day for which the action is noticed for trial.

N. Y. Cty. Supreme Court, Trial Term, Rule IV. See

$ 241 

local court rules. A copy of the notice of motion is served with the note of issue on the adverse attorney. The original notice of motion with proof of service thereof is filed with the clerk of Trial Term, Part II, at any time up to twelve o'clock noon on the day for which it is made returnable. If the defendant feels that for some reason the plaintiff is not entitled to a preference, he may file with the clerk of Trial Term, Part II, on the return day, an affidavit or memorandum in opposition thereto. In 

Kings County, the application is returnable in Trial Term, Part I, of the Supreme Court, and the moving party is required to file the motion papers with the clerk thereof three days before the return day. See local court rules.

An application pursuant to the rules of the court is likewise made by notice of motion accompanied by affidavit, and is returnable at the time and place aforementioned, but it is made after the case has been placed on the calendar. New York County Supreme Court, Trial 

Term, Rule V. See other local court rules.

The court as a rule will not hear oral argument upon an application for a preference. Where application is made pursuant to subdivision 20 of Section 138, the granting thereof is within the discretion of the court, and only where extraordinary circumstances justify a departure from the regular order. Shapiro v. Rockland 

Light & Power Co., 140 Misc. 204, 249 N. Y. S. 407; 

Greene v. McDermott, 245 A. D. 726, 280 N. Y. S. 68. An order granting or denying a preference is not appealable.

Where, however, a party feels aggrieved thereby, he may move in the usual manner for a reargument, in which case the motion papers may be made returnable on any day of the term before the same judge who decided the motion originally.

The decision appears in the New York Law Journal under Trial Term, Part II, decisions in New York County and under Trial Term, Part I, decisions in Kings County.

If the See local papers in other parts of the State. motion is granted, a copy of the order entered thereon, with notice of entry, is served upon the adverse attorney. 

A certified copy thereof is served upon the calendar clerk, who places it on his calendar of cases for the day specified in the order or gives it the preferred position otherwise indicated in the order.

§ 256. Procedure in New York City Court. 

In New York City Court actions, a case is likewise noticed for trial by the service and filing of a note of issue in the form already described, except that in addition to the nature of the action one must also state the nature of the defense and indicate the classification number. 

New York City Court Act, § 30; Rule IIa of the Rules of the New York City Court. Unlike the practice of the 

Supreme Court, however, there are no terms for which a case may be noticed. It may be noticed for trial for any day. The note of issue is served five days before the day for which it is noticed and filed with the clerk three days before the return day. New York City Court Act, §§ 29, 30. Calendar numbers are obtained at the time of such filing. If a jury is desired, a demand therefor is served and filed.

Where the note of issue contains the statement that the action is an equity cause, it is placed on the equity calendar. All actions of a tortious nature (except actions in replevin and for conversion), as set forth in subdivision (A) of Rule IIa, are placed upon the proper general calendar. All actions of a commercial nature, as set forth in subdivision (B) of Rule IIa, as well as all actions in replevin and for conversion, are placed on the proper commercial calendar, but no action for personal injury or for property damage, whether predicated on a tort or upon breach of contract, may be placed on the commercial calendar. No action which could have been brought in the Municipal Court may be placed on the commercial calendar, and an action which could have been brought in the Municipal Court will be placed on the proper gen-

$ 257 

eral calendar and if improperly placed on the commercial calendar will be stricken therefrom on motion. Rule II of the New York City Court. A case placed on the commercial calendar will be reached for trial sooner than one placed on the general calendar. 

§ 257. Procedure in Municipal Court of New York City -Notice of Trial-Form. 

A case is noticed for trial in the Municipal Court of New York City by the service and filing of a notice of trial. An action may be noticed for any day, but the day thus set must not be less than five nor more than eight days after the service of the notice of trial. N. Y. City

Mun. Ct. Code, § 95. A copy is served upon the adverse attorney five days before the return day. The original notice with proof of service thereof is filed with the clerk of the court three days before the return day. N. Y. Mun.

Ct. Rule 3. Where either party appears in person, the clerk sets a day for trial not less than five nor more than fifteen days after the joinder of issue and notifies the parties by mail of such date. And the case is actually reached for trial on the day thus set unless an adjournment is requested. But where both parties appear by attorney and either side serves a notice of trial, the case may not be reached for trial for months.

The practice with respect to calendar numbers differs from that of the other courts. In this court, all jury cases and some non-jury cases are transferred from the district courts in which they were originally brought, to a court known as Central Jury Part. As soon as the transfer is effected there appears in the New York Law Journal, a list of such cases together with the calendar numbers. As to the non-jury cases which remain, the calendar numbers may be obtained from the clerk shortly after the notice of trial has been filed. 

If a jury is requested, the usual form is prepared,

$ 245 

served, and filed with proof of service within three days after joinder of issue. N. Y. Mun. Ct. Code, § 118, subd. 

1. The jury fee is six dollars since it is customary to have only six jurors unless twelve are requested. See 

New York City Mun. Ct. Rule XXVII, subd. c and rule

XXXIII for cases entitled to a preference and the manner in which application is made. 

The notice of trial is in the following form:

§ 258. Dismissal of Action Upon Failure to Notice Case for Trial. 

If the attorney neglects to serve and file a note of issue within six months after joinder of issue or if a note of issue is not served and filed and it is shown that later cases have been tried in regular order, a motion may be made by the defendant to dismiss the complaint for failure to prosecute. C.P.R. 156. See also C.P.A., §§ 180, 181. 

The notice of motion and accompanying affidavit are prepared, served and filed in the usual manner. The motion papers are returnable in Special Term Part III 

of the Supreme Court in New York County and in Special 

Term Part I of the New York City Court. 

If the motion is granted, an order is entered thereon. 

Costs are taxed and judgment entered therein. 

In the New York City Municipal Court, however, the court will on its own motion, dismiss every action wherein issue has been joined for a year, and the case has not been noticed for trial. This is done sometime during the early summer. An announcement to this effect appears in the New York Law Journal and an opportunity is given to the plaintiff to submit an affidavit excusing the failure to so notice the case. 

§ 259. Notice of Motion to Dismiss-Form. 

A notice of motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute may read as follows:

§ 261. New York Law Journal and Other Publications Wherein Court Calendars and Decisions are 

Published. 

It has previously been explained that when a case is noticed for trial, a number is received by the attorney indicating the position of the particular case on the general calendar of the court. The case subsequently advances to the day reserve calendar and finally to the ready day calendar whence it is sent to a part for trial. 

And during the period of time which is required for a case to reach the day calendar, it is the duty of the attorneys for both sides, or their representatives who are charged with that duty, to watch the progress so that they will know the approximate time that the case will be reached for trial and thus be prepared to try it. 

This is done through the medium of the New York Law Journal. It is a paper published daily except Sundays 249

8 262 

and holidays. Briefly, it covers the First and Second 

Judicial Departments and publishes court calendars and decisions, opinions of the judges and various notices and advertisements. It also publishes the decisions of the 

United States Supreme Court and of the Court of 

Appeals. 

In other parts of the state where there is no regular law publication, the court calendars and decisions are published in the local newspapers. This is true in Albany where such information is available in the Times Union and The Knickerbocker News. 

A study of the calendars of some of the courts will enable one to better understand how cases may be followed. 

§ 262. Calendar Practice-Supreme Court-New York County Ready Trial Calendar. 

Each day, there is published in the New York Law Journal, a ready jury calendar of the New York County Supreme Court, at the foot of which appears the highest calendar number reached in regular order. 

Directly following it, is the non-jury calendar. If a case appears on either of these calendars, the attorneys for both sides wait until the clerk of the court notifies them by telephone to appear in court either the afternoon of the same day or the morning of the following day, and prepare to try the case. Counsel for both sides attend in Trial Term Part II. This is the court room which is devoted almost exclusively to the work of the calendar of jury and non-jury actions. Equity and matrimonial actions are called in Special Term Part 

III. As the clerk calls the cases in the order in which they appear on the calendar, the attorneys answer in accordance with the disposition to be made thereof and the clerk makes notations beside the name of the case thus: "Ready", "Settled", and where an adjournment 1

$ 251 

is requested, the adjourned date is noted. When disputes arise as when one attorney requests an adjournment and the other desires to proceed to trial, the former must submit an affidavit which he has prepared in advance and which states the reason for the adjournment. The judge settles the question immediately. 

The ready jury calendar appears in the New York Law 

Journal thus:

READY JURY CALENDAR. 

Court opens and calendar called in Room 139 at 10 A.M. 

The following cases, other than inquests, or those directed to appear on a specified date without further notice, heretofore answered "Ready," will not be called again. They will be assigned to the parts for trial as reached in their regular order. The assignments will be made by telephone calls to attorneys at a reasonable interval before the trial. 

Any changes in status of a ready case must be noticed to the opposition and presented by affidavit to the court at the calendar part immediately after receiving telephone call and not when the cause has been assigned for trial. Both sides must appear.

§ 263. Inquest-Dismissal. 

If the plaintiff's attorney is present and answers the case "Ready", but the defendant's attorney fails to appear, the former may answer the case "Inquest", and inform the clerk on what day he will be prepared to prove his case. his case. On the day thus specified, he appears in Trial Term Part II with his witnesses and tries the case in the usual manner before the court with or without a jury depending on whether a jury is demanded, and without the presence of the defendant. It is advisable, however, to answer the case ready for both sides and to notify the defendant's attorney that the case has been called, otherwise the latter may take steps to open the default and thus both sides may be put to trouble and expense unnecessarily.

If the defendant's attorney is present but the plaintiff's attorney fails to appear when the case is called, the former may answer "Dismissed". And here again, the defendant's attorney should extend the adverse attorney the courtesy of answering the case "Ready" for

§ 253 

both sides rather than take advantage of a situation which is likely to occur in any office because it does require a great deal of care to be able to follow cases, especially in courts where there are congested court calendars, and know when they appear on the calendar, and although the clerk of the court may notify the attorney's office, the message may not always reach the person in charge of the case. 

§ 264. Sending Cases Out. 

The judge concerns himself chiefly with the cases which have been answered "Ready". He calls before him the attorneys in those cases and takes up the question of a possible settlement. If the parties cannot agree upon the terms of settlement, the judge sends the case out for trial to any one of twenty courtrooms. Each such courtroom is known as a part and numbered consecutively from II to XXI. And as each such part completes the trial of the case, the judge of that part sends word to the judge of Part II requesting that another case be sent to him. The latter calls out the ready case next in order and directs counsel to go to that part.

If parts are not available to all those whose cases have been marked ready, the attorneys who are thus awaiting an assignment to a part, are directed to return from day to day until a part is available. Announcements, as to how many cases will be held over until parts are found, and as to remaining ready cases, are made at the conclusion of the call of the calendar.

As the cases advance to the ready day calendar from the day reserve calendar, cases are added to the latter from a general reserve calendar, which is published on a Friday once in about four or five weeks, depending on whether cases are required to be added to the day reserve calendar. The general reserve calendar may properly be regarded as the starting point; for the case will first appear there, and when it does, it must be answered in the same manner as already described. The clerk, however, does not notify counsel with respect to cases appearing on this calendar. The burden is upon the attorney's office to watch for this calendar; and if this is not done, the case will be dismissed or marked for inquest and may thus never reach the ready calendar in the regular routine manner. § 267. Calendar Practice - City Court - New York County. 

On February 26, 1937, a new system became effective in the City Court of New York County with respect to calendar practice. On that day the Jury and Non-Jury calendars were called at ten o'clock in Trial Term Part I and the Commercial calendar was called at twelve o'clock in the same part. Causes on those calendars were assigned in sequence to the several parts for trial on the Monday following. When the parts were filled, the cases following were placed on a reserve ready calendar for assignment to parts during the ensuing week on telephone calls by the clerk to the respective attorneys. Thereafter, the three calendars appeared daily in the New York Law Journal, each such calendar containing cases theretofore marked "Ready" and in addition, a list of cases indicated by numbers only. The cases on the latter list appeared on subsequent Fridays as required. Thus calendars are called on Fridays rather than daily during the week as formerly. And where the attorneys can agree upon an adjournment, they may sign the usual stipulation and file the original thereof with the calendar clerk on or before the preceding Wednesday. This makes it unnecessary for attorneys or their representatives to appear on the calendar call and is a means of great convenience to them.

§ 268. Calendar Practice New York City Municipal Court. 

The attorneys for the parties must watch the calen dars of the New York City Municipal Court closely and appear on the date indicated in the Law Journal to answer the cases. There is no notification by the court. 

In the district courts, the cases are, as a rule, called in 

Trial Term Part I at nine-thirty in the morning. In Central Jury Part, in the Borough of Manhattan, tort cases are called in Part I at nine o'clock in the morning and commercial calendar cases at nine-thirty in Part 

VIII. 

The cases are answered in the manner already described. In Central Jury Part, however, jury cases are not sent directly to a part for trial. They are sent to 

Trial II where a jury is selected. The attorneys remain there until a part wherein the case may be tried, is available.

Municipal Court of the various districts is published daily in the Law Journal indicating by numbers, which actions will be called for trial, thus: 7744

§ 269. Court Calendars of Other Counties. 

In addition to the foregoing, the calendars of the various courts of the counties of Bronx, Kings, Richmond, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester are also published. 

§ 270. Additional Calendars. 

The court calendars of the Federal Court, Surrogates Court and Criminal Courts are published. 

§ 271. General Calendar Call. 

The New York Law Journal should be watched for an announcement of a general calendar call. This appears about once a year. It means that every case on the 

General Calendar is called, so that those which have been settled, discontinued or dismissed may be taken off the calendar. 

§ 272. New Calendar Numbers. 

Sometime during the month of August and prior to the commencement of the Fall Term of court, it is customary to make inquiries of the various courts to learn whether calendar numbers have been changed, and if

8 272 

so, to obtain the new numbers and to make the necessary change in the office list of pending cases. As a rule, calendar changes are made in the Supreme Court of New York County and in the Federal Court of the Southern District. Announcement as to the changes may be found in the New York Law Journal.

§ 273. Examine File. 

267 268 268 269 It is assumed that the case has already been prepared for trial to the extent at least of making the necessary motions to correct the pleadings; that a bill of particulars and an examination before trial have been obtained, where possible, and that the file contains a statement of each witness; the trial brief, and such other papers as are necessary, so that just before a case is about to appear on the day calendar, it will only be necessary to re-examine the papers in order to have the facts and circumstances fresh in the lawyer's mind and to attend to a few further details which could not be taken can of too far in advance of the trial. 

§ 274. Evidence. 

The pleadings are examined and note made as to what evidence is necessary to support the allegations of fact. 

If one intends to use the testimony of witnesses as proof, they should be summoned by subpoena. If proof is to be made by documentary evidence, one should be sure that such papers are in the file or readily obtainable. 

And each such paper which will be offered in evidence as an exhibit should be carefully arranged in the order in which it will be used. If the exhibit is required to 263

8 275 

be certified before it can be introduced into evidence, this should be done before the trial. If the suit is based upon a foreign judgment, an exemplified copy thereof must be obtained. If there is reason to believe that objection will be made to the introduction of an exhibit or to the testimony of a witness, one should be prepared with authorities to support the claim that it is proper evidence. 

§ 275. Subpoena Witnesses. 

If a witness is to be summoned, it is always advisable to serve a subpoena upon him to insure his presence in court at the trial. A list containing the names and addresses of all witnesses in the order in which they will be required to testify should be made. The attorney, as an officer of the court may prepare the subpoena, printed copies of which may be obtained at law stationers. 

It is served by his clerk or by a regular process server. 

The subpoena must be served personally upon the witness and in order that it may be binding upon him, he should be paid the regular fee of fifty cents for each day's attendance, and if he resides more than three miles from the place of attendance, eight cents for each mile going to the place of attendance. C.P.A., § 1539. The form of subpoena is the same as that considered under examinations before trial except that it indicates that the witness is to testify at a trial and before the judge of the part in which the action is to be tried. If the case has not been assigned to a part, the subpoena may be made returnable in the calendar part; for example, Trial Term Part II of the Supreme Court of New York 

County and before the judge there presiding.

The process server should fill in and sign the affidavit of service which appears on the reverse side of the printed form of subpoena, so that if the witness should fail to appear, the necessary steps may be taken to

276 265 

PREPARATION FOR TRIAL. 

punish him for contempt or secure a body attachment authorizing the sheriff to bring the witness to court. 

C.P.A., §§ 405, 406. 

§ 276. Notice to Produce-Form. 

If the attorney has a copy of a letter or other exhibit which he desires to offer in evidence, the original of which is in the possession of the adverse attorney or party, a demand may be served, requiring the production of the original upon the trial. If the party fails to produce the original, a copy may be offered in evidence for the reason that a foundation has been laid for the introduction of secondary evidence. The demand is known as a notice to produce. It may be served a day before the trial, but in any event, a demand for an original exhibit in the possession of the adverse attorney may always be made during the course of the trial. 

A notice to produce is in the following form:

RAYMOND FOLEY, Plaintiff, -against- 

EDWARD CARSON, Defendant. 

SIR: 

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that you are hereby required to produce on the trial of the above entitled action, the following described papers: 

I. A certain note dated January 7, 1935, in the sum of five thousand dollars made by Ray Anderson to the order of Joseph 

Frick payable July 1, 1935 and endorsed by the defendant.

II. Letter dated July 10, 1936, written by the plaintiff and addressed to the defendant.

III. All other documents, notes, papers, books, letters and

8 277 

writings whatsoever in your possession or control containing any entry, memorandum or other matter in any way relating to the above cause.

In case of your failure to produce any of the foregoing, secondary evidence of the contents of the same will be offered. 

Dated: New York, March 3, 1937. 

Yours, etc.,

MILTON BARTLETT, 

Office and Post Office Address, 

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. 

To: 

MARTIN ADAMs, Esq., Attorney for Defendant.

§ 277. Subpoena Duces Tecum. 

If one does not have copies of the papers sought to be introduced into evidence but requires certain books and papers which are in the possession of the adverse party, then, of course, something more than a notice to produce is necessary. A subpoena duces tecum should be served, the form of which has already been outlined under examination before trial. And if the books and papers are not furnished pursuant to the subpoena duces tecum, the person so served is liable for contempt. 

It may be well to remember that in the case of a corporation, if books and papers only are required, the service of the subpoena duces tecum is sufficient and anyone employed by the corporation who has the requisite knowledge to identify them and testify as to their purpose will be permitted to bring them to court, but if it is desired to have an officer of the corporation personally appear it will be necessary to serve the officer personally

$ 267 

PREPARATION FOR TRIAL. 

with a subpoena in addition to the subpoena duces tecum. 

The latter should be served five days before the return day. C.P.A., §§ 411, 412, 413, 414. 

§ 278. Memorandum of Law on Motion to Dismiss Com plaint. 

If the defendant's attorney has reason to believe that the plaintiff will not be able to establish a prima facie case; that is, to prove upon the trial, each allegation of the complaint, and may as a result, be successful upon a motion to dismiss the complaint, he should prepare a list of authorities to show that proof of the various essential allegations contained in the complaint is necessary to establish the plaintiff's case, and wherein the plaintiff failed in such proof, and at the proper time, make his motion and submit his brief in support thereof. 

§ 279. Requests to Charge. 

After each side has summed up to the jury, the judge proceeds to give a brief resumé of the facts which were brought out by the testimony during the course of the trial, and to state the contention of each side. He advises the jury that they are the sole judges of the facts; and that they alone must determine whom they will believe and whom they will not believe. And to aid them in arriving at a just verdict, where a question of law is involved, the judge explains the law which is applicable to the facts of the case. When he has finished, the attorney for either side may request the judge to advise the jury as to some point of law which he feels is applicable to the facts and favorable to his side. If the judge is of the opinion that the additional charge is proper, he may so charge. If not, he may refuse to do so, whereupon the attorney may take an exception.

Thus it is advisable to prepare a list of charges

8 281 

which are to be requested. The importance of this will be considered under this title in a discussion of the trial of an action. 

§ 280. Trial Brief. 

In as much as the judge is not familiar with the case before him, it is always advisable to prepare a trial brief. It is similar in appearance to the briefs submitted on motions and serves the same purpose. It states the nature of the case, outlines the pleadings, sets forth a resumé of the evidence which will be introduced, and cites authorities in support of the propositions of law involved therein. In other words, the judge is furnished with whatever information is necessary to give him a clear understanding of the case over which he will preside. And, in a jury case, since it is the judge's duty to see that the case is conducted in a fair and just manner, he will, if he has a thorough knowledge of the case, be better able to rule as to what is proper evidence and what is not and at the proper time to convey a clear picture of the case to the jury who must render the verdict. 

§ 281. Trial Folder. 

It is helpful to have some means to enable one to arrange in chronological order all papers necessary for use upon the trial. For this purpose, one may purchase a thirty page folder with finger index, numbered from one to thirty in which may be placed the various papers and exhibits; some of which will appear as follows: 

1. Pleadings. 

2. Motions and orders. 

3. Examination before trial. 

4. Bill of Particulars. 

5.

Exhibits consisting of correspondence and other documentary evidence.

§ 269 

PREPARATION FOR TRIAL, 6. Notice to produce. 

7. Subpoenae. 

8. List of witnesses and statement of each. 

9. Requests to charge. 

10. Memorandum in support of motion to dismiss the complaint. 

11. Trial brief. 

This enables one to refer to a paper immediately and return it to its proper place to be used again when the occasion arises. Frequently, during the confusion of a trial, papers are mislaid causing unnecessary delays which may be obviated by the use of a folder of this sort. 

§ 282. Interview Client and Witnesses. 

Just before the trial, the attorney should review the facts and examine the papers in the case with his client because the latter, more than anyone else, knows the facts and circumstances and to review them helps to fix them in the minds of both himself and the attorney. The latter may also be better advised as to what points he should stress. He should make note of them. Witnesses should also be interviewed for the same reason. The attorney may find it helpful to make a list of the witnesses in the order in which they will be called and the points to be stressed.
