§ 283. Marked Pleadings Furnished to Court Before Commencement of Trial. 

When an action pending in either the Supreme Court or the New York City Court is sent to a part for trial, the attorneys for both sides proceed to the assigned part immediately and notify the clerk that they have been sent there. The clerk makes note of the case and notifies counsel as soon as the previous case has been disposed of or it may be necessary for them to make inquiry later in the day as to the progress of the cases which precede their case. The plaintiff's attorney furnishes the clerk with a set of marked pleadings for the purpose of acquainting the judge with the nature of the case in advance of the trial. C.P.R. 160. 270

284 271 

THE TRIAL. 

In the New York City Municipal Court, the attorneys proceed at once to the part assigned to them and await their turn. In the Central Jury Part in the Borough of 

Manhattan, the attorneys proceed from the calendar part to Part II, select their jury and await an assignment to a part. 

§ 284. Selection of Jury. 

If the case is to be tried by a jury, the attorneys proceed to the particular room wherein the jurors are selected. There, the clerk, upon being advised that the attorneys wish to select a jury, draws from a box, twelve ballots containing the names of jurors, and calls together the twelve men. In Central Jury Part in the 

City of New York, six men are chosen unless twelve are requested. The clerk provides the plaintiff's attorney with a card holder containing six or twelve cards, as the case may be, on each of which is written the name and occupation of a juror. The plaintiff's attorney examines the cards and questions the jurors in an effort to find if any of the jurors is biased or otherwise prejudiced in favor of either side so as to render him unsatisfactory. 

If so, the juror is excused, and replaced by another. 

This is known as challenging jurors. C.P.A., §§ 450–455. 

Either side is permitted six peremptory challenges; that is, without stating the reason therefor. One may also challenge to the favor. This occurs when a juror is found to be an employee of a party to the action, or where the action is to recover damages for injuries and the juror is an employee, shareholder or stockholder of a corporate party, or a shareholder, stockholder, officer or otherwise interested in an insurance company issuing protection against liability for damages resulting in injury. The attorney briefly explains the nature of the case, asks whether any one of the jurors knows either of the parties or their attorneys and whether

$ 285 

there is any reason why he cannot decide the issue fairly. What the attorney asks will depend on the circumstances and the nature of the case. For example, if the action is brought to recover damages for the alleged conversion of bonds deposited with the defendant stock broker, the latter at least, will not want a juror who has lost money in the stock market. Having in mind the purpose of the questions, an attorney should have no difficulty in formulating them. See Wait's N. Y.

Practice, Vol. 4 (3rd Ed.) 166–178. A jury implies twelve competent and disinterested men. 

Blair v. 

McCormack Construction Co., 123 A. D. 30, 107 N. Y. S. 

750. As the court in Butler v. Glens Falls, etc. Co., 121 

N. Y. 118 said: "The question for the triors is whether the juror is, as he avowedly should be, altogether indifferent, and if they find he is not, it is their duty to reject him."

When the plaintiff has expressed his satisfaction with the jury, he turns the cards over to the defendant's attorney who proceeds to examine the jurors in the same manner. He too, excuses any jurors which he may find objectionable. And when he has expressed his satisfaction with the jurors, the plaintiff's attorney resumes the questioning of any new jurors chosen by his adversary. This continues until both sides are satisfied with the jurors. The jurors thus chosen proceed to the courtroom, enter the jury box and are sworn by the clerk. 

§ 285. Opening to the Jury. 

Although it is important to afford the judge an opportunity to become familiar with the case in advance of the trial by furnishing him with marked pleadings and a trial brief, nevertheless, if it is a jury case, it is equally important to acquaint the jurors with the facts, for they will ultimately decide the case and if they are provided with information before the actual trial thereof,

§ 273 

THE TRIAL. 

they will better understand the technical procedure which follows. For this reason, the attorney for each side, opens to the jury. C.P.R. 161. The attorney who has the affirmative opens first and he is, is as a rule, the plaintiff's attorney. But where the answer, for example, admits the allegations of the complaint and sets up an affirmative defense or a counterclaim, the defendant's attorney opens first, for he has the burden of establishing the case. And the attorney who first opens, has the right to close; that is, he sums up last or as the expression goes, he "has the last say" to the jury. The advantage of this privilege is obvious and sometimes it becomes the subject of a great deal of argument which the judge may be called upon to settle. 

If the defendant's attorney, therefore, believes that he is entitled to this privilege, he should have in court, authorities to prove his contention.

In the usual case, the plaintiff's attorney opens by stating to the jurors, the nature of the case, and explains as briefly as possible what he intends to prove. The adverse attorney, in turn explains what he intends to prove. 

The attorney should never dwell at length on what he intends to prove; for the jury may expect too much of him. It is always advisable to be brief. Some attorneys waive the opening and proceed immediately with the case. 

§ 286. Commencement of Trial Proper-Introduction of Evidence. 

Unless a motion is made directly after the opening, to dismiss the complaint on the ground that it does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action or that the court does not have jurisdiction of the person or the cause of action, the plaintiff's attorney calls his first witness who, in all probability is the plaintiff. 

Sanders v. Saxton, 182 N. Y. 477. He is sworn by the 18

8 286 

clerk and gives his name and address to the court stenographer before he testifies. C.P.A., §§ 360–365. 

The witness should recite his story in a simple, straightforward, honest and direct manner, giving the facts in chronological order without prompting by his attorney. 

A jury is always favorably impressed by testimony of this sort. But because a witness may not always know what is relevant and what is not, he usually recites facts which are not necessary or otherwise proper. Under such circumstances, the attorney may ask questions to guide him, but in so doing, he must not ask leading questions unless the witness is hostile or illiterate. For example, where suit is brought to recover the purchase price of goods sold and delivered and the defendant claims he returned the goods because they were defective and not the kind he ordered, the attorney should not ask the question, “And when you received the goods, you immediately returned them and notified the seller that they were defective and not the kind you ordered, did you not?" But rather he should ask, "And what did you do when you received the goods?" As soon as an improper question is asked, the adverse attorney may immediately rise and object to it, giving his reason thus: "I object on the ground that it is irrelevant and immaterial." The judge may sustain the objection or overrule it and direct the witness to answer. If he overrules the objection, the adverse attorney may have the court stenographer note his exception on the minutes by merely saying: "Exception" or "I respectfully except".

Again, where a witness volunteers information which is not called for by a question, the adverse attorney may ask the court to strike out the entire answer or so much thereof as is not responsive to the question.

The plaintiff's attorney thus follows the narrative, putting in a question here and there as a guide. When the witness refers to any papers such as a letter which

$ 275 

THE TRIAL. 

he has written, his attorney produces the letter, asks the witness if that is the letter to which he referred. If the witness answers in the affirmative, he may offer it in evidence. C.P.A., §§ 329-420. The court stenographer may note upon it the words "Plaintiff's Exhibit 1". The defendant's exhibits are usually marked by letters thus: "Defendant's Exhibit A". However, either numbers or letters may be used. If the adverse attorney wishes to object to the introduction of the paper in evidence, he may ask to examine it and then state his objection. The judge decides whether or not it is to be admitted. If the judge is of the opinion that it is not proper evidence, the plaintiff may ask that it be marked for identification and the stenographer makes the notation upon it; to wit, "Plaintiff's Exhibit 1 for Identification". This is done for the purpose of appeal. Although objection may be made to the introduction of papers in evidence, anything at all may be marked for identification. 

§ 287. Cross-Examination. 

As soon as the plaintiff's attorney has finished questioning his witness, the defendant's attorney may crossexamine for the purpose of making the testimony appear more favorable to his side; or of bringing out discrepancies therein; or otherwise attack the witness' credibility. 

§ 288. Redirect Examination. 

As soon as the defendant's attorney concludes the cross-examination, the plaintiff's attorney endeavors by further questioning to harmonize the alleged discrepancies and thus rehabilitate his witness. Each witness in turn is called and the same procedure is followed. The one attorney "builds up", the adverse attorney seeks to destroy and the first attorney returns to mend the damage thus caused. Where a witness, for example,

$ 290 

who has been asked on cross-examination if he made certain statements in a designated conversation, he may state what the conversation was, on redirect examina tion. People v. Buchanan, 145 N. Y. 1. 

§ 289. Withdrawing a Juror. 

As the plaintiff's attorney proceeds, he may find that he does not have sufficient proof and may therefore desire to discontinue the trial in the belief that on a new trial he may be better prepared. Or it may be that the adverse attorney has said something which has prejudiced his case and he does not for that reason wish to continue. Under such circumstances, he may move to withdraw a juror. Leave to withdraw a juror is a favor, not a right, and has always been held to rest within the sound discretion of the court and is not subject to review. Cattano v. Metropolitan Street Ry. 

Co., 173 N. Y. 565; citing Chesebrough v. Conover, 140

N. Y. 382. If it is granted, the trial is at an end. The reason for this is that the jury can function only if all its members are present, and if a juror be absent by reason of illness or other cause, its usefulness is at an end and it ceases to function. Either side may ask for the withdrawal of a juror. 

§ 290. Plaintiff's Case-Motion to Dismiss Complaint. 

In order that the plaintiff may be assured that his case will reach the jury, he must establish a prima facie case; that is, he must prove everything he is required to prove to entitle him to the relief he asks. To do this, assuming that the complaint sufficiently alleges a cause of action, he offers proof in support of each allegation of the complaint except as to those allegations which have been admitted by the defendant in his answer. And when the plaintiff has thus made out his case, he says: "The plaintiff rests".

$ 277 

THE TRIAL. 

This is the defense attorney's cue. He rises and moves to dismiss the complaint, stating his reason therefor; that is, if he feels reasonably certain that the plaintiff has failed to prove his case. If the motion is granted, the case is at an end. If the judge denies the motion or reserves decision, the defendant continues with his case, upon having his exception noted. 

§ 291. Defendant's Case. 

After the plaintiff rests, the defendant proceeds with proof in support of his claim. The defendant's attorney calls the first witness for the defense, which in all probability will be the defendant, and examines him. The plaintiff's attorney cross-examines the witness and the defendant's attorney rehabilitates his witness. The procedure is similar to that of the plaintiff's case. When the defendant's proof is all in, the defense attorney says: "The defendant rests". 

§ 292. Rebuttal. 

After the defendant rests, the plaintiff may endeavor to discredit any new fact brought out by the defense. 

This is known as rebuttal testimony. 

§ 293. Surrebuttal. 

The defense may proceed to discredit or otherwise reply to matter brought out in rebuttal. This is known as surrebuttal. 

§ 294. Renewing Motion to Dismiss the Complaint. 

The motion to dismiss the complaint may be renewed at the close of the case and after all proof is in. 

§ 295. Motion for Direction of Verdict. 

The statute provides that a judge may direct a verdict when he would set aside a contrary verdict as against

§ 297 

the weight of evidence. C.P.A., § 457-a. In other words, a verdict may be directed, for example, in favor of the plaintiff if it is conclusively established that he is entitled to a verdict there being no issue of fact raised by the defense. In an action to recover damages for personal injury, it was held the court can direct a verdict for the defendant where the testimony of the plaintiff's witnesses describes the accident in a manner which is physically impossible and overwhelming evidence clearly shows absence of liability. Serina v. New York Rys. 

Corp., 238 A. D. 302, 264 N. Y. S. 107. 

§ 296. Summation. 

At the conclusion of the defendant's case, the defendant's attorney proceeds to sum up to the jury and he is in turn followed by the plaintiff's attorney. Each seeks to present a resumé of the testimony brought out during the trial in so far as it is favorable to his side; that is, he states briefly what the facts constituting his claim are; how he supported those facts by proof; in what respects the effort of the adversary to overcome such proof is unavailing; and finally that the jury must bring in a verdict for his side. The attorneys confine themselves to a review of the facts only and do not instruct as to the law because that lies within the province of the judge. 

§ 297. Charge to Jury. 

Following the summation, the judge proceeds to state the respective contentions of the parties and the manner in which they were supported by the testimony. He advises the jurors that they are the sole judges of the facts; that they are to determine by what was said and the manner in which it was said, how much weight to give to it. If any law is involved, he explains how the various propositions of law are to be applied to the

$ 279 

THE TRIAL. 

facts. At the conclusion of the charge, either attorney may object to such part thereof as he deems improper. 

This may form the basis of an appeal for reasons to be considered under the next section following. 

§ 298. Requests to Charge. 

After the judge has concluded his charge to the jury and either attorney finds that no reference has been made to certain propositions of law which are applicable to the facts, either attorney may ask the judge to further charge the jury with respect thereto. If the judge refuses to do so, the attorney may have his exception noted. This forms the basis of an appeal. Ordinarily there is no appeal from a verdict of a jury, because the jury is the judge of the facts and where there is conflicting testimony, the jurors have a right to believe either side and decide in favor of the side which they think is telling the truth unless, of course, it can be shown among other things, that the verdict is against the weight of evidence; that is, that there is no evidence to support the facts. Franklin Coal Co. v. Hicks, 46 

A. D. 441, 61 N. Y. S. 875, citing Duffus v. Schwinger, 92 

Hun 70, aff'd 157 N. Y. 685. And, as the court in

Hospital Supply Co. v. O'Neill, 10 Misc. 655, 31 N. Y. S. 

792, aff'd 155 N. Y. 634, said: "We have no authority to substitute our judgment for the judgment of the jury and to say proof persuasive with us should have been convincing to them." But where a party can show that the charge was improper and thus prejudiced the jury or that if the judge had charged the jury in accordance with the charge as requested, the jury might have arrived at a different verdict, then there is a basis for an appeal and ground for reversal. It is, therefore, advisable for either attorney to prepare, in advance of the trial, a list of requests to charge. The list may be submitted to the judge before the latter instructs the

8 301 

jury or the attorney may wait until the judge concludes his charge to the jury and then make his requests to charge.

At the conclusion of the judge's charge, the jurors file out to the jury room to deliberate. They may take with them such papers which were admitted in evidence, as the court permits. 

§ 299. The Verdict-Entry Thereof. 

When the jury returns to the jury box, the foreman announces the verdict, whereupon the clerk makes the entry in his minutes specifying the time and place of the trial; the names of the jurors and witnesses; the verdict, or the questions and findings thereon, as the case requires; and the direction, if any, which the court gives with respect to the subsequent proceedings. C.P.R. 165. 

§ 300. Motion to Set Aside Verdict. 

After the jury has announced its verdict, the attorney for the party adversely affected may move to set aside the verdict and for a new trial on all the grounds set forth in Section 549 of the Civil Practice Act. The judge rules on the motion, an exception is noted, if the ruling is adverse, and the jury is discharged. 

It may be well to note that under the new section 463-a of the Civil Practice Act, effective September 1, 1937, unanimous verdicts are no longer required in civil cases. 

The statute provides that a verdict may be rendered by not less than five-sixths of the jurors constituting a jury in any civil case. 

§ 301. Non-Jury Case-Decision. 

A case tried without a jury follows the procedure already outlined, omitting of course such parts as have reference to a jury; to wit, the opening and closing address of counsel, the charge and requests to charge.

$ 281 

THE TRIAL. 

Actions tried without a jury are equity actions and actions at law wherein a jury has been waived. 

And instead of the verdict of the jury, there is the decision of the court which may be oral or in writing and, except where a non-suit is granted, must state the facts which it deems essential. The decision forms part of the record. C.P.A., § 440. 

§ 302. Trials and Hearings Before Referees. 

Referees to Hear and Determine. If the parties prefer, they may consent to have their case tried by a referee instead of a judge. C.P.A., §§ 464–471; C.P.R. 170-174. 

This they may do either by written stipulation or by stipulation in open court and enter an order thereon. 

Federal Fuel Co. v. Macy, 130 Misc. 192, 223 N. Y. S. 

710. The referee may be chosen by them or by the court. Except by consent of all parties in interest, no person, unless he be an attorney, may be appointed sole referee. C.P.R. 172. Where the parties consent, the court has no alternative but to grant the preference. 

However, in the cases mentioned in Section 465 of the Civil Practice Act, notably among which are matrimonial actions, the court may in its discretion grant or refuse a reference. In these cases also as well as in foreclosure cases to compute the amount due; to sell mortgaged premises; or to report on application for surplus moneys, the referee must be designated by the court rather than by the parties. C.P.R. 265.

The statute furthermore provides that the court on its own motion, or upon the application of either party, without the consent of the other, may direct a trial of the issues of fact, by a referee, where the trial will require the examination of a long account on either side and will not require the decision of difficult questions of law. C.P.A., §§ 466, 467. The pleadings of course will determine whether or not the action is such as to

$ 302 

compel a reference. Brooklyn Public Library v. City of 

New York, 240 N. Y. 465.

Where the reference is one to hear and determine; that is, where the case is to be tried by a referee instead of a judge, the trial is brought upon like notice and conducted in like manner as a case tried by a court without a jury. C.P.A., § 469. The referee exercises upon such a trial, the same powers as the court, among other things, to grant adjournments; to preserve order, to punish a violation thereof; to subpoena a witness to attend before him and in a proper case to bring with him a book, document or other paper. The referee's decision is known as a report and it must comply with certain regulations; to wit, among other things, the requirements as to a decision by the court in a like case; and where the whole issue is an issue of fact, the report stands as a decision of the court. C.P.A., § 470. The right of either party to submit requests to find, which he deems established by the evidence and the rulings upon questions of law which he desires the referee to make, as well as the form thereof are considered in Chapter XX; 

C.P.A., § 471. 

Reference for Information of Court. If the court desires information for its own use in order to determine a question of fact, it may order a reference at any stage of an action. C.P.A., § 467. 

C.P.A., § 467. In an action for divorce, for example, where the wife moves for an order requiring the husband to pay her $150.00 a week alimony, during the pendency of the action, and the husband insists that he can pay only $15.00 a week, the court in fairness to both sides, may order that proof with respect to the true condition of the husband's finances be taken before a referee. The practice is to enter the usual long form order, leaving a blank space in the clause appointing a referee, for the insertion of the latter's name by the court. As soon as the order

$ 283 

THE TRIAL. 

is signed, a certified copy thereof is obtained and served upon the referee named therein. The latter directs the attorney to serve a notice upon the adverse attorney indicating the time when and the place where the hearing is to be held. The attorneys and their witnesses attend at the hearing and such testimony and proof is taken as to establish the true state of the husband's finances. 

Another example is a reference in foreclosure actions to compute the amount due or to report on the application for surplus money.

In instances of this sort, the referee does not have broad powers but is limited by the order of appointment and to the purpose for which he was appointed.

§ 303. In General. 

Immediately upon the termination of an action, some official record thereof is required to be made in order that proceedings may be taken to collect the amount involved or otherwise enforce the relief sought. The successful party, as a rule, takes the necessary steps for the entry of such record. It is known as a judgment-roll and consists of the judgment which is a determination of the rights of the parties, and all papers which form the basis thereof. C.P.A., § 472. 

The following are some of the common forms of judgment: 284

304 ENTRY OF JUDGMENT-TAXATION OF COSTS. 285 

Judgment after trial

Judgment by default 

Judgment upon dismissal of complaint 

Judgment by confession 

§ 304. Preparation and Service of Proposed Judgment— Form. 

When the action is terminated, the attorney for the successful party prepares a judgment which, among other things, recites the time when and the place where the trial took place, whether before a judge and jury or the court sitting alone, setting forth merely the result thereof; that is, the verdict of the jury, decision of the court or report of the referee, as the case may be, but not the provisions thereof. C.P.R. 185. Unlike an order, it does not contain a recital of the papers upon which it is based. If the action is to recover money, it specifies the sum and directs that execution issue therefor. It is signed by the clerk. In uncontested actions, the facts upon which the jurisdiction depends are required to be stated and the default recited. A copy of the proposed judgment is served upon the adverse attorney. A space is left blank wherein the clerk of the court will insert the amount of costs as taxed by him. C.P.A., § 1532. This he does by examining a bill of costs which is prepared by the same attorney and served with the proposed judgment. 

The form of judgment is not specifically prescribed for except that it is to be entered in such form as may be required by the nature of the case and by the recovery or relief awarded. C.P.R. 185.

The following is a form of judgment after trial by a jury:

$ 305 

RAYMOND FOLEY, Plaintiff, -against- 

EDWARD CARSON, Defendant. 

The issues of this action having duly come on for trial before 

Honorable Julius Miller, and a jury at Trial Term, Part VI of this Court at the Courthouse thereof in the Borough of Manhattan, City of New York on the 10th and 11th days of February 1937, and the plaintiff having duly appeared by Milton Bartlett, his attorney, and the defendant having appeared by Martin Adams, his attorney, and the court and jury having heard and considered the proofs offered and the jury having brought in a verdict for the plaintiff and against the defendant; 

Now, on motion of Milton Bartlett, attorney for the plaintiff, it is 

ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED, that the plaintiff recover of the defendant, the sum of $10,500 as found by the jury together with the sum of $150 costs and disbursements as taxed, amounting in the total sum of $10,650 and that said plaintiff have execution therefor.

Dated: New York, February 14, 1937. 

ALBERT MARINELLI, Clerk. 

§ 305. Bill of Costs-Form. 

Upon the rendition of a final judgment, the successful party is entitled to recover from the losing party certain fixed sums and certain disbursements as a matter of right in actions enumerated in Section 1470 of the Civil Practice Act. In all other cases, the right thereto lies within the discretion of the court. C.P.A., §§ 1477, 1492. The fixed sums prescribed by statute are known as statutory costs, as, for example, ten dollars for procuring the appointment of a guardian or guardian ad litem; and ten

§ ENTRY of Judgment—TAXATION OF Costs. 

287 dollars for taking the deposition of a witness. C.P.A., § 1504, subds. 1.c, 3.h. In addition to statutory costs, the successful party is entitled to be reimbursed for such sums as were actually paid by him, as, for example, the sum of twelve dollars paid as a jury fee, as well as the fees paid to witnesses. C.P.A., § 1518. 

Printed forms of bills of costs are available. To facilitate the preparation of a bill of costs, it will be noted that in the printed forms beside the blank spaces reserved for the insertion of the amounts, there is a reference to the particular statute which one may read to determine if one is entitled to the payment of the particular sum. The amounts may vary in the different counties. For example, see C.P.A., § 1554-a, for fees charged by the county clerk in such counties as Albany, Schenectady, Monroe, Orange, etc.; also see C.P.A., § 1554-b, for fees charged by the county clerk of the county of Putnam. The correct amounts are inserted and totalled, and the affidavit at the foot thereof is executed. 

C.P.A., § 1538. When thus completed, a copy of the bill of costs with notice of taxation is served upon the adverse attorney in order that he may examine the items before they are submitted to the clerk for allowance.

§ 306. Notice of Taxation of Costs-Form. 

The usual procedure is to serve a copy of the proposed judgment and bill of costs on the adverse attorney together with two days' notice of taxation. Where the attorneys do not reside or have their offices in the city or town where the costs are taxed, at least five days' notice is required. C.P.A., § 1534. The notice appears on the reverse side of the printed form of the bill of costs and reads as follows: 

RAYMOND FOLEY, Plaintiff, -against- 

EDWARD CARSON, Defendant. 

SIR: 

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that the within is a copy of a bill of costs which will be presented for taxation and adjustment to the Clerk

$ 307 

of the Supreme Court, New York County, at his office in the 

Courthouse thereof, Pearl and Center Streets, in the Borough of Manhattan, City of New York, on the 10th day of January, 1937, at 10 o'clock in the forenoon of that day.

Dated: New York, January 8, 1937. 

Yours, etc.,

MILTON BARTLETT, 

Office & P. O. Address, 

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. 

'To: 

MARTIN ADAMS, ESQ., 

112 Broadway,

§ 307. Procedure Upon Taxation and Re-Taxation of Costs. 

At the time and place indicated in the notice of taxation, the attorney for the successful party appears before the particular clerk of the court whose duty it is to enter judgments, and presents to him the original judgment and bill of costs with proof of service thereof, together with receipted bills or other evidence to prove that the disbursements indicated have been made. The attorneys for both sides or their representatives attend. If the adverse attorney is satisfied that the bill is correct, he does not attend, but permits judgment to be entered without opposition. In any event, the clerk examines each item, and if he finds that any one of them is improper, he notes in the margin thereof the word "disallowed", and deducts the sum from the original total. C.P.A., § 1537. 

He makes a notation on the bill to the effect that costs were taxed, and in the particular sum indicated, the date thereof and signs his name. Adverse counsel may object to any of the sums indicated and request the clerk to disallow such item. If the clerk refuses to do so, counsel may have his exception noted on the bill and make appli-

§ ENTRY OF JUDGMENT-TAXATION OF COSTS. 293 

cation to the court on motion for a new taxation. Upon the application, the court will review the taxation or the retaxation, as the case may be. C.P.A., § 1536.

The bill of costs may be presented to the clerk and taxed in the first instance without giving notice thereof to the adverse attorney. But where this is done, notice of retaxation must be given immediately afterwards by the party at whose instance they were taxed. A copy of the bill of costs may be served upon the adverse attorney with notice of retaxation, using the usual form of notice of taxation as already described except that the prefix "re" is added to the word "taxation" wherever it appears in the notice of taxation and the same procedure is followed. It would, however, seem to be better practice to serve notice of taxation, tax costs and enter judgment at one and the same time. However, where notice of taxation is not given in the first instance, and notice of retaxation is not given immediately thereafter, the party entitled to notice may apply to the court therefor and the party in default will be obliged to pay the costs of the motion. C.P.A., § 1535; Hesse-Schnitt v. Brahe, 134 Misc. 

67; 234 N. Y. S. 535. 

§ 308. Entry of Judgment After Trial by Jury—Judg ment-Roll.

Just before the clerk is asked to examine the bill of costs, the attorney for the successful party assembles and presents to the clerk all papers which make up the judgment-roll, and which involve or necessarily affect the judgment. C.P.R. 202. If the case is one wherein a trial was had, the following papers are required:

Summons Pleadings 

Note of issue 

Extract of minutes; that is, the verdict

Proposed judgment 

If any of the aforementioned papers have not been previously filed, as in actions pending in the Supreme Court or

$ 309 

New York City Court, the original papers are taken from the office file. Copies of papers may be used where the originals are not available. If the original papers are filed in court, they are requisitioned; that is, the file containing all papers in the particular case is obtained by filling in a printed blank form provided for the purpose, with the date, name of the case, index number, name and address of the applicant, and presenting it to the clerk who has charge of the files. The extract from the minutes is a record of the result of the trial, and is obtained from the clerk of the Trial Term part in which the case was tried. In addition to the papers already mentioned where an interlocutory judgment has been entered, it, too, may be made part of the judgment-roll. Motion papers and orders are not part thereof unless to show jurisdiction was obtained as in attachment proceedings. 

Where amended pleadings have been served, they are submitted rather than the pleadings which they supersede. 

With the judgment-roll before him, the clerk examines the bill of costs, notes the correct total, examines the proposed judgment and inserts in the blank space provided for the purpose the amount of the verdict recovered, if any, plus the total costs and disbursements. C.P.A., § 495. He signs his name thereto and notes therein the time it was filed and entered, specifying the year, month, day, hour and minute. The judgment is annexed to the papers aforementioned and the judgment-roll is complete. 

§ 309. Service of Judgment with Notice of Entry. 

The attorney for the successful party makes a conformed copy of the judgment and serves it upon the adverse attorney with notice of entry. This is done to limit the time to appeal; for the time within which one is permitted to appeal begins to run from the date of the service of the judgment with notice of entry. A copy of the bill of costs as taxed may also be served.

§ 310. New York City Municipal Court Judgment- Form.

Another form is used upon default in answering. The procedure is substantially the same as already outlined. New York City 

Municipal Court Code, § 164, specifies the sums which may be allowed. On default judgments, statutory costs in one-half the regular sum are allowed. See pertinent sections of other local court acts, as, for example, Albany 

City Court Act, § 312, and Syracuse Municipal Court Code, § 164.

§ 312. Procedure After Service of Judgment with Notice of Entry. 

Filing Transcript of Judgment. In order that the judgment may constitute a charge upon the property of the debtor for a period of ten years after the filing of the judgment-roll with respect to real property and chattels real, either already owned by the debtor or thereafter acquired within ten years, a transcript of the docket of the judgment is obtained from the clerk who entered the judgment and filed in the county wherein the property is situated. C.P.A., §§ 502, 510, 511. 

Steps to Be Taken to Enforce Judgment Unless Stayed. 

The successful party may immediately take steps to collect the judgment as described in Chapters XXII and XXIII, unless the losing party has been granted a stay in open court or applies for an order therefor. The losing party may effect a stay, however, by serving and filing a bond. Thereafter, and within the period of time permitted to take an appeal, he may serve a notice of appeal. 

§ 313. Entry of Judgment After Non-Jury Trial-Judg ment-Roll.

The procedure upon entry of judgment and taxation of costs, in non-jury cases, where costs are allowed, is the same as that considered under jury actions, except that the decision of the court takes the place of the verdict of a jury, and is made part of the judgment-roll.

$ ENTRY OF JUDGMENT-TAXATION OF COSTS. 299 § 314. Findings-The Decision of the Court and Report of Referee. 

Upon a trial by the court without a jury, each party is afforded reasonable opportunity, before the cause is finally submitted to the court, to submit requests to find the essential facts which he deems established by the evidence. Each request is numbered. If the court fails to grant a request either specifically or by embodying it in the decision, it is deemed to have been refused. C.P.A., § 439. The decision of the court may be oral or in writing and, except where a nonsuit is granted, must state the facts which it deems essential. So far as is practicable, the court by its decision grants one or more motions for judgment which each party is deemed to have made in his favor. The decision forms part of the record. C.P.A., 8 440. See C.P.A., § 441, for decision where nonsuit is granted. The decision must be rendered within sixty days after the final adjournment of the term where the issue was tried. If it is not so rendered, either party may move at a special term for a new trial upon that ground. If the decision has not been rendered when the motion is heard, the court must make an order for a new trial, either absolutely or unless it is rendered within a time specified in such order. C.P.A., § 442. See C.P.A., 

§§ 445-447, with respect to exceptions. 

In actions tried before a referee, before the cause is finally submitted, the attorney for either party may submit in writing a statement of the essential facts which he deems established by the evidence and of the rulings upon questions of law or of fact, or of both, separately stated; each of which must be numbered and so prepared with respect to its length and the subject and phraseology thereof that the referee may conveniently pass upon it. 

At or before the time when the report is rendered, the referee must note in the margin of the statement the manner in which each proposition has been disposed of, and must file the statement thus noted; but an omission

$ 315 

so to do does not affect the validity of the report. C.P.A.

, 

§ 471. 

When preparing a list of findings, it may be helpful to remember that one proceeds to enumerate therein such of the allegations of the complaint which have been established by the evidence at the trial, and, in addition, any further facts which have been brought out and established upon the trial. The list of conclusions of law consists of such rulings of law as govern the case and which it is desired that the judge or referee make and, in addition, the relief to which the successful party deems himself entitled. See form, § 476. 

The referee's report must either be filed with the clerk or delivered to the attorney for one of the parties within sixty days from the time when the cause or matter is finally submitted; otherwise either party, before it is filed or delivered, may serve a notice upon the attorney for the adverse party that he elects to end the reference. 

In such a case, the action thenceforth proceeds as if the reference had not been directed. C.P.A., § 470. See also 

Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 4 (3rd Ed.) 293–350. 

§ 315. Judgment by Default-Form of Affidavit. 

Where in an action for breach of contract to recover a sum of money which is fixed or capable of being ascertained by computation only, the defendant defaults in appearing or answering, judgment may be taken without application to the court. C.P.A., §§ 485-494; C.P.R. 189, 

191. The judgment is entered in the manner previously described by preparing and submitting to the clerk of the court, the judgment-roll, consisting of the summons with notice or a copy of the complaint with proof of service thereof; the affidavit showing default as provided in 

C.P.A., § 486; the proposed judgment and bill of costs. 

C.P.A., § 486, provides that where the summons was personally served upon the defendant, and a copy of the complaint or a notice stating the sum of money for which

$ ENTRY OF JUDGMENT-TAXATION OF COSTS. 

301 judgment will be taken was served with the summons, or where the defendant has appeared but has made default in pleading, the plaintiff may take judgment by default, as follows: 

1. If the defendant has made default in appearing, the plaintiff must file proof of the service of the summons and of a copy of the complaint or the notice; and also proof by affidavit that the defendant has not appeared. 

Whereupon the clerk must enter final judgment in his favor. 

2. If the defendant has seasonably appeared but has made default in pleading, the plaintiff must file proof of the service of the summons and of the appearance or of the appearance only; and also proof by affidavit of the default. Whereupon the clerk must enter final judgment in his favor.

The clerk computes the amount of the default judgment in accordance with C.P.A., § 487. 

An affidavit submitted upon a default judgment may read as follows: 

MUNICIPAL COURT OF THE CITY OF NEW YORK Borough of Manhattan: First District. 

JOHN DOE, et al., Plaintiff, -against- 

RICHARD ROE,  )  Defendant. 

John Doe, being duly sworn, deposes and says that he is one of the plaintiffs in the above-entitled action and a member of the firm of Doe & Doe, stock and commodity brokers and members of the National Raw Silk Exchange, Inc. of New York City and of other Exchanges, having their principal office and place of

8 315 

business at 25 Broad Street, Borough of Manhattan, City,

County and State of New York. 

That this action was commenced by the personal service of a summons, bearing the endorsement "Action on an account stated by and between the plaintiffs and the defendant for $750 on November 13, 1929, duly demanded but unpaid", upon the defendant on the 18th day of September, 1930, which summons, together with the affidavit of service, was filed in the office of the Clerk of this Court on the 22nd day of September, 1930.

That the last day of the defendant to plead was the 23rd day of September, 1930, and that an examination of the records of the Clerk's office on the 25th day of September, 1930, disclosed that the defendant had defaulted in filing his answer. 

That heretofore, on the 3rd day of July, 1930, defendant gave plaintiff firm his check to the order of the plaintiff firm, drawn on the Bank of the United States, for $150 as payment on account of the said indebtedness of $750, which said check was returned by the said bank marked "not sufficient funds" on the 

7th day of July, 1930; that thereafter, on the 10th day of July, 1930, defendant gave plaintiff firm another check for $150, which said check was similarly returned unpaid for the same reason on the 12th day of July, 1930. That such checks so offered as payments on account, although worthless, establish the defendant's acknowledgment of the correctness of his indebtedness to the plaintiffs in the amount of $750 with interest from 

November 13, 1929. 

WHEREFORE, deponent respectfully prays that the Clerk of this Court enter judgment in favor of the plaintiffs and against the defendant in the sum of $750 together with costs and disbursements. 

3rd day of October, 1930.

JOHN DOE. 

Where the summons was personally served upon the defendant within the state and he has made default in appearing, or where the defendant has appeared but has

§ ENTRY of Judgment-TAXATION OF COSTS. 

303 made default in pleading, and the case is not one where the clerk can enter final judgment, as prescribed in C.P.A., §§ 486 and 487, the plaintiff may apply to the court or to a judge thereof for judgment. C.P.A., §§ 489,. 

490. The plaintiff is not obliged to serve the defendant with notice thereof unless the latter has served a notice of appearance or a demand for notice of application for judgment. C.P.R. 190. Where the case appears on the calendar for trial and the defendant defaults, the plaintiff proceeds to have the case marked for inquest as already explained and the case is set down for a hearing for a day certain, at which time the plaintiff proceeds with his proof as upon a trial. Where, however, the casedoes not appear upon the calendar, and it becomes necessary to make application to the court, Rule 191 provides as follows: 

"If, in an action in the supreme court, the plaintiff be entitled to judgment on the failure of the defendant to answer the complaint, and the relief demanded requires. application to be made to the court, such application may be made at any special term in the district including the county in which the action is triable, or, except in the first district, in a county adjoining the county in which the action is triable. Such application, except in the first and second judicial districts, may be made also at a trial term in the county in which the action is triable. When a reference or writ of inquiry shall be ordered, the same shall be executed in the county in which the action is triable, unless the court shall direct otherwise. In any county where a separate special term for the hearing of motions only, or for the transaction of ex parte business, is regularly held pursuant to assignment therefor, applications under this rule shall be made only to such a special term as may be designated for that purpose in the special or local rules applicable to such county. Any judgment granted in violation of this provision may be vacated by a special term at which the application might

§ 316 

have been made. Except in an action for the annulment of a marriage, for a divorce or for a separation, no finding of fact in writing shall be necessary to the rendition of a judgment on default in appearance or pleading." 

Following the submission of proof, the plaintiff's attorney prepares and submits to the clerk the judgment-roll which includes the judgment and the bill of costs and judgment is entered accordingly. 

§ 316. Entry of Judgment Where Complaint is Dismissed Before Trial-Form. 

Where the complaint is dismissed before trial pursuant to Rules 106 or 112 of the Rules of Civil Practice on the ground that it fails to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, an order is first entered thereon and thereafter, judgment is entered upon the said order, and costs are taxed, following the procedure already outlined. 

A judgment dismissing the complaint may read as

EDWARD LYONS, Defendant. 

The defendant having moved this Court, at a Special Term, Part III thereof, before the Honorable Julius Miller, on the 

4th day of January, 1937, for judgment dismissing the complaint herein on the ground that it does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, and the Court, after due deliberation, having granted the motion, and an order having been entered thereon, and the costs of the defendant having been duly taxed

Now, upon motion of Warren Cutler, attorney for the defendant, it is hereby

305 ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED that the complaint be and the same is hereby dismissed; and it is further 

ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED that the defendants recover of the plaintiff the sum of $26.25 costs as taxed and that said defendants have execution therefor.

ALBERT MARINELLI, Clerk. 

§ 317. Entry of Judgment Where Complaint is Dis missed Either at Close of Plaintiff's Case or 

After Trial-Form of Judgment. 

Where the complaint is dismissed either at the close of the plaintiff's case, or after trial, the procedure upon entry of judgment is the same as already described under entry of judgment after trial. The important thing to remember in this connection, however, is that a final judgment dismissing the complaint before the close of the plaintiff's case does not bar a new action for the same cause, unless it expressly states that it is rendered on the merits. But a dismissal of the complaint at the close of the plaintiff's case or the dismissal of a counterclaim at the close of the defendant's case, as the case may be, or a dismissal of either the complaint or the counterclaim at the conclusion of the trial, is a final determination of the cause of action on the merits, and bars a new action between the same parties or their privies for the same cause of action unless the court shall dismiss the action without prejudice. C.P.A., § 482.

A judgment to dismiss the complaint after the close of the plaintiff's case may read as follows: 20

8 318 

CHARLES MILLER, Plaintiff, -against- 

HERBERT RYAN, Defendant. 

The issues of this action having duly come on for trial before 

Honorable Philip J. McCook, and a jury at Trial Term, Part VI 

of this Court at the Courthouse thereof in the Borough of 

Manhattan, City of New York on the 10th and 11th days of

January, 1937, and the plaintiff having duly appeared by Martin Adams, his attorney and the defendant having appeared by Milton Bartlett, his attorney, and the Court having heard the plaintiff's proof, and the defendant by his counsel having duly moved this Court at the conclusion of the plaintiff's case for judgment dismissing the plaintiff's complaint herein on the ground that the plaintiff had failed to make out a cause of action herein against the defendant, and due deliberation having been had thereon, and the said motion having been duly granted; 

Now, on motion of Milton Bartlett, attorney for the defendant, it is 

ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED, that the plaintiff's complaint be and the same hereby is dismissed upon the merits; and it is further

§ 318. Judgment by Confession. 

Where a debtor executes a judgment by confession, it may be entered without an action. C.P.A., §§ 540-544;

New York City Court Act, § 16, subd. 4; New York City 

Mun. Ct. Code, § 6, subd. 3.

It may be either for money

$ ENTRY OF JUDGMENT-TAXATION OF COSTS. 307 

due or to become due or to secure a person against contingent liability in behalf of the defendant, or both. It is a written statement made and signed by the defendant under oath stating the sum for which judgment may be entered and authorizes the entry of judgment therefor. 

It must state concisely the facts out of which the debt arose and that the sum confessed therefor is justly due or to become due. The statement is filed within three years after execution. The clerk enters judgment thereon, in like manner as in an action, for the sum confessed, with costs which he taxes in the amount of fifteen dollars, besides disbursements which are taxable as in an action. 

C.P.A., § 543. Judgment cannot be entered thereon after the defendant's death.

If the confession of judgment is in excess of $3000, it is entered in the Supreme Court and filed with the county clerk of the county in which the defendant was a resident at the time of the execution of the statement. If the amount is $3000, and not less than $1000, it is filed with the clerk of the New York City Court. If the amount is $1000, or less, it is filed with the clerk of the New York 

City Municipal Court.

§ 320. Procedure Upon Settlement of Action Before Judgment—In General. 

Frequently, after an action is commenced and before judgment is entered, the defendant, realizing the futility of defending an action to recover a claim which is justly owing, will concede the indebtedness and make payment; or the circumstances may become such that no further purpose can be served by continuing the action, and so the parties consent to a discontinuance thereof, whereupon the plaintiff's attorney executes and delivers to the defendant's attorney the following papers:

Stipulation of Discontinuance General Release § 321. Stipulation of Discontinuance-Form. 

A stipulation discontinuing an action may be executed at any stage of the action. And, although a party is entitled to costs where the action is discontinued after the defendant has appeared, it is not customary to exact such a penalty. The original stipulation is delivered to the defendant's attorney, who retains it in his file unless papers in the action have previously been filed in court, 310

$ PROCEDURE UPON SETTLEMENT OF ACTION. 

311 in which event the stipulation may also be filed. No order is required to be entered. C.P.A., § 301.

The stipulation reads as follows: 

HARRY WEBSTER, Plaintiff, -against- 

CHARLES KING, Defendant.

IT IS HEREBY STIPULATED, CONSENTED AND AGREED by and between the attorneys for the respective parties hereto that the above entitled action be and the same hereby is discontinued without costs to either party as against the other and that an order to that effect may be entered thereon without further notice. 

Dated: New York, February 11, 1937. 

§ 322. General Release-Form. 

WARREN CUTLER, 

Attorney for Plaintiff,

HAROLD BARBOUR, 

Attorney for Defendant.

A release is executed by the plaintiff and delivered to the defendant so that the latter may be assured that the former will not again assert the same claim against him at some future date. The release bars all claims from the beginning of the world to the date of the release, so that if the parties intend that it cover any other matters of dispute between the parties upon which suit may be brought, the release may refer to those matters. It is customary to exchange releases; that is, both parties execute and deliver to each other releases. Printed forms are available at law stationers and read as follows:

§ 323. Stipulation of Settlement-Form. 

If, after the summons has been erved, the parties desire to settle the action, they may enter into a stipulation embodying the terms of the settlement. For example, where the defendant is unable to pay a claim in full

$ PROCEDURE UPON SETTLEMENT OF ACTION. 

313. but is willing to make installment payments, the defendant may agree, among other things, that upon his failure to make any of the payments as provided in the stipulation, the plaintiff may enter judgment by default and. proceed to issue execution allowing credit for any payments made on account of the claim. The plaintiff, on. the other hand, agrees that if the terms are complied with, he will execute a stipulation of discontinuance and general release.

If the case is settled after the joinder of issue, the stipulation may contain a provision whereby the defendant agrees that the answer be withdrawn in order to facilitate the entry of judgment, for if there is no answer, the judgment may be entered as upon a default. 

Assuming that the action is settled after the service of the summons, and before the answer is served, the stipu lation of settlement may read as follows: 

HARRY WEBSTER, Plaintiff, -against- 

CHARLES KING, Defendant. 

IT IS HEREBY STIPULATED, CONSENTED AND AGREED by and between the attorney for the plaintiff and the defendant in person that the above entitled action be settled on the following terms: 

1. The plaintiff agrees to receive and the defendant agrees. to pay $1,125.00 in full settlement of the plaintiff's claim herein. 

2. Said defendant agrees to pay said sum as follows: (a) $450.00 upon the signing of this stipulation, the receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged by the plaintiff. (b) $450.00 on the 27th day of February, 1937. (c) $225.00 on the 27th day of March, 1937.

3. Upon the final payment, plaintiff agrees to execute and deliver a stipulation of discontinuance of the above entitled action. 

4. Upon the failure of the defendant to make any of the payments aforesaid, the plaintiff is hereby authorized to enter judgment against the defendant, without notice, for the amount of his claim with costs and interest, but crediting the defendant with any payments which have been made by said defendant pursuant to this stipulation prior thereto. 

Dated: New York, February 11, 1937. 

WARREN CUTLER, 

Attorney for Plaintiff,

CHARLES KING, Defendant in Person. 

§ 324. Procedure Upon Settlement After Judgment—In General. 

After judgment has been entered for a sum of money and no appeal is taken therefrom, the matter is finally disposed of by payment of the claim. When this is done, the judgment creditor's attorney must execute a satisfaction of judgment. 

§ 325. Satisfaction of Judgment—Form. 

After judgment has been entered, the judgment creditor is entitled to payment of the full amount of the judgment and, in addition, interest from the day of entry thereof, and if a verdict has been rendered, or the report or decision was made, interest is computed from the time the verdict was rendered or the report or decision was made to the time of entering judgment. C.P.A., §§ 480, 481. When payment is made, the judgment debtor is entitled to receive a certificate to the effect that the judgment has been satisfied and is called a satisfaction of judgment. If the judgment is paid within two years. after the entry thereof, the satisfaction piece may be executed by the attorney for the party in whose favor the judgment was entered, otherwise it must be executed by

$PROCEDURE UPON SETTLEMENT OF ACTION. 

315 the party or his executor or administrator. C.P.A., 530; see also C.P.A., § 531.

The satisfaction piece is filed with the clerk of the county wherein the judgment was entered so that the docket may be cancelled; that is, the clerk's books will show that the judgment has been paid and any lien against or charge upon property which existed by reason of the judgment will be cancelled. C.P.A., § 537. 

A satisfaction of judgment reads as follows: 

RICHARD ROE, 

Judgment entered on 

November 10, 1936, for $4,526.10 in favor of the plaintiff.

Defendant. 

WHEREAS a judgment was on the 10th day of November, 1936, recovered by the plaintiff against the defendant in the above entitled action for the sum of Four Thousand Five Hundred 

Twenty-Six and 10/100 ($4,526.10) Dollars which judgment was, on the 10th day of November, 1936, duly entered in the judgment book in the office of the Clerk of the above named Court and said judgment has been wholly paid, and it being further certified that there are no outstanding executions with any Sheriff of any County of the State of New York, or with any Marshal of the City of New York,

THEREFORE, satisfaction of said judgment is hereby acknowledged, and the clerk of said Court is hereby authorized and directed to cancel, satisfy and discharge the same. 

JAMES SMITH. 

 County of New York, SS.: 

On the 15th day of November, 1936, before me personally came James Smith to me known and known to me to be the

$ 326 

attorney for the plaintiff, John Doe, in the above entitled action, and to be the same person described in and who executed the within satisfaction of judgment and acknowledged to me that he executed the same.

MARY MITCHELL, Notary Public-New York County. 

§ 326. Transcript of Satisfaction of Judgment—Cancel ling Bond.

If the debtor's property is located in counties other than the one in which the judgment was entered and transcripts of the judgment have been filed therein, transcripts of the satisfaction of judgment may also be filed in such counties. The transcript is a certificate furnished by the clerk with whom the satisfaction piece was filed, and indicates that the judgment has been paid. 

If a bond has been obtained from a surety company to stay execution of a judgment, a transcript of the satisfaction piece may be sent to the surety company in order that it may have notice thereof and cancel the bond of record, and so that no further claims for the payment of premiums will be made.

§ 327. Proceedings Supplementary to Judgment. 

After a judgment has been recovered, the next consideration is how it may be collected. And before this question can be determined, it is necessary to know what assets the debtor has, if any, and if the nature of the assets is such as to authorize the sheriff or marshal to seize them and apply them to the payment of the judg- 317

$ 329 

ment. To examine one for this purpose, one proceeds by what is known as proceedings supplementary to judg ment. Article 45 of the Civil Practice Act. See Wait's 

New York Practice, Vol. 6 (4th Ed.), page 182, for a comparison of the procedure under the old and the new statutes. 

§ 328. In What Cases the Judgment Creditor May Main tain Proceedings.

C.P.A., § 773, provides that to entitle a judgment creditor to maintain a special proceeding authorized by Article 45, the judgment must have been rendered in any sum by any court of this state, whether or not of record. A decree or order awarding the payment of money is deemed a judgment for the purpose of this article. The proceeding may be maintained until the judgment is satisfied, vacated or barred by the statute of limitations. 

§ 329. How Proceedings are Instituted-Procedure for Examination of Debtor. 

Pursuant to the recently amended statute, effective 

September 1, 1938, supplementary proceedings may be instituted in the following ways:

By order of the court, served upon the judgment debtor, a third party or a witness. The judgment creditor is entitled to an order for the examination of the judgment debtor concerning his property, income or other means for satisfying the judgment upon proof by affidavit that the judgment is unpaid in whole or in part. The order requires the attendance of the judgment debtor to whom it is directed to appear for examination at a time and place to be specified therein, and may require the production at such examination of any books, papers or records in his possession or control which have or may contain information concerning his property or income. 

The order may also contain a provision restraining the judgment debtor from transferring or disposing of any of his property then held or thereafter acquired by or becoming due to him not exempt by law from application

$ 319 

SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

to the satisfaction of the judgment, and such other provisions as the court may deem proper. Such restraining clause remains in force for two years unless previously vacated. C.P.A., §§ 774, 775. 

Printed forms of the order and affidavit are available. 

When prepared, they are submitted to the clerk in the court wherein ex parte business is transacted, and when signed by the judge, a copy of the order to which is annexed a copy of the affidavit is served personally upon the debtor.

By subpoena. Procedure by service of a subpoena is perhaps most common, because relief can be obtained in a shorter time than that required by procedure by order, since the subpoena can be issued immediately by the judgment creditor's attorney and does not require the judge's signature. For this reason, the procedure will be herein after discussed in more detail. C.P.A., §§ 774, 775. 

By warrant. Whenever it appears by affidavit to the satisfaction of the court that there is danger that the judgment debtor will leave the state or conceals himself, and that there is reason to believe that the judgment debtor has in his possession or control property which may be reached by the judgment creditor under this article, the court may issue a warrant requiring the sheriff of any county within the state where the judgment debtor may be found, to arrest him and bring him before the court, judge or justice issuing the warrant. Under such circumstances, the warrant may be issued though a proceeding be pending under an order or subpoena. 

C.P.A., 88 774, 775.

By service upon a financial institution, within two years from the date of the judgment, of a subpoena, as provided for in C.P.A., § 782a. 

§ 330. In What Court Proceeding is Instituted. 

C.P.A., § 777, provides that the proceeding may be instituted in the civil court of record in which the judgment was recovered and in the county where the judgment

$ 331 

debtor resides or has a place for the regular transaction of business in person. Where the debtor neither resides nor has such place of business in the county of such court, then the proceeding is instituted in the county court or supreme court of the county wherein he resides or has such place of business. Where the debtor neither has his residence nor such place of business in any county within the state, then the proceeding is instituted in the court of record in which the judgment was recovered or in the county court or the supreme court of the county wherein the judgment-roll or a transcript of the judgment is filed or wherein the debtor is served with the order or the subpoena. Where the judgment has been recovered in a court not of record, the proceeding is maintained in the supreme court or county court as above provided. Where the judgment is recovered in the municipal court of the City of New York, the proceeding is instituted in the city court of the City of New York, whether or not any transcript has been filed in the office of any county clerk. 

The order or subpoena is made returnable in the court as hereinbefore provided. This section also means that where, for example, a judgment is recovered in the municipal court of the City of New York, the order or subpoena is prepared with the title of a city court action and made returnable therein as if the judgment had been recovered in the city court. 

§ 331. Procedure by Subpoena-Time and Manner of 

Service.

The attorney for the judgment creditor may at any time within two years from the date of such judgment, issue a subpoena directed to the judgment debtor requiring his appearance for examination concerning his property, income or other means for satisfying the judgment. But a subpoena may not be issued where the debtor has been previously examined on such judgment or has previously been required to and did attend a court

$ 321 

SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

of record pursuant to an order or subpoena for examination in proceedings supplementary to such judgment. 

The subpoena must state the court in which the supplementary proceeding is instituted and the names of the judgment creditor and of the judgment debtor, and must be subscribed in the name of the attorney for the judgment creditor, together with his office address. C.P.A., $ 775. 

Except as provided in C.P.A., § 411, a copy of the subpoena is served upon the debtor personally not less than three days nor more than twenty days before the return day unless otherwise ordered. C.P.A., § 783. (Effective 

Sept. 1, 1938.) 

The subpoena may read as follows:

Annexed to the subpoena is an affidavit of service which is executed by the individual who served it. 

§ 332. Attendance Upon and Conducting Examination— Examination of Books. 

On the return day of the subpoena, the attorney for the judgment creditor appears in the part of the court designated therein, with the subpoena and proof of service thereof, and prepared to record the testimony of the debtor. In some courts the subpoena may be made returnable on certain days only. It is therefore advisable to consult local court rules for method of procedure. 

Generally, the practice does not differ very much. The procedure in the Supreme Court of New York County is as follows: At ten o'clock, the subpoena is exhibited to the clerk of Special Term, Part II, who calls the name of the debtor. If the latter is not present, the name is called

$ 323 

SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

again at ten-thirty. This is known as the last call. In the City Court of New York County, the practice requires the filing of a note of issue, together with the original subpoena, two days in advance of the return day so that the clerk may have a record of the names and call them in the order of filing. N. Y. City Court Rule XII, subds. b, c. This is similar to the practice of placing motions on the calendar for call in court, and was made necessary by the fact that the debtors were so numerous that some means had to be found to dispose of the debtor proceedings more speedily. 

If the debtor fails to appear, the clerk stamps the subpena to indicate that the debtor has defaulted in appearance. This forms the basis for a motion to punish for contempt. If the debtor appears, he is sworn by the clerk and proceeds to the room in the courthouse which is provided for the purpose of examining debtors and witnesses. Although the judgment debtor's attorney may attend upon the examination, he does not, as a rule, do so. 

The judgment creditor's attorney proceeds to record in longhand all questions and answers. C.P.A., § 784. The procedure outlined under examinations before trial may be followed whereby the attorney stipulates with the judgment debtor to hold the examination in the attorney's office and provide that it be taken before a notary public or commissioner of deeds with the same force and effect as if such testimony had been taken in or before the court. C.P.A., § 791. 

One may obtain at law stationers a printed copy of questions to be asked upon such an examination. Briefly the attorney examines as to the following: the debtor's name; where he resides and with whom; how much rent he pays; name of landlord; whether he has signed a lease, and furnished security to the landlord; occupation; salary; all other sources of income and how he disposes of it; whether he is an officer of a corporation, member of a partnership; whether he has a bank account of any kind anywhere; the name of the bank, and the

$ 332 

amount on deposit; if the answer is in the negative, he is asked if he ever had a bank account, the name of the bank, the date the account was closed, and the amount on deposit at that time; whether he has a postal savings account; whether he now owns or ever did own real property regardless of location; whether he has jewelry or pawn tickets; whether he owns a library, whether he has a collection of curios, or rare coins; whether he owns stocks or bonds; if he is entitled to royalties; whether he has made a will; whether he is a legatee under a will; whether he carries insurance; the name of any beneficiaries; whether anyone is indebted to him; whether any judgments have been recovered against him and when, also whether he has paid anything on account of the judgments.

If the debtor refuses to answer a question, he may be taken before the judge sitting in Special Term Part II 

where the latter will direct him to answer if the question is proper. 

It should be remembered that a debtor may be honest and otherwise willing to discharge a just obligation but may be in straitened circumstances or it may be that he is sincere in his belief that the judgment creditor is not entitled to payment despite the recovery of judgment and it is very unpleasant, to say the least, to be obliged to divulge the information asked, and therefore the judgment creditor's attorney should not approach the debtor in a hostile manner. It may be that in a quiet talk, off the record at the outset of the examination, the attorney may be convinced that the debtor actually lacks sufficient means to satisfy the judgment in the full amount and may be able to arrange to accept a lesser sum in full settlement if the client is agreeable. If, however, the depleted condition of the debtor's finances is only temporary, it may be that the debtor will stipulate to pay the full amount in installments. And, very often, if this practice is followed on an examination before trial, an action may be amicably settled. 

C.P.A., § 784-a, a new section, effective September 1,

§ 325 

SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

1938, provides that any books, papers or records produced by a judgment debtor, third party, or witness at his or its examination pursuant to an order or subpoena, may be examined and inspected by the judgment creditor and his attorney, so far as the same are relevant to the proceedings, except that in the case of books, papers and records produced by a third party or a witness, the judge, justice or referee presiding at such examination, upon proof to his satisfaction, that any such book, paper or record contains business or trade secrets, or that its disclosure might substantially prejudice the third party or witness, may restrict the examination and inspection of such book, paper or record to such part or parts thereof as do not contain such business or trade secrets and do not create such prejudice. If books of account of a third party or witness are subpoenaed, the third party or witness may, unless the court otherwise orders, produce in place of the original books of account, a sworn transcript of such accounts as are relevant to the proceedings.
