§ 334. Adjourning the Examination. 

At the conclusion of the examination, the debtor is asked to read each page of the testimony and to write his name along the margin of each page as well as at the foot of the last page. If the attorney does not wish to close the examination, he may adjourn it. A printed stipulation of adjournment is obtained from the clerk and is signed by the debtor in person and by the attorney

$ 327 

SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

for the judgment creditor. C.P.A., § 790. If the debtor refuses to consent to an adjournment and insists upon closing the examination, the attorney and the debtor may appear before the judge sitting in Special Term

Part II for a ruling. The judge grants the first adjournment as a matter of course. This is done to permit the judgment creditor's attorney to check the answers and thereafter if necessary to question the debtor with respect thereto on the adjourned date. Although it is customary to obtain only one adjournment, some attorneys stipulate from time to time for further adjournments believing that if the examination remains open and the debtor realizes that he will have to attend court and be examined again, he may be prevailed upon to pay the claim. The court, however, discourages this means of harassing a debtor, and the latter may refuse to consent to further adjournments unless it is shown that they are necessary. In the City Court, there may not be any more than two adjournments, except with the approval of additional adjournments noted on the papers by the judge presiding in Special Term Part II. New York City Court Rule XII (e). Where further adjournments are consented to, the practice is for the judgment creditor's attorney to prepare the stipulation and send it to the debtor so that the latter may sign a copy before the return day of the examination and return the original. The debtor's admission of service appears on the original stipulation so that if the debtor fails to appear upon the examination, on the adjourned date, the attorney for the judgment creditor will be able to show that the debtor had notice thereof and is liable to punishment for contempt. New York City

Court Rule XII (d). 

§ 335. Closing the Examination. 

When the judgment debtor has been examined, and there is no further need for an adjournment, the examination is closed by having the debtor again appear before the clerk and sworn that the questions given are true.

8 336 

The clerk then writes to the left of the debtor's signature the following: 

day of and signs his name. 

§ 336. Summoning Witnesses. 

The judgment creditor's attorney may summon witnesses for questioning concerning the debtor's property referred to in the testimony, or otherwise discovered. 

For example, upon the examination, it may develop that the debtor has in his possession a valuable piece of jewelry which he claims belongs to a relative or friend. 

If the attorney for the judgment creditor doubts the statement and believes that he can establish ownership in the debtor in order to apply its value on account of the claim, he may prepare and serve a subpoena upon the alleged owner. The same form of subpoena as that used to summon witnesses upon a trial, may be served, but changed so as to indicate that the witness is to appear upon an examination. The witness is paid the usual fee and mileage. C.P.A., § 782. The statute provides that in such proceedings commenced by the service of an order or subpoena upon a judgment debtor or a third party, the examination of witnesses may be had simultaneously with or separately from the examination of the debtor or third party and the completion of one or more examinations shall not have the effect of terminating either the proceeding in which the examination was conducted or any other proceeding. Such examinations, however, are more effective when held separately. Until the close of the examination of the judgment debtor or third party or within six months thereafter or otherwise as provided in Article 45, a subpoena may be issued, requiring the appearance in court of the witnesses and the production of books, records and papers necessary to discover property of the judgment debtor, his income or other means for satisfying the judgment. C.P.A., § 782.

329 

SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

Apart from proceedings commenced by the service of an order or subpoena upon a judgment debtor or third party, C.P.A., § 782, as recently amended, effective September 1, 1938, provides that a witness may be examined where there is reason to believe that he has knowledge or information concerning property of the judgment debtor exceeding ten dollars in value or concerning any debt owed to the judgment debtor, his income or other means for satisfying the judgment. The attendance of such witness for examination may be compelled by the service upon him of an order or a subpoena. The order may require the production of books, records and papers. The form of the subpoena is substantially as provided in C.P.A., § 775, except that it must contain a statement that it is void unless served within two years from the date of the judgment.

C.P.A., § 782-a, a new section, effective September 1, 1938, provides that the attorney for the judgment creditor may, within the time allowed for examination of witnesses under C.P.A., § 782, issue a subpoena directed to any financial institution, the main office or any branch office whereof is located within the jurisdiction of the court in which proceedings supplementary to judgment can be instituted on such judgment, requiring the office on which the subpoena is served to state in writing whether it has a record of any demand or time deposit account or safe deposit box maintained at such office in the name of the judgment debtor at the time of the service of the subpoena or within a period of one year prior thereto, except that as to time deposit accounts in a financial institution other than a savings bank, such period shall be limited to the current and next preceding calendar months. The contents of the subpoena is prescribed by subdivision 3. It is accompanied by an affidavit and also a form readily detachable therefrom, on which the financial institution may, if it so desires, furnish the required information. It is served personally or by ordinary or registered mail and is accompanied by a fee of twenty-five cents and a stamped envelope ad-

$ 337 

dressed to the attorney for the judgment creditor. The information is required to be furnished within seven days from the receipt of the subpoena. The statute further provides that a financial institution which wilfully fails to obey a subpoena served pursuant to this section or wilfully furnishes false information shall be liable to the judgment creditor in the sum of fifty dollars. 

§ 337. Appointment of Receiver-Form of Order. 

Upon the examination of the debtor, the attorney for the judgment creditor usually brings along a printed form of order for the appointment of a receiver. This is done so that in the event any property is disclosed, the attorney may appear before the judge of Special Term Part II with the debtor, exhibit to the judge the testimony to prove that the debtor has property whereupon the judge will sign the order. It is to be noted, however, that such proof is no longer required to obtain the order. C.P.A., § 804, as recently amended, effective September 1, 1938, provides that at any time after the institution of a proceeding, the court must make an order appointing a receiver of the property of the judgment debtor, upon application of the judgment creditor, whether or not it shall appear that the judgment debtor has property applicable to the payment of the judgment. 

No further notice thereof is required to be given the debtor where the order is signed at the conclusion of the examination or upon the return day of the order or warrant. Otherwise two days' notice of the appointment is given to the debtor personally unless dispensed with by the judge. C.P.A., § 804. The order together with papers upon which it is based is submitted for signature, leaving a blank space for the judge to insert the name of the receiver. When signed, a certified copy thereof is served upon the receiver. A bond in the amount required is obtained and filed. See C.P.A., § 804-a, for allowances to receiver. (Effective Sept. 1, 1938.) 

The order appointing a receiver may read as follows:

§ 338. Extension of Existing Receivership. 

Before the order is signed, it should be ascertained whether a receiver has already been appointed in a previous proceeding. If so, an order is made extending the receivership so as to include the subsequent proceeding for the reason that only one receiver may be appointed for the debtor's property. C.P.A., § 806. See also C.P.A., §§ 804, 807, 808, 809, 810, 796, 787. 

§ 339. Examination of Third Party. 

Upon proof by affidavit that any person or corporation has, or that there is reason to believe that he or it has, property of the judgment debtor, exceeding ten dollars in value, or is indebted to him, in a like sum, the court will make an order requiring that person or corporation to attend at a time and place specified in the order, to be examined as a third party, concerning such property, money or indebtedness. The order may contain a provision prohibiting the third party from transferring or disposing of any property claimed to belong to the judgment debtor or to which he may be entitled, or from paying out any money due or to become due to such judgment debtor until the further order of the court. For the effect of an injunction provision or stay in a third party order or subpoena, see C.P.A., § 799-a.

Unless previously vacated by order of the court or by stipulation of the parties, or the entry of an order pursuant to C.P.A., §§ 794, 796, a restraining provision remains in full force and effect for two years from the date thereof. C.P.A., § 779, subd. 1. 

Here again, instead of applying to the court for an order, the attorney for the judgment creditor may, at any time within two years from the date of the judgment,

340 333 

SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

serve the third party with a subpoena requiring his attendance for examination. C.P.A., § 779, subd. 2. The form is substantially the same as that provided in § 775 of the Civil Practice Act except that it shall contain a statement that it is void unless served within two years from the date of the judgment. To effect a restraining provision, a copy of C.P.A., § 781, is indorsed upon the copy of the subpoena served upon the third party. 

§ 340. Order for Examination of Third Party-Form. 

If one wishes to proceed by order and provide therein that the third party be enjoined from disposing of the judgment debtor's property until the further order of the court, printed forms are available which read as follows:

§ 342. Procedure After Service of Third Party Order. 

Where a third party is served, he does not, as a rule, appear upon the examination, but prepares an affidavit in which he states the details with respect to the property. If it is money, he states the amount and any other information affecting its ownership. The judgment debtor thus has the information he desires, and does not require an actual examination. 

If no affidavit is served in lieu of the examination, the judgment creditor's attorney attends at court and examines the third party, and proceeds in the same manner as upon an examination of a judgment debtor. 

§ 343. Permissive Order. 

C.P.A., § 794, as recently amended, effective September 

1, 1938, provides as follows: "1. At any time after the commencement of a special proceeding authorized by this article, the court, upon proof by affidavit to his satisfaction that a person or corporation is indebted to the judgment debtor, and upon

334-b § 343 

such notice given to such persons as it deems just, or without notice, may make an order, permitting the person or corporation to pay to a sheriff designated in the order, a sum on account of the alleged indebtedness, not exceeding the sum which will satisfy the judgment or execution, or to pay to the judgment creditor a sum on account of the alleged indebtedness not exceeding the judgment with interest unless a receiver has been appointed or a receivership has been extended to the special proceeding, and in that case to the receiver. 

2. At any time after the commencement of a special proceeding authorized by this article, the judgment creditor may by notice of motion served either personally or as the court may direct, upon the judgment debtor and such third party as described in the preceding subdivision of this section, apply to the court for an order directing the said third party to pay to the judgment creditor, unless a receiver has been appointed or a receivership has been extended to the special proceeding and in that case to the receiver, a sum on account of the alleged indebtedness not exceeding the judgment with interest. If it shall appear to the satisfaction of the court that the said third party is indebted to the judgment debtor, the court must grant such an order unless the said third party or judgment debtor shall show such facts as may be deemed by the court sufficeint to entitle the said judgment debtor or third party to a trial of the issues in an action brought by the judgment creditor or a receiver of the judgment debtor or any claimant to said indebtedness. Disobedience of such an order may not be punished as a contempt, but said order may, at any time after five days from the entry thereof, be docketed as a judgment and shall be enforceable as such. 

3. A payment thus made under either an order permitting such payment or an order directing it is, to the extent thereof, a discharge of the indebtedness, except as against a transferee from the judgment debtor in good faith and for a valuable consideration, of whose rights

$ 335 

SUPPLEMENTARY PROCEEDINGS. 

the third party had actual or constructive notice prior to the entry of the order." 

§ 344. Contempt Proceedings Upon Debtor's Failure to Appear. 

If the judgment debtor ignores the subpoena or order requiring his attendance in court upon the examination, the attorney for the judgment creditor prepares what is known as an order to show cause why an attachment should not issue for contempt. C.P.A., § 801. 

§ 345. Order to Show Cause to Punish for Contempt- Form. 

In New York County, in the City Court, the order to show cause is made returnable in Special Term Part II 

at twelve o'clock noon in accordance with the new rules. 

In other counties, it is returnable in the regular motion part; to wit, Special Term Part I. Annexed to the order to show cause, as referred to therein, are the affidavit and subpoena with proof of service thereof. Except for good cause shown, the motion to punish for contempt must be made within thirty days after the commission of the alleged contempt. It is made returnable not less than three days from the date of service. New York City 

Court Rule XIII, subds. (a), (b). 

The order to show cause is in the following form:

§ 347. Service of Order to Show Cause to Punish for Contempt. 

Care should be taken to serve the debtor personally with a copy of the order to show cause to punish for contempt. The signature of the judge who signed it and which appears on the original, is exhibited to the debtor at the time of making the service. 

§ 348. Procedure After Service of Order to Show Cause. 

The motion to punish for contempt is placed on the calendar of motions in the same manner as other motions. 

On the return day, the judgment debtor's name is called. 

If he is present, the judge as a rule, orders the attorney for the judgment creditor to proceed in the same manner to examine the judgment debtor as if the latter had appeared pursuant to the subpoena originally served upon him. 

§ 349. Procedure Upon Failure to Appear Pursuant to Order to Show Cause. 

If the judgment debtor ignores the order to show cause, the motion to punish for contempt is granted by default. The decision appears in the New York Law 

Journal. The next step is to prepare an order that attachment issue; that is, an order authorizing the sheriff to arrest the debtor. 

§ 350. Body Attachment-Form. 

In accordance with the decision of the court, a body attachment issues to the sheriff. It must be prepared

$ 350 

for signature within thirty days after the entry of the order directing its issuance. New York City Court Rule

§ 351. Procedure Following Preparation of Body Attach ment.

The attachment order with the papers upon which it is based, is submitted for signature. The original and a certified copy thereof are delivered to the sheriff's office together with the sheriff's fee. A deputy sheriff is assigned to make the arrest but before he can execute the order, he must know when and where the debtor can be found and there must be someone present who can identify the debtor; otherwise the wrong person may be arrested and the judgment creditor will be liable in an action for false arrest. Arrangement is therefore made, whereby the judgment creditor's attorney telephones the deputy sheriff just as soon as he learns of the whereabouts of the debtor. The deputy sheriff and the person who is to identify the debtor proceed immediately to the place where the debtor is to be found. The debtor invariably pays the judgment rather than submit to arrest. If he does not do so, he is taken into custody and brought before the judge sitting in Special Term Part II. The latter, as a rule, fines him the amount of the judgment which is payable in installments, and directs that upon failure to pay any of the installments, the entire amount shall become due and payable and the debtor shall be arrested and committed to jail until the fine is paid. 

§ 352. Order Imposing Fine for Contempt—Form. 

The order imposing the fine for contempt together with the papers upon which it is based is submitted for signature. When signed, a certified copy thereof is served upon the judgment debtor.

§ 353. In general. 

Assuming that the examination of the debtor in supplementary proceedings has disclosed property, the next step is to issue execution; that is, to seize or levy upon the property or otherwise take such steps as are necessary to apply it in payment of the judgment. 

§ 354. Exemptions. 

The debtor's property is subject to execution and sale to satisfy the judgment on the theory that the debtor will not be permitted to full enjoyment of property while his creditor remains unpaid. Despite this, however, certain kinds of property are exempt from execution, as for example, implements of trade; the tools of 342

§ 343 

EXECUTION. 

a mechanic, professional instruments of a physician, law books of an attorney; also, wearing apparel, furniture and cooking utensils. Certain property is exempt in a limited value only. With respect to real property, exemptions include the house ocupied as a residence; 

and also burial ground. C.P.A., § 664-678. 

§ 355. Kinds of Execution. 

There are four kinds of execution as follows: (C.P.A., 

§ 638.) 

1. Against property. 

2. Against the person. 

3. For the delivery of the possession of real property with or without damages for withholding the same. 

4. For the delivery of the chattel, with or without damages for the taking or detention thereof. 

§ 356. To Whom Executions are Directed. 

If a judgment has been rendered in the Supreme Court, the execution is directed to the sheriff. C.P.A., § 636. 

This is also true with respect to judgments recovered in New York City Court actions, except that a marshal may execute certain mandates only but not an order of arrest, a warrant of attachment or a requisition to replevy a chattel. New York City Court Act, § 28. If the judgment has been recovered in a New York City Municipal Court action, and no transcript has been issued and filed, the execution is directed to a marshal. 

N. Y. City Mun. Ct. Code, § 130. 

§ 357. To What Counties Executions May Issue. 

An execution against property can be issued only to a county wherein the judgment is docketed. An execution against the person may be issued to any county. An execution for the delivery of the possession of real property is issued to the county wherein the property

$ 359 

or a part thereof is situated. An execution for the delivery of the possession of a chattel may be issued to any county wherein the chattel is found, or to the sheriff of the county wherein the judgment-roll is filed. 

C.P.A., § 648. 

§ 358. Time Within Which Executions May Issue. 

Execution may issue as of course at any time within five years after the entry of judgment. After the lapse of five years, execution may issue in one of the following cases only: (C.P.A., §§ 652, 653). 

1. Where an execution was issued thereupon within five years after the entry of the judgment, and has been returned wholly or partly unsatisfied or unexecuted. 

2. Where an order is made by the court granting leave to issue the execution. The question of leave is discretionary and not reviewable on appeal. Van Rensselaer v. Wright, 121 N. Y. 626.

The time within which execution may issue as of course may vary in the different courts. For example, the time limit in the Albany City Court is six years. 

Albany City Court Act, § 260. This is also true in the 

New York City Municipal Court. N. Y. City Mun. Ct. 

Code, § 130. 

§ 359. Execution to Marshal-Form. 

Assuming that a judgment has been recovered and duly entered in an action brought in the New York City Municipal Court, and no transcript has been filed, the next step is to issue execution to the marshal; that is, direct the marshal, among other things, to collect the amount due on the judgment out of the personal property of the debtor and to pay the same to the clerk or to the party entitled thereto. N. Y. City Mun. Ct. Code, § 135. 

There are a number of marshals, any one of whom may be chosen to perform this duty. The execution is prepared

$ 345 

EXECUTION. 

and subscribed by the attorney for the judgment creditor. It is directed to a marshal. It states, among other things, the names of the parties, the district where and the time when rendered, the amount of the judgment and the amount due thereon. If it is an action wherein the defendant cannot be arrested, it must direct the officer to collect the amount due, if it is an action wherein the defendant may be arrested, then in addition to the foregoing, it may direct the officer, that if sufficient property cannot be found to satisfy the judgment, that he arrest the defendant and commit him to the jail of the county in the district in which the judgment was entered until he pays the judgment or is discharged according to law. The original execution with the marshal's fee of one dollar, and the address of the judgment debtor are mailed to the marshal.

The execution reads as follows:

endorsed stating the manner in which you have executed the same. 

WITNESS, Hon. William T. Keleher, one of the Justices of the said Municipal Court of the City of New York, Borough of Man hattan, Ninth District, the 14th day of February, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-six. 

§ 360. Making a Levy. 

WARREN CUTLER, 

Upon receipt of the execution, the marshal proceeds to the debtor's residence or place of business, as the case may be, and makes demand for the payment of the judgment. It is always well to advise the marshal to collect his fees from the debtor in addition to the amount of the judgment so that there will be no question as to who shall be liable therefor. New York City Mun. Ct. Code, § 178. If payment is refused, he may proceed to seize such merchandise or other articles of property as is not subject to exemption and sell it at public auction. Such seizure is known as making a levy, and consists of such acts as are necessary to subject the property to the dominion and control of the marshal. For example, where a levy is made at the debtor's place of business, the marshal posts a notice of levy upon the door, and may place a lock on the door or may hire someone to remain on the premises to watch the property levied upon. A marshal or sheriff may seize only enough property to satisfy the judgment. 

§ 361. Return of Execution. 

Within twenty days after the marshal receives the execution, he must make his return; that is, he must file the execution which he received from the attorney for the judgment creditor, with the clerk of the court wherein the judgment was entered, and endorse thereon his report to the effect that the judgment was wholly or

364 347 

EXECUTION. 

partly satisfied or returned unsatisfied, as the case may be. The marshal also notifies the judgment creditor's attorney as to the disposition. Executions, of course, may be renewed. N. Y. City Mun. Ct. Code, § 138. 

§ 362. Effect of Filing Transcript. 

Where a judgment has been recovered in the New York City Municipal Court, and a transcript thereof has been filed with the county clerk, the judgment becomes a judgment of the Supreme Court and execution is issued to the sheriff and not to the marshal. 

§ 363. Execution to the Sheriff. 

An execution issued to a sheriff is substantially in the form already considered. It differs therefrom, among other things, by requiring the sheriff to satisfy the judgment out of the personal property of the judgment debtor; and, if sufficient personal property cannot be found, then out of the real property belonging to him at the time when the judgment was docketed or at any time thereafter. C.P.A., § 643. It also requires the sheriff to return it to the proper clerk within sixty days after the receipt thereof. C.P.A., § 640. The return is made to the clerk with whom the judgment roll is filed. 

C.P.A., § 640. And where a transcript is filed, the return is made with the clerk with whom the transcript is filed. 

C.P.A., § 641. Upon receipt of the execution, the sheriff endorses thereon, the day, hour and minute he receives it. C.P.A., § 637. Printed forms of the execution are available. 

§ 364. Order of Preference Among Executions. 

When two or more executions against property are issued against the same judgment debtor, the one first delivered to an officer has preference, notwithstanding that a levy is first made by virtue of an execution subsequently delivered; but if a levy upon and sale of

8 366 

personal property has been made by virtue of the junior execution before an actual levy by virtue of the senior execution, the same property may not be levied upon or sold by virtue of the latter. C.P.A., § 680. 

§ 365. Levy Upon Earnings or Income of Judgment Debtor. 

If it develop upon the examination of the judgment debtor that the latter is employed and receives wages or a salary or that there is due and owing to him income from trust funds or profits in the amount of twelve dollars or more a week, and execution has been issued and returned wholly or partly unsatisfied, the judgment creditor's attorney may apply to the court in which the judgment was recovered without notice to the judgment debtor and upon satisfactory proof of the facts by affidavit or otherwise, for an order directing that an execution issue against such wages, debts, earnings, salary, income from trust funds or profits due. C.P.A., $ 684.

§ 369. Service of Garnishee Execution. 

After the execution has been signed, the original and copy are delivered to the marshal who files the original with the clerk of the court after he makes his return and serves the copy on the employer. The execution thus becomes a lien and a continuing levy upon the salary due or to become due to the judgment debtor to the amount specified therein and it becomes a continuing levy until both the execution and the expenses thereof are fully satisfied. Each week, therefore, the employer is obliged to deduct ten per cent of the salary and hold it for the marshal who either calls for it or arranges to have it forwarded to him. If the employer, or other person or corporation to whom the execution is directed, fails or refuses to pay the amount to the marshal, the former becomes liable in an action therefor by the judgment creditor. If more than one execution has been issued and served on the employer, the latter must satisfy the executions in the order in which they are served upon him; that is, he must pay the first execution in full before proceeding to make payment on the next execution served upon him. C.P.A., § 684.

The marshal in turn forwards the amounts so received to the judgment creditor's attorney. 

§ 370. Modification of the Execution. 

The statute provides that either party may apply on notice to the other party for a modification of the execution and that if and when the execution is modified, it continues in full force and effect until fully paid and satisfied or until further modified. C.P.A., § 684. 

§ 371. In Matrimonial Actions. 

In matrimonial actions, where the decree directs the husband to pay his wife alimony, the statute provides that she may sequester his property and have a receiver

$ 371 

appointed thereof. C.P.A., §§ 1171, 1171-a. And where it appears presumptively, to the satisfaction of the court, that payment cannot be enforced by means of the sequestration of the husband's property, the wife may move by order to show cause to punish him for contempt for failure to make payment. C.P.A., § 1172. Execution may issue, however, where application is first made for an order to docket the arrears of alimony as a money judgment. For example, assuming that the plaintiff has been granted a final decree of divorce awarding her alimony and the husband has failed to make payments pursuant thereto, she may apply for an order directing the clerk to make a docket at the foot of the final decree in the total sum of the arrears. The practice on a motion of this sort is described in Chapter XXVI.

§ 372. In General. 

Where a party feels aggrieved by reason of an adverse decision, or verdict, he may ask an appellate court to review the proceedings if there is reason to believe that a favorable decision or verdict should have been rendered. Before an appeal is taken, however, it is advisable to consult the authorities to determine whether there is a basis for it. For example, if the ground of appeal involves a question of law, such as an erroneous charge to the jury or the exclusion of evidence which should have been admitted, one is justified in proceeding therewith, because the judges can decide the question from a mere reading of the record and supporting briefs. 

But where the case involves a question of fact, which has been decided by a jury, a different situation arises; for the jury in the lower court had the advantage of observing the witnesses and the manner in which they testified and were thus in a better position to determine whom to believe and whom not to believe; whereas the appellate judges would be obliged to determine from a mere reading of the testimony which side was telling the truth. This would be obviously unfair. obviously unfair. Under the circumstances, appellate courts refuse to disturb the verdict of a jury based upon the determination of a pure question of fact unless some other circumstance arises as, for example, where the verdict is against the weight of evidence; that is, where there is no evidence to support the verdict and this, of course, would be obvious from a mere reading of the record. 

§ 373. Parties to Appeal. 

The party who appeals is the appellant.

The adverse party is the respondent. C.P.A., § 561. 

§ 374. Time Within Which to Appeal. 

One may appeal from an order as well as from a judgment. Immediately upon receipt of a judgment or

$357 

APPEALS. 

order with notice of entry, the attorney for the appellant should make a diary entry thirty days hence as the last day within which to appeal; that is, to serve a notice of appeal. This is the time limit for appeals taken from orders and judgments of the Supreme Court and New 

York and Albany City Courts. C.P.A., § 612; N. Y. City Court Act, § 62; Albany City Court Act, § 286. An appeal to the Court of Appeals is taken within 60 days.

C.P.A., § 592. In the Municipal Courts, of New York 

City and Syracuse, the notice of appeal is served within twenty days. New York City Mun. Ct. Code, 156, Syracuse Mun. Ct. Code, § 156. It is important to note that a court is without power to extend the time within which to appeal. $ 375. Where Heard.

Appellate Term-Appeals from judgments and orders of the City Court or the Municipal Court of the City of New York are heard by not less than three justices of the Supreme Court in each of the first and second judicial departments. They are designated for that purpose by the justices of the appellate division and constitute the Appellate Term of the supreme court in the first and second departments respectively. After an appeal has been heard by the Appellate Term and the decision is adverse, the aggrieved party may ask for a re-argument of the appeal or in the alternative for permission to appeal to the next higher court; to wit, the appellate division. If the application is denied, the aggrieved party may move in the appellate division for permission to appeal thereto. C.P.A., § 627.

Appellate Division Appeals from judgments and orders of the supreme court as well as appeals from decrees and orders of the surrogate's court are heard in the appellate division. There is an appellate division in each of the four departments. An appeal from a

& 376 

judgment or order of the supreme court must be heard in the department embracing the county in which the judgment or order appealed from is entered, unless otherwise ordered. C.P.A., § 617. After an appeal has been heard and the decision is adverse unless the case is one in which a further appeal may be taken, as of course, the aggrieved party may ask for a re-argument of the appeal or in the alternative for permission to appeal to the next higher court; to wit, the Court of 

Appeals. If the application is denied, the aggrieved party may move in the Court of Appeals for permission to appeal thereto. C.P.A., §§ 608-621. 

Court of Appeals-One may appeal to the Court of Appeals as of right where among other things, the judgment or order has been reversed or modified by the appellate division or where one of the justices of the latter court dissents from a decision thereof. Seven judges preside. C.P.A., §§ 588-607. 

Other Appellate Courts-Appeals from the orders and judgments of the Albany City Court are taken to the 

County Court of the County of Albany. Albany City Court Act, § 285. See other local court acts. 

§ 376. Notice of Appeal-Form. 

The first step necessary to commence an appeal is to prepare, serve and file a notice of appeal. The notice is to the effect that the appellant appeals from the judgment or order or from a specified part thereof. 

C.P.A., § 562. The title of the notice of appeal is that of the court in which the judgment or order was rendered. 

Assuming that the appeal is taken to the Appellate Division from an order of the Supreme Court, it would read as follows:

§ 377. Service and Filing Notice of Appeal. 

A copy of the notice of appeal is served upon the attorney for the adverse party. The original with proof of service thereof is filed with the clerk of the court wherein the judgment or order appealed from is entered. For example, where a party appeals to the appellate division from an order of the Supreme Court,

$$ 380 

the notice is filed in the County Clerk's office. Upon an appeal to the Court of Appeals from an order of the appellate division, made upon an appeal from the surrogate's court, the notice of appeal is filed with the clerk 

· of the surrogate's court. C.P.A., § 562. 

§ 378. Undertaking. 

Where appeals are taken to the Appellate Term or Appellate Division, it is not necessary for the appellant to furnish a bond unless, of course, it is an appeal from a judgment for a sum of money and the purpose is to stay the marshal or sheriff from levying upon the property pending the decision on the appeal. But with three exceptions however, where appeals are taken to the Court of Appeals, an undertaking in the sum of five hundred dollars must be furnished to perfect the appeal; that is, to render the notice of appeal effectual, otherwise, it may be dismissed. C.P.A., § 593. The bond may be furnished by a surety company in the manner previously considered, or in lieu thereof, a sum of money may be deposited with the clerk, or a written undertaking by other sureties may be given. Approval of the undertaking is not necessary; but exceptions to sureties may be made and disposed of as provided by law. C.P.A., $566. 

§ 379. Service and Filing of Undertaking. 

A copy of the undertaking may be served with the notice of appeal and the original with proof of service is filed with the clerk with whom the judgment or order appealed from is entered. C.P.A., § 567. 

§ 380. Case on Appeal-In General. 

After the notice of appeal has been served, the next step is to assemble all papers, which are to be sent to the printer, and consisting of the pleadings, testimony

$ 361 

APPEALS. 

and evidence which were before the lower court at the time the decision or verdict was rendered, in order that the justices of the appellate court may examine them and determine whether the lower court erred in its decision or the jury rendered an unfair verdict. This is known as the record or case on appeal. C.P.A., §§ 575, 616. 

§ 381. Case on Appeal from Order. 

Where one appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, the following papers constitute the record or case on appeal: (C.P.A., § 576, Rule 234) Notice of Appeal. 

Order Appealed From. 

Notice of Motion or Order to Show Cause. 

Affidavit in Support of Motion. 

Complaint. 

Answer. 

Affidavits in Opposition to Motion.

Opinion or Affidavit of No Opinion. 

Stipulation Waiving Certification. 

When making up this list, the first two items as well as the last two must always be included. What the remaining papers will be depends upon what is recited in the order appealed from which will be either in long form or short form. Copies of these papers will no doubt be found in the office file. If the appeal is taken from an order denying a motion to strike out defenses, there will, of course, be no affidavits because the notice of motion and pleadings only were submitted on the motion. 

§ 382. Affidavit of No Opinion—Form. 

If a judge renders an opinion, it must appear in the same form as given. If there is no opinion, there should

§ 383 

be an affidavit to this effect and prepared for the printer to read as follows: 

Affidavit of No Opinion  

SS.: 

George Arnold, being duly sworn, deposes and says that he is the attorney for the plaintiff-appellant herein, and is familiar with all the proceedings had herein in making the order appealed from.

That no written opinion was rendered by the Court below. 

GEORGE ARNOLD. 

 11th day of February, 1936.

MARION MARTIN, Notary Public; New York County. 

§ 383. Stipulation Waiving Certification-Form. 

Since the papers which comprise the case on appeal are required to be exact copies of the original papers on file in the clerk's office, it would ordinarily involve a great deal of expense if the clerk were obliged to read the entire case and compare it with the papers in his office and to certify that they are exact copies. To obviate this expense, it is customary for the attorneys for the parties to stipulate to waive certification. Such a stipulation may be prepared for the printer, without the title and reading as follows: 

Stipulation Waiving Certification Pursuant to Section 170 of the Civil Practice Act, it is hereby stipulated and agreed by and between the attorneys for the respective parties hereto that the foregoing are true and correct copies of the notice of appeal, the order appealed from and all the papers upon which the Court below acted in making the order appealed from and the whole thereof and are now on file in the office of the Clerk of the County of New York and certifica-

$ 363 

APPEALS. 

tion thereof, pursuant to Section 616 of the Civil Practice Act is hereby waived.

Dated: New York, February 3, 1936. 

GEORGE ARNOLD, 

Attorney for Plaintiff-Appellant.

Attorney for Defendant-Respondent.

§ 385. Statement Under Rule 234—Form. 

The statement under Rule 234 recites the time the action or proceedings were commenced, the time of the

$ 387 

service of the respective pleadings, the names of the original parties, and whether there has been any change in parties. It reads as follows: 

NEW YORK SUPREME COURT Appellate Division-First Department. 

JOHN DOE, Plaintiff-Appellant, -against- 

RICHARD ROE,

Defendant-Respondent.

This action was commenced by the service of a summons and complaint, June 26, 1933. The defendant's answer was served 

July 14, 1934.

The action is brought to recover the sum of five thousand dollars as salesman's commissions. The answer was a general denial.
