There has been no change of attorneys or parties since the commencement of this action. 

§ 386. Extract from Clerk's Minutes. 

The extract from the minutes is a record of the result of the trial and may be obtained from the clerk of the trial term part in which the case was tried. 

§ 387. Case and Exceptions. 

The case and exceptions are the stenographer's minutes of the trial consisting, among other things, of the

389 365 

APPEALS. 

testimony, exceptions, and charge to the jury. The transcript of the minutes may be obtained from the stenographer who was assigned to the trial and recorded. the testimony in shorthand. The stenographer is entitled. to a fee for furnishing the transcript. 

§ 388. Exhibits. 

The exhibits used on the trial become part of the record. If they are voluminous, the parties may stipulate to dispense with the printing thereof and submit them upon the argument of the appeal. Again, if an exhibit requires too much space, the parties may stipulate to describe it briefly, in lieu of printing, and submit it upon the argument. 

§ 389. Stipulation Settling Case Form. 

Occasionally mistakes are made in taking down the testimony. When this happens, it may be necessary to serve a notice upon the adverse attorney for a hearing before the judge who tried the case who may make the changes relying on his memory of the trial. The attorneys, as a rule, stipulate to make the changes.. 

When the case is corrected and settled, the attorneys enter the following stipulation which becomes part of the record and reads as follows: 

Stipulation Settling Case 

It is hereby stipulated and agreed that the foregoing case contains all the evidence given upon the trial of this action and that the same be settled, signed and ordered on file and annexed to the judgment-roll herein. 

Dated: New York, February 15, 1936. 

GEORGE ARNOLD, 

Attorney for Plaintiff-Appellant.

ROLAND MANNERS, Attorney for Defendant-Respondent..

$ 392 

§ 390. Order Settling Case-Form. 

An order is required to be entered upon the stipulation settling the case. It is prepared for the printer as indicated with the name of the judge typewritten.

The printer leaves the necessary blank space in the three original copies for the judge to sign personally. 

Order Settling Case 

Upon the above stipulation, the foregoing case containing all the evidence given on the trial of this action is hereby settled and signed by me and ordered on file, and annexed to the judgment-roll herein.

Dated: New York, February 15, 1936. 

Julius Miller,

J. S. C. 

§ 391. Order Filing Record in Appellate Division-Form. 

If the appeal is taken from a judgment, the case is ordered filed by the justice or referee before whom the case is tried. The order reads as follows: 

Order Filing Record in Appellate Division Pursuant to Section 616 of the Civil Practice Act, it is ordered that the within case and exceptions be filed with the clerk of the Appellate Division. 

Dated: New York, February 15, 1936. 

Julius Miller,

J. S. C. 

§ 392. Case on Appeal to the Court of Appeals. 

The record on appeal as prepared for the Appellate Division with the additional papers such as the notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals, the order or judgment of the Appellate Division, etc., constitute the case on appeal to the Court of Appeals. Where there is reason to believe that a case will ultimately reach the Court of Appeals, it is customary to ask the printer to hold the type.

$ 367 

APPEALS. 

§ 393. Printing Case. 

Where appeals are taken from the orders or judgments of the Supreme Court or the New York City Court, the case on appeal is required to be printed. Therefore, as soon as either of the foregoing sets of papers is assembled, it is sent to the printer. Care, of course, should be taken to engage a reliable and experienced printer; for, unless the printed case complies with certain requirements as to size, margin, spacing, etc., one may experience difficulty in filing it with the clerk. The printer sets up the type and prepares three proofs which he sends to the attorney for the appellant for possible corrections. 

Where appeals are taken from New York City Municipal Court judgments, the entire case on appeal with the exception of the stenographer's minutes, is typewritten on regular brief paper. When the record is filed with the clerk of the court, he inserts therein the minutes, which were previously filed with him by the stenographer. 

§ 394. Service of Proposed Case-Form of Notice. 

Upon receipt of the proof from the printer, the attorney for the appellant sends one copy of the proposed case to the respondent's attorney for corrections, with the following notice:

NEW YORK SUPREME COURT Appellate Division-First Department. 

JOHN DOE, Plaintiff-Appellant, -against- 

RICHARD ROE, Defendant-Respondent. 

24

$ 395 

SIR: 

PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that the within is the plaintiff-appellant's proposed case on appeal.

Dated: New York, February 15, 1936. 

To: 

ROLAND MANNERS, ESQ., 

Yours, etc.,

GEORGE ARNOLD, 

Attorney for Plaintiff-Appellant,

Office and Post Office Address, 

119 Broadway,

Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. 

Attorney for Defendant-Respondent, 140 East 42nd Street,

The respondent's attorney examines the proposed case for possible corrections which he may indicate on the proof or he may write the appellant's attorney a letter indicating what corrections are to be made. The appellant's attorney examines his copy of the proof, indicates thereon all corrections which either he or the respondent's attorney has found and returns it to the printer to be made up in final form. Thirty copies are printed, three of which are originals. The latter are distinguished by the fact that the names of the attorneys are not printed in the stipulation nor is the name of the judge printed in the orders, but spaces are left blank so that they may be inserted by them in ink together with the date of such signing. They may be further distinguished by the use of different colored covers. 

§ 395. Service and Filing of Case. 

On appeals to the Court of Appeals, three copies of the case on appeal are served on the respondent. An admission of service is obtained on one original which together with seventeen copies making a total of eighteen

$ 369 

APPEALS. 

copies are filed with the clerk of the Court of Appeals.

Court of Appeals Rules VI, VII. 

On appeals to the Appellate Division, three copies are served on the respondent's attorney. Nineteen copies are filed with the Clerk of the Appellate Division. 

Appellate Division, First Department Rules IV, V. The stipulations and orders contained in the original copies must be signed before they are served and filed. 

On appeals from orders or judgments of the New York City Court, three copies are served and ten copies filed with the clerk of the Appellate Term. Rule II of the 

Rules of the Appellate Term, First Department. 

On appeals from a judgment of the New York City Municipal Court, in the First Department, one copy is served, the original with proof of service is filed with the clerk of the Municipal Court in the district wherein the action was commenced. N. Y. City Mun. Ct. Code, § 161. 

The clerk inserts the stenographer's minutes in its proper place in the case on appeal and sends it by messenger to the clerk of the Appellate Term for filing. 

The appellant's attorney, of course, has arranged, in advance, with the court stenographer for the preparation of the transcript of the testimony and the filing thereof with the clerk. 

§ 396. The Brief. 

After the case has been served and filed, the next step is to prepare the brief. In the case of the record, it was merely necessary to gather together the various papers and send them to the printer and the latter could be relied upon to arrange the papers and print them in proper form. The situation with respect to the brief is different. The success of an appeal may depend very largely upon the submission of a carefully planned and well written brief. To obtain the best results, the brief

$ 396 

should be drafted many times before it is finally submitted to the printer. 

The first page may contain, in addition to the title, a statement in whose behalf the brief is submitted, thus: 

APPELLANT'S BRIEF 

or 

BRIEF ON BEHALF OF APPELLANT 

The First Department rule provides that the name of the attorney who is to argue the appeal should appear in the upper right-hand corner.

The brief proper is divided into the following parts: 

Statement, Facts, Points of Law and authorities in sup port thereof.

Statement. The brief begins with a short introductory note known as the Statement, which indicates what the appeal is and whence it came. For example, if it is an appeal from an order, it may read as follows:

This is an appeal from an order of Mr. Justice Mitchell, entered herein on or about the 12th day of November, 1935, directing the defendant to serve an additional bill of particulars. 

If it is an appeal from a judgment, it may read as follows: 

This is an appeal from a judgment in defendant's favor entered in the City Court of the City of New York, New York County, on the jury's verdict after trial before Mr. Justice 

Schimmel and a jury.

Facts. Following the statement is a brief recital of the facts of the case in the order of their happening. The purpose of a narration of this sort is to acquaint the court at the outset with the nature of the controversy and each step from the beginning thereof, to the entry of the order or judgment. The parties must be identified and their relation to the case indicated. When preparing

§ 371 

APPEALS. 

this part of the brief, one should bear in mind that the appellate judges are not familiar with the case and that it is practically impossible for them to examine the entire record of each case in order to learn what the facts are; whereas, if the facts are presented to them in a clear and concise manner and in chronological order, they will be in a position to grasp the situation clearly to the end that they will be better able to apply the law which follows.

To test.whether the account of the facts serves the purpose for which it is intended, the attorney should put himself in the position of the appellate judge and determine for himself from a reading thereof whether he is sufficiently apprised of the facts to enable him to apply the law.

Every such statement of fact must be true and one which is contained in the record. And for the convenience of the judges the folio number in the record where it is found should appear in parentheses beside each statement of fact. If there are disputed facts, reference thereto is made and the attorney should indicate how they are overcome. They should not be ignored. A party may feel more confident of success upon an appeal if each challenge is thus met.

Perhaps instead of grouping the facts under the one heading, it may sometimes be more effective to give a separate account of the pleadings or the testimony and label the matter under the specific title. 

The Law. Following the recital of facts are the propositions of law which govern the case. Each such proposition is labelled a point and numbered consecutively. The number of points will, of course, depend upon the number of propositions of law involved. They should not, however, be numerous. They appear in sequence, as, for example, in a case wherein judgment has been entered upon a verdict in favor of the plaintiff, the defendant in appealing therefrom may state as the first point that

§ 396 

there was no evidence to support the verdict, and for the next point that the verdict should be reversed with costs. 

A point begins with the argument in favor of the proposition of law stated therein and is followed by the authorities in support thereof. For example, if the defendant claims that there is no evidence to support the verdict, he proceeds to show how he arrives at that conclusion. He may show what the plaintiff would have to prove in order to entitle him to the verdict and then show wherein the evidence was deficient. If the plaintiff were suing for a broker's commission and was required, among other things, to prove that he produced a buyer ready, able and willing to purchase, but the testimony showed that the prospective purchaser did not have funds to buy the property, the defendant would call attention to this fact as the reason why the verdict in favor of the plaintiff was erroneous. Cases may then be cited to show what the courts hold is sufficient to prove an allegation of the complaint that the buyer was ready, able and willing. It is not necessary to cite too many cases. If there are numerous authorities, those of the highest courts are chosen. If there is a decision of the Supreme Court of the United States, that should be cited. A decision of the 

New York Court of Appeals is preferable to that of the Appellate Division and the latter is preferable to a 

Miscellaneous Report. And wherever possible, the cases decided in the department wherein the appeal is to be heard should be cited. One may recite the facts of the cited case briefly and state the holding of the court, or if the language is appropriate, that may be quoted. However, if a quotation is lengthy, only the parts which best fit the situation should be quoted. If any part thereof is omitted, the omission should be indicated by asterisks. 

A quotation may be taken from one or two cases and the remaining cases may be cited. When citing cases, the official report is given; that is, the New York Supple-

$ 373 

APPEALS. 

ment citation is not given if the Appellate Division or 

Miscellaneous Report citation is available. 

Before the draft of the brief is finally submitted to the printer, a final check is made to see that the spelling of the citations and the page numbers are correct. In addition, each case should be carefully traced through Shepherd's to see that it still represents the law and has not been reversed.

The last point to the effect that the judgment or order should be reversed or affirmed does not require explana tion or citations. 

The brief concludes with the name of the attorney for the party in whose behalf it is submitted and below this and to the left appears the name of the attorney who prepared the brief. The latter is not necessary but is customary. 

§ 397. Brief on Appeal from Order-Form. 

The following is a copy of a brief which was successfully used in a libel action to reverse the order of the lower court which denied the plaintiff's motion to strike out the defenses contained in the answer. Levey v. N. Y. 

Evening Journal, 237 A. D. 255; 260 N. Y. S. 654. It is. self-explanatory. It may also serve as a guide in the preparation of memoranda of law submitted on motions. 

To be argued by

RICHARD ROE. 

NEW YORK SUPREME COURT Appellate Division-First Department. 

JOHN E. DOE, Plaintiff-Appellant, -against- 

NEW YORK EVENING JOURNAL, INC., Defendant-Respondent.

$ 397 

BRIEF FOR PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT. 

Statement. 

This is an appeal from so much of an order of Mr. Justice 

Cohn entered herein on the 14th day of July, 1932, which denied the plaintiff's motion to strike out the first and second separate defenses and the first, second and third partial defenses from the defendant's amended answer. 

The Complaint. 

This action is brought to recover damages for libel by reason of the publication of plaintiff's photograph in defendant's newspaper together with the following false, scandalous and defama tory article (fol. 14) : 

"Records, files and 'sucker lists' were seized by raiders from the District Attorney's Office when they descended on the office of J. E. Doe, and arrested him for investigation of his deals. He is shown (at left) on his way to face quiz by the District Attorney. With him is Deputy George McCall of that office, one of the raiders." (Italics ours.)

The plaintiff pleads (Paragraph "Fifth", fol. 15): 

"That by the words above quoted which were printed, published and widely circulated by the defendant as aforesaid, the defendant meant and intended to mean that plaintiff was charged with a crime and that said words were so understood by the readers of defendant's said newspaper." 

The Answer. 

The answer admits the publication; admits that the plaintiff was the president of the corporation known as J. E. Doe & Co.,

Inc., engaged in the sale of securities and in substance denies the remaining allegations of the complaint. 

In addition, there are set up two complete defenses and four partial defenses. The fourth partial defense was stricken out by the order of the Court at Special Term and is not in issue on this appeal.

$ 375 

APPEALS. 

THE DEFENSES. 

The First Defense. 

The first defense attempts to justify the truth of the publication by alleging that prior to the date of publication there was pending in the office of the Attorney General of the State of New York a complaint that the plaintiff had induced one Louise Roe to enter into an agreement to purchase certain Hearst-Brisbane bonds for $1600. upon certain alleged false representations; that pursuant to the complaint so set forth, the Attorney General of the State of New York, by his assistants and deputies, proceeded to the plaintiff's office and "commanded the plaintiff to attend forthwith at the office of the Attorney General of the State of New York, together with all his books and papers, pursuant to the complaint set forth in Paragraph 4 of this amended answer, whereupon the said plaintiff submitted to the command of the Attorney General without physical resistance, and was thereupon immediately taken to the office of the said Attorney General by officers of the State of New York, and examined pertaining to the practices of himself and J. E. Doe & Company, Inc., on the issuance, sale, etc., of securities in or from the State of New York.' (Italics ours.) 

The defense further alleges that prior to the bringing of the plaintiff to the office of the Attorney General, the plaintiff was conducting business in violation of Article 23-A of the State of 

New York and Chapter 649 of the Laws of 1921 and Acts amendatory thereto, in that the books and records which dealers in securities were and are required to keep, were not properly kept; that the plaintiff had and used in connection with his stock selling activities a list of names of individuals to whom he intended to sell Hearst-Brisbane bonds at a price far in excess of their true market price, and that the plaintiff intended to induce the said individuals to enter into contracts for the purchase of the said bonds without specifying the date and maturity and to reap a large and unconscionable profit, and to treat the said individuals as, what is commonly known in the field of selling stock, "suckers." That prior to the publication of the matter complained of, the plaintiff was engaged in the selling of bonds on the instalment plan for future delivery without.

$ 397 

delivering the bonds and without holding title to them, at the same time assuming to levy a carrying charge to the purchaser for the bonds.

The Second Defense. 

For a second defense, the defendant alleges that the publication of the matter was a fair and true report of certain “public, official and judicial proceedings, to wit, an inquiry pursuant to Article 23-A of the General Business Law of the State of New York and Chapter 649 of the Laws of 1921, and acts amendatory thereto, in regard to the practices of plaintiff and J. E. Doe & Company, Inc., in the issuance, sale and negotiation of securities in and from the State of New York by the Attorney General of said State; was published without malice and privileged." (Italics ours.)

The First Partial Defense. 

The first partial defense realleges the first complete defense.

The Second Partial Defense. 

The second partial defense realleges the first complete defense and pleads that the facts therein stated had been communicated to the defendant by trustworthy persons from trustworthy sources and were believed to be true. 

The Third Partial Defense. 

The third partial defense realleges the second complete defense.

ARGUMENT. 

The libel charges an arrest of the plaintiff by the District Attorney. The defenses sought to be stricken out show affirmatively that the statement published was untrue. These defenses, we submit, are insufficient either as a justification of the libel, or as pleas of privilege, or in mitigation of damages. 

POINT I. 

The facts set forth in the first defense and in the First Partial Defense as an alleged justification in no way sustain the truth of the publication complained of.

$ 377 

APPEALS. 

The rule is well settled that a plea of justification must set forth the facts justifying the libel. Mere assertions of truth are insufficient. 

Bingham v. Gaynor, 203 N. Y. 27 at 34;

Nunnally v. Mail & Express Co., 113 App. Div. 831; 

Wachter v. Quenzer, 29 N. Y. 547.

The gist of the libelous statement in the instant case is that raiders from the District Attorney's office arrested the plaintiff ; that Deputy George McCall of that office (to wit, the District Attorney's office) was one of the raiders, and that the plaintiff was being taken to the District Attorney's office. 

The answer shows affirmatively that this statement is untrue. 

It alleges, on the contrary, that representatives of the Attorney General "commanded the plaintiff to attend forthwith at the office of the Attorney General." The defendant carefully avoids making the statement or giving the inference in its answer that the plaintiff was arrested.

In libelous publications, words must be taken in their ordinary and accepted meaning. 

Brush v. Blot, 16 App. Div. 80;

Morse v. Press Publishing Co., 49 App. Div. 375 at 378, 379. 

The distinction between an arrest and a command to attend is marked both in common parlance and in legal definition. Arrest is defined in Funk & Wagnalls New Standard Dictionary (1924) 

at page 158; 

"Arrest. V. * * *2. Law. To take into legal custody; 

seize and hold by legal authority; apprehend;

as, to arrest a thief * **"" The word arrest is defined in Bouvier's Law Dictionary (p.

240) 

as follows: 

'Arrest.

To deprive a person of his liberty by legal authority. "A restraint, a restriction of the right of locomotion which cannot be implied in the mere notification, or summons on petition, or, any other service of such process by which no bail is required, nor restraint of liberty.' Hart v.

Flynn's Ex'r. 8 Dana (Ky.) 190." (Italics ours.)

$ 397 

The implication of the use of the term arrest is the actual taking into custody, and, when coupled with a reference to the office of the District Attorney, can leave no inference except that a person has been taken into custody charged with a crime. 

An arrest must, of necessity, carry with it the deprivation of a person's liberty and right of locomotion. The mere fact that a person is told to come before an officer and goes voluntarily, without submission to legal authority, a warrant, or force, does not constitute an arrest. To constitute an arrest, there must be custody and control importing actual restrain or detention; authority, real or assumed, to make the arrest, and intention to effect an arrest. 

Foulke v. New York Consolidated Railroad Co., 180 

App. Div. 848, aff'd 228 N. Y. 269;

People v. McKay, 166 App. Div. 614; 

Tobin v. Bell, 73 App. Div. 41.

The law is well settled that a plea of justification must be co-extensive with the libel. The facts shown in the affirmative defense must support the gist of the libel. Justification is not properly pleaded by allegations tending to show that the plaintiff was guilty of crimes other than those charged or that there were facts or circumstances which might have justified the publication of a different statement or even a slightly modified statement. 

As said by the court in Fero v. Ruscoe, 4 N. Y. 162, at pages 165 and 166: "The justification must be as broad as the charge; and if the defendant fails in an attempt to prove it true, he is entitled to no benefit from the evidence which may have tended in that direction. There is no such thing as a halfway justification. When several distinct things are charged, the defendant may justify as to one, though he may not be able to do so as to all; but as to any one charge, the justification will either be every thing or nothing. If the charge be of stealing a horse, it is not half of a defense, nor any part of one, to show that the plaintiff took the horse by a mere trespass: or if the charge of perjury, proof that the plaintiff swore falsely through an innocent mistake amounts to nothing. If the plaintiff offers evidence which goes only part of the way towards a justification, all will agree that it should be rejected, because it does not cover the whole ground; and clearly the defendant ought not to gain any

$ 379 

APPEALS. 

thing by offering to prove more than he can, and thus getting in evidence which would otherwise have been excluded." 

For instance, in Mann v. Press Publishing Co., 133 App. Div. 

29, where the libel alleged forgery, it was held that a defense setting forth facts showing that certain names had been used without authority was insufficient.

In Stock v. Keele, 86 App. Div. 136, where a statement was made that "Stock is short $6000 in his accounts in Cheektowaga, and if he had his just dues he would be behind the bars; * * it was held that a defense that Stock had been guilty of various wrongs and dishonest acts was insufficient. 

In Block v. Nussbaum, 160 App. Div. 678, where the libel charged that the plaintiff had been guilty of obtaining money by false representations, the court held that a defense showing that the plaintiff had made misrepresentations promissory in their nature was insufficient.

In Christianson v. O'Neil, 39 Misc. 11, aff'd. 82 App. Div. 636, there was a slanderous charge that the plaintiff, a tenant of the defendant, had said: "I want that gas radiator returned to me at once and if you don't I will have you arrested and behind the bars before sundown. The radiator belongs to me and you stole it from my place. You are a thief and a skin."

The defendant attempted to plead in justification that the plaintiff "wrongfully removed and took away from said premises a gas chandelier, *** the property of the defendant." The court held that the plea in justification was bad. 

See also: 

Sawyer v. Bennett, 20 N. Y. Supp. 835.

We submit that it appears from these examples of decisions of the courts that the defendant cannot equivocate. He must, if he relies on justification, present facts substantiating not misconduct of another sort, not a similar sort of facts, not a portion of the facts, but the very state of facts which the libel charges. 

As said by this court in Schieffelin v. Hylan, 205 App. Div. 360, at page 362: "It is fundamental that a plea in justification must be as broad as the charge (Xavier v. Oliver, 80 App. Div. 292; 

Young v. Fox, 26 id. 261). In determining what the charge

§ 397 

is, the scope and object of the whole article must be considered, and such a construction put upon the language used as would naturally be given to it (More v. Bennett, 48 N. Y. 472). *** It is, however, urged by the respondent that if the defense is a complete justification of any of the libelous charges it is not demurrable. This is not a correct statement of the law, as I understand it. The justification must be as broad as the libel itself, that is, of all the libelous charges made." (Italics ours.)

It is respectfully submitted that the learned Court below was in error when it held that the justification was as broad as the charge. 

The charge is that the plaintiff was arrested by a representative of the District Attorney's office. The alleged justification is that he was commanded to appear by a representative of the Attorney General at the office of the Attorney General. In considering the scope and the natural construction to be put upon the words used by the defendant in its publication, it cannot be said that the defense is the same as the libel. 

The defendant, in its defense, uses the term "commanded to attend". Due to the facts set forth in the complaint, there is no ambiguity as to what the term means. The authority of the 

Attorney General to investigate complaints in connection with the sale of securities lies in the so-called "Martin Act" (Article 

23-A of the General Business Law of the State of New York). 

Under Section 352 of the General Business Law, the Attorney 

General may require a person complained of to submit a written statement under oath or he may subpoena witnesses. A subpoena is a command to appear and is the means given to the Attorney General by the statute to compel the appearance of a witness. 

The service of a subpoena, however, does not constitute an arrest. Subpoena is defined in Bouvier's Law Dictionary 

"SUBPOENA. A process to cause a witness to appear and give testimony, commanding him to lay aside all pretenses and excuses and appear before a court or magistrate therein named, at a time therein mentioned, to testify for the party named under a penalty therein mentioned.” 

Disobedience of the subpoena without reasonable cause is made a misdemeanor, which may subsequently lead to an arrest by a

$ 381 

APPEALS. 

proper officer. But the service of the subpoena itself and the command to appear in pursuance thereof do not constitute an arrest. This Court has held (prior to the amendment of the statute making a demand for a subpoena fee a prerequisite to refusing to obey) that the failure to answer a subpoena, in the absence of payment of the subpoena fee, did not justify a 

People v. De Valdor, 234 App. Div. 50. 

There is no allegation in the defense that the plaintiff refused to obey the command to appear or the subpoena, if one was served. Nor is there any allegation that the Attorney General instituted any criminal prosecution pursuant to Section 358 of the Martin Act and that there was any arrest as a result of such prosecution.

The fact that the plaintiff went to the Attorney General's. office does not change the situation. There is no allegation that he was subjected to arrest or that the Attorney General's representative put him under arrest or threatened to put him under arrest or to take him into custody. The sole justification claimed by the defendant is that the Attorney General's representative commanded the plaintiff to appear before the Attorney General and that the plaintiff did so appear. If these facts were proven, we submit that they would not constitute evidence of an arrest. 

On the very allegations set forth in the defense, we submit that there is no evidence of justification of the libel. 

There being no ambiguity the question we submit is one of law to be determined by the Court. 

Shanks v. Stumpf, 23 Misc. 264 and 267; aff'd 34 A. D.. 623. 

POINT II. 

The Second Defense, namely, the alleged claim of privilege, is insufficient. 

In the second defense, the defendant attempts to plead privilege by reason of the fact that the publication was a fair and true report of certain "public, official and judicial proceedings, to wit, an inquiry pursuant to Article 23-A of the General Business Law of the State of New York and Chapter 649 of the Laws of 1921

$ 397 

By the very terms of the defense, the privilege is limited to the inquiry of the Attorney General under a specific statute. We submit that this inquiry cannot give rise to a privileged report. 

Section 337 of the Civil Practice Act reads as follows: 

"Sec. 337. Privileges of Newspapers in action for libel.

An action, civil or criminal, cannot be maintained against a reporter, editor, publisher, or proprietor of a newspaper, for the publication therein of a fair and true report of any judicial, legislative or other public and official proceedings, or for any heading of the report which is a fair and true headnote of the article published. 

This section does not apply to a libel contained in any other matter added by any person concerned in the publication; or in the report of any thing said or done at the time and place of the public and official proceedings which was not a part thereof."

The inquiry before the Attorney General was not judicial, legislative or public.

Section 352 of Article 23-A of the Business Law of the State of New York provides as follows: 

66 'Any officer participating in such inquiry and any person examined as a witness upon such inquiry who shall disclose to any person, other than the Attorney General, the name of any witness examined or any other information obtained upon such inquiry, except as directed by the Attorney General, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor."

In Dunham v. Ottinger, 243 N. Y. 423, the Court of Appeals said at page 432: 

66* * *the Attorney General as an administrative official charged with the duty of enforcing the statute is given the power to secure from a person whom he suspects of violation of the statute by means of questionnaire, oral examination and inspection of books, under conditions of absolute secrecy, the information which will enable him to determine whether the foundation does exist for further proceedings and which information, subject to the immunity hereinafter to be referred to, may be utilized in the prosecution authorized by the statute.

I find no bestowal upon the Attorney General of any of those judicial powers which by our Constitution are lodged with the courts. He decides nothing in a judicial way. 

He passes upon no question of civil violation or of criminal guilt. The ultimate and only end to which he can proceed

$ 383 

APPEALS. 

is by action or criminal prosecution to submit to the courts the question whether a person has been guilty of such unlawful practices that he should be enjoined from further pursuing them or should be subjected to a criminal prosecution. 

Everything which he does leading up to this point is the performance of an executive or administrative power such as has long been recognized as perfectly appropriate and valid and whatever judicial decision follows is made by the courts." ." (Italics ours.)

Since the proceeding is a secret one under the statute and since it has been held to be both secret and non-judicial by the Court of Appeals, we respectfully submit that a report of what takes place at such a proceeding cannot come within Section 337 of the Civil Practice Act or give rise to a claim of privilege. 

Furthermore, the libelous publication does not refer to anything which transpired at the hearing. The gist of the libel is not that the plaintiff appeared before the Attorney General and that certain proceedings took place; on the contrary, the libelous article states that the plaintiff was arrested by the District Attorney. Not a word is stated in the libelous article about an Attor ney General's inquiry. 

Under no circumstances would a report of a non-judicial inquiry give rise to a claim of a privileged publication. Where the proceeding is neither judicial, legislative nor public, the rule of privilege does not apply Nunnally v. Press Publishing Co., 110 

App. Div. 10. 

There is no allegation that the Attorney General exercised his discretion to make the inquiry public. Even if there had been a public inquiry, it is respectfully submitted that the rule of privilege would not apply, since it appears from the answer itself that the report was false.

As said by the court in Schaffran v. Press Publishing Co., 258 

N. Y. 207, at page 210: **Looking at the matter as a pure proposition of law, without intimating that the reporter acted wilfully or recklessly, we think that the article was not a fair and true report of the default divorce action and does not come within the protection of section 337 of the Civil Practice Act (Lee v. Brooklyn Union Publishing Co., 209 N. Y. 245; 

Campbell v. New York Evening Post, Inc., 245 N. Y. 320).

The evidence which the reporter heard did not prove to the mind of the judge, as he stated that it did, the adultery of 25

$ 397 

Mrs. Schaffran. He made a guess at what the judge would find and guessed wrong.' 

A defense of privilege is not sufficient if the report is false.

See: O'Neill v. Star Co., 121 App. Div. 849. 

We submit that the second defense, namely, that of privilege, is wholly insufficient.

POINT III. 

The First and Third Partial Defenses are insufficient. 

The first partial defense is a repetition of the first complete defense. 

The third partial defense is a repetition of the second complete defense. 

We submit that if, as we claim, the defenses are insufficient, by the same token these facts cannot be pleaded in mitigation of damages. 

There is in the complaint just one charge, namely, that the plaintiff was accused of having been arrested by the District Attorney. The only purpose of a partial defense in mitigation of damages is to show that the defendant honestly believed the facts to be true and was not actuated by malice. 

As said by the court in Mattice v. Wilcox, 147 N. Y. 624, at page 634: "Mitigating circumstances are those which, while not proving the truth of the charge, do yet tend in some appreciable degree towards such proof and thus permit of an inference that defendant was not actuated by malice in his charge. They must be of such a nature as to show that defendant, though mistaken, believed the charge to be true when it was made. The mitigating facts must be connected with or bear upon the defamatory charge. (Bush v. Prosser, 11 N. Y. 347; Bisby v. Shaw, 12 N. Y. 67; Hamilton v. Eno, 81 N. Y. 116.) Mitigating circumstances under the old system, when a justification was set up, could not be proved because they did not amount to a justification. The reasons are stated in the cases in 11 and 12 N. Y. (supra). There have been circumstances admitted as mitigating where from prior acts or publications of the plaintiff the feelings of defendant have been exasperated. They do not apply here. 

The circumstances must otherwise be such as tend to disprove malice by showing that the words were spoken in the

$385 

APPEALS. 

honest belief that they were true, with some reason for such belief and without actual malice or evil design. 

The defendant in the instant case published the report that the plaintiff had been arrested by the District Attorney. Assuming that it knew the facts it set out in the answer, how can it be said that the defendant believed the plaintiff to have been arrested by the District Attorney?

The test of malice is whether "the communication was made in good faith, believing the statements are true." See, Bingham v. Gaynor, 203 N. Y. 27, at 32.

Even a belief that the statement is true is not sufficient. As quoted by the court in Hess v. New York Press Co., 26 App. Div. 

73, at page 75, from Hartman v. The Morning Journal Association (46 N. Y. St. Repr. 184): 

'Mere belief in the truth of a publication is not sufficient to constitute good faith on the part of the publisher; he must be free from negligence as well as improper motives in making it. It is his duty to take all reasonable precaution to verify the truth of the statement and to prevent untrue and injurious publications against others.' 

The defendant does not even attempt to plead that it believed the report of the plaintiff's arrest by the District Attorney which it published or that it had any information that the plaintiff had been arrested by either the Attorney General or the District Attorney. It sets forth facts which show a totally different situation. 

We submit, therefore, that the first and third partial defenses are insufficient.

POINT IV. 

The Second Partial Defense is insufficient. 

The second partial defense is a statement by the defendant that prior to the publication of the matter complained of, the facts set forth in the first separate defense were known to the defendant and had been communicated to it by trustworthy per-

$ 398 

sons; that these facts were relied upon and were believed to be true.

In the previous point we discussed this situation as it applied to the other partial defenses. The same element vitiates the second partial defense.

The defendant realleges the first defense in the second partial defense and says in effect it had been informed that the Attorney General called on the plaintiff, commanded him to attend, and the plaintiff did attend. It did not publish that fact; it published the statement that the plaintiff had been arrested by the 

District Attorney. 

The only inference that could be drawn from the statement so published is that the plaintiff had been charged with a crime and had been apprehended and taken into custody by the criminal prosecuting authorities. The plaintiff in Paragraph "Fifth" 

of the complaint (fols. 14-15) states that as the inference. The defendant does not meet that charge; does not even submit any facts to the court which would justify a belief that the plaintiff had been arrested and charged with a crime by the District Attorney. Its defense of publication in good faith, therefore, cannot be sustained.

POINT V. 

Wherefore, it is respectfully submitted that the order of the Court below be reversed to the extent of striking out the first and second complete defenses and the first, second and third partial defenses with costs. 

Respectfully submitted,

RICHARD ROE, ROE & ROE, Attorneys for Plaintiff.

Of Counsel.

BRIEF ON BEHALF OF THE APPELLANT. 

This is an appeal from a judgment in defendant's favor entered in the City Court of the City of New York, New York County, on the jury's verdict after trial before Mr. Justice 

Schimmel and a jury.

The Nature of the Action. 

The plaintiff sued to recover from the defendant, a former salesman, the excess of moneys advanced over commissions earned by him.

The Pleadings. 

The cause of action herein involved, alleged that between 

April 1, 1931 and January 6, 1933 the plaintiff advanced to the defendant the sum of $7,081.97, which the defendant agreed to repay; that no part of the same has been repaid except $5,844.17, leaving a balance due of $1,237.80 (fols. 15-17). 

The answer is a general denial (fol. 19).

The Evidence. 

There were but two witnesses, the plaintiff's president and the defendant. The agreement of employment arose out of a conversation between these persons in March or April, 1931. 

Mr. Jones, plaintiff's president, says that in this conversation he told defendant that a salesman employed by the plaintiff is practically in business for himself (fol. 36); a commission is paid on business returned by the salesman or received from

$ 398 

the salesman's territory and type of trade (fols. 36, 37); plaintiff preferred to have their men finance themselves, but if Mr. 

Smith did not have sufficient funds to finance himself, the plaintiff was willing to advance him such weekly sums against his commissions, that might be necessary to carry him until such time as he was earning large enough commissions to carry himself (fols. 37-38). Smith (Jones says) explained that he did not have enough funds to carry on and that he would require some advance every week for his home expenses and when traveling (fol. 39); it was agreed that $75 a week was to be advanced against his commission (fols. 38-40). Jones said 

"I explained very carefully he was in business for himself, that his earnings depended on his own efforts and results, and any earnings he got would be credited to him and all sums due him would be paid him. Any sums which we advanced that he did not earn was due us at some future date when he was called upon to pay it." (Italics ours.) 

To this the defendant agreed (fol. 41).

The defendant remained in plaintiff's employ until January 1933 (fol. 71). By that time there had been advanced to him an aggregate of $7,113.48 which had been reduced by credits to $1,237.80 (fol. 53).

One searches the record in vain to find direct denial by the defendant of the portion of the employment agreement requiring repayment of advances. He says that he was employed "as a salesman covering the New England territory, which was this $75 was a drawing account charged against commission" (fol. 

156). On direct examination defendant testified (fol. 169): "Q. Mr. Jones testified that on a number of occasions you said you would return moneys that you overdrew in 1931. Was there any such conversation ever had in which you said any such thing? A. Aboslutely not. 

Q. Did Mr. Jones up to the time that you were in the employ of the plaintiff at the end of 1932 ever speak to you about returning any overdrafts either in 1932 or 1931? 

A. No."

Obviously these questions and answers relate to conversations after the hiring and after the money had been advanced. 

On cross examination, however, defendant admitted (fols. 204-206):

$ 389 

APPEALS. 

"Q. Then there was some talk about your overdraft, wasn't there? A. The 1931 overdraft, right.

Q. There was talk about that, wasn't there? A. The 

1931 overdraft. 

Q. And Jones stated you owed it to them, didn't he? 

A. He said that he would wipe it off. 

Q. He said you owed them twelve hundred and some odd dollars? A. Whatever the amount was, correct. 

Q. And you didn't deny it, owing it to him, did you? 

A. No, I did not. 

Q. And now you say that they cancelled it; is that right? 

A. Not "they"; Mr. Jones, otherwise I—

Q. Didn't you testify that you never denied owing that money to Doe? A. Not for 1931, I never denied it. 

Q. Didn't you say that there was no conversation where you admitted that you owed that money? A. Not for 1931. 

I never denied it. 1932, yes. 

Q. In 1931 you did owe them $1200? A. Right.” 

Seizing upon the circumstance that some nine months after the employment there had been a change of territory, duties and rates of commission, defendant's counsel upon cross examination of plaintiff's witness, injected a new and unpleaded element into the case. He asked (fols. 121–123) : "Q. We will come to the indebtedness. I ask you to look at your bill of particulars again. All of this indebtedness or practically all resulted by the end of 1931, didn't it? A. At the end of 1931 he owed us $1224.

Q. I said all of this indebtedness that you claim is shown to have accrued as claimed at the end of 1931? A. At the end of 1931, according to our claim he owed us $1,224. 

Q. And if you segregate and separate 1931 from 1932, in 1932 the payments you gave him whether as advances or commissions just about equalled his earned commission; isn't that right? A. Slightly below, his earnings were slightly below the segregation of 1932. 

Q. A matter of less than $100. A. That is correct.

Q. And at the end of 1931 and at the beginning of 1932 you made this new arrangement with him of which this memorandum is some evidence, is that right? A. That is correct. 

The memorandum referred to is Defendant's Exhibit A (p. 

99), which is silent, as to advances or drawing accounts. merely recites additions to territory, and provides for additional compensation for handling a department store division. There

$ 398 

is no mention of the cancellation, release or relinquishment of the $1200 indebtedness.

No such defense was set up in the answer, and therefore no such issue could properly be considered by the jury. Yet by the sequence and purport of these questions the jury may well have been misled into believing that such an issue was presented. 

Where as a result of that situation, the question arose in the cross examination of defendant on the query whether defendant had asked for a provision cancelling the indebtedness, he did not deny owing the $1200 for 1931 but said that Jones had said he "would wipe off my overdraft of 1931" (fol. 204).

Since the only issue to be considered was whether there had been an agreement to repay the advances, and since the question of cancellation had been injected by defendant's counsel, plaintiff requested the court to charge (fol. 246) "if the jury finds that there was an agreement to repay there is no issue in this case of cancellation since there was no cancellation or waiver of payment, or payment pleaded.” 

This request the court refused, saying (fol. 247) : "I decline to so charge having already defined the only issues in this case. 

POINT I. 

The charge requested should have been granted. 

The sole question of fact to be decided by the jury was whether an agreement had been made to repay the advances. 

If defendant had desired to present an issue of cancellation or relinquishment of the indebtedness it was incumbent upon him to plead that defense. It was not available to him under a general denial.

As said by the Court in Ramme v. Long Island R. R. Co., 226 

N. Y. 327 at 332: "Where the defendant relies upon new matter by way of confession and avoidance of the claim of the plaintiff it must be specially pleaded. 

In Brazil v. Islam, 12 N. Y. 9, the Court said at page 17: "The plaintiff in his complaint had stated a prima facie 

To meet the case thus made by new

$ 391 

APPEALS. 

matter constituting a defense, it must be set forth plainly in the answer. 

Not only was no such defense pleaded in the answer, but no motion was made by defendant at the trial to set up that defense. It is apparent therefore that he was prepared to stand or fall on the sole question of the existence of an agreement to repay the advances.

It is true that in his charge the learned trial judge presented this issue to the jury.

We submit however that the jury having had instilled in their minds the theory presented in the first instance by the defendant's counsel that a new arrangement had been made later on, should have been instructed specifically that no issue of cancellation of the indebtedness was before it. 

In Sedwards v. Long Island Railroad Co., 155 App. Div. 596, the Court, at pages 599-600, said: "The instructions thus given correctly and clearly stated the general rules applicable to such questions; but in the particular circumstances of the case at bar, where the allegations of the complaint and the statement in the bill of particulars and the testimony of the plaintiff are all definite and show that the accident occurred on the twenty-first of June, we are of opinion that the right of the plaintiff to recover should have been confined to an accident occurring on that day."

In the instant case the defendant made no attempt to correct his pleading to set up the issue of cancellation, but rested entirely on his denials. The requested instruction would have made that situation clear to the jury. See: 

Matter of Taylor, 197 App. Div. 865. 

In Franklin v. Hoadley, 145 App. Div. 228, the Court, at page 231, said: "And whenever such issue is presented at a trial before a jury, then specific instructions should be given to this effect." 

In Smith v. Green Fuel Economizer Co., 123 App. Div. 672, at page 674: "There was some evidence about the floor of the shop being to some extent greasy, but only as is necessarily the

$ 398 

case in all machine shops; and yet the learned trial judge spoke of that to the jury, and apparently left them to find a verdict for the plaintiff on that ground; but the accident did not happen from a greasy floor, nor is there any allegation in the complaint that it did, nor was there any proof that the floor was dangerous from grease. 

The issue to be considered by the jury is that which is pre- 'sented by the pleadings. Although the following case was decided under the Ohio laws, nevertheless it presents a concise and sound statement of the law. In Henkel & Sullivan v. Robinson, 27 Ohio App. 341, the Court, at page 343, said: "An issue is a single, certain, and material point deduced from or arising out of the pleadings. The pleadings, and not the evidence, must be looked to in determining the issue to be presented to the jury. These rules have been deduced from judicial decisions in order that the lay mind may grasp the issue and be able to determine the questions presented for its consideration."

In the face of the defendant's admission that he never denied owing the $1200 for the year 1931, it is inconceivable that the jury should have found a verdict in his favor unless it believed that it could do so on the ground of cancellation. 

It is not sufficient for defendant to argue that he might have amended his answer to conform to the state of the record at the close of his case to raise this issue. Nor is it sufficient for the defendant to argue that the plaintiff questioned the defendant about the injected theory of cancellation, the defendant elected to stand strictly on the issue of the denial. Had the answer been amended, plaintiff would have had an issue to rebut. The jury would have had before it the full question with appropriate instructions as to that issue.

In view of the fact that defendant elected to stand on his denials, we respectfully submit that the charge requested was not only a proper one, but was necessary to define the issue and should have been granted.

POINT II. 

The judgment should be reversed with costs. 

Respectfully submitted,

ROE & ROE, Attorneys for Plaintiff-Appellant.

§ 399. Serving and Filing Brief. 

The proposed brief is sent to the printer. The proof is examined, and returned with the corrections noted thereon. When it is received from the printer in final form, the requisite number of briefs is served and filed in the same manner as the case on appeal. See pertinent court rules. On appeals from the New York City Municipal Court, however, although the record is required to be filed in the district court, nevertheless the briefs are filed directly with the clerk of the Appellate Term. 

§ 400. Respondent's Brief and Reply Thereto. 

Within a specified time after the service of the appellant's brief, the respondent must serve and file the requisite number of briefs as prepared by him. Thereafter the appellant may serve a reply brief either pursuant to the rules or with the permission of the court. 

See pertinent court rules. 

§ 401. Notice of Argument—Form. 

Just as it is necessary to serve and file a note of issue in order that a case may be placed upon the calendar by the clerk and reached for trial in its regular order, it is equally necessary, in the case of an appeal, to prepare, serve and file a notice of argument. Before drawing the notice, the rules of the Appellate Division of the various departments should be studied. For example, in the First 

Department, appeals are divided into enumerated and non-enumerated appeals. The former includes, among other things, appeals from judgments and orders denying motions to strike defenses. The latter includes appeals from orders. The enumerated appeals may be noticed for any day of the term; the non-enumerated appeals may be noticed for motion days only. There are two such motion days in a term, and occur on a Friday. To determine which days are motion days, it is necessary to know on what day a term begins. This varies in the dif-

8 401 

ferent departments. In the First and Second Departments, the information is available in the New York Law 

Journal. In other courts, the clerk may be consulted.

A copy of the notice of argument is served upon the adverse attorney. The original with proof of service is filed with the clerk of the appellate court. It reads as follows: (Rule IV of the Rules of the Appellate Division, First Department).

§ 404. Calendar Practice. 

Court of Appeals. The calendar of appeals is published in the New York Law Journal and the attorneys

$ 404 

for the parties watch the progress thereon from day to day. The clerk of the court sends the attorneys notice by telegram the evening before the day on which the hearing is scheduled to be heard.

Appellate Division. The clerk of the Appellate Divi sion, First Department, prepares two calendars, one for the non-enumerated appeals and the other for the enumerated appeals. If the appeal is a non-enumerated appeal, the attorneys appear on the day for which the appeal is noticed for argument, and may either argue it or mark it "submitted". It is heard immediately after the motion calendar which is called at nine o'clock in the morning. If the appeal is an enumerated appeal, the

Law Journal must be watched until the list of new appeals appear with calendar numbers. Note should be made of the calendar number so that the daily progress of the appeal may be watched until it appears on the regular calendar. When that happens, the attorneys appear and answer the calendar call. The court convenes at two o'clock in the afternoon. The appeal may be marked "submitted". If it is to be argued, counsel for each side is asked to state how much time his argument will require. After the calendar call, or as soon thereafter as is practicable, the court announces how many of the appeals which have been marked "ready" will be heard. The remainder are adjourned until the following day.

In the Appellate Division of the Third and Fourth 

Departments, the clerk of each such department prepares two calendars, to wit, the order calendar and general calendar. Because the rules vary somewhat, it is advisable to consult the local department rules. 

Appellate Term. The calendar of appeals from New 

York City Court judgments or orders is called on a Monday and that of the New York City Municipal Court is called on a Tuesday of a week to be announced in the Law Journal. The calendar is published some days in ad-

407 397** 

APPEALS. 

vance. And, on the day thus specified, the attorneysappear to mark the appeals "submitted" or to argue them.

See local court rules for the practice on appeals to the county courts. 

§ 405. Decision. 

The decisions of the appellate courts, that is, those of the United States Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals,. 

and the Appellate Divisions of the First and Second De partments, appear in the New York Law Journal from time to time. The decisions of the Appellate Division of the First Department are published on a Saturday, but are available to those who call the clerk on Friday morn-ing. See local newspapers in other parts of the state. 

§ 406. Service of Order With Notice of Entry. 

When the decision appears in the Law Journal, one may call at the Clerk's office, make a copy of the order embodying the decision, and serve a copy thereof with notice of entry. 

§ 407. Taxation of Costs-Remittitur. 

As a rule, the order will state the amount of costs to be paid by the adverse party. If not, and costs are awarded, a bill of costs may be taxed in the manner already considered. And as already stated, the costs are taxed in the court from which the appeal was taken and not in the appellate court. But before this can be done, the judgment or order of the appellate court must be remitted to the court below. C.P.A., § 606.

On appeals from the supreme court or county court where, for example, an order of affirmance is made by the appellate division, a certified copy thereof and the original case or papers upon which the papers were heard are transmitted by the clerk of the appellate division to the clerk of the county where the judgment or order-

$ 409 

appealed from was entered. Thereafter judgment is entered in the county clerk's office and becomes the judgment of the appellate division. Foley v. Carter, 214 

A. D. 292, 212 N. Y. S. 381. Costs may then be taxed and a further appeal taken. C.P.A., § 621. See also

C.P.A., §§ 621 and 629, for practice where appeals have been taken from other and inferior courts. 

§ 408. Dismissal of Appeal for Failure to Prosecute. 

Appeals, like actions, may be dismissed for failure to prosecute. Where, for example, the appellant serves and files his notice of appeal within the time limited therefor, but fails to prepare and serve the proposed case on appeal or to serve and file a brief within the time limited therefor or for any other unreasonable delay, the respondent may move on three days' notice to dismiss the appeal. Appellate Division, First Department, Rule V. 

See pertinent rule of the appellate division of other departments.

§ 411. Calendar Practice. 

In the First Department the notice of motion is served five days before the return day and is made returnable on one of the two Fridays of the term which is designated as a motion day. A note of issue is prepared and filed with the clerk before twelve o'clock noon on the day preceding the return day. The motion is marked "submitted" on the return day. II. See also Appellate Division, Fourth Department, 

Rule IV, and pertinent rule of other departments.

§ 412. Decision. 

The decision on a motion to dismiss an appeal is invariably to the effect that the motion is granted unless the appellant proceeds with the appeal and places it upon the calendar for the term indicated therein. The court also imposes costs.

§ 413. Mortgage Defined. 

Under the early common law of England, where real property was conveyed, the legal estate was vested in the mortgagee, to be defeated by the performance of a condition subsequent; to wit, payment at the law day. In default of such payment, the title became absolute and irredeemable in the mortgagee. This rather drastic rule was modified by equitable principles to relieve mortgagors against forfeitures with the result that in England, the New England States, and in many States. of the Union, the courts hold that legal title passes to the mortgagee and becomes by default absolutely vested in him at law, and the mortgagor has after default, nothing but an equity of redemption; that is, a right to redeem the mortgaged premises, to be enforced in a court of equity. In this State, however, the common law has never been adopted to its full extent. Here, the mortgagor has, both in law and equity, been regarded as the owner of the fee, and the mortgage has been regarded as a mere chose in action; a security of a personal nature. Trimm v. Marsh, 54 N. Y. 599; Becker v. McCrea, 193 N. Y. 423. The mortgagor, both before and after default, is entitled to the possession of the premises of which he cannot be deprived without his

414 403 

consent, except by foreclosure. Trimm v. Marsh, 54 N. Y. 

599; Prudence Co. v. 160 W. 73rd St. Corp., 260 N. Y. 

205. And since the mortgagor continues to own the land, while the mortgagee's interest is that of a creditor only, payment at any time after the mortgage debt becomes due and before foreclosure, destroys the lien of the mortgage and restores the mortgagor to his full title without a reconveyance. Trimm v. Marsh, 54 N. Y. 599.

And therefore, until the sale, a mortgagor in sole possession of the mortgaged premises, is entitled to such possession as against a receiver appointed in an action to foreclose the mortgage and cannot be compelled to pay for the value of the use and occupation of the property. 

Holmes v. Gravenhorst, 263 N. Y. 148. 

§ 414. Foreclosure of Mortgage-Methods. 

A mortgage, like any other contract, contains certain terms and conditions, the breach of any of which entitles the mortgagor to relief known as foreclosure of the mortgage whereby the equity of redemption is fore closed and extinguished. C.P.A., §§ 1077–1088-a; Rules 255-267 of the Rules of Civil Practice. Failure to pay principal and interest as provided for in the instrument, is an example of such a breach. The following are the methods by which a mortgage may be foreclosed: 

1. Foreclosure by action in equity. This is an action whereby all persons who acquired liens subsequent to the execution of the mortgage are sued to the end that their equity of redemption may be forever barred and extinguished; and where the judgment entered therein, authorizes a sale of the property and decrees that the proceeds thereof be applied in satisfaction of the mortgage indebtedness, the expenses of the action and of the sale, and other liens and encumbrances as provided therein, and to distribute the surplus, if any, to those entitled thereto in the order of their priority. Wilkinson et al. v. Paddock et al., 57 Hun 191, 11 N. Y. S. 442, aff'd 125 N. Y. 478. Because this method is most fre-

8 414 

quently employed, each step in the action will, hereinafter, be discussed in detail. 

2. Strict foreclosure. Although this is likewise by action in equity, it nevertheless is seldom employed; for, as the court in Silver v. Berger, 228 A. D. 591, 240 N. Y. S. 

468 points out, the remedy is regarded as harsh and generally inequitable and not to be encouraged in this state, citing Bolles v. Duff, 43 N. Y. 469; Moulton v. 

Cornish, 138 N. Y. 133; Denton v. Ontario County 

National Bank, 150 N. Y. 126. Unlike the other two methods, absolute title is transferred without a sale. 

C.P.A., 1082 provides that the judgment instead of directing a sale of the property, shall fix the time within which the property shall be redeemed by a person having or claiming the right to redeem or foreclose a second or subsequent mortgage or lien that has been matured for at least five years and shall provide that a failure to redeem or commence an action for the foreclosure of such mortgage or lien within such time, will preclude the mortgagee or lienor from redeeming the property or foreclosing the mortgage and exclude such person from claiming title or interest therein and all such title and interest therein, will be extinguished or terminated. See 

Wait's N. Y. Practice Vol. 5 [4th Ed.] pages 245-248. 

3. Foreclosure by advertisement. This method is used in a case where the mortgage instrument itself provides for the exercise of the power to sell by a person or his assignee. This method is not looked upon with favor because it is strictly statutory and requires a strict compliance with the statute. In other words, statutory proceedings to foreclose a mortgage are not proceedings in court, so as to authorize the courts to remedy defects in them. Dwight v. Phillips, 48 Barb. 116. Real

Property Law, §§ 540-563; see Wait's N. Y. Practice 

Vol. 1 [3rd Ed.] 191-200. 

4. Action at law on bond. A party is not, however, obliged to proceed in the first instance by suit to foreclose the mortgage but may, at his option, commence an action at law upon the bond to recover the mortgage

$ 

405 debt. But he cannot avail himself of both remedies at the same time. C.P.A., § 1078 expressly provides that while an action to foreclose a mortgage upon real property is pending or after final judgment for the plaintiff therein, no other action shall be commenced or maintained to recover any part of the mortgage debt, without leave of the court in which the former action was brought. Such leave is within the discretion of the court and is dependent upon the circumstances of the case. Tousey v. Barber, 132 Misc. 861, 231 N. Y. S. 133.

The general rule is that leave will not be granted except for "good reasons". Carlin v. Lindtveit, 175 A. D. 940, 161 N. Y. S. 1120. The reason for this rule is that otherwise the plaintiff would be able to recover costs in two actions and subject the defendant to the trouble and annoyance of the dual litigation. In re Byrne, 81 A. D. 

74, 80 N. Y. S. 977; Equitable Life Ins. Soc. of the United 

States v. Stevens, 63 N. Y. 341; McKernan v. Robinson, 84 N. Y. 105.

C.P.A., § 1077 further provides that where final judgment for the plaintiff has been rendered in an action to recover any part of the mortgage debt, an action shall not be commenced or maintained to foreclose the mortgage, unless an execution against the property of the defendant has been issued upon the judgment and has been returned wholly or partly unsatisfied. Scheidell, et al v. Llewellyn Realty Co., 177 N. Y. S. 529. 

§ 415. Moratorium Laws. 

An action to foreclose a mortgage may be maintained only in the event that it does not come within the mortgage moratorium laws which were enacted in 1933 when the legislature declared the existence of an emer gency as defined in Section 1077-g of the Civil Practice 

Act. C.P.A., § 1077-a provides that during the emergency period, no action shall be maintained to foreclose a mortgage on real property solely for or on account of a default in the payment of principal or any installment thereof. C.P.A., § 1077-b provides that no action shall

8 415 

be maintained or judgment entered, during such period, upon a bond or other evidence of indebtedness for like defaults. In defending the constitutionality of these measures, the court in McCarty et al. v. Prudence Bonds 

Corp., 149 Misc. 13, 266 N. Y. S. 629, pointed out that in enacting these laws, the legislature sought to protect the mortgagor of real property against foreclosure of the mortgage and against an action on the bond, in the expectation that in the meantime, business and finance, and the conditions of real property, in particular, might rectify themselves; that this purpose could not be secured merely by suspending the foreclosure of mortgages, but it was necessary also to suspend enforcement of bonds secured by the mortgage, for otherwise the property would frequently be sold to satisfy a judgment recovered on the bond. 

It is to be noted, however, that the legislature required the payment of interest, taxes and other carrying charges, and as to property not used for farming or dwelling purposes, it imposed additional conditions. 

C.P.A., § 1077-c. Johnson v. Meyer, 268 N. Y. 701; Cole v. Miller, 150 Misc. 32, 268 N. Y. S. 443; McCarty v. 

Prudence Bonds Corp., 149 Misc. 13, 266 N. Y. S. 629.

The period of emergency as originally defined, was extended to July 1, 1938, except that any payments of principal, or installments thereof which became due prior to July 1, 1934 would become due and payable six months after the expiration of the emergency period while those payments which became due and payable between July 1, 1934 and July 1, 1937, would become due one year after the expiration of the emergency period. C.P.A., §§ 1077-a, 1077-b. Chapter 500 of the 

Laws of 1938 further extended the emergency period to 

January 1, 1940. This statute covers Sections 1077-a to g inclusive, and 1077-cc of the Civil Practice Act, and amends C.P.A., § 1077-g. 

Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions, C.P.A., § 

1077-c provides that any person who would otherwise have the right to foreclose a mortgage, shall have the

415 407 

right to make an application to any court in which such foreclosure action might be brought upon eight days' notice, and if, upon such application, it shall appear that the mortgaged property during the six months. prior to the application, shall have produced a surplus over and above the taxes, interest and all other carrying charges, the court may make an order directing the payment of such surplus or such part thereof as the court may determine to the mortgagee to apply toward the reduction of any past due principal. In the event of default in making of such payment for thirty days. after service of a copy thereof with notice of entry thereof, then and in such event, the applicant may maintain an action to foreclose the mortgage. 

And during the emergency period, C.P.A., § 1077-cc, provides that the rate of interest on such bond or other evidence of indebtedness contracted for simultaneously with the mortgage and secured by such mortgage shall not be increased by reason of the maturity of such obligation during the emergency period. And any covenant or agreement whereby the mortgagor agrees to waive the protection intended to be afforded him by C. P. A., §§ 

1077-a, 1077-b, and 1077-cc, shall be deemed void. C.P.A., 1077-d. 

The moratorium laws were made applicable to pending cases, and provided, among other things, that with respect to actions instituted before or after the emergency period, where the action has not proceeded to final judgment, the action may be dismissed upon payment by any defendant to the plaintiff of taxable costs and disbursements and remedying any default other than the payment of principal or any installment thereof. And where the action had proceeded to judgment directing a sale of the premises, the sale could be stayed in like manner. C.P.A., § 1077-e. It was further provided that the statute of limitations shall not run during the period of emergency with respect to actions or proceedings within the act which otherwise would have been main tainable. C.P.A., § 1077-f. Section 1077-g of the Civil

8 416 

Practice Act refers to the mortgages which are not affected by these laws. 

Section 1083-a provides for a limitation upon deficiency judgments during the emergency period and the manner of determining the fair and reasonable market value of the mortgaged premises. The purpose of this section was to set up a new equitable standard for dealing with the question of deficiency judgments growing out of foreclosures; on the one hand to protect the unfortunate mortgagors, and, on the other, to allow mortgagees, when equitable in the circumstances to secure deficiency judgments. Heiman v. Bishop et al., 272 N. Y. 83.

Section 1083-b provides that in an action to recover a judgment for an indebtedness secured by a mortgage, the defendant shall be entitled to set off the fair and reasonable market value of the mortgaged premises less the amounts owing on prior liens and encumbrances. 

This section when read with §§ 1077-a, 1077-b, and 1083-a, affords protection not only to makers of original mortgages, bonds and guarantors thereof, but also to any party who is contingently liable as guarantor. City 

Bank Farmers Trust Co. v. Ardlea Corp., 267 N. Y. 224; 

Klinke v. Samuels, 264 N. Y. 114; Kramer v. Relgov 

Realty Co., Inc., 268 N. Y. 592.

Chapter 501 of the Laws of 1938 extended the emergency period with respect to Sections 1083-a and b of the 

Civil Practice Act, to July 1, 1939. This statute does not apply to mortgages dated on or after July 1, 1932.

Chapter 510 of the Laws of 1938, effective April 7, 1938, however, amends C.P.A., § 1083, to include the provisions of C.P.A., § 1083-a, and applies to mortgages dated before or after July 1, 1932; but unlike C.P.A., § 1083-a, the relief provided for is permanent and is not limited to the emergency period. 

§ 416. Procedure in General. 

A foreclosure action is commenced by the service of the summons in the same manner as other actions. If an answer is interposed, the issue proceeds to trial; if

§ 409 

not, and the court does not compute the amount due, application is made for the appointment of a referee to compute, and subsequent steps are taken for the entry of judgment and the sale of the premises. 

§ 417. When and in What Court Action is Commenced. 

If the action is not barred by the moratorium laws, a mortgage, being an instrument under seal, could formerly be foreclosed any time before the expiration of twenty years from the time the debt became due. Hulbert v. 

Clark, 128 N. Y. 295, aff'd 57 Hun 558, 11 N. Y. S. 417; 

Brooklyn Savings Bank v. Wechsler Estate, 232 A. D. 

565, 251 N. Y. S. 62; Kelley v. Hall, 144 Misc. 759, 259 

N. Y. S. 383. Under the recent amendment, however, this period was reduced to six years. C.P.A., § 47-a. (Effective Sept. 1, 1938.) 

The action is brought in the Supreme Court in the county in which the property or some part thereof is situated. C.P.A., § 183; Railroad Fed. Savings & Loan 

Ass'n v. Zelkind, 247 A. D. 110, 286 N. Y. S. 158; Manu facturers' Trust Co. v. Roerich Museum, 236 A. D. 76, 

258 N. Y. S. 284. A county court likewise has jurisdiction where the real property to which the action relates is situated within the county. C.P.A., § 67, subd. 1. 

Delaware Nat. Bank of Delhi N. Y. v. Wiss, 158 Misc. 

276, 284 N. Y. S. 615. And in the latter instance, C.P.A., § 69 provides that the county court may render any judgment or grant either party any relief which the supreme court might render or grant in a like case, and may enforce its mandates in like manner as in the supreme court. 

§ 418. Notice of Pendency-Form. 

The first step in bringing a foreclosure action is to prepare and file a notice of pendency. The purpose of such a notice is to protect the status of the property and of the parties. Bond Realty v. Pounds, 128 A. D. 91, 112 N. Y. S. 433. It is notice to the world that the plaintiff has a right of action affecting the title to, or the possession, use, or enjoyment of the property

8 418 

described therein. It states the names of the parties, the object of the action, and contains a brief description of the property in the county, affected thereby. 

C.P.A., § 120. It recites the date of the mortgage and the time and place of recording it. C.P.A., § 1080. 

The notice may be in the following form:

-against- Plaintiff,
