§ 487. Action to Annul Marriage. 

An action may be maintained to procure a judgment declaring the nullity of a void marriage or annulling a voidable marriage. C.P.A., § 1132. 

A marriage may be annulled for the following reasons:

Nonage. A marriage is void from the time its nullityis declared by a court of competent jurisdiction if either party thereto is under the age of legal consent. However, nonage in itself is not an absolute ground for annulment, but it lies within the discretion of the court which takes into consideration the facts and circumstances surrounding the marriage. C.P.A., § 1133; Dom. Rel. Law, §7; Keegan v. Keegan, 209 A. D. 74, 204 N. Y. S. 405.

Incest. A marriage is incestuous and void between an ancestor and a descendant; a brother and sister; an uncle and niece, or an aunt and nephew. Dom. Rel. Law,.

$ 487 

85. In Audley v. Audley, 196 A. D. 103, 187 N. Y. S. 652, the plaintiff, who married her uncle, brought suit for divorce. The court held that the marriage was forbidden by law and was therefore void. It was as if no marriage had taken place, and there was therefore no basis for an action for divorce. It should be noted that a divorce presupposes a valid marriage.

Mental Incapacity. A marriage is void from the time its nullity is declared by a court of competent jurisdiction if either party is incapable of consenting to a marriage for want of understanding. Dom. Rel. Law, § 7. The action may be maintained on the ground of idiocy or lunacy of either party. C.P.A., §§ 1136, 1137, 1138. 

Physical Incapacity. A marriage is void from the time its nullity is declared by a court of competent jurisdiction if either party is incapable of entering into the married state from physical cause. Dom. Rel. Law, § 7; C.P.A., § 1141. 

Fraud and Duress. A marriage is void from the time its nullity is declared by a court of competent jurisdiction if either party consents to the marriage by reason of force, duress, or fraud. Dom. Rel. Law, § 7; C.P.A., § 1139. The free and full consent which is the essence of all ordinary contracts is expressly made necessary by statute to the validity of the marriage contract. The minds must meet in one intention. It is the general rule that every misrepresentation of a material fact made with the intention to induce another to enter into an agreement and without which he would not have done so, justifies the court in vacating the agreement. Di Lorenzo v. Di Lorenzo, 174 N. Y. 467. In the cited case, the court held that a gross fraud had been practiced upon the plaintiff, whose consent to marry the defendant had been obtained by fraudulent representations, causing him to believe that he was the father of the defendant's child. 

Duress is defined as an actual or threatened violence or restraint of a man's person contrary to law, to compel

$505 

MATRIMONIAL ACTIONS. 

י. ​2 PA ​2 The him to enter into a contract or to discharge one. plaintiff must show that the duress of the party asking to be relieved was occasioned by the other contracting party, or that he knowingly used or availed himself of such duress as a means of procuring the contract sought to be annulled and that the threats constrained the will of the promisor and induced the promisee. Fraletto v. Fraletto, 193 N. Y. S. 865. In the cited case, the plaintiff was granted an annulment on the ground of duress. The plaintiff claimed the defendant and his uncle, in the presence of the plaintiff's family, informed her that if she did not marry the defendant, she would be kidnapped; taken to New York; her face would be disfigured and her home would be blown to pieces. The court held that the plaintiff was impelled to marry the defendant by fear that the threats so made would be carried into execution. 

Prior Marriage. An action to annul a marriage may be maintained on the ground that the former husband or wife was living and the former marriage was in force when the subsequent marriage was contracted. C.P.A., $ 1134. 

§ 488. Conditions Attached to Maintenance of Annul ment Action.

Assuming that the plaintiff has ground for maintaining an action for annulment, he must show that one of the following conditions exists: (C.P.A., § 1146-a) 

1. Both parties are residents of the state when the action is commenced. 

2. The parties were married within the state and either the plaintiff or the defendant is a resident thereof when the action is commenced. (Effective Sept. 1, 1938) 

3. The parties were married without the state and either the plaintiff or the defendant is, and has been, a resident of the state one year when the action is commenced.

§ 490. Jury Trial. 

In an action to annul a marriage, except where it is founded upon an allegation of the physical incapacity of one of the parties thereto, the court, upon the application of either of the parties, must make an order directing the trial by a jury of all the issues of fact; or, of its own motion, it may make an order directing the trial by a jury of one or more issues of fact, for which purpose, the questions to be tried are prepared and settled. C.P.A., § 1142. 

§ 491. Procedure in an Annulment Action. 

The procedure in an annulment action is the same as that outlined under an action for divorce. 

§ 492. Action to Dissolve a Marriage. 

Under certain conditions, where a spouse has been absent for five years, application may be made for what is known as an Enoch Arden divorce on the theory that a presumption of death arises from absence. Pitcairn v. 

Pitcairn, 119 Misc. 37, 195 N. Y. S. 275. And if a spouse contemplates another marriage, it is advisable to obtain an adjudication, thus transferring the probability of death to a legal certainty so that unpleasant consequences may thereby be avoided, should the absentee spouse reappear. Matter of Kotlik, 153 Misc. 355, 274 N. Y. S. 

838. See also Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 6 (4th Ed.), page 975. 

Section 7a of the Domestic Relations Law deals with this remedy. The courts have jurisdiction to grant relief under this section to a wife, who, although a bona fide resident of this state, nevertheless was married in another state wherein she was wilfully deserted and compelled to support herself, on the theory that she possessed the matrimonial res and therefore had a right to bring the res of the matrimonial status into this state. Dodge v. Campbell, 239 A. D. 534, 242 N. Y. S. 534, aff'g 135 Misc. 644, 238 N. Y. S. 666.

$ 493 

§ 493. Procedure. 

The Domestic Relations Act provides that a party to a marriage may present to the Supreme Court a duly verified petition showing that the husband or wife of such party has absented himself or herself for five successive years without being known to such party to be living during that time; that such party believes such husband or wife to be dead; and that a diligent search has been made to discover evidence showing that such husband or wife is living, and no such evidence has been found. The court thereupon, by order, requires notice of presentation and object of such petition to be published in a newspaper in the English language designated in the order as most likely to give notice to such absent husband or wife, once each week for three successive weeks. The notice is directed to the husband or wife who absented himself or herself, and states the time and place of the hearing on the petition, which time is not less than forty days after the completion of the publication of the notice. notice is subscribed with the name of the petitioner and with the name of the petitioner's attorney and with his office address. The notice may appear in the following form: "Supreme Court,

§ 494. Alimony and Counsel Fees. 

In an action for divorce or separation, the court in its discretion, during the pendency thereof, from time to time, may make and modify an order or orders requiring the husband to pay any sum or sums of money necessary to enable the wife to carry on or defend the action, or to provide suitably for the education and maintenance of the children of the marriage, or for the support of the wife, having regard to the circumstances of the respective parties. C.P.A., § 1169. Where an award of alimony is made during the pendency of the action, it is known as alimony pendente lite; when made after judgment, it is known as permanent alimony. The award of alimony, and the amount thereof, whether temporary or permanent, is based on practically the same considerations and are matters of discretion with the court. 

Where the wife sues, in order to entitle her to an order for the payment of alimony, she must present to the court some evidence tending to show that there is reasonable probability that she will succeed in establishing her charges. Domb v. Domb, 195 A. D. 526, 186 N. Y. S. 306;

Desbrough v. Desbrough, 29 Hun 592. In the Domb case, a quarrel arose between the husband and wife because the husband would not rent an apartment preferred by the wife. As a result, the wife refused to return to their home. The court held that the wife was not entitled to alimony because the facts disclosed that there was not an abandonment but a refusal without justification to live with her husband.

The amount of the award depends on the wife's means,

$ 495 

if any, and the ability of the husband to pay. The court considers the husband's income as well as all the duties and burdens chargeable upon him. Forrest v. Forrest, 25 N. Y. 501. In Paterson v. Paterson, 4 A. D. 146, 38

N. Y. S. 637, the court held that suitable support is not simply what will supply the wife with the bare necessaries of life, but such a sum as will keep her in the situation and condition in which her husband's means entitle her to live.

No alimony will be granted if suitable provision has been made for the wife in the separation agreement and the husband has not defaulted in payment. 

Although the statute does not expressly authorize the award of alimony and counsel fees in an action to annul a marriage, nevertheless, it is the settled law that the court has such power where the action is brought against the wife. Jones v. Brinsmade, 183 N. Y. 258, citing 

Griffin v. Griffin, 47 N. Y. 134; Higgins v. Sharp, 164 N. Y. 

4. But a different situation arises where the wife brings the action. Since the theory of an annulment action is that there never was a valid marriage, the courts argue that by bringing the action, the wife denies the existence of the marriage and therefore cannot consistently claim that the husband is under any obligation to provide her with the means to carry on her suit against him. Jones v. Brinsmade, 183 N. Y. 258, citing Brinkley v. Brinkley, 50 N. Y. 184. In other words, one who elects to rescind a contract cannot claim anything under it, and furthermore, that it would be unjust and unwise for the wife to establish the invalidity of the marriage with means furnished by her husband.

The motion papers for alimony and counsel fees may be served with the summons and complaint.

J. S. C. $499. Collection of Alimony.

Where a husband is directed to pay alimony and fails to do so, payment may be enforced by sequestration of his property. C.P.A., §§ 1171-1172. And where this cannot be done, contempt proceedings may be brought. But the court may at any time order that arrears of alimony be docketed as a money judgment and execution issue thereon.

§ 504. In General. 

The statute provides in which court an action may be brought, and also in which division thereof, if there is more than one such court. For example, where an action is required to be brought in a supreme court, it is provided which of the several counties in which a supreme court is located, is the proper county. This is also true with respect to city court actions. In municipal court actions, the pertinent statute provides which of the several districts is the proper one. Despite these provisions, however, the plaintiff may commence the action in the wrong county or district and it will be tried therein unless the defendant objects thereto and takes the necessary steps to change the place of trial; otherwise he is deemed to have waived any objection thereto. C.P.A., § 186. In 

Hull v. Trainor, 233 A. D. 351, 252 N. Y. S. 845, it was 520

$ 521 

held that the court had no discretion to change the place of trial to another county, when no party asked for such relief. The question of a county court's jurisdiction as to residence is waived by the defendant by answering and taking part in the trial. Lindemann v. Wolf, 234 A. D. 

291, 254 N. Y. S. 274; Meyers v. American Locomotive 

Co., 201 N. Y. 163. 

§ 505. Proper County-Supreme Court Actions. 

In supreme court actions, unless it is an action speci fied in Sections 183 and 184 of the Civil Practice Act, the action must be tried in the county in which one of the parties resided at the commencement thereof. If neither of the parties then resided in the state, it may be tried in any county which the plaintiff designates for that purpose in the title of the complaint. A party having or maintaining a residence in more than one county is deemed a resident of either county. C.P.A., § 182. The plaintiff's 

"residence" within the statute determining the place of trial must be characterized by the element of permanency, but it does not necessarily contemplate a permanent home or domicile. Hurley v. Union Trust Co. of Rochester, 244 A. D. 590, 280 N. Y. S. 474.

With respect to the real property actions enumerated in Section 183 of the Civil Practice Act, they must be brought in the county in which the subject of the action or some part thereof is situated. Such actions include the following: 

1. An action of ejectment. 

2. For the partition of real property. 

3. For dower. 

4. To foreclose a mortgage upon real property, or upon a chattel real. 

5. To compel the determination of a claim to real property. 

6. For waste.

§ 507  

7. For a nuisance. 

8.

To procure a judgment directing a conveyance of real property. 

9. Every other action affecting real property or a chattel real.

The statute further provides that certain actions must be brought in the county where the cause of action arose. 

These include an action to recover a penalty or forfeiture imposed by statute; an action against a public officer; and an action to recover a chattel distrained or for dam ages thereof. C.P.A., § 184. 

§ 506. Grounds for Change of Venue. 

A party may seek a change of venue on the following grounds: 

1. Where the county designated for that purpose in the complaint is not the proper county. 

2. Where there is reason to believe that an impartial trial cannot be had in the proper county. 

3. Where the convenience of material witnesses and the ends of justice will be promoted by the change. C.P.A., § 187. 

§ 507. When to Ask for Change. 

If the defendant seeks to change the place of trial on the ground that the county designated is not the proper county, a demand therefor is required to be served on the plaintiff's attorney with the answer, or before the service of the answer. C.P.R. 146.

If the defendant seeks to change the place of trial for the remaining two reasons specified, to wit, that an impartial trial cannot be had in the proper county; or for the convenience of witnesses, application may be made to the court therefor at any time before trial, and it is not necessary that a demand be first served. Saal Products 

Sales, Inc. v. Schatz Manufacturing Co., 216 A. D. 544, 

215 N. Y. S. 530.

$ 523 

§ 508. Procedure in General. 

Where a demand is served, the plaintiff's attorney must serve his written consent thereto within five days after the service of the demand; otherwise the defendant's attorney may, within ten days after the expiration of the five-day period, serve notice of a motion to change the place of trial. C.P.R. 146. 

§ 509. Demand for Change of Venue-Form. 

A demand for a change of venue to be served by the defendant's attorney must specify the county where the defendant requires the action to be tried, and reads as follows: 

SIR:

Dated: New York, March 16, 1937. 

Yours, etc.,

WILLIAM ANDREWS, Attorney for Defendant.

In other words, an order changing the place of trial be-comes effective upon the entry thereof in the office of the clerk of the county from which the place of trial is.

changed; but for the purpose of an appeal therefrom, the place of trial is deemed unchanged. C.P.R. 147. 

§ 513. Notice of Motion to Change Venue-Form. 

Inasmuch as the defendant, if he proceeds in time, has an absolute right to change the place of trial to the proper county, there should be no need to apply to the court for such relief. Veeder v. Baker, 83 N. Y. 156. The plaintiff cannot, for example, contend that although the county is not the proper one, it should, nevertheless, remain therein because it serves the convenience of his witnesses. 

The proper procedure, under such circumstances, is to consent to the change and thereafter move for an order changing the place of trial for the convenience of witnesses. Culver v. Union National Bank, 212 A. D. 766, 210 N. Y. 370. But where the defendant moves to change the place of trial to the proper county, the plaintiff may by cross-motion, pursuant to C.P.A., § 117, ask that the court retain the action in the county in which it was brought upon the ground of the convenience of witnesses. 

McDaniels v. Doubleday, 241 A. D. 51, 270 N. Y. S. 306, citing Behrman v. Pioneer Pearl Button Co., 190 A. D. 

843, 181 N. Y. S. 59; Ackerman v. Cummiskey, 236 A. D. 

519, 259 N. Y. S. 489.

If the defendant refuses to consent to change the place of trial, a notice of motion may be prepared to read as follows:

§ 516. Change of Venue to Secure Impartial Trial. 

Where there is reason to believe that an impartial trial cannot be had in the proper county, the defendant may, at any time before trial, make application to change the place of trial. Although applications of this sort are not frequent, nevertheless circumstances may arise which make it necessary to ask for relief of this sort. For example, an action may be pending in a very small community wherein the only newspaper published therein contained adverse comment or the persons who were likely to be called as jurors expressed an opinion with respect to the action pending therein which was unfavorable. Under such conditions, it is obvious that a fair trial cannot be had and it is necessary to change the place of trial.

A notice of motion and supporting affidavit as already outlined may be used for this application, making the necessary changes to conform to the facts and circumstances.

§ 531 

§ 517. Change of Venue for Convenience of Witnesses. 

A change of venue for the convenience of witnesses is frequently made. And unlike an application for a change to the proper county, the right thereto is not an absolute one. Various considerations are taken into account. It is not sufficient, for example, for the supporting affidavit to state that the moving party expects to prove certain facts by certain witnesses. It must contain positive statements. It must set forth the names of the witnesses proposed to be called, a statement of the substance of the testimony to be given by each witness, and the material ity thereof. Bartrop v. Sobel Realty Co., 214 A. D. 799. 

See also Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 3 (4th Ed.), page 

730; also page 733, for the requirements of the supporting affidavit in the different departments. The rule that the convenience of parties and of expert witnesses will not be consulted on a motion to change the venue of an action, for the convenience of witnesses, does not apply to expert witnesses who will testify from their personal knowledge of the matter in controversy as distinguished from those experts who will give their opinions on an assumed state of facts. Roche v. Holbrook, 159 Misc. 

796, 287 N. Y. S. 829, citing Groff v. Rome Metallic Bed stead Co. et al., 98 A. D. 152, 90 N. Y. S. 691, 693; Taylor v. Jacobs, 168 A. D. 260, 153 N. Y. S. 778. 

§ 518. Removal of Action from County Court to Supreme Court. 

C.P.A., § 189 provides for the removal of an action pending in the county court to the supreme court by reason of the incapacity of the judge. Where removal is sought for other reasons, however, the procedure already outlined may be followed. 

§ 519. Venue and Change Thereof in City Court Actions. 

With respect to a City Court action, it is required to be brought in the division of the court located in the county

$ 520 

in which either the plaintiff or the defendant, or one of the plaintiffs or one of the defendants, resides, or has a place for the transaction of business, unless all the plaintiffs or all of the defendants reside out of the City of New York, or have no place for the transaction of business therein, in which case the action may be brought in any county. New York City Court Act, § 48. 

The defendant proceeds by notice of motion based upon an affidavit of the defendant or his attorney showing the residence or the location of the place of business of the parties and specifying the county to which the defendant desires the action to be transferred. 

§ 520. Venue and Change Thereof in New York City Municipal Court Actions. 

A New York City Municipal Court action may be brought in a district in the borough wherein one of the parties resides or has a place of business unless all of the plaintiffs or all of the defendants reside out of the city of New York, in which case, the action may be brought in any borough, except that an action for rent, or to recover possession of real property, must be brought in the district wherein the property is located. N. Y. City Mun. 

Ct. Code, § 17, subd. 1. 

If the action is brought in the wrong borough, the court may on its own motion, and must on the motion of the defendant, transfer the action to the proper borough, and may thereupon, in its discretion, impose five dollars costs against the plaintiff. N. Y. City Mun. Ct. Code, § 17, subd. 2. See other local court acts.

§ 521. When Defendant May Require Plaintiff to Furnish Security for Costs. 

The statute provides that in certain instances, the defendant may require the plaintiff to furnish security for costs. The purpose is to protect defendants from groundless suits in courts of record of this state prosecuted by foreign entities, natural and corporate, without property within this jurisdiction out of which a successful defendant may be made whole for his statutory costs. 

State v. Saal, 239 A. D. 420, 267 N. Y. S. 558; Morek v. 

Smolak, 245 A. D. 355, 282 N. Y. S. 418.

C.P.A., § 1522 provides that the defendant in an action brought in a court of record may, except where permission is given to sue as a poor person, require security for costs to be given: "A. Where the plaintiff, when the action was commenced, either was 533

8 521 

1. A person residing without the state; or, if the action is brought in a county court, except in the counties of 

Albany, Kings, Queens, Rensselaer and Richmond, or in the city court of the city of New York, the city court of Yonkers, or the city court of Albany, residing without the city or county, as the case may be, wherein the court is located; or 

2. A foreign corporation; or 

3. A person imprisoned under execution for a crime; or 

4. The official assignee of a person so imprisoned; the official assignee or official trustee of a debtor; or an assignee in bankruptcy; where the action is brought upon a cause of action arising before the assignment, the appointment of the trustee or the adjudication in bankruptcy.

B. Where, after the commencement of the action, the plaintiff either 5. Ceases to be a resident of the state; or, where the action is brought in either of the local courts specified in subdivision one of this section, ceases to be a resident of the city or county, as the case may be, wherein the court is located; or 

6. Is adjudicated a bankrupt, or discharged from his debts, or exonerated from imprisonment, pursuant to a law of the state or of the United States; or 

7. Is sentenced to the state prison for a term less than for life. 

8. In a case specified in this section, if there are two or more plaintiffs, the defendant cannot require security for costs to be given unless he is entitled to require it of all the plaintiffs. 

9. The word 'city' as used in this section, so far as applies to the city court of the city of New York, shall be construed to mean and apply to the territory within the city of New York as it now exists or may hereafter be constituted."

§ 535 

§ 522. When Court May Require Plaintiff to Give Security for Costs. 

C.P.A., § 1523 provides that in an action by or against an executor or administrator, in his representative capac-ity, or the trustee of an express trust, or a person expressly authorized by statute to sue or to be sued; or by an official assignee, the assignee of a receiver, or the committee of a person judicially declared to be incompetent to manage his affairs; the court, in its discretion, may require the plaintiff to give security for costs. 

§ 523. When and How to Make Application. 

The defendant proceeds under C.P.A., § 1522 as a matter of right; and the application for an order pursuant thereto, may be made ex parte. Where, however, application is made pursuant to C.P.A., § 1523, the granting thereof is within the discretion of the court and must be predicated upon notice of motion. Weiss v. Kanarek, 136 Misc. 848, 241 N. Y. S. 345.

C.P.A., § 1524 provides that an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish security for costs may be made at any time. It is, however, customary to make the application before serving the answer; and the advantage of doing so is that the proceedings are stayed, except to review the order, until the security is furnished. In Snyder v. Gris-wold, 140 Misc. 82, 250 N. Y. S. 26, the court explained. that it was held previous to 1915, that the defendant waived his absolute right to security unless application was made prior to answering, and that after answering, the granting of security was within the discretion of the court, citing W. A. Ives Mfg. Co. v. Smith & Hemenway 

Co., 166 A. D. 910, 151 N. Y. S. 275; Belah v. Delaware &· 

Hudson Co., 173 A. D. 867, 160 N. Y. S. 74. But by the

Laws of 1915, c. 635, the legislature amended the then code by inserting the words "at any time" (Code Civ. 

Proc., § 3272, now C.P.A., § 1524), and since such amendment, the rule has been that application may be made and

$ 524 

must be granted at any stage of the action, citing Hun garian General Credit Bank v. Titus, 175 A. D. 507, 161 

N. Y. S. 1078. 

§ 524. Order-Form. 

Application under C.P.A., § 1522, by reason of the fact that the plaintiff is a nonresident or a foreign corporation, is perhaps most frequently made, and therefore the procedure will hereinafter be described in more detail. 

The order requires the plaintiff, within a time specified, either to pay into court the sum of two hundred and fifty dollars, to be applied to the payment of the costs, if any, awarded against him, or, at his election, to file with the clerk an undertaking and to serve a written notice of the payment or of the filing upon the defendant's attorney; and staying all other proceedings on the part of the plaintiff, except to review or vacate the order, until the payment or filing, and notice thereof, and also, if an undertaking is given, the allowance of the same. C.P.A., § 1524. The amount of security varies in the lower courts. 

See local court acts.

The order made pursuant C.P.A., § 1522, is made ex parte, and reads as follows: 

PRESENT: 

At a Special Term, Part II, of the Supreme 

Court of the State of New York, held in and for the County of New York at the County Courthouse in the Borough of Manhattan, City of New York, on the 10th day of March, 1937.

HON. JULIUS MILLER, Justice.

§ 537 

On reading and filing the affidavit of William Andrews, verified the 9th day of March, 1937, and the statement of plaintiff's address, annexed hereto, by which it appears that the plaintiff in this action does not reside in the State of New York, but resides in the City of Philadelphia in the State of Pennsylvania, and that she so resided at the time of the commencement of this action.

Now, upon motion of William Andrews, attorney for the defendant herein, it is hereby ORDERED, that the plaintiff be and he hereby is required, within ten days from the day of the service of this order upon Martin Lee, his attorney, exclusive of the day of service, either to pay into court the sum of Two Hundred and Fifty ($250) Dollars to be applied in payment of the costs of this action, if any, awarded against him, or, at his election, to file with the Clerk of this Court an undertaking in due form of law executed to the defendant by one or more sufficient sureties, to the effect that they will pay upon demand to the said defendant all costs which may be awarded to him in this action not exceeding the sum of Two Hundred and Fifty ($250) Dollars. And the plaintiff is further directed and required to serve a written notice of such payment or filing of such undertaking upon the attorney for the said defendant; and it is further

J. S. C. 

§ 525. Affidavit-Form. 

An affidavit in support of an application for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish security for costs, reads as follows:

§ 526. Submitting Order for Signature. 

As soon as the order and affidavit have been prepared, the papers are submitted for the judge's signature in the part of the court where ex parte business is transacted. 

§ 527. Service of Order. 

When the order is signed, a conformed copy thereof and of the affidavit and any other paper upon which it is based, with notice of entry thereof, are served upon the plaintiff's attorney. 

§ 528. Effect of Order. 

When the order has been served, all proceedings on the part of the plaintiff are thereby stayed until the plaintiff furnishes the security. 

§ 529. Time Within Which Plaintiff Must Furnish Security. 

Within the time specified in the order, the plaintiff may either deposit the amount with the clerk of the court or more often serves a copy of the bond on the plaintiff's attorney and files the original bond with proof of service thereof with the clerk of the court. 

§ 530. The Undertaking-How Obtained and Requisites 

Thereof.

The plaintiff's attorney, as a rule, arranges with a surety company to furnish the bond. The company inquires into the financial status of the plaintiff and if satis-

$ 532 

fied with the information it receives, it sends to the plaintiff's attorney an original and two copies of the bond. It also sends an application blank to the plaintiff to be filled in and returned. And for this service the company receives a premium of ten dollars a year. 

The undertaking must be executed to the defendant, by one or more sureties, and must be to the effect that they will pay upon demand to the defendant all costs which may be awarded to him in the action, not exceeding the sum of two hundred and fifty dollars. C.P.A., 

§ 1525. 

§ 531. Dismissal of Complaint on Failure to Obey Order. 

If the plaintiff does not file the bond or otherwise furnish security pursuant to the order, the defendant may move to dismiss the complaint, and in his favor for costs. 

C.P.A., § 1529. 

§ 532. Liability of Attorney for Costs. 

The plaintiff's attorney is liable for the payment of costs to the extent of one hundred dollars pending the furnishing of security whether or not application has been made therefor. This applies to the actions enumerated in Section 1522, subdivisions one to four, of the

Civil Practice Act. 

Read also Chapter on Security of Costs in Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 1 (3rd Ed.), page 639.

§ 533. Reason for Appointment of Guardian Ad Litem. 

and When to Make Application. 

An infant, unlike an adult, cannot sue or be sued nor can he engage counsel for that purpose. Some one can, however, prosecute or defend an action for him. This person is known as a guardian ad litem and is appointed. by the court. Where, therefore, an infant has a meritorious cause of action upon which it becomes necessary to institute suit, application is made to the court for the appointment of a guardian ad litem before the action is commenced. The failure to appoint a guardian ad litem prior to the service of the summons, is a mere irregularity and does not affect the jurisdiction of the court, but the application must be made and the proper person appointed nunc pro tunc; that is, as of a date prior to the 541

8 536 

commencement of the action. C.P.A., § 202. Holmes v. 

Staib Abendschain Co., 198 A. D. 354, 190 N. Y. S. 449.

Where an infant is sued, and application for the appointment of a guardian ad litem is not made in his behalf within twenty days after the completion of the service of the summons upon him, the application may be made by any other party to the action as provided in Section 203 

of the Civil Practice Act. C.P.R. 39. 

§ 534. Who May Act as Guardian Ad Litem. 

The parent of the infant, as a rule, applies for the appointment as guardian ad litem. The general guardian of the infant or other person fully competent to understand and protect the rights of the infant may be appointed. Any trust company, however, which is authorized by the laws of the state to act as a general guardian without furnishing security may be appointed, as well as an attorney or officer of the court. C.P.R. 40. 

§ 535. By Whom Application is Made. 

If the infant is of the age of fourteen years or upwards, he may make application in his own behalf. If the infant is under the age of fourteen, application may be made by his general or testamentary guardian if he has one, otherwise by a relative or friend; and in the case of an infant defendant, if no such application is made, then any other party to the action may apply for the appointment.

C.P.A., § 203. 

§ 536. Qualifications of a Guardian Ad Litem. 

The statute provides, among other things, that a guardian ad litem shall be a person fully competent to understand and protect the rights of the infant; that he shall have no interest adverse to that of the infant, nor be connected in business with the attorney or counsel of any adverse party, nor shall he be nominated by any person having an adverse interest. The statute further pro-

$ 543 

vides that a person so appointed shall be of sufficient ability to answer for any damage which may be sustained by his negligence or misconduct, and such ability shall be shown by affidavit stating facts in respect thereto. C.P. R. 40. 

§ 537. Duty of Guardian Ad Litem. 

It is the duty of the guardian ad litem to examine into the circumstances of the cause or matter so far as to enable him to protect the rights of the infant. It is also his duty to account for all moneys received by him and to invest the same according to the directions of the court, and to faithfully execute his trust. C.P.R. 42. 

§ 538. Security Furnished by Guardian Ad Litem. 

Rule 41 of the Rules of Civil Practice provides that except in a case specially prescribed by law, a guardian ad litem is not permitted to receive money or property other than costs and expenses allowed to the guardian by the court, until he has given sufficient security, to account for and apply the same under the direction of the court. 

But where the money or the value of such property does not exceed one hundred dollars, security may be dispensed with in the discretion of the court. Where a trust company authorized by the laws of this state to act as general guardian of the estate of the infant without giving security, is appointed guardian ad litem, the order of the court may dispense with the giving and filing of security. The rule does not apply to a general guardian of an infant who has been appointed guardian ad litem, but at any time the court may require the general guardian to give additional security for the faithful discharge of his trust before receiving money or property of the infant under a judgment or order in the action or proceeding. The security to be furnished by a guardian ad litem shall be a bond to the infant conditioned for the faithful 35

8 540 

discharge of the trust, for the paying over and investing of and accounting for all moneys received and for the observance of any provision of law or the rules and the directions of the court in relation to the trust. New or additional security may be required by the court at any time. 

The purpose of the rule is to safeguard the interest of the infant. Maxwell v. Klein, 151 Misc. 485, 271 N. Y. S. 886. 

§ 539. Compensation of Guardian Ad Litem. 

A guardian ad litem is entitled to such compensation for his services as the court may deem reasonable. And to secure it, he must show by his affidavit, if he is an attorney, or if not, then by his affidavit and an affidavit to be made by an attorney who has acted in the matter in his behalf, that he has examined into the circumstances. of the case and, to the best of his ability, has made himself acquainted with the rights of the ward and that he has taken all of the steps necessary for the protection of such rights to the best of his knowledge and as he believes, stating what has been done by him for the purpose of ascertaining the rights of the ward. 

If he is appointed for an infant defendant who is not entitled to any money or property under the terms of the final judgment, he may nevertheless receive such compensation as the court deems just and reasonable, which is paid by any party to the action or proceeding, or out of the proceeds of any property which is the subject matter of the action, as the court may direct. C.P.R. 43. 

§ 540. Liability for Costs. 

A guardian ad litem for an infant is not liable for costs unless specially charged therewith by the order of the court. C.P.A., § 205; Johnson v. Johnson, - A. D. -, 209 N. Y. S. 854. 

---

542 545 

§ 541. Procedure in General. 

An application for the appointment of a guardian ad litem is made in the court in which the action is brought or about to be brought or a judge thereof; and if the action is in the Supreme Court, the guardian may be appointed by the county judge of the county where the action is triable; provided, however, that in an action for partition, the guardian ad litem can be appointed by the court. C.P.A., § 202. 

If the application is made by a relative or friend, notice thereof is required to be given to his general or testamentary guardian, or if he has none, to the person with whom the infant resides.

Where the application for the appointment of a guardian ad litem for an infant defendant is made by a person other than the infant, notice thereof is required to be given to the general or testamentary guardian if he has one within the state, or if he has none, to the infant himself if he is of the age of fourteen years or upwards and within the state, or if he is under that age and within the state, to the person with whom he resides. C.P.A., § 204. 

The application is based upon the following papers:

Petition. 

Written Consent. 

Affidavit of Ability to Answer.

Order. 

§ 542. Petition-Form. 

Upon an application for the appointment of a guardian ad litem, if a person has been designated to receive summons, pursuant to the provisions of C.P.A., § 225, that fact must affirmatively appear in the affidavit presented upon such application. C.P.A., § 203.

The petition of the parent of an infant under the age of fourteen years may read as follows:

§ 549. Removal of Action from State Court to Federal 

Court.

Where an action is commenced in the State court, it. may, where certain conditions exist, as provided in the statute, be removed by the defendant from the State court. to a district court of the United States for the proper district. The application for the removal is perhaps. most frequently made where the action is between citizens of different states and the amount in controversy is in excess of three thousand dollars exclusive of inter est and costs. Judicial Code, § 28. 

Judicial Code, § 28. Ross v. Pacific 

Steamship Co., 272 Fed. 538. If, for example, the action were originally commenced in the Supreme Court of New York County, the action would be removed, by the defendant, to the United States Court for the Southern District of New York. If the action were originally 551

8 552 

commenced in the County Court or the Supreme Court of the County of Albany, it would be removed to the United States Court for the Northern District of New York.

The practice in the federal court is similar to that of the State court unless otherwise prescribed. 

§ 550. When to Remove Action. 

If a case is one which may be removed to the federal court, steps to effect such removal must be taken within the time required by the laws of the State or by the rule of the State court in which the action is brought, to serve an answer; that is, in this State, within twenty days after the service of the complaint, with the exception, of course, of those actions which are removable on the ground of prejudice or local influence. Judicial 

Code, § 29. 

§ 551. Procedure-In General. 

To remove an action, for example, from the supreme court to the federal court, the defendant's attorney secures a bond and in addition, prepares the following papers: (Judicial Code, § 29) Notice of Filing of Petition and Bond for Removal. 

Petition. 

§ 552. Notice of Filing of Petition and Bond for Removal-Form. 

The notice is to the effect that on a certain date therein stated, the petition for the removal of the action to the federal court, and the bond will be presented to the justice presiding at special term or such part wherein ex parte business is transacted. Two days' notice to the adversary is sufficient.

The notice reads as follows:

§ 553. Petition-Form. 

The petition for the removal of an action is in the nature of a process to transfer the case after due notice

8 553 

to the plaintiff. Hull v. Payne, 274 Fed. 237. Although the statute does not prescribe what the petition shall contain, it must, nevertheless, set forth jurisdictional facts; that is, facts sufficient to entitle the party to transfer the action. The right to removal exists only in certain enumerated classes of cases. To exercise that right, therefore, it is essential that it be shown that the case comes within one of those classes and this is done by a verified petition setting forth, agreeably to the ordinary rules of pleading, the particular facts, not already appearing, out of which the right arises. It is not sufficient to allege in terms that the case is removable or belongs to one of the enumerated classes, or otherwise to rest the right upon mere legal conclusions. As in other pleadings, there must be a statement of the facts relied upon, and not otherwise appearing, in order that the court may draw the proper conclusion from all the facts. Little York Gold-Washing, etc., Co. v. Keyes, 96 U. S. 199. 

The petition may read as follows: 

SUPREME COURT OF THE  County of New York. 

JOHN DOE, for himself and all others similarly situated, Plaintiff, -against- 

X Y Z STORES, INC., RICHARD ROE, JOHN ROE and RAY BOLLES, Defendants. 

TO THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK, COUNTY OF NEW YORK: 

The petition of X Y Z Stores, Inc., one of the defendants in the above entitled action, respectfully shows to this Honorable 

Court as follows:

$ 555 

1. That this action was commenced on the 16th day of September, 1936, by the service of a summons and complaint herein on the defendant, Richard Roe, individually, and by the service of a summons and complaint herein on the 16th day of September, 1936, on Richard Roe, as President of the defendant, X Y Z Stores, Inc.; that your petitioner has not answered or pleaded to the complaint; that your petitioner now appears herein specially for the purposes of this petition without generally submitting itself to the jurisdiction of this Court and without admitting the validity of the purported service of process upon it in this cause. 

2. That this action is wholly of a civil nature and that the matter and amount in dispute therein and in that portion of this action in which your petitioner is interested exceeds the sum of $3,000, exclusive of interest and costs. 

3. That your petitioner is a foreign corporation duly organized and existing under and by virtue of the laws of the State of Delaware, and was at the time of the commencement of this action and still is a non-resident of the State of New York, and was and still is citizen and resident of the State of Delaware. 

That the plaintiff herein was at the time of the commencement of this action and still is a citizen and resident of the State of 

New York, having his residence in the Borough of Manhattan,

City, County and State of New York, in the Southern District of New York. 

4. That there is in this action a separate and distinct controversy which is wholly between citizens of different states; to wit, between the plaintiff, a citizen of the State of New York, and your petitioner, a citizen of the State of Delaware, as more fully appears from the complaint in this action, a copy of which is hereto annexed and made part hereof. 

5. That said controversy between the plaintiff and your petitioner is of the following nature:

The plaintiff in his complaint herein alleges in substance that the directors of your petitioner, the individual defendants named herein, failed and neglected to perform their official duties as such and were guilty of alleged gross, deliberate, wilful and malicious acts of misfeasance, mismanagement, waste and dissipation of assets. $555. Bond on Removal. 

H. SAM PRIEST, Clerk Circuit Court. 

The party who petitions for the removal of the action is required to file a bond with good and sufficient surety for his entering in the federal court within thirty days from the date of filing of the petition, a certified copy of the record in such suit, and for paying all costs that may be awarded by the federal court if it shall hold that the action was wrongfully or improperly removed thereto. Judicial Code, § 29. A bond in the sum of five hundred dollars may be secured from a surety company and is submitted with the petition on the return day. 

§ 556. Filing in State Court. 

On the return day of the notice, the petition, bond, summons and complaint are submitted to the judge sitting in Special Term or in such part wherein ex parte business is transacted. In New York County, it is pre sented to the clerk of Special Term, Part II. If the petition is granted and the bond approved, the papers are filed. The statute provides that it shall be the duty

$ 559 

of the State court to accept the petition and proceed no further in the suit. Judicial Code, § 29. No order is required to be entered thereon. 

§ 557. Filing Record in Federal Court. 

Within thirty days after the filing of the record in the State court, a certified copy of all of the papers filed therein; to wit, the petition, notice, bond, summons and complaint are filed in the office of the clerk of the district court of the United States to which the action has been removed. Judicial Code, § 29. 

§ 558. Time to Plead. 

The defendant is required to serve his answer within thirty days after the filing of the record in the federal court. Judicial Code, § 29. 

§ 559. Remanding Cause Back to State Court. 

Section 37 of the Judicial Code provides that if in any suit commenced in a district court or removed from a State court to a district court of the United States, it shall appear to the satisfaction of the said district court, at any time after such suit has been brought or removed thereto that such suit does not really and substantially involve a dispute or controversy properly within the jurisdiction of the said district court, or that the parties to said suit have been improperly or collusively made or joined, either as plaintiffs or defendants, for the purpose of creating a case cognizable or removable under this chapter, the said district court shall proceed no further therein but shall dismiss the suit or remand it to the court from which it was removed, as justice may require, and shall make such order as to costs as may be just.

The plaintiff may proceed by notice of motion. It may be remanded even on motion of the party who removed it where it appears that the federal court had no juris- 36

8 556 

authorized to take and certify the same by the laws of the said State, and to take and certify the acknowledgment and proof of deeds, to be recorded in the State, and that the same is taken and certified in all respects as required by the laws of said State. That I am well acquainted with the handwriting of said Richard Smith, and verily believe that the signature attached to the foregoing Certificate is the genuine signature of said Richard Smith. 

WITNESS my hand and seal of the Circuit Court, City of 

St. Louis, at my office in said City, this 1st day of October nineteen hundred and thirty-five. (SEAL.) 

No seal is necessary to be filed by said Notary under the laws of this State. 

§ 555. Bond on Removal. 

H. SAM PRIEST, Clerk Circuit Court. 

The party who petitions for the removal of the action. is required to file a bond with good and sufficient surety for his entering in the federal court within thirty days from the date of filing of the petition, a certified copy of the record in such suit, and for paying all costs that may be awarded by the federal court if it shall hold that the action was wrongfully or improperly removed thereto. Judicial Code, § 29. A bond in the sum of five hundred dollars may be secured from a surety company and is submitted with the petition on the return day. 

§ 556. Filing in State Court. 

On the return day of the notice, the petition, bond, summons and complaint are submitted to the judge sitting in Special Term or in such part wherein ex parte business is transacted. In New York County, it is pre sented to the clerk of Special Term, Part II. If the petition is granted and the bond approved, the papers are filed. The statute provides that it shall be the duty

$ 559 

of the State court to accept the petition and proceed no further in the suit. Judicial Code, § 29. No order is required to be entered thereon. 

§ 557. Filing Record in Federal Court. 

Within thirty days after the filing of the record in the State court, a certified copy of all of the papers filed therein; to wit, the petition, notice, bond, summons and complaint are filed in the office of the clerk of the district court of the United States to which the action has been removed. Judicial Code, § 29. 

§ 558. Time to Plead. 

The defendant is required to serve his answer within thirty days after the filing of the record in the federal court. Judicial Code, § 29. 

§ 559. Remanding Cause Back to State Court. 

Section 37 of the Judicial Code provides that if in any suit commenced in a district court or removed from a State court to a district court of the United States, it shall appear to the satisfaction of the said district court, at any time after such suit has been brought or removed thereto that such suit does not really and substantially involve a dispute or controversy properly within the jurisdiction of the said district court, or that the parties to said suit have been improperly or collusively made or joined, either as plaintiffs or defendants, for the purpose of creating a case cognizable or removable under this chapter, the said district court shall proceed no further therein but shall dismiss the suit or remand it to the court from which it was removed, as justice may require, and shall make such order as to costs as may be just.

The plaintiff may proceed by notice of motion. It may be remanded even on motion of the party who removed it where it appears that the federal court had no juris- 36

$560 

diction. Mansfield, etc., R. Co. v. Swan, 111 U. S. 379; 

Torrence v. Shedd, 144 U. S. 527. On a motion to remand, after a delay of over a year, it was held that in the absence of an explanation therefor, the defendant lost his right to insist that the petition for removal was not filed in time. Miller v. Kent, 18 Fed. 561. 

§ 560. Notice of Motion to Remand-Form. 

A notice of motion to remand is in the usual form of a notice of motion used in supreme court actions, and reads as follows:

§ 561. Affidavit-Form. 

An affidavit in support of a motion to remand which controverts the allegations of the petition for removal may be considered by the court. Smith v. Crosby Lumber 

Co., 46 Fed. 819, aff'd 51 Fed. 63. It reads as follows:

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT, Southern District of New York. 

JOHN DOE, for himself and all others similarly situated, -against- Plaintiff,

X Y Z STORES, INC., RICHARD ROE, JOHN ROE and RAY BOLLES, Defendants. 

SS.: 

 MARTIN LEE, being duly sworn, deposes and says: I am the attorney for the plaintiff herein and am familiar with all the facts and circumstances herein stated.

§ 561 

1. This motion is to remand the above entitled case back to the Supreme Court of the State of New York, County of 

New York. 

2. The action was commenced in the Supreme Court of the 

State of New York,  on September 16, 1935, by the service of a summons and complaint on the defendant, Richard Roe, a New York resident, individually. Service was also attempted to be made upon X Y Z Stores, Inc., by leaving a copy of the summons and complaint with Richard 

Roe, as president thereof. The corporate defendant appeared specially and "without admitting the validity of the purported service of process upon it in this cause. 

3. On October 2, 1935, the corporate defendant served a petition for removal, notice of presentation thereof and a removal bond. These were presented to the Supreme Court of the State of New York, at Special Term, Part II, on October 4, 1935. 

The petition was duly granted, the bond approved and the said. papers filed. 

4. A certified copy of the petition, notice, bond, summons and complaint was duly filed in the Clerk's office of this Court on November 1, 1935. 

5. The ground upon which remanding to the Supreme Court is based is that the controversy as it now stands is between citizens of the same state, namely, citizens of New York. Furthermore, even if citizens of other states were duly served, the controversy is still between citizens of the same state, New York, because the controversy is an inseparable one as to all defendants. The controversy is between a stockholder of the defendant corporation as plaintiff and defendant corporation and its directors and officers. Unless the directors were guilty of waste and dissipation of assets as alleged, there could be no judgment against the corporation. Inextricably interwined with each other are the directors and the corporation. If the directors were not derelict in their duties, there can be no judgment against the corporation. If the directors were and the Court so finds, judgment against the corporation must follow. No determination of the controversy could be had unless both the corporation and the directors were present. of the individuals, a director of the corporation is a necessary and indispensable party without whom and without the corporation as a defendant, there could be no adjudication.

§ 563 

6. It is a curious coincidence that the only two defendants as to whom service was concededly made are Richard Roe and John Roe, each of whom is a resident of the State of New York. Therefore, so far as now appears, the controversy is between a resident of the State of New York as plaintiff and two residents of the State of New York as defendants. Service was attempted to be made on X Y Z Stores, Inc., by leaving with Richard Roe individually served and a resident of the State of New York another copy of the summons and complaint. 

As already stated, the corporation appeared specially and challenged the validity of the service. 

7. On November 4, 1935, the corporation obtained an order to show cause returnable November 15, 1935, to vacate the service upon the corporation on the ground that it was not doing business in this State; that its officer when served was not doing business here and that no valid service was obtained on the corporation. 

8. I verily believe that there is no local prejudice against the defendants or any of them in the Supreme Court of the State of New York,  and that they may try their case there without fear of favor or local prejudice against them. 

WHEREFORE, I respectfully pray that an order be made herein remanding this case to the Supreme Court of the State of New York, County of New York, whence it came, and for such other, further and different relief as to the Court may seem just and proper in the premise. 

8th day of November, 1935.

§ 562. Calendar Practice. 

MARTIN LEE. 

The motion to remand is placed upon the calendar for hearing. In the District Court of the United States for the Southern District, the motion is placed on the calendar, by filing a note of issue. The calendar of motions is published in the New York Law Journal. See local papers in other parts of the State. On the return day,

$ 564 

the attorneys appear prepared either to submit or argue the motion. The original motion papers are submitted on the hearing of the motion. Memoranda of law may be prepared and submitted with the original motion papers or within such further time as may be permitted by the court. 

§ 563. Decision. 

The decision on a motion to remand will appear in the same manner as the decisions of other courts. 

§ 564. Order-Form. 

An order is entered upon a decision of a federal court in the same manner as upon a decision of a State court, and when signed by the judge, a copy thereof is served upon the adverse attorney with notice of entry. Where, for example, the motion to remand, is denied, an order entered thereon, may read as follows:

§ 565. In General. 

In a civil action, under certain extraordinary circumstances, where the need for immediate relief is urgent and the delay attendant upon a trial will render thejudgment ineffectual, the plaintiff is not obliged to await the trial but may obtain temporary relief by application for a provisional remedy. The application is made in connection with an action and is based upon affidavits. which present facts to show that the party is entitled to the relief. Unless dispensed with in certain cases, a bond is required to be furnished upon the application, so that the defendant may be indemnified against costs, disbursements, and damages if he succeeds in vacating the order or warrant or otherwise succeeds in the action.. 

The provisional remedies are as follows: 

Attachment. 

Injunction.

Arrest. 

Receiver. 

Replevin. (Although this is not classified as a provisional remedy, nevertheless it is similar in character.)

Read also Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 2 [3rd Ed.] for a comprehensive study of the subject.

§ 566. Attachment-In General. 

Ordinarily, where a party sues another, he must wait until the trial of the action, and if he is successful, he

8 568 

may seize the debtor's property and apply it in payment of the judgment. But in certain cases, where among other things, personal service of process cannot be made because the debtor is a non-resident or a foreign corporation, but property belonging to the debtor is situated within the jurisdiction of the court, the plaintiff may have it seized before commencement of action and hold it as security for the payment of the judgment when and if rendered in his favor. This he proceeds to do by applying for a warrant of attachment. C.P.A., §§ 

902-973. 

§ 567. In What Actions Attachment May Issue. 

A warrant of attachment may be obtained in an action to recover a sum of money only as a tax or as damages for one or more of the following causes: (C.P.A., $$ 

902, 904). 

1. Breach of contract, express or implied other than a contract to marry. 

2. Wrongful conversion of personal property. 

3. An injury to person or property in consequence of negligence, fraud or other wrongful act. 

4. A wrongful act, neglect or default by which the decedent's death was caused when the cause of action arose in this State before or after the passage of this act and the action is brought by an executor or administrator against a natural person who, or a corporation which, would have been liable to an action in favor of the decedent by reason thereof if death had not ensued. 

5. Peculation and deceit. 

§ 568. Against Whom Attachment May Issue. 

A warrant of attachment may issue against non-residents; also against a resident who among other things has departed from the state for the purpose of defrauding creditors or to avoid the service of the summons, or keeps himself concealed therein with like intent; or has

571 569 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

removed or is about to remove property from the state in fraud of creditors, or has assigned, disposed of or secreted, or is about to assign, dispose of or secrete property with like intent; or has been continuously absent from the city for six months without designating a person upon whom service can be made or has made a false financial statement in order to secure credit. An attachment may also issue against a foreign corporation; and against a domestic corporation where no person can be found within the State after diligent effort, upon whom a summons can be served.

Under such circumstances, it is obvious that no personal service can be made upon the defendant and therefore, in order to invoke the jurisdiction of the court, it is necessary that some property of the debtor be found within the state upon which a levy may be made. 

§ 569. When and by Whom Warrant is Granted. 

A warrant may be granted to accompany the summons or at any time after the commencement of the action, but it may not be granted after final judgment, except as otherwise specially prescribed by statute. C.P.A., § 818. The warrant may be granted in a proper case either by the court in which the action is brought or a judge thereof or any county judge. C.P.A., § 817. 

§ 570. Papers Used Upon Application. 

It is not necessary to prepare a complaint to secure a warrant of attachment. The plaintiff's attorney prepares a warrant, affidavit and summons, and in addition, secures an undertaking. 

§ 571. The Warrant-Form. 

The warrant may be directed either to the sheriff of a particular county, or generally, to the sheriff of any county. It requires the sheriff to attach and safely keep so much of the property within his county, which the

8 571 

defendant has or which he may have, at any time before final judgment in the action, as will satisfy the plaintiff's demand, with costs and expenses. The amount of plaintiff's demand must be specified in the warrant, as stated in the proofs on which the warrant was granted. 

C.P.A., 910; Bloomingdale v. Cook, 35 A. D. 350, 54

N. Y. S. 924. Since no notice of the application for a warrant is required to be given either before or after the defendant's appearance in the action (C.P.A., § 815), the warrant is submitted for the judge's signature and subscribed by the plaintiff's attorney.

The warrant reads thus: 

THE PEOPLE OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK. 

To THE Sheriff of the County of New York: 

WHEREAS, an application has been made to the undersigned by the plaintiff, JOHN DOE & COMPANY, INC., for a Warrant of Attachment against the property of the defendant, X Y Z 

ALCOHOL COMPANY, LIMITED, and a summons and complaint having been duly issued in an action in the Supreme Court of the State of New York,  and it appearing to my satisfaction by the affidavit of JOHN DOE, duly sworn to the 15th day of May, 1931, and the verified complaint herein, that the action is brought to recover a sum of money only over and above all counterclaims known to the plaintiff, to wit, the sum of Thirty Thousand ($30,000) Dollars and interest from the 17th day of April, 1931, as damages for breach of express contracts to pay money, to wit, the failure on the part of the defendant to purchase and accept molasses pursuant to written agreements entered into whereby the plaintiff agreed to sell and deliver, and the defendant agreed to purchase and accept said molasses, and that said cause of action is one specified in Section 902 of the Civil Practice Act, and that the defendant, X Y Z ALCOHOL COMPANY, LIMITED, is a foreign corporation, and the plaintiff having given an undertaking required by law;

YOU ARE HEREBY COMMANDED to attach and safely keep so much of the property within your County which the said defendant, X Y Z ALCOHOL COMPANY, LIMITED, has, or which it may have at any time before final judgment in this action

as will satisfy plaintiff's demand herein, to wit, Thirty Thousand ($30,000) Dollars and interest thereon from April 17th, 1931, with costs and expenses, and that you proceed hereon in the manner required of you by law.

§ 572. The Affidavit-Form. 

The affidavit in support of a warrant of attachment must contain evidentiary facts tending to prove a cause of action; that is, the affidavit must contain such evidence from which the court can determine that the ultimate facts stated in the pleading can be substantiated. Sicklick v. Schasseur, 221 A. D. 742, 225 N. Y. S. 279; Abdun 

Nur v. Arbeed, 198 A. D. 795, 191 N. Y. S. 38. The reason for this requirement is that under the provisional remedy, the defendant's property is taken from his possession in advance of the trial of the issues, and to the end that there may be no injustice to him, the evidentiary facts are required to be presented, so that the court may see that the plaintiff, at least, has a prima facie cause of action for a recovery of damages to the extent claimed. 

Dexter & Carpenter, Inc., v. Lake & Export Coal 

Corporation, 196 A. D. 766, 188 N. Y. S. 623.

To entitle the defendant to a warrant, he must show that a cause of action specified in C.P.A., § 902 exists against the defendant, and, if the action is to recover

8 572 

damages for breach of contract, that the plaintiff is entitled to recover a stated sum, over and above all counterclaims known to him. He must also show that the defendant 

1. Is either a foreign corporation or not a resident of the state; or 

2. If a natural person and a resident of the state, has departed therefrom with intent to defraud his creditors or to avoid the service of the summons, or keeps himself concealed therein with like intent; or 

3. If a natural person or domestic corporation, has removed or is about to remove property from the state with intent to defraud his or its creditors, or has assigned, disposed of or secreted, or is about to assign, dispose of or secrete property with the like intent or if the defendant is a domestic corporation that no person can be found within the state after diligent effort, upon whom a summons can be served; or 

4. Has made a false statement in writing, under his own hand or signature, or under the hand or signature of a duly authorized agent made with his knowledge and acquiescence, as to his financial responsibility or standing, for the purpose of procuring credit or the extension of credit; or 

5. If an adult and a resident of the state, has been continuously without the state for more than six months next before the granting of the order of publication of the summons against him and has not made the designation, provided for by statute, of a person upon whom to serve a summons in his behalf, or a designation so made no longer remains in force, or service upon the person so designated cannot be made within the state after diligent effort. C.P.A., § 903.

In this connection, it is well to note that owing to the harshness of the remedy it is construed strictly in favor of those against whom it is invoked. Courtney v. Eighth 

Ward Bank, 154 N. Y. 688. If, therefore, the affidavit

572 573 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

does not contain the required evidentiary facts, the attachment may be vacated. For example, it would not be sufficient to allege that the defendant who is a resident of the state departed therefrom or keeps himself concealed therein with intent to avoid service of the summons. There would have to be some reference to the fact that the defendant knew that the plaintiff intended to serve him. To state merely that the defendant departed from the state would be insufficient because it may well be that the defendant merely left the state for a short visit and intended to return, and had no knowledge that a summons was to be served upon him. 

Again under subdivision 4 of Section 903 which authorizes the issuance of a warrant of attachment in a case where a debtor makes a false statement in writing as to his financial standing, for the purpose of securing credit, a court nevertheless will refuse to grant the warrant in a case where the debtor made a false statement in writing but it did not come to the knowledge or notice of the creditor until after credit had been given to the debtor. The case of Penoyar v. Kelsey, 150 N. Y. 77, indicates how reluctant courts are to grant a remedy of this sort unless the facts are such as to clearly entitle the applicant thereto and will go beyond the mere wording of the statute to apply the ordinary principles of law. The court there argued that the law furnished a remedy only for a wrongful act which results in injury; that if a false statement is made for the purpose of securing credit, but without having that effect, no creditor is injured; and furthermore that if it is made to one who does not believe it, or does not act upon it, it cannot become the basis of a summary remedy, for no right has been violated, no wrong suffered and no damages sustained. The court further points out that it would be an anomaly in commercial law to permit a wrongful act that injured no one to disrupt a man's

$ 572 

business by allowing any creditor to seize his property at any time.

The affidavit in support of a warrant of attachment may read as follows: 

JOHN DOE & COMPANY, INC., 

-against- Plaintiff,

X Y Z ALCOHOL COMPANY, LIMITED, Defendant. 

 S 

JOHN DOE, being duly sworn, deposes and says:

That John Doe & Company, Inc., the plaintiff in the above ⚫entitled action, is a corporation duly organized and existing under and by virtue of the laws of the State of New York, having its principal place of business at No. 100 Broadway, in the Borough of Manhattan, City of New York. That deponent is the President of said corporation, and personally represented the plaintiff in the transactions had with the defendant hereinafter set forth, and is fully familiar with such transactions. 

That the defendant, X Y Z Alcohol Company, Limited, is justly and truly indebted to the plaintiff, and the plaintiff is entitled to recover from the defendant, the sum of Thirty Thousand ($30,000) Dollars, with interest thereon from the 

17th day of April, 1931, over and above all counterclaims known to the plaintiff, on causes of action on contracts express or implied, which arose from and are based on the following facts, to wit: 

On or about the 8th day of October, 1930, the plaintiff and defendant duly entered into an agreement in writing, wherein and whereby the plaintiff agreed to sell and deliver to the defendant, and defendant agreed to purchase and accept from the plaintiff, thirty-five (35) tank cars of Refinery Blackstrap

$ 575 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

Molasses, f.o.b. seller's tank cars Boston, Mass., for shipment to the defendant at Belleville, Ontario, shipments to commence on or about October 8th, 1930, and extending over a period ending December 31st, 1930.

On October 9th, 1930, a further contract was entered into between the plaintiff and defendant covering forty (40) tank cars of similar molasses for shipment to the defendant at Belleville, Ontario, shipments to commence from October 9th, 1930, up to February 1st, 1931.

On October 9th, 1930, a further contract was entered into between plaintiff and defendant calling for five hundred thousand (500,000) gallons of the same molasses, f.o.b. seller's tank cars Boston, Mass., for shipment to the defendant at Belleville, Ontario, shipments to commence in April, 1931, and spread out evenly until December 31st, 1931. 

The prices of such molasses under the aforementioned agreements ranged from 4½¢ to 5¢ per United States wine gallon. 

The total amount of molasses covered by the three orders approximated 1,100,000 gallons. 

Between about the 15th day of October, 1930, and the 30th day of January, 1931, the plaintiff delivered to the defendant on the 35 and 40 tank car orders, fifty-eight (58) tank cars, amounting to approximately 464,000 gallons of molasses, leaving a balance of about 136.000 gallons still due. 

On December 12th, 1930, and at various times thereafter, the defendant requested the plaintiff to delay shipment of the balance of said orders until further notice to the plaintiff, which the plaintiff agreed to do but advised defendant that it would not suspend shipments indefinitely.

On or about the 13th day of April, 1931, the plaintiff wrote the defendant demanding that the defendant give the plaintiff definite instructions with reference to the shipment of the balance of said molasses on or before April 24th, 1931. Thereafter defendant attempted to vary the terms of the said agreements by directing the plaintiff to ship the balance of said molasses to places in the United States instead of Belleville, Ontario, as provided in said agreements, and notified the plaintiff that unless such shipments were made, to consider said contracts cancelled. The plaintiff refused to consent to such variation of the terms of said agreements and insisted upon 37

8 572 

delivery of the molasses as provided in the contracts, as a result thereof the defendant notified the plaintiff to consider said agreements cancelled.

With reference to the agreement entered into on October 9th, 1931, covering five hundred thousand (500,000) gallons of Blackstrap Molasses, the defendant likewise requested that deliveries thereunder be suspended until further notice. On or about the 13th day of April, 1931, plaintiff demanded that the defendant give plaintiff definite instructions as to shipments by April 24th, 1931, which the defendant failed and refused to do and sought to vary the contract in the manner above set forth. On or about the 17th day of April, 1931, this contract, too, was cancelled by the defendant.

That the plaintiff duly performed all the terms and conditions of the aforementioned agreements on its part to be performed, and was ready, able and willing to make delivery of the molasses covered by said agreements and would have delivered the same but for the acts of the defendant aforesaid. 

Deponent respectfully submits that by reason of the failure of the defendant to purchase and accept the aforesaid molasses in violation of the terms of the agreements, plaintiff has been damaged in the sum of $30,000. Deponent has estimated plaintiff's loss by reason of the following:

Deponent has been actively and continuously engaged in the business of buying and selling molasses for thirty-three years, during which period he has bought and sold millions of gallons of such molasses. He is thoroughly familiar with domestic and foreign market conditions and the market prices of blackstrap molasses at the times herein mentioned. 

It will be noted that under the aforementioned contracts, the molasses was to be shipped to Belleville, Ontario. These contracts are designated "export contracts" and the prices fixed therein were the export prices for blackstrap molasses then in effect. Export prices of blackstrap molasses at the time of the making of the contracts, and at all times prior and subsequent thereto, have been substantially lower than the domestic prices (i.e., molasses for delivery in the United States), due to the fact that where molasses is exported, the supplier is entitled to a refund of duty from the United States Government known as a "drawback.'

$ 577 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

Deponent is compelled to base his estimate of the plaintiff's damages on the prevailing domestic market price of blackstrap molasses on April 17th, 1931, the date when the aforementioned contracts were breached by the defendant, for the reason that neither on said date, nor at any time thereafter, has there been an export market for this commodity, and such molasses could not readily be sold for export to Canada, which country offers the only available market for export molasses. 

The prevailing domestic market price of blackstrap molasses: on October 9th, 1930, at the time the aforementioned contracts were entered into, was 10¢ per gallon (which is the price the defendant would have had to pay if the molasses were destined for domestic use), and the market price of blackstrap molasses for domestic use from April 1st, 1931, to date, and particularly on April 17th, 1931, the date when the aforementioned contracts were breached, is 434¢ per gallon. Plaintiff's damage is therefore 5¢ per gallon. The amount of molasses which the defendant refused to accept and which is still undelivered under the contracts, is 636,000 gallons. Plaintiff's damage therefore is the sum of $33,390, a sum in excess of the amount claimed.

The defendant is a foreign corporation, created by and under the laws of the Dominion of Canada, and has its principal office in the Canada Cement Company Building, Philips Square, Montreal, Canada. That deponent has a great many letters and cables in his possession showing conclusively that the defendant conducts business in Canada. Plaintiff has also made inquiry of the Bureau Du Protonotaire of Montreal, Canada, and was advised by such Bureau that the defendant corporation has been incorporated by Letters Patent of the
