Deputy Prothonotary § 573. Undertaking. 

The bond or undertaking furnished by the plaintiff before the warrant is granted, is to the effect that if the defendant recovers judgment, or if the warrant is vacated, the plaintiff will pay all costs which may be awarded to the defendant and all damages which he may sustain by reason of the attachment, not exceeding the

§ 579 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

sum specified in the undertaking, which must be at least two hundred and fifty dollars. C.P.A., § 907. Failure to furnish the security required, results in the loss of the attachment. McCann v. Schnitzler, 254 N. Y. 107.

The bond may be secured from a surety company in the manner previously described. 

§ 574. Procedure. 

C.P.A., 906 provides that the plaintiff, procuring the warrant, must cause the affidavits and papers comprising the proof upon which it was granted to be filed in the office of the clerk, within ten days after the granting thereof. It may be interesting to note more specifically the steps which actually take place following the preparation of the papers. 

Assuming that the action is pending in the Supreme Court, New York County, the original warrant, affidavit, summons and undertaking are submitted separately to the clerk of Special Term, Part II, which is the part wherein ex parte business is transacted. When the warrant is signed by the judge sitting in Special Term, Part II, the clerk returns all the papers except the affidavit which he retains. The plaintiff's attorney thereupon proceeds to the sheriff's office and files the summons and warrant, and at the same time pays the mileage and filing fees. A deputy sheriff is assigned to the case and he proceeds to the address furnished by the plaintiff's attorney. If, as in the illustrated case, the debtor is a foreign corporation, and the property levied upon is personal property, the deputy sheriff serves a copy of the summons, together with a copy of the warrant and all other papers upon which it is based, upon the debtor or other person holding the defendant's property. He also leaves a notice showing the property attached. The copy of the warrant must be certified. C.P.A., § 917. 

Thereafter the action proceeds in the same manner as any other action at law.

$ 575 

§ 575. Levy by Sheriff. 

The sheriff executes the warrant immediately, by levying upon so much of the personal and real property of the defendant, within his county, as will satisfy the plaintiff's demand, with costs and expenses. He must take into his custody all books of account, vouchers, and other papers, relating to the personal property attached, and all evidences of the defendant's title to the real property attached, which he must safely keep, to be disposed of as provided by the act. The sheriff, to whom a warrant of attachment is delivered, may levy, from time to time and as often as is necessary, until the amount for which it was issued has been secured, or final judgment has been rendered in the action, notwithstanding the expiration of his term of office. C.P.A., § 912. 

See also Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 2 [3rd Ed.], page 219. 

In making the levy, care should be taken that it is made in the manner prescribed in Section 917 of the Civil Practice Act, otherwise it may be ineffectual. Real property may be levied upon and includes any interest therein, either vested or not vested which is capable of being aliened by the defendant. C.P.A., § 913. It made by filing with the clerk of the county wherein te property is situated a notice of attachment. It is p pared by the plaintiff's attorney. It states the nan s of the parties to the action, the amount of the plainti's claim and a description of the property levied up n. 

It is subscribed with the name and address of the pla tiff's attorney. This is recorded in like manner effect as a notice of pendency previously descri 

C.P.A., & 917, subd. 1.

In the case of personal property, capable of mai delivery such as a bond, promissory note or other ins ment for the payment of money, the sheriff takes it his custody. And where the sheriff fails to take a r for example, into his actual custody, the attachment 1d. al 11e,

$ 581

levy are ineffectual. Schmid v. Berkheimer, 222 A. D. 

694, 224 N. Y. S. 726. In the case of other personal property, the sheriff leaves a certified copy of the warrant, and a notice showing the property attached, with the person holding the property. Prahl Construction 

Corporation v. Jeffs, 126 Misc. 802, 215 N. Y. S. 96. 

§ 576. Certificate to Be Furnished the Sheriff. 

Upon application of a sheriff holding a warrant of attachment, a corporation or a debtor of the defendant or a person holding property, including a bond, promissory note or other instrument for the payment of money, belonging to the defendant, must furnish to the sheriff a certificate specifying the defendant's interest in the property so attached, so held or of the debt or demand, owing to the defendant, as the case requires. C.P.A., § 918. Failure on the part of the sheriff to demand a certificate does not invalidate the levy, if the essential elements of the levy are otherwise complete. This statute is for the protection of the sheriff, and he may, in his discretion, waive its provisions. The statute does not require him to make the demand. But where the demand is made, he must be furnished with the required information. Prahl Const. Corp. v. Jeffs, 126 Misc. 802, 215

N. Y. S. 96. But where a person refuses to furnish a certificate or furnishes one which is not true or otherwise fails to set forth fully the facts required to be shown thereby, the plaintiff's attorney may move for an order requiring that person to appear and be examined under oath concerning the same. C.P.A., § 919. 

§ 577. Inventory. 

Immediately after the levy, the sheriff is required to make, with the assistance of two disinterested freeholders, a description of the real property and an inventory of the property attached and file it in the office of the clerk of the county wherein the property is attached,

$ 580 

within five days after the levy is made. C.P.A., § 921. 

Failure to file the inventory does not, however, affect the validity of the levy. C.P.A., § 921 is for the protection of creditors. Prahl Const. Corp. v. Jeffs, 126 

Misc. 802, 215 N. Y. S. 96; Korytkowski v. Greniewicki, 

220 A. D. 237, 221 N. Y. S. 119. 

§ 578. Filing Papers. 

The sheriff makes his return and the plaintiff's attorney thereupon files the return, undertaking and summons in the county clerk's office. This must be done within ten days after the warrant of attachment has been signed. 

C.P.A., § 906. 

§ 579. Service of Summons Where Attachment Issues Before Commencement of Action. 

If the warrant of attachment has been granted before the service of the summons, personal service of the summons must be made upon the defendant within thirty days after the signing of the warrant, or if the summons is to be served by publication, service must be commenced within the same period of time. C.P.A., § 905. 

Failure to begin publication of the summons within the thirty day period is fatal. Bakalas v. Moscahlades, 203 

A. D. 554, 196 N. Y. S. 682. And if the order of publication is granted upon insufficient papers, the warrant of attachment falls. Friedman v. Prescetti, 199 A. D. 385, 192 N. Y. S. 55. 

§ 580. Vacating Warrant. 

Application may be made at any time before the actual application of the attached property or the proceeds thereof to the payment of a judgment recovered in the action, to vacate or modify the warrant or to increase the security given by the plaintiff. C.P.A., § 948. The application may be founded only upon the papers upon which the warrant was granted, or upon new proof as

$ 583 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

provided by statute. Such new proof, however, cannot be used to supply jurisdictional defects. C.P.A., §§ 948951; Dexter & Carpenter, Inc., v. Lake and Export Coal 

Corporation, 196 A. D. 766, 188 N. Y. S. 623. See also

§ 581. Discharge of Attachment. 

The defendant may at any time, after he has appeared in the action, apply for an order to discharge the attachment in whole or in part. Upon such application, however, he must give an undertaking to the effect that on demand, he will pay to the plaintiff the amount of any judgment which may be recovered in the action against him, not exceeding the sum specified in the undertaking, with interest. C.P.A., §§ 952-959. 

§ 582. Injunction-In General. 

There are two kinds of injunctions, temporary and permanent. The former is granted prior to judgment and the latter is granted after judgment. It is, however, with the temporary injunction only that the statute concerns itself and provides two instances wherein a temporary injunction is granted. One is where the right depends upon the nature of the action; such as the ordinary equity action. A common example is an action to enjoin the use of a trade name. C.P.A., § 877; Martin v. 

Martin's Department Store, Inc., 245 N. Y. 513. In such a case, it must appear from the complaint that the plaintiff demands and is entitled to a judgment of injunction restraining the commission and continuance of an act, the commission or continuance of which during the pendency of the action would produce injury to the plaintiff. And the allegations of that complaint must be sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to the remedy prayed for. Vandervoort v. City of Troy, 130 Misc. 151, 223 

N. Y. S. 454. In other words, a temporary injunction will not be granted in the absence of evidence showing

$ 582 

a clear right to the permanent injunction for which the suit is brought. Village of Great Neck Estates v. Bemak 

& Lehman, Inc., 128 Misc. 441, 218 N. Y. S. 359.

The other instance wherein a temporary injunction is granted is any other action, other than the equity action, wherein the right thereto depends upon extrinsic facts as follows: 

1. Where it appears that the defendant during the pendency of the action, is doing, or procuring or suffering to be done, or threatens, or is about to do, or to procure or suffer to be done an act in violation of the plaintiff's rights respecting the subject of the action and tending to render the judgment ineffectual, an injunction may be granted to restrain him therefrom. 

2. Where it appears that the defendant during the pendency of the action threatens or is about to remove or to dispose of his property, with intent to defraud the plaintiff, an injunction order may be granted to restrain the removal or disposition. C.P.A., § 878. 

A case wherein the right to a temporary injunction depends upon extrinsic facts is that of Adams v. Ball, 24 A. D. 69, 48 N. Y. S. 778, where the plaintiff brought an action to recover the proceeds of a sale by defendant assignee of certain stocks alleged to have been the property of the plaintiff. It seems the defendant assignee was about to apply the assets to certain preferred debts in accordance with the terms of the assignment. The court held that the case came directly within Section 878 of the Civil Practice Act, as it appeared that the defendant was about to do an act, viz., to pay to the preferred creditors the money realized from the sale of plaintiff's stock, tending to render the judgment demanded ineffectual. The court further held that the injunction was very properly granted to restrain the disposition of these moneys until it could be determined in the action whether the plaintiff was entitled to recover the moneys as the proceeds of the sale of stocks belonging to him and to

$ 585 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

which the preferred and other creditors had no right whatever. 

The purpose of an injunction pendente lite, therefore, is to leave the matters in statu quo until the cause can be tried. 

§ 583. Persons Affected. 

It is elementary that an injunction order is not binding upon a person who is not a party to the action for the court may deal with those persons only who have been brought before it and have had an opportunity to be heard. Dixon v. Talerico, 217 A. D. 191, 217 N. Y. S. 

482. But a person not a party to the action, and who has knowledge of the injunction may be bound thereby if he is a servant or agent of the defendant or acts in collusion or combination with them. Rigas v. Livingston, 178 N. Y. 20, citing Daly v. Amberg, 126 N. Y. 490. 

§ 584. When Application Is Made. 

The order may be granted to accompany the summons or at any time after the commencement of the action, but it may not be granted after final judgment, except as otherwise specially prescribed by statute. C.P.A., § 

818; People ex rel. Cauffman v. Van Buren, 136 

N. Y. 252. 

§ 585. Procedure-In General. 

An action to secure an injunction is commenced by the service of a summons and complaint and brought to trial in the same manner as other actions in law and in equity. 

Where a temporary injunction is sought, it cannot be granted ex parte. C.P.A., § 882 provides that the order may be granted only upon notice. And where an application is made upon notice, either before or after answer, the court or judge may enjoin the defendant until the hearing and decision of the application; but only upon

8 586 

such notice as the court or judge, in his or its discretion, may direct. 

§ 586. Order to Show Cause Form. 

Although one may proceed by order to show cause, nevertheless it may not, as it formerly did, contain a stay pending the hearing and determination of the motion, since C.P.A., § 882, as amended, specifically provides that such preliminary relief may only be granted upon notice.

The order to show cause may be in the following form:

§ 588. Necessary Papers. 

If the papers are prepared pursuant to Section 877, they will consist of the summons, complaint, affidavit and order to show cause or notice of motion. If they are prepared pursuant to Section 878, the complaint may be omitted, but it, nevertheless, is served as a matter of practice, and in any event, it is served after the defendant serves a notice of appearance.

$ 593 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

§ 589. Submitting Order for Signature. 

Assuming that the plaintiff proceeds by order to show cause, the order is submitted to the clerk of Special Term, Part II (or such part in other courts wherein ex parte business is transacted), for the judge's signature, together with the supporting affidavit and the summons, with or without the complaint, as the case may be. 

§ 590. Service of Order to Show Cause. 

A copy of the order to show cause and affidavit may be served upon the defendant with the summons and complaint, at the same time exhibiting the original order containing the judge's signature. C.P.A., § 883. 

§ 591. Hearing-Security. 

On the return day, counsel for both sides may appear and argue the motion. It may be granted or denied. In 

New York County, where an answer has been interposed, and the motion for an injunction is denied, the court may, if the parties consent thereto, order an immediate trial and direct the action, cause or issue to be placed upon the appropriate calendar for trial for a day certain. 

New York County Supreme Court, Special Term, Rule 

III, subd. 11. If the motion is granted, the judge, unless otherwise provided, will fix the amount of the bond to be furnished, which will be to the effect that the plaintiff will pay to the party enjoined, such damages, not exceeding a sum, specified in the undertaking, as he may sustain by reason of the injunction, if the court finally decides that the plaintiff was not entitled thereto. 

C.P.A., § 893. 

§ 592. Entry and Service of Injunction Order. 

If the motion is granted, a long form order is entered thereon in the usual manner. Care should be taken to draw the order so that it will plainly indicate to the defendant specifically all the acts which he is thereby

$595 

restrained from doing. It must not be vague nor uncertain but must be so expressed that the defendants may understand what is prohibited. Lyon v. Botchford, 25 

Hun 57.

The order with notice of entry is served upon the defendant and those affected thereby. C.P.A., § 883 provides that where the injunction order is granted by the court, it must be served by delivering a certified copy thereof; where it is granted by a judge, it must be served by showing the original order and delivering a copy thereof. Copies of papers upon which the order was granted must be delivered with the copy of the order. 

§ 593. Vacating or Modifying Order. 

The party enjoined may move to vacate or modify the injunction order as provided by statute. $$ 897-901. 

§ 594. Arrest-In general. 

C.P.A.,

Arrest is, perhaps the most severe of the provisional remedies and great care should be exercised in utilizing it. The courts are inclined to grant it in those cases where no other relief will suffice. For example, where an attachment gives complete protection, an order of arrest should not be granted. Todd-Buick, Inc., v. 

Smith, 118 Misc. 102, 192 N. Y. S. 459, aff'd 202

A. D. 774. 

§ 595. Actions Wherein Remedy is Available. 

An order of arrest may be obtained in both law and equity actions.

Section 826 of the Civil Practice Act provides that a defendant may be arrested, where the action is brought for either of the following causes: 

1. To recover a fine or penalty. 

2. To recover damages for personal injury. 

3. To recover damages for wrongful taking, detention or conversion of personal property.

§ 

595 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

4. To recover damages for breach of promise to marry. 

5. To recover damages for misconduct or neglect in office, or in a professional employment. 

6. To recover damages for fraud, or deceit. 

7. To recover a chattel where it is alleged in the complaint that the chattel or a part thereof has been concealed, removed or disposed of so that it cannot be found or taken by the sheriff and with intent that it should not be so found or taken, or to deprive the plaintiff of the benefit thereof. 

8. To recover for money received, or to recover property or damages for the conversion or misapplication of property, where it is alleged in the complaint that the money was received or the property was embezzled or fraudulently misapplied by a public officer or by an attorney, solicitor or counselor, or by an officer or agent of a corporation or banking association in the course of his employment, or by a factor, agent, broker or other person in a fiduciary capacity. Where such allegation is made, the plaintiff cannot recover unless he proves the same on the trial of the action; and a judgment for the defendant is not a bar to a new action to recover the money or property. 

9. To recover for conversion or wrongful disposition of public money or property. 

10. In an action upon contract, where it is alleged in the complaint that the defendant was guilty of a fraud in contracting or incurring the liability, or that since the making of the contract, or in contemplation of making of the same, he has removed or disposed of his property with intent to defraud his creditors, or is about to remove or dispose of the same with like intent. 

These provisions, however, do not give the plaintiff an absolute right to an order of arrest; the language is permissive only. It rests in the sound discretion of the

$ 596 

judge to grant or refuse the order. Gelles v. Rosenbaum, 141 Misc. 588, 252 N. Y. S. 827.

Section 827 of the Civil Practice Act refers to equity actions and provides that a defendant may be arrested in an action wherein the judgment demanded requires the performance of an act, the neglect or refusal to perform which would be punishable by the court as a contempt, where the defendant is not a resident of the state, or, being a resident is about to depart therefrom by reason of which non-residence or departure, there is danger that a judgment or an order requiring the performance of the act will be rendered ineffectual. In a case specified in this section, the order of arrest can be granted only by the court, is always in its discretion and may be granted or served either before or after final judgment unless an appeal from the judgment is pending upon which security has been given sufficient to stay the execution thereof. 

§ 596. Persons Privileged from Arrest. 

A woman cannot be arrested as prescribed in Articles 

47 and 48 except where the order can be granted only by the court, and in actions to recover damages for a wilful injury to person, character or property. C.P.A., $ 829. 

A lunatic, an idiot, or an infant under the age of fourteen years, if arrested, may be discharged from arrest as a privileged person, in the discretion of the court or judge. The application for his discharge may be made in his behalf by a relative or by any other person whom the court or judge permits to represent him for that purpose. C.P.A., § 830. 

A person prosecuted in a representative capacity, as heir, executor, administrator, legatee, devisee, next of kin, assignee, or trustee cannot be arrested, as prescribed in Articles 47 and 48, except for his personal act.

C.P.A., 831.

$597 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

§ 597. Necessary Papers. 

The following papers are submitted upon an application for an order of arrest: Order Affidavit

Summons required unless already served. 

C.P.A., § 818. 

Complaint. As a matter of practice, it is submitted upon the application although it is not always necessary to do so. In actions under Section 827 and subdivisions 7, 8 and 10 of Section 826, a complaint should be submitted since an allegation of the complaint is necessary to an arrest. C.P.A., § 833. And as the court stated in Lichstrahl v. Lichstrahl, 38 Misc. 331, 77 N. Y. S. 900, that it was difficult for the court to know what is alleged in the complaint when there is no complaint. 

Undertaking. 

§ 598. Order-Form. 

An order for the arrest of a party is subscribed by the attorney for the party obtaining the order, and, unless granted by the court, is also signed by the judge. 

C.P.R. 82. It may be directed to the sheriff of a particular county or generally, to the sheriff of any county. 

C.P.A., § 838. It requires the sheriff forthwith to arrest the party against whom it is directed, if found within his county, to hold him to bail in a specified sum, and to return the order, with his proceedings thereunder, as prescribed by law. C.P.R. 82. The plaintiff's attorney, at his option, by an indorsement upon the order, or, where it was granted by the court, upon the copy thereof delivered to the sheriff, may fix a time within which the defendant must be arrested. In such case, he cannot be arrested afterward under the same order, unless the time be extended by the court, for cause. C.P.A., § 838. 

The amount of bail is left blank in the order to be filled

$ 598 

in by the judge. The order also briefly recites the ground or grounds on which it is granted. C.P.A., § 821.

§ 599. Affidavit-Form. 

Before an order of arrest is granted, the existence of a cause of action sufficient to establish the right to an arrest, or where the right to arrest depends partly on extrinsic facts, the existence of a cause of action and facts sufficient to authorize the order, must be shown to the satisfaction of the court or judge. It must also show facts and circumstances from which the amount of bail to be required may be determined.

The affidavit in support of the order may read as follows:

The action was commenced by the service of a summons on the defendant on or about the 7th day of February, 1928. The defendant subsequently appeared herein and after the service of an amended complaint duly filed an amended answer. A copy of the pleadings is annexed hereto and made a part of the moving papers herein.

The action is one for specific performance. The defendant Roe and the plaintiff are husband and wife. Shortly after their marriage in 1923, plaintiff gave to her husband securities of the value of approximately $850,000, and subsequently in July, 1923, the defendant with these securities established a trust, naming the Loan & Trust Company and Harry Parker as trustees. Disputes arose between the parties, as a result of which they separated. 

On January 12, 1928, at Paris, France, the parties entered into an agreement providing among other things for the custody of the children of the parties and also providing that defendant would request the trustees to terminate the trust theretofore created to the extent that $250,000 would be withdrawn from the trust and paid over to the plaintiff. Defendant, however, refused to proceed with the agreement and as a result plaintiff commenced this action in the Supreme Court of the State of New York. The defendant and trustees appeared and the issue was referred to Hon. Charles A. Boston, as Referee. Over 900 pages of testimony have been taken and the hearings have consumed many months. The defendant had among other things interposed a plea that the agreement was void under the laws of Illinois, where, he contended, the parties had their legal domicile. Thereafter the Referee filed an opinion, among other things sustaining the validity of the agreement of January 12, 1928, and directing the defendant specifically to perform the same. 

While the opinion herein has been filed, the formal report of the Referee is still incomplete, due to his desire to hear arguments on additional questions of law involved in the case. The decision at the present time has been prepared by the Referee and will be signed within a very short time and final judgment entered. The

A motion to enjoin defendant Roe from prosecuting the Illinois action has been made and is at present before the court awaiting a decision. § 600. The Undertaking. 

RICHARD SMITH. 

The undertaking, unless dispensed with, is to the effect that if the defendant recovers judgment or if it is finally decided that the plaintiff was not entitled to the order of arrest, the plaintiff will pay all costs which may be awarded to the defendant and all damages which he may sustain by reason of the arrest, not exceeding the sum specified in the undertaking, which must be at least equal to one-tenth of the amount of bail required by the order and not less than two hundred and fifty dollars. 

C.P.A., § 835. Where the order can be granted only by the court, an undertaking on the part of the plaintiff may be dispensed with. If it is required, its form and the security to be given thereupon must be such as the court prescribes. C.P.A., § 836. Security shall not be required where the action was brought for a cause specified in C.P.A., § 826, subd. 9. 

§ 601. Procedure. 

The order of arrest, or where it was granted by the court, a certified copy thereof, subscribed by the plain-

$603 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

tiff's attorney, and, in either case, the papers upon which the order was granted, with the undertaking, if any, must be delivered to the sheriff, who, upon arresting the defendant, must deliver to him copies thereof. C.P.A., § 839. The sheriff executes the order by arresting the defendant if he is found within his county, and keeping him in custody until discharged by law. C.P.A., § 840. 

§ 602. Filing Papers. 

Within ten days after the defendant is arrested, if he does not give bail, or if he gives bail, within ten days after the justification of the bail, the sheriff must file with the clerk the order of arrest, or, where it was granted by the court, the certified copy thereof delivered to him, with his return thereupon endorsed, the papers upon which the order of arrest was granted and the undertaking, if any, given on the part of the plaintiff. C.P.A., 

§ 864. Rule 80 of the Rules of Civil Practice provides that the attorney shall file the affidavit on which the order was granted within ten days after it is granted, otherwise the opposing party may move to vacate the order and the court will vacate it unless the time to file the affidavit is extended. 

§ 603. Procedure After Arrest. 

Immediately upon his arrest, the defendant may give bail or make a deposit of the sum specified in the order of arrest at any hour of the day or night, and he must have reasonable opportunity to send for and to procure bail before being committed to jail. C.P.A., § 847. The defendant's attorney may furthermore move to vacate the order of arrest where the complaint fails to set forth a cause of action in which an arrest is authorized or an allegation essential to the right of arrest. He may also move to reduce the bail or increase the security. C.P.A., S 842-845; C.P.R. 83. 

§ 604. Receivers-In General. 

In addition to the cases wherein the appointment of a receiver is specifically provided for by law, a receiver

$606 

may be appointed for the purpose of preserving property where, before final judgment, the property which is in the possession of an adverse party is in danger of being removed beyond the jurisdiction of the court or otherwise lost or injured; where by or after final judgment, it is necessary to carry the judgment into effect, or to dispose of the property in accordance with its provisions; and where, after final judgment, it becomes necessary to preserve the property pending the appeal. C.P.A., § 974.

The receiver before entering upon his duties is required to furnish security in a sum fixed by the court. C.P.A., § 976. See also Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 2 (3rd Ed.), 524. 

§ 605. Replevin-In General. 

Where a party is the owner of a chattel or otherwise entitled to possession thereof, and it is wrongfully detained by the defendant, he may commence suit in the usual manner to recover it. And if he wishes to have the chattel seized in advance of instituting suit so that he may have it until his right to possession thereto can be ascertained, he may take the necessary steps provided by the remedy known as replevin. C.P.A., §§ 1089-1131; 

C.P.R. 270-273; New York City Mun. Ct. Code, §§ 57-69; 

Albany City Court Act, §§ 95-129. See also Wait's N. Y. 

Practice, Vol. 2 (3rd Ed.), 685. This corresponds to at tachment. Although replevin is not a provisional remedy, nevertheless it is similar in nature thereto. Where, for example, a chattel is seized before the service of the summons, it is regarded as equivalent to the granting of a provisional remedy for the purpose of giving jurisdiction to the court and enabling it to control subsequent proceedings. C.P.A., § 1092. 

§ 606. When Application May be Made. 

A chattel may be replevied before the summons is served, or at any time thereafter and before the entry of final judgment. C.P.A., §§ 1092; 1094.

$ 605 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

§ 607. Procedure-In General. 

A written undertaking is furnished to the sheriff, and in addition, an affidavit, together with a written requisition indorsed upon or annexed to the affidavit and subscribed by the plaintiff's attorney to the effect that the sheriff is required to replevy the chattel described therein. The requisition is the mandate of the court and may be directed to the sheriff of a particular county or generally to the sheriff of any county where the chatter is found. C.P.A., § 1095. 

§ 608. Requisition—Form. 

The requisition reads as follows:

RAYMOND SMITH, 

Attorney for Plaintiff,

Borough of Manhattan,  

Note: In some of the lower courts, the requisition is required to be issued by the clerk. See Albany City Court Act, § 101;

New York City Municipal Court Code, § 59.

$ 609 

§ 609. Affidavit-Form. 

The affidavit to be delivered to the sheriff in behalf of the plaintiff with a requisition to replevy a chattel may be made by the plaintiff's agent or attorney if the material facts are within his personal knowledge; or if the plaintiff is not within the county where the attorney resides or has his office. C.P.A., § 1110. It must particularly describe the chattel to be replevied. This is necessary not only for the protection of the sheriff but the defendant as well. And the description required is such that there can be no doubt as to what property is to be taken. It must also state the value of the chattels. 

C.P.A., § 1096; National Enameling & Stamping Co. v. 

Kaplan, 53 A. D. 96, 65 N. Y. S. 732; Croker Fire Prevention Corp. v. Jacobs, 235 A. D. 216, 256 N. Y. S. 775.

It must contain allegations; to wit, that the plaintiff is the owner of the chattel, or is entitled to the possession thereof, and the facts with respect thereto; that it is wrongfully detained by the defendant; the alleged cause of the detention thereof; that it has not been taken by virtue of a warrant against the plaintiff for the collection of a tax, assessment or fine issued in pursuance of a statute of the state or of the United States; or, if it has been taken under color of such a warrant, either that the taking was unlawful, by reason of defects in the process, or other causes specified, or that the detention is unlawful by reason of facts specified which have subsequently occurred; that it has not been seized by virtue of an execution or warrant of attachment against the property of the plaintiff or anyone through whom he has derived title since the seizure thereof; or if it has been so seized, that it was exempt from seizure or that its detention is unlawful; and its actual value.

The following form of affidavit may be used in any of the courts:

§ 610. Undertaking. 

The undertaking to be delivered to the sheriff with a requisition to replevy a chattel must be executed by at least two sureties, who must be approved by the sheriff.

§ 609 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

It must be to the effect that the sureties are bound in a specified sum, not less than twice the value of the chattel, as stated in the affidavit, for the prosecution of the action, for the return of the chattel to the defendant, if possession thereof is adjudged to him, or if the action abates, or is discontinued before the chattel is returned to the defendant; and for the payment to the defendant of any sum which the judgment awards to him against the plaintiff. C.P.A., § 1099. 

§ 611. Complaint Form. 

A complaint may be served with the papers although it is not necessary to do so. An allegation in a pleading interposed by either party to the effect that the party pleading, or a third person, was, at the time when the action was commenced, or the chattel was replevied, as the case may be, the owner of the chattel, or that it was then his property, is a sufficient statement of title, unless the right of the action or defense rests on a right of possession by virtue of a special property, in which case, the pleading must set forth the facts upon which the special property depends, so as to show that at the time the action was commenced, or the chattel was replevied, as the case may be, the party pleading, or the third person, was entitled to the possession. C.P.R. 70. If in an action to recover a chattel, the complaint contain a sufficient statement of the plaintiff's title, a general allegation that the defendant wrongfully took the chattel, is sufficient without setting forth the facts showing that the taking was wrongful. If the taking of the chattel is not complained of, but the action is founded upon its wrongful detention, the complaint must set forth the facts showing that the detention was wrongful. C.P.R. 71.

The following form of complaint may be used in any of the courts:

§ 612. Replevying Chattel. 

After the affidavit, requisition and undertaking are delivered to the sheriff, or if it is a municipal court action to the marshal, he immediately proceeds to take the

§ 614  

chattel into his possession, if it can be found in the possession of the defendant, or the latter's agent; since the purpose of the action is to obtain possession of the chattel and the defendant cannot elect as between the delivery of the chattel and the payment of the award. Tanenbaum 

Son & Co. v. Bauman & Co., 261 N. Y. 85. And at the 'same time, he serves a copy of the affidavit, requisition and undertaking upon the defendant or the latter's agent, from whose possession the chattel is taken, and if neither can be found, a copy of the papers is left at the usual place of abode of either with a person of suitable age. 

C.P.A., § 1100. The sheriff then retains possession of the chattel until the person entitled to possession thereof is ascertained. He delivers it to that person after payment of his fees and expenses. C.P.A., § 1101. If the goods is of a perishable nature, an order may be obtained directing the sheriff to sell the goods and retain in his possession the proceeds of the sale to be delivered to the person entitled thereto. C.P.A., § 1101a. 

The defendant may, in such a case, except to the sureties in accordance with Section 1102 of the Civil Practice Act, reclaim the chattel as provided in Section 1103 of the Civil Practice Act, or simply await the trial of the action. 

§ 613. Return by Sheriff. 

Within twenty days after the sheriff has delivered a chattel replevied, to the party entitled to the possession thereof, as provided in Section 1105 of the Civil Practice 

Act, he files with the clerk, the plaintiff's affidavit, and requisition with a return, stating in what manner he executed the latter. C.P.A., § 1113. And these papers are made a part of the judgment-roll. C.P.A., § 1115. 

§ 614. Trial-Judgment-Execution. 

A replevin action proceeds in the usual manner to trial regardless whether the sheriff was required to replevy

$ 613 

PROVISIONAL REMEDIES. 

the chattel or has been unable to do so. C.P.A., § 1116. 

The issue to be determined in the replevin action is the present right to possession. Roach v. Curtis, 191 N. Y. 

387, aff'g 115 A. D. 765, 101 N. Y. S. 333.

The final judgment must award to the plaintiff the chattel or its value, together with damages for the detention thereof or for injury or depreciation, if any. C.P.A., 

§§ 1118; 1124. 

Where the judgment, among other things, awards a sum of money, if possession of the chattel is not delivered to the prevailing party, execution may issue requiring the sheriff, if the chattel cannot be found in his county, to satisfy the sum so awarded, with interest and his fees, out of the property of the party against whom the judgment is rendered.

§ 615. In General. 

PAGE 

614 615 616 616 616 617 621 621 621 It has been pointed out that in order to secure relief, it is necessary to commence suit therefor by the service of a summons, and that certain steps are required to be taken before judgment can be entered, and in some instances this procedure requires a long period of time, which may result in rendering ineffective the remedy which is finally obtained. It was further pointed out that in certain instances where immediate relief was urgent, one could apply for the provisional remedies. The latter, however, are temporary and jurisdiction acquired thereby is conditional and liable to be divested in a case where the jurisdiction was dependent on some act to be done after the granting of the remedy. C.P.A., § 825. Unlike either the civil action or the provisional remedy is the special proceeding. There are a number of special proceedings, each of which is used for a particular purpose. They consist of habeas corpus, certiorari, mandamus, prohibition and contempt proceedings. In addition, there is the special proceeding for the appointment of a committee of an incompetent person and arbitration proceedings. 614

§ 615 

SPECIAL PROCEEDINGS-HABEAS CORPUS. 

These follow more or less the same method of procedure; to wit, application for the relief by petition or affidavit and the entry of the final order. 

With respect to three of the foregoing special proceedings, the legislature passed a law May 22, 1937, effective 

September 1, 1937, whereby Articles 78, 79, and 80 of the

Civil Practice Act, dealing with certiorari, mandamus and prohibition, respectively, were repealed, and in the place thereof was substituted Article 78. This article abolishes the separate classification of certiorari, mandamus and prohibition. The relief heretofore obtained by such writs or orders may be obtained as provided in 

Article 78, and in the manner therein prescribed. See 

Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 6 (4th Ed.).

The procedure with respect to one of the aforementioned special proceedings; to wit, an application for a writ of habeas corpus, will be more fully discussed. 

§ 616. Writ of Habeas Corpus. 

The writ of habeas corpus has come down to us through the centuries, having for its object the speedy release by judicial decree of one who is illegally restrained of his liberty or illegally detained from the control of those who are entitled to his custody. The importance and urgency of the writ is so well recognized by the law that provision is made that unless the petitioner is prohibited by law from prosecuting the writ, the judge must grant it or forfeit the sum of one thousand dollars to the prisoner. 

The writ may be issued on Sunday. C.P.A., § 1235.

Although the purpose of the writ was to secure individual freedom, nevertheless it has come to be applied to many uses, among which is the ascertainment and enforcement of the right of the custody of infant children. 

Ordinarily the basis of the issuance of the writ is illegal detention, but where a writ is issued for the detention of a child, the question to be determined is not the legality

$ 619 

of the detention but rather the welfare of the child. The law regards the unauthorized absence from legal custody as the equivalent of illegal restraint and imprisonment. 

People ex rel. Pryne v. Watts, 122 N. Y. 238; see also 

Domestic Relations Law, §§ 70, 71. 

§ 617. Persons Entitled to the Issuance of a Writ of 

Habeas Corpus. 

A person imprisoned or restrained of his liberty, within the state, except by virtue of a mandate of a Federal Court having exclusive jurisdiction or by virtue of a final judgment and decree of a state court of competent jurisdiction, is entitled to the issuance of a writ of habeas corpus. C.P.A., § 1231. 

§ 618. Procedure-In General. 

The writ takes the place of a summons and is the process by which jurisdiction is obtained. Although it is prepared by the attorney, nevertheless, unlike a summons, it must be signed by the judge and issued under the seal of the court. The applicant for the writ is the relator. It is directed to the person who is charged with wrongful distraint and he is known as the defendant. The papers consist of the writ and petition. The latter may be signed either by the person for whose relief it is intended or by some person in his behalf. C.P.A., § 1232. 

The writ must be issued, although no application has been made therefor, where the judge has evidence that a person is illegally imprisoned or restrained of his liberty. 

C.P.A., § 1241. 

§ 619. The Writ-Form. 

The form of the writ is prescribed by statute. C.P.A., § 1237. It may be made returnable forthwith or at some future date. A writ for the custody of a child, made re turnable in Special Term, Part II, of the Supreme Court, New York County, may read as follows:

$ 617

ROE -against- 

RICHARD ROE, Writ of 

Habeas Corpus.

§ 620. Petition-Form. 

BERNARD SHIENTAG, Justice of the Supreme Court. 

The petition must be verified and state in substance that the person in whose behalf the writ is applied for, is

8 620 

imprisoned or restrained of his liberty; the place where and the officer or person by whom he is imprisoned or restrained; that he has not been committed and is not detained by virtue of any judgment, decree, or final order of a state court of competent jurisdiction; or the mandate of a federal court of exclusive jurisdiction; the cause or pretence of the imprisonment or restraint; if the imprisonment or restraint is by virtue of a mandate, a copy thereof must be annexed if it can be obtained; if the imprisonment is illegal, it must state why it is illegal; whether any previous application has been made for the writ and whether an appeal has been taken from any order upon an application for a writ. C.P.A., § 1234. 

A petition in support of a writ for the custody of a child may read as follows:

§ 621. Service of Writ. 

After the writ is signed by the judge, a copy thereof and of the petition may be served upon the defendant, by any person of the age of twenty-one years and upwards. 

C.P.A., § 1243. 

§ 622. The Return. 

It has already been stated that the writ takes the place of the process or summons. The petition, in turn, may be regarded as the complaint. The return which the writ requires the defendant to make, may be regarded as the answer, which in substance, states, among other things, whether the defendant has custody of the person in whose behalf the writ was issued and by what authority he holds that person. It must be verified unless it is signed by a public officer. C.P.A., § 1245. 

§ 623. Hearing. 

On the return day, the person upon whom the writ is served, must obey it according to the command thereof. 

C.P.A., § 1244. The parties may appear by attorney. 

C.P.A., § 1247.

The hearing is held before the judge of 

Special Term, Part II, and is in the nature of a trial. If the hearing is one for the custody of a child, the judge hears the witnesses and may question the child. The court is concerned only with the best interests of the child, and where it does not appear that the health, morals or the welfare of the child are in danger, it will not interfere. For example, in a case which involved a dispute between the parents as to the education of the child in

§ 623  

their joint custody, a writ whereby the mother obtained exclusive custody and control of the child was dismissed on the ground that the courts cannot regulate the internal affairs of the home, and it did not appear that the health or morals of the child were affected. People ex rel. Sisson v. Sisson, 271 N. Y. 285.

§ 624. In General. 

A will is an instrument by which a person makes a disposition of his property to take effect after his death. 

There may be an oral will which is known as a nuncupa- 40 623

$ 625 

tive will and is valid under certain circumstances, such as when drawn by sailors at sea or soldiers in actual service. 

Up to the form of execution, there is no prescribed form for a will or the language to be used except that it must clearly set forth the intent of the testator; that is, one should be able to determine from a reading thereof how the testator intended to dispose of his property. But inasmuch as a person, as a rule, informs his attorney how he wants his property distributed, it is the attorney who should be responsible for drawing it in the proper language and advise the testator whether he may lawfully dispose of his property in the manner he wishes. 

The person who makes a will is the testator. The person to whom real property passes is the devisee. The legatee is one to whom personalty passes. The testator devises real property and bequeaths personalty. The executor is the person nominated in the will to execute the will; that is, to carry it into effect. An administrator is one who administers or manages the estate of an intestate. The latter term is applied to one who dies without leaving a will. 

§ 625. The Will-Form. 

Although no particular form of will is prescribed, the following may be observed as to form and contents:

I, JOHN DOE, of the City and State of New York, being of sound and disposing mind, memory and understanding, do hereby make, publish and declare this to be my Last Will and Testament, hereby revoking all other wills by me heretofore made. 

FIRST: I hereby direct that all my just debts and funeral expenses be paid as soon after my demise as practicable. 

SECOND: I give and bequeath the sum of Two Thousand 

($2,000) Dollars to my nephew, HUGH SMITH, residing at 100

§ 626. Manner of Execution. 

When the will has been prepared by the attorney, it is submitted to the client for careful examination. If the latter is satisfied that it complies with his wishes, the next step is to have it executed in proper form. The attorney calls in two witnesses and proceeds to read the attestation clause to the testator. This clause appears just below the signature of the testator. The client signs his name at the end of the will and also along the margin of each sheet of paper as a precautionary measure; that is, in order that no other page may be substituted for those which constitute the will as signed. The testator states to the witnesses that the instrument is his will and requests them to sign. In actual practice, the attorney introduces the witnesses to the testator and says in substance, "You request Miss Jones and Mr. Smith to act as witnesses to your will and sign their names thereto?"

The testator replies in the affirmative. Each witness in turn signs his name together with his address. It is well to note that failure to indicate the address may subject

$ 627 

the witness to payment of a fine. Two copies of the will are conformed at the time of the execution. The original and a copy may be delivered to the client, who may deposit the original with the Surrogate for safe-keeping. 

Dec. Estate Law, § 30. A copy thereof may be retained by the attorney. It should also be remembered that at some future time, when it becomes necessary to prove the will, the subscribing witness may not be able to remember what occurred upon the execution of the will. The Decedent Estate Law, § 30, provides, therefore, that a subscribing witness may make and sign an affidavit setting forth the facts of the execution. The affidavit may be annexed to and filed with the will. 

§ 627. Changing Will. 

The testator may make an entire new will from time to time, and as often as he chooses. Or, he may desire to change parts of the will already executed, in which case, he may execute what is known as a codicil and follows the formalities attendant upon the execution of a will. 

§ 628. Procedure on Death of Testator. 

Upon the death of the testator, the executor who is lawfully entitled to the custody of the will, proceeds to take the necessary steps to qualify, pay the debts of the decedent and distribute the estate. 

§ 629. Court Wherein Will Is Probated—Jurisdiction and Procedure.

The Surrogate's Court is one wherein all matters relating to the affairs of decedents are administered. 

Among other things, it takes proof of wills, admits wills to probate, grants and revokes letters testamentary and letters of administration; directs and controls the conduct of, and settles the accounts of executors and administrators; enforces the payment of debts and legacies; directs

$629 

the disposition of real property and interests therein; and the disposition of the proceeds thereof; appoints guardians for infants; and determines the validity, construction or effect of any disposition of property con tained in the will. Surr. Ct. Act, § 40. 

Proceedings in the Surrogate's Court are commenced by the filing of a petition. Surr. Ct. Act, § 48. This cor responds to a complaint in a civil action in the supreme court and may be verified in the same manner. Surr. Ct. 

Act, § 50. Where the applicant resides out of the county, and the matters are peculiarly within the attorney's knowledge, the attorney may properly verify the petition. 

In re Riess, 170 A. D. 951, 155 N. Y. S. 1136. The petition must set forth the title of the proceeding, the name and residence of the person to whose estate or fund the proceeding relates, and the name and residence of the petitioner; the facts upon which the jurisdiction of the court depends; the names and post-office addresses of all persons interested in the proceeding who are required to be cited or concerning whom the court is required to have information; that there are no other persons than those mentioned interested in the application; a request for the relief to which petitioner is entitled; also information. with respect to any who are infants, or who are adjudged or alleged incompetent. Surr. Ct. Act, § 51. 

The process of the court is a citation to show cause or an order to show cause. Surr. Ct. Act, § 52; In re Eno's 

Estate, 111 Misc. 69, 180 N. Y. S. 889. Unless otherwise prescribed by law, it is returnable in the surrogate's court from which it was issued and may be served or executed in any county. Surr. Ct. Act, § 52. It sets forth the name and address of the petitioner, and of the person to whose estate or fund the proceeding relates; the names of all the persons to be cited who have not waived its issue and service, or have not appeared unless the number of such persons constitute a class exceeding five

$ 629 

hundred, in which case it may be directed to such class by appropriate description; the time and place it is returnable, which time must not be more than four months after the date thereof; the object of the proceeding and the date when it issues. It is attested in the name of the surrogate, and by the seal of his court. Surr. Ct. Act, 

§§ 53, 54. 

The citation is served in practically the same manner as a summons. Surr. Ct. Act, §§ 56-62. Proof of service of the citation is also made in the manner similar to that of proof of the service of a summons. 

The petitions, answers, and objections if any, contain a plain and concise statement of the facts constituting the claim, objection or defense, and a demand for the decree, order or other relief, to which the party supposes himself to be entitled and are duly verified. The surrogate may require that a copy thereof be served upon any person interested in such manner as he may direct. A party who fails to comply with such requirement may be treated as a party in default. Surr. Ct. Act, § 49. The only recognized pleadings are the petition and answer. In re 

Work's Estate, 76 Misc. 403, 137 N. Y. S. 97.

In this court, also, a person may appear and prosecute or defend a special proceeding in person, or by attorney. 

The appearance must be evidenced by a notice of appearance signed by the party or his attorney and filed in the Surrogate's Court. And where no citation has been served on the person appearing, or where citation has been served personally without the state or by publication, such appearance and notice must conform to the re quirements of Section 41 of the Surrogate's Court Act. 

Surr. Ct. Act, § 63. The appearance of a party against whom a citation is issued, has the same effect as the appearance of a party in an action in the supreme court. 

In re Gregory's Estate, 13 Misc. 363, 35 N. Y. S. 105. 

The surrogate must appoint a special guardian where

$ 629 

a party who is an infant, does not appear by a general guardian, or where a party is a lunatic, idiot or habitual drunkard and does not appear by his committee, and where such party appears by a general guardian or committee, as the case may be, inquires into the facts to find if such general guardian or committee is fully competent to take care of the interests of such party, otherwise a special guardian must be appointed in addition thereto. 

A special guardian is also appointed where there are unknown persons or persons whose whereabouts are unknown. Surr. Ct. Act, & 64. 

In a special proceeding other than one instituted for the probate of a will and subject to the right of trial by jury of any question of fact, the surrogate may in his discretion appoint a referee to take and report to the surrogate the evidence upon the facts; to examine an account rendered, to hear and determine questions arising upon the settlement of such an account and make a report thereon subject to confirmation or modification by the surrogate. But no referee to examine an account rendered, or to hear and determine questions arising upon the settlement of such account, may be appointed where the estate or fund does not exceed one thousand dollars in value, or in any case where the item or items in such account to which objections have been made do not aggregate more than two hundred dollars. Surr. Ct. Act, 

§ 66. 

A jury may be obtained to decide controverted questions of fact, in which case, the surrogate makes an order that such trial be had either before himself and a jury or at a trial term of the supreme court to be held within the county, or in the county court of the county. Surr. Ct. 

Act, 88 67-70. If there is no jury, the surrogate must file in his office his decision in writing which shall direct the decree to be entered, and need not contain either the facts found or the conclusions of law. Surr. Ct. Act, § 71.

§ 631 

The determination of the rights of the parties to a special proceeding in a surrogate's court is a decree. A direction made or entered in writing, and not included in a decree, is an order. It is enforced in like manner as a similar order made by the supreme court in an action. 

Surr. Ct. Act, § 78. See Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 7 

(4th Ed.), 143. A decree directing the payment of a sum of money may be enforced by an execution against the property of the party directed to make the payment. The execution is issued by the surrogate, or the clerk of the surrogate's court, under the seal of the court, and is made returnable to the court. In all other respects the procedure for the collection of the judgment corresponds to that taken upon a judgment recovered in the supreme court, the decree being for that purpose regarded as a judgment. In order to commence proceedings supplementary to judgment, no execution need be issued and the decree has the same force and effect as if it were a judgment of the county court, or in the city of New York, of the supreme court. Surr. Ct. Act, § 83. See People ex rel. Sackett v. Woodbury, 70 A. D. 416, 75 N. Y. S. 236. 

§ 630. Probate of Will-In General. 

The first step in the probate of a will is to obtain the decedent's will. If it is in a safe deposit box, it will be necessary to procure an order from the Surrogate for the opening of the box. A certified copy of the order is served upon the company which owns the box and also upon the State Tax Commission. An appointment is made with a representative of the State Tax Commission who is required to be present when the safe deposit box is opened. The purpose is to insure payment of the transfer tax.

If the will is in the possession of a person and there is reason to believe that the person has destroyed or is concealing it, or has knowledge of such facts, the court must

§ 631  

make an order requiring that person to attend and be examined, and it may require the production of the will. 

Matter of Hardy, 216 N. Y. 132. See also Sielcken's

Estate, 115 Misc. 385, 188 N. Y. S. 386. The person is served with a certified copy of the order and is paid the usual witness fee. Surr. Ct. Act, § 137. 

The trial of an issue in the Surrogate's Court follows practically the same procedure as that of other courts. 

See Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 7 (4th Ed.), 207.

Because in the majority of cases the probate of a will is uncontested, it may be well to follow the steps in such a proceeding. A complete set of forms to be used may be obtained from the clerk of the particular surrogate's court in which the proceeding is to be brought. 

§ 631. Affidavit of Comparison-Form. 

Assuming one has obtained the original will, an exact copy thereof is made so that it may be filed with the original. This is compared with the original by two adult persons. An affidavit is executed to the effect that these persons have compared the copy with the original will and that the copy is true and correct. New York 

County Surrogate's Court Rule VII. See local court rules. It reads as follows: 

In the Matter of Proving the Last 

Will and Testament of 

Affidavit Proving a 

JOHN DOE,

Correct Copy of the 

Will Filed for Probate. Deceased.

COUNTY AND  SS. : 

We, MARY BROWN and LOUISE NEWMAN, being duly and severally sworn say, each for herself, that she has carefully compared the foregoing paper with the original thereof, dated

$ 633 

the 15th day of March, 1930, about to be filed for probate, and that the same is in all respects a true and correct copy of said instrument and of the whole thereof. 

MARY BROWN, LOUISE NEWMAN. 

15th day of February, 1933.

ROBERT ADAMS, Notary Public-New York County. 

§ 632. Petition—Form. 

A petition for the probate of a will may be presented by any person designated in the will as executor, devisee, legatee, testamentary trustee or guardian, or by the general guardian of any infant legatee or devisee; a creditor of the decedent, or any other person interested in the estate; any party to an action brought, or about to be brought, in which action the decedent, if living, would be a proper party. And where a will has been filed in the surrogate's office for over sixty days, and no other person who is entitled to petition for its probate has done so, the surrogate's court may direct the public administrator or county treasurer to present a petition. Surr. Ct. Act, § 139. The general contents of the petition are enumer ated in Surr. Ct. Act, § 51. 

Assuming that the petition is to be presented on behalf of the executor, the latter's attorney may draw the peti tion to read as follows: 

In the Matter of Proving the Last 

Will and Testament of

JOHN DOE,

Deceased, as a Will of Personal Property.

§ 633. Citation and Waiver Thereof-Form of Waiver. 

Certain persons must be cited upon a petition for the probate of a will. The person designated in the will as

§  

637 executor, testamentary trustee or guardian or beneficiary in any other will of the same testator filed in the surrogate's office, must be cited, as well as the husband or wife, if any, and all the distributees of the testator. In addition to the general contents contained in sections 53 and 54 of the Surrogate's Court Act, the citation sets forth the name of the person by whom the will is propounded; whether the will relates exclusively to real property or to personal property, or to both; and if the will is nuncupative, that fact. Surr. Ct. Act, § 140. See also Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 7 (4th Ed.), 51. 

Such persons may, however, waive the issue or service, or both, of the citation, by an instrument in writing which is signed, acknowledged or proved and duly certified. 

Surr. Ct. Act, § 41, subd. 3a. The waiver may read thus: 

In the Matter of Proving the Last 

Will and Testament of 

JOHN DOE, Deceased,

Waiver of Citation in Probate Proceeding. 

As a Will of Real and Personal

Property. 

I, HUGH SMITH, the undersigned, an heir at law and next of kin of JOHN DOE, deceased, do hereby appear in person and waive the issuance and service of a citation in the matter of proving the last will and testament of said deceased, bearing date March 15th, 1930. 

Dated, February 28th, 1933. 

Signed in the presence of

ROBERT ADAMS. 

HUGH SMITH.

8 634 

BE IT KNOWN, that on the 28th day of February, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-three before me a Notary Public in and for the State of New York, duly commissioned and sworn, residing in the Borough of Brooklyn, personally came and appeared HUGH SMITH to me personally known, and known to me to be the same person described in and who executed the above waiver and he acknowledged that he executed the same.

IN TESTIMONY WHEREOF, I have hereunto subscribed my name and affixed my seal of office, the day and year above written.

ROBERT ADAMS, Notary Public, New York County. 

§ 634. Notice of Probate-Form. 

In order that all other persons who are interested in the will and who are not next of kin or heirs-at-law, may have notice of the probate of the will and claim their legacy, a notice is sent to all such persons. The notice states the name of the testator, that his last will and testament has been offered for probate, or probated, as the case may be, and the name and post-office address of the proponent and of each and every legatee, devisee or other beneficiary, as set forth in the petition, who has not been cited or has not appeared or waived citation. The notice may be mailed to each beneficiary. An affidavit of such mailing is filed in the surrogate's office together with the original notice before letters are issued. Surr. Ct. 

Act, § 146. 

The notice of probate reads as follows:

§ 635. Executor's Oath-Form. 

The official oath or affirmation of an executor, administrator, guardian, or testamentary trustee, to the effect that he will well, faithfully and honestly discharge the duties of his office, must be filed in the surrogate's court before letters are issued to him, or he is permitted to act. 

Surr. Ct. Act, § 98. The executor must qualify or renounce within fifteen days after the will has been pro bated. Surr. Ct. Act, § 157. 

The oath is in the following form:

Will and Testament of

Deceased,

§ 636. Designation of Clerk Upon Whom to Serve Process-Form. 

Every person, before letters are granted, is required to file in the surrogate's court, an instrument, acknowledged or proved, and duly certified, designating the clerk of the surrogate's office, and his successor in office, on whom service of any process issuing from the surrogate's court may be made in like manner and with like effect as if it were served personally upon himself, whenever the person so receiving letters cannot be found and served within the state of New York, after due diligence used. 

Surr. Ct. Act, § 95. 

Assuming that the designation is filed on behalf of the executor, it will read as follows:

§ 637. Order for Publication-Form. 

If, among other things, and as more specifically set forth in Surr. Ct. Act, § 56, there is a possibility that there may be heirs and next of kin of the decedent whose names and places of residence are unknown, an application may be required to be made for an order directing the service of a citation either personally without the state or by publication. Publication of the citation may be directed to be made in two newspapers therein designated unless it appears that the estate or fund amounts to less than five thousand dollars, in which case only one paper may be designated and for a specified time, as the surrogate deems reasonable, not less than once in each of four successive weeks, and by mailing a copy of the citation as provided in Surr. Ct. Act, § 59, except that mailing may be dispensed with if, among other things, the names or addresses are unknown. Surr. Ct. Act, § 58.

§ 640. Procedure Upon Filing of Petition. 

Where the parties waive service of citation, the petition for the probate of the will may be filed two days before the day set for the hearing. With the petition are filed the original will and a copy thereof to which is annexed the affidavit of comparison; also the waivers of citation; the executor's oath and designation of the clerk. New 

York County Surrogate's Court Rule VII. See local court rules. Where the citation is served upon persons who have not waived service, affidavits of service are prepared and filed. If service of the citation is to be made by publication, the order is filed and the citation is signed by the clerk. Steps are then taken to have the citation published as required. At the expiration of the period of publication proof of such publication is filed with the clerk of the court.

The subscribing witnesses are notified of the return day of the citation and the place of probate.

$ 647 

§ 641. Proof Deposition of Subscribing Witness Form. 

Before a will can be admitted to probate, the two subscribing witnesses must be produced and examined if they are within the state. Surr. Ct. Act, § 141. When two witnesses are available, both must testify to the publication of the will by the testator, and that they signed it at his request. The purpose is that the surrogate may be satisfied by proof that the requirements of law were observed in the execution and publication of the paper propounded as a will. Under such circumstances, it is not sufficient to merely ask the subscribing witnesses to identify his signature. In re Huber's Will, 81 A. D. 635, 168 

N. Y. S. 890. The proofs must be reduced to writing and is done by preparing the deposition of the subscribing witness. It states in substance, among other things, the date the will was made, that it was signed in the presence of the deponent and the other subscribing witness, that the decedent declared the instrument was his last will and testament, and that the deponent signed the instrument at the request of the decedent and in his presence. It reads as follows: 

In the Matter of Proving the Last 

Will and Testament of JOHN DOE, Deposition of a Subscribing Witness. 

Deceased, As a Will of Personal Property. 

COUNTY AND  SS. : 

ALICE MYERS of 1200 West 5th Street, Brooklyn, New York, being duly sworn as a witness in the above-entitled matter, and examined on behalf of the applicant to prove said will, says: I was acquainted with JOHN DOE, now deceased. The subscription of the name of said decedent to the instrument

8641 

now shown to me and offered for probate as his last will and testament, and bearing date the 15th day of March, in the year one thousand nine hundred and thirty was made by the decedent at the City of New York, on the 15th day of March in the year one thousand nine hundred and thirty, in the presence of myself and LILLIAN DAVIS, the other subscribing witness. 

At the time of making such subscription the said decedent declared the said instrument so subscribed by him to be his last will and testament; and I thereupon signed my name as a witness at the end of said instrument, at the request of said decedent, and in his presence.

The said decedent at the time of so executing said instrument was upwards of the age of twenty-one years, and in my opinion of sound mind, memory and understanding, not under any restraint or in any respect incompetent to make a will. 

I also saw said LILLIAN DAVIS, the other subscribing witness, sign her name as witness at the end of said will, and know that she did so at the request and in the presence of said decedent. I knew said decedent for thirty years before the execution of said instrument.

ALICE MVERS. 

Witness sworn and examined before me this 16th day of February, 1933.

CHARLES P. SHERIDAN, Assistant to the Surrogate, New York County. 

It may be that only one subscribing witness is available. 

In such case, the statute provides that the death, absence from the state, or incompetency by reason of lunacy, or otherwise, of a subscribing witness required to be examined, or the fact that such witness cannot, with due diligence, be found within the state, or cannot be examined by reason of his physical or mental condition, may shown by affidavit. In such case the surrogate may by the decree or by an order entered in the minutes, dispense with the testimony, or if the witness is out of the state, the testimony may be required to be taken before a commission. Where the testimony of a subscribing witness be

$ 649 

has been dispensed with, and one subscribing witness has been examined, the will may be admitted to probate upon the testimony of such subscribing witness alone. And in the event neither subscribing witness can be present or forgets the occurrence or testifies against the execution of the will, the will may nevertheless be established upon proof of the handwriting of the testator, and of the subscribing witnesses, and of such other circumstances as would be sufficient to prove the will upon the trial of the action. Surr. Ct. Act, § 142. 

§ 642. Hearing. 

On the return day of the citation the attorney appears before the probate clerk with the subscribing witnesses and submits to the clerk the depositions which he has prepared. The witnesses sign the deposition in the presence of the probate clerk. N. Y. County Surrogate's Court 

Rule VII. See local court rules. 

§ 643. Decree of Probate. 

If it appears to the surrogate that the will was duly executed, and that the testator, at the time of executing it, was in all respects competent to make a will and not under restraint, the will is admitted to probate. 

After the hearing, there appears in the Law Journal, under the name of the surrogate and under the title of 

Decrees Admitting Wills to Probate, the names of the various decedents whose wills have been admitted to probate. See other local papers wherein decisions are published. 

In those counties wherein the clerk does not prepare and enter the decree admitting the will to probate, it is necessary to draw the decree and submit it for signature. 

§ 644. Letters Testamentary-Form. 

After the will has been admitted to probate, any person entitled to letters thereunder, who is competent by law to

8 644 

serve, and who appears and qualifies, is entitled to letters testamentary thereupon. Surr. Ct. Act, § 155. See also 

Wait's N. Y. Practice, Vol. 7 (4th Ed.), 279. Letters testamentary are secured from the clerk of the surrogate's court. The original letter and a sufficient number of certificates to the effect that letters have been granted, should be obtained. Each such certificate is evidence, for example, of the authority of the executor to act as such. And, in order to withdraw funds from a bank which are on deposit in the decedent's name, the bank requires the executor to present such a certificate. 

The letters testamentary read as follows:

Foley, a Surro gate of our said county, the last will and testament of John Doe, deceased, was proved, and is now approved and allowed by us; and the said deceased having been at the time of his death a resident of the County of New York, by means whereof the proving and registering said will and the granting administration of all and singular the goods, chattels and credits of the said testator and also the auditing, allowing and final discharging the account thereof doth belong unto us, the administration of all and singular goods, chattels and credits of the said deceased in any way concerning his will, is granted unto

§ 645. The Executor-Duties. 

The executor should reduce all personalty to possession. He inquires whether the testator had a safe deposit box, securities or bank deposits. If the decedent was a policy holder or member of a death benefit association, the various companies are notified. Forms for proof of death are filled in and the insurance collected. 

The executor collects debts owing to the estate. If someone has property belonging to the estate, the executor may petition the surrogate's court to compel the delivery thereof.

Assuming that the estate consists of money only, which is distributed in several banks, the executor may apply at these banks to withdraw the money. Upon such application, the bank requires the following:

Presentation of Pass Book. 

Certificate of letters testamentary. 

Waiver from the Transfer Tax Bureau. Waiv ers may be obtained upon presentation of a certificate that letters testamentary were issued. 

When the executor has drawn the money from the several banks, he opens an account in a bank in his representative capacity and to the credit of the estate. Surr. Ct. 

Act, § 231. 

The executor pays all the charges and debts of the estate by check so that he may have a record thereof. 

The executor must, within three months after qualifying and after notice to the legatees and next of kin, make an inventory of the personal property of the dece-

$ 646 

dent. An order is then entered in the surrogate's court appointing two disinterested appraisers. The appraisal is made. The inventory is filed in the surrogate's court and a copy is retained by the executor. Surr. Ct. Act, 88 195-199. This is not, however, done as a matter of practice except where, among other things, the estate is a complicated one and there may be misunderstandings. 

§ 646. Notice to Creditors-Payment of Claims. 

At any time after the granting of letters testamentary, the executor or administrator may insert a notice once a week for six months in such newspaper or newspapers printed in the county as the surrogate directs, requiring creditors of the decedent to present claims on a specified day therein named which must be at least six months from the day of the first publication of the notice. The claims are accompanied by vouchers and an affidavit that the claim is justly due, and that there are no offsets against the same to the knowledge of the claimant. Surr. 

Ct. Act, § 207. 

The executor may allow the claim if it is a just claim. 

But where he doubts the validity of the claim, he may reject it by serving a notice to that effect upon the claimant. The claimant must thereupon commence suit within three months, otherwise he is barred from maintaining the action. The claim, however, may be tried on the judicial settlement of the accounting. Surr. Ct. Act, 

§ 211. A claim may very properly be presented to the executor before it is due. International Harvester Co. v. 

Champlin, 155 A. D. 847, 140 N. Y. S. 842.

The executor pays the funeral expenses of the decedent out of the first moneys received by him. Surr. Ct. Act, 

§ 216. Other debts are paid in the following order: debts entitled to a preference under the laws of the United 

States and the state of New York; taxes assessed on property of the deceased previous to his death; judg-

$ 653 

ments docketed and decrees entered against the deceased. according to the priority thereof respectively, and finally all recognizances, bonds, sealed instruments, notes, bills and unliquidated demands and accounts. No preference,. however, may be given in the payment of a debt over other debts of the same class. Surr. Ct. Act, § 212. 

If the executor does not publish the notice aforementioned, then the creditors are permitted to present their claims within seven months. Surr. Ct. Act, § 218. If a claim is not presented on or before the day fixed for presentation of claims in the notice to creditors, or if no notice is published within seven months from the date of the issue of the letters, the executor is not charged with any assets or moneys that he may have paid in satisfaction of lawful claims or legacies or in making distribution. to the next of kin before such claim was presented. Surr.. 

Ct. Act, § 208. 

§ 647. Payment of Legacies. 

No legacies are paid before the completion of the publication of notice to creditors if such notice is published, or if none is published before the expiration of seven months from the time of the granting of letters testamentary or of administration unless otherwise directed by the will or decree on an accounting. Surr. Ct. Act, § 218.. 

§ 648. Transfer Tax Proceeding. 

The Tax Law imposes a tax upon the transfer of property of the decedent either by will or if he dies intestate. 

It is therefore necessary to move for an order fixing the tax, or if no tax is to be paid, then for an order exempting the estate from the payment of a tax. See Wait's N. Y. 

Practice, Vol. 7 (4th Ed.), 605.

Forms may be obtained at the office of the attorney for the State Tax Commission.

$ 650 

§ 649. Notice of Motion-Form. 

The notice of motion to fix the amount of tax in a transfer tax proceeding is returnable in the surrogate's court and reads as follows:

§ 651. Service and Filing of Motion Papers. 

Two copies of the motion papers are served upon the attorney for the State Tax Commission. The original with proof of service thereof is filed with the clerk of the court. The motion appears on the motion calendar and is answered on the return day. 

§ 652. Order Form. 

An order duly entered on the motion and setting forth the amount of tax to be paid, reads as follows:
